stories.Headline: SAP CFO Dominik Asam reports a 70 basis point fall in cloud gross margin
stories.Summary:
SAP shares closed Friday at €181.10, down 2.1%, as a wave of selling in AI and technology names rolled from Wall Street and Asia into European markets. The retreat came even as Anthropic made its market debut, an event that, according to Reuters, failed to restore investor confidence in the AI sector. Questions over whether hefty AI spending will eventually translate into durable returns continued to hang over software stocks. The selling pressure hit SAP alongside other technology names despite the company's own AI announcements during the week.

Speaking Thursday at Morgan Stanley's technology conference, CFO Dominik Asam said SAP's cloud gross margin fell 70 basis points year on year on a currency-adjusted basis. He pointed to the product mix and introductory offers for AI products as contributing factors, Reuters reported. The disclosure landed as a reminder that SAP's AI build-out carries a near-term cost. To give investors a clearer read on that business, Asam said SAP will introduce a new metric in January covering revenue from its Business AI Platform. The gauge targets a specifically defined slice of SAP's AI operations, while his margin commentary addressed the cloud segment as a whole.

On the corporate front, SAP has completed its acquisition of TechWolf, a provider of an AI platform for work intelligence. SAP expects the business to become the intelligent core of its SuccessFactors portfolio, supporting AI-driven personnel and workforce planning. The company's retail ambitions were on display as well: on 11 November, SAP and VF Corporation opened the S.Fashion innovation space at SAP headquarters in Walldorf, where the partners will test AI-powered processes for the fashion trade, including a smart fashion store. These moves extend SAP's AI reach into workforce planning and retail processes beyond its core software business.

Separately, board member and Chief Customer Officer Thomas Saueressig has announced he will leave to take a role outside the company. He will remain in his post until the end of March 2027, with Emmanuel Raptopoulos set to take over his duties on an interim basis from January. IONOS has appointed Saueressig as its CEO effective 1 April 2027, and Achim Weiß will step down from that role on 31 March 2027. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these dates and appointments.

Articles.Title: SAP's AI Push Comes With a Margin Bill as Stock Slips 2.1%

stories.headline_source: SAP's AI Push Comes With a Margin Bill as Stock Slips 2.1%

stories.Headline: Taiwanese banks deploy AI tools to detect and block cyberattacks
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese banks have recently begun deploying artificial intelligence to detect suspicious activity and strengthen their defenses against growing cyberattacks. Taiwan Cooperative Bank Ltd reported that monthly external probes during the first ten months of this year were roughly double those of last year. First Commercial Bank Ltd noted that its web application firewall blocked approximately 2.2 million attacks between January and October. These attacks primarily targeted corporate banking services, online banking platforms, and various internet facing services.

The banks are now implementing AI powered tools to monitor network traffic and analyze suspicious connections to respond more quickly to threats. First Commercial Bank Ltd introduced endpoint detection systems to link security incidents, while Bank of Taiwan Co uses AI assisted tools for threat detection. Taiwan Cooperative Bank Ltd is currently testing AI based technologies to improve its incident response and overall detection capabilities. These systems allow financial institutions to identify unusual behavior and assess potential risks before they lead to successful breaches.

Consultant Chen Chia-hung from Rays Technology Co stated that banks should use AI to simulate attacks and identify system weaknesses. He suggested that companies incorporate AI driven attacks into their routine cybersecurity drills to refine their response procedures. The banks noted that while they have not definitively attributed any attacks to autonomous AI systems, automated methods are making detection harder. They believe that relying solely on tools that detect attacks after they occur is insufficient for modern security.

Articles.Title: Taiwan banks deploy AI to prevent cyberattacks

stories.headline_source: Taiwan banks deploy AI to prevent cyberattacks

stories.Headline: Delhi high court justice Arora urges law firms to keep hiring fresh graduates despite AI cost savings
stories.Summary:
Delhi High Court Justice Manmeet Pritam Singh Arora urged law firms not to stop recruiting fresh law graduates to save costs amid the growing use of artificial intelligence, warning that the legal profession cannot afford to stop training its next generation of lawyers. She was speaking at the first meeting of the Indian Commercial Litigators' Forum, hosted by JSA Advocates and Solicitors in New Delhi on November 20. Justice Arora said she had heard that some law firms in India had stopped hiring A0 associates, even as concerns grow over the potential impact of AI on employment opportunities for young lawyers. She asked who would train new lawyers for three years if firms only took on people after they had gained experience, and told the audience that while they are saving costs they should not cut down on the future, because firms that do not take in A0 associates today will not have themselves tomorrow. Responding to her observation, JSA Managing Partner Amar Gupta said firms were conscious of the need to retain training opportunities for fresh graduates even as the firm integrates AI into its operations.

He said the firm has in mind to reserve some kind of work entirely without any AI aid or assistance, and that this first-level training will continue to be imparted to new associates who join the firm. Gupta said that roadmap is quite clear in their minds, and that the firm has onboarded AI models deliberately, with some method and planning. Justice Robin Knowles of the High Court of England and Wales moderated the session virtually from London, and he emphasised the value of bringing insights from both the judiciary and legal practitioners to the upcoming seventh full meeting of the Standing International Forum of Commercial Courts. Delhi High Court Justice Prathiba M Singh shared global figures from a recent WIPO IP Judges Forum survey in Geneva covering 146 courts and tribunals.

The survey stated that 35% of courts worldwide already have AI policies in place, 19 courts reported that 30% of their drafting involves AI, and an on-the-spot poll revealed that 52% of judges want to use AI for drafting. Delhi High Court Justice Anish Dayal, who is leading the Indian judiciary's input on SIFOCC's AI workstream ahead of the seventh meeting in Zambia, pointed to the Supreme Court of India's draft AI regulations alongside existing guidance from the High Courts of Kerala and Gujarat. Justice Dayal highlighted the need to guard against hallucinations and confidentiality breaches, while identifying where human decision-making remains irreplaceable, and he also advocated for peer-to-peer judicial training and standardised operating procedures. Justice Prateek Jalan welcomed CLF India and encouraged the forum to eventually expand its membership to include individual and small-firm practitioners who form a vital part of the Indian bar.

Articles.Title: Don't stop training young lawyers: Justice Manmeet Arora on law firms using AI to cut costs

stories.headline_source: Don't stop training young lawyers: Justice Manmeet Arora on law firms using AI to cut costs

stories.Headline: Tech stocks plunge as Anthropic loses 109 billion dollars in value
stories.Summary:
Wall Street suffered its worst tech selloff in years during the week of November 22, 2026. The S&P 500 fell 8.6 percent, marking its biggest weekly drop since April 2025. The Dow lost 8 percent, its worst week since March 2020. The Nasdaq Composite fell 10 percent, also its worst week since March 2020. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged about 17 percent, its worst week since September 2001.

Anthropic hit the market this week and lost 109 billion dollars in value on Friday. The stock finished Thursday with a market cap of 1.28 trillion dollars. President Donald Trump says his administration will ban U.S. companies from building data centers overseas. Companies that build these centers will face a tremendous tax. Meta and Alphabet signed agreements worth billions of dollars to build overseas data centers.

Attorney General Rob Bonta said California is examining potential criminal violations of state law. He stated the legal framework involves prohibitions against misleading investors and the public. Analyst Michael James McDonald says extreme bearish sentiment supports a near-term rally. He noted long-term indicators suggest the correction could last three to four months. Dividend Value Investor called HP revenue growth spectacular due to AI PC demand.

Hyperscalers are worrying about data center opposition and increased costs after the Democratic midterm sweep. Nvidia is being probed for unlawfully selling advanced chips to China and misleading investors. Gen Z is expected to lead a rebound in in-store Black Friday shopping. A CivicScience survey found 41 percent of shoppers plan to shop in stores. This is the highest share of in-store shoppers since 2014.

The Nasdaq is in the red for the year. The S&P and Dow are in correction territory for the first time since Liberation Day. An Anthropic mathematician says he and Claude solved the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis. Two independent groups verified the proof, but formal recognition is still pending. HP operates on thin margins, and rising memory prices threaten its profitability recovery.

HP and Dell report earnings on Tuesday, while Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom report Monday. The October core PCE price index is expected to rise 3.2 percent on Wednesday. Hyatt Hotels goes ex-dividend Monday, and Johnson and Johnson goes ex-dividend Tuesday. Newmont and S&P Global go ex-dividend Wednesday. The articles leave open whether the current market correction will end soon.

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger says AI needs a 10,000-fold efficiency gain beyond incremental chip upgrades
stories.Summary:
Former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger used a fireside chat called “Reality Check: Beyond Chips” at the COSM Technology Summit 2026 in Scottsdale, Arizona, to argue that small generational chip upgrades cannot meet the demands of artificial intelligence, which he said needs a 10,000-fold gain in computing efficiency. He appeared alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. After the event he wrote on X that Moore’s Law should be woken up rather than declared dead. He said the revival depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five engineering fronts.

Gelsinger said the needed advances span light, power, cooling, composition and packaging, and that turning one gigawatt of electricity into ten gigawatts of AI token output requires far more than shrinking transistors. He pointed to U.S. energy capacity growing only in the low single digits over the past decade, gas turbine supply backlogs of eight years and nuclear projects that take a decade to build. He cited NVIDIA’s Kyber racks built on the Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power needs to 600kW, enough to supply 500 homes, and a Harvard study finding U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as Chile. He also noted that major AI foundation models now ship roughly every four weeks.

Since joining the venture firm Playground Global as a general partner in March 2025, Gelsinger has backed startups aimed at these hardware bottlenecks, including the government-supported lithography venture xLight, which seeks to move past ASML’s 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, and the nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy. His roadmap also points to optical interconnects and silicon photonics to carry data with light instead of copper. He said that after more than 40 years in semiconductors he believes the greatest innovations are still ahead. On an earlier occasion he called HBM a hideous memory while conceding it is the best technology the industry has now, and he proposed Z2RAM as an alternative with potentially better density, performance and power draw.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act amendment delays high-risk rules but adds new prohibitions and enforcement powers
stories.Summary:
The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and amends the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, on a number of points. It is widely described as a postponement, and in one important respect it is, because the obligations for high-risk AI systems will now apply later than originally planned. That description is incomplete, however, because much of the AI Act already applies and the Omnibus also introduces new prohibitions and stronger enforcement tools. The note by Logan & Partners sets out the main changes and what they mean in practice for companies that develop, procure or use AI systems in the European Union. The AI Act is not a future regime, since its first provisions have applied since 2 February 2025.

Since 2 February 2025 the practices prohibited under Article 5 have been unlawful, including manipulative or deceptive techniques, social scoring, untargeted scraping of facial images, and emotion recognition in the workplace and in education, subject to limited exceptions. Infringements may lead to fines of up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. Providers of general-purpose AI models have been subject to Chapter V since 2 August 2025 and must maintain technical documentation, put in place a copyright policy and publish a summary of the content used for training. The Commission's power to fine these providers has applied since 2 August 2026, and the transparency obligations in Article 50 have also applied since that date. Users must be informed when they interact with an AI system, synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format, and deepfakes must be disclosed.

Under new Article 111(4), providers of generative AI systems placed on the market before 2 August 2026 have until 2 December 2026 to comply with the marking obligation in Article 50(2). The requirements and obligations in Sections 1 to 3 of Chapter III will apply from 2 December 2027 to the systems listed in Annex III, which covers areas such as recruitment and workforce management, creditworthiness assessment, risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, education, biometrics, critical infrastructure, law enforcement, migration and the administration of justice. They apply from 2 August 2028 to AI systems that are safety components of products, or are themselves products, covered by the EU legislation listed in Annex I, such as medical devices, toys and lifts. The recitals explain that the postponement responds to the late availability of harmonised standards and to delays in setting up national authorities, and the legislator chose fixed dates. The Omnibus does not link application to the publication of standards, so companies should not plan on the assumption of a further extension.

The transitional rule in Article 111(2) has also been adjusted, so high-risk systems placed on the market or put into service before the relevant application date fall within the AI Act only if their design is significantly changed after that date. According to the recitals, this assessment is made per type and model, and systems intended for use by public authorities must in any event comply by 2 August 2030. The Omnibus adds two prohibitions to Article 5, which apply from 2 December 2026, the first covering AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic intimate images or sexually explicit content of an identifiable person without that person's explicit consent and the second covering AI-generated child sexual abuse material. Under new Article 5(1a), a provider may be caught even where its system was not designed for this purpose, where such output is a reasonably foreseeable outcome that can be reproduced without significant technical modification and the system lacks adequate safeguards to prevent it.

A deployer, by contrast, is caught only where it uses the system for the purpose of generating such material, so providers of general-purpose image and video generation tools should review their technical safeguards. Article 25 now specifies the information, technical access and assistance that an initial provider must give to the party that becomes the provider of a high-risk system, and it also requires written agreements with suppliers of AI models, tools and components. A breach of these obligations may now be fined up to EUR 15 million or 3% of turnover under new Article 99(4)(da). At EU level, the AI Office has obtained exclusive competence over certain AI systems, including systems based on a general-purpose AI model where the model and the system are developed by the same provider, and AI systems that constitute or are integrated into very large online platforms or search engines, with some exceptions.

The AI Office now has inspection powers and may impose periodic penalty payments. Article 4 on AI literacy now requires providers and deployers to take measures to support the AI literacy of their staff, and it states expressly that no specific level of literacy has to be guaranteed. SMEs and the new category of small mid-cap enterprises may provide technical documentation in a simplified form and apply a quality management system proportionate to their size, and where they are fined, the lower of the fixed amount and the percentage of turnover applies. New Article 4a allows providers of high-risk systems to process special categories of personal data where this is strictly necessary to detect and correct bias, subject to specific safeguards, and in exceptional cases the same possibility extends to deployers of high-risk systems and to providers and deployers of other AI systems and models.

The Commission has published draft guidelines on classification under Article 6, the consultation closed in July 2026 and, at the time of writing, the final guidelines have not been adopted. Article 6(3) allows certain Annex III systems to be treated as not high-risk, for example where they perform only a narrow procedural or preparatory task, but this exception never applies to systems that perform profiling. Providers relying on it must document their assessment before placing the system on the market and register the system. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US attracts elite AI researchers while China trains them and India loses its top talent
stories.Summary:
A global competition for artificial intelligence supremacy is unfolding as nations fight to attract and retain elite scientific talent. This struggle for human intelligence now outweighs the importance of oil, gold, or rare earth minerals for geopolitical power. Chidanand Rajghatta reported on these developments on November 22, 2026, highlighting the roles of China, America, and India. The United States acts as a magnet for researchers, while China functions as a talent factory. India is described as an also-ran that fails to produce or keep its best minds.

The Carnegie Endowment tracked 10,280 researchers from NeurIPS 2025 to analyze the concentration of global AI talent. China educated nearly 60 percent of these researchers, while the United States educated only 13 percent. In the US, 35.7 percent of 3,514 researchers were China-educated, and 34.5 percent were educated in America. India produced 411 researchers in this cohort, but 90 percent, or roughly 370 people, moved abroad. Only 285 India-educated researchers, representing 8.1 percent, were part of the elite group studied.

The Department of Homeland Security disputes the study authorization of Eva Yi Xie, a Chinese-born doctoral student. Xie was detained Friday at Reagan National Airport while returning from a neuroscience conference despite having valid work authorization. Her lawyers state she has a pending asylum case and was not accused of espionage or Nvidia investigations. The US national security establishment is increasingly suspicious of Chinese access to advanced technology following a recent Nvidia controversy. This restrictive immigration climate unsettles the international scientific community that supports American technological leadership.

India is affected by an inability to produce enough advanced researchers and a failure to retain them. New Delhi has engaged in much talk but only modest action regarding AI education for its citizens. The Carnegie study found India's share of elite AI researchers declined by two percent between 2022 and 2025. No Indian institution appeared among the leading universities producing talent, whereas Peking University topped the rankings. India's share of global computer science AI research citations rose from 3.2 percent in 2013 to 6 percent in 2023.

China's 22.5 percent citation share and 70 percent of 2023 AI patents reflect two decades of investment. China awarded 53,000 science and engineering doctorates in 2022, while the US awarded 45,000 in 2023. India awarded 23,000 such doctorates in 2021 but produced only 621 computer science PhDs compared to 2,874 in America. Stanford University's 2025 AI Index noted US institutions produced 40 notable models in 2024, while China produced 15. India produced no models meeting that threshold, though Bengaluru-based Sarvam is developing ambitious models for 2026.

The New York Times reported Saturday that Beijing ran a secret campaign to acquire AI chips and gather intelligence. No such intelligence issues have been reported regarding New Delhi, which faces purely homegrown educational failures. Sarvam's 30-billion and 105-billion-parameter models will arrive in 2026, but they were too late for 2024 comparisons. The articles leave open whether India can improve its education front to stop the talent drain. It remains unclear if the US will further restrict immigration for Chinese-born researchers in the future.

Articles.Title: The AI talent war: China is the factory, America the magnet, India an also-ran

stories.Headline: AI industry workers in Westminster propose a national regulator and stronger whistleblower protections
stories.Summary:
A coalition of organizations representing artificial intelligence industry workers gathered in Westminster on November 20, 2026, to advocate for regulation and labor rights. This group, which included whistleblowers, civil society organizations, and unions, held a conference titled AI: Worker Voice as Critical Internal Condition. The event aimed to establish a network that empowers workers to act as a force for regulating the sector. Participants sought to create formal channels so that those who build and are ruled by AI can influence its deployment.

The coalition proposed strengthening whistleblower protections in Britain and establishing a national AI regulator, which the country currently lacks. They called for a negotiated slowdown of development between private companies to ensure the frontier is governed by workers and government. John Chadfield of the Communication Workers Union suggested that contracts for data workers, content moderators, and defense staff include statutory ethics clauses. These clauses would grant employees the legal right to negotiate over matters concerning public safety.

John Chadfield based his suggestions on discussions with workers at Google DeepMind to encourage these contractual changes. Adam Cantwell-Corn from the TUC tech project stated that his organization is leading the movement to define what workers want from AI. He noted that this includes collective bargaining in the workplace and shaping the economy through industrial strategy. Alex Sobel, the Labour and Co-operative MP for Leeds Central and Headingley, argued that Britain should model global behavior by moving first on regulation.

The conference was hosted by the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard and the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford. Alex Sobel compared the need for immediate AI legislation to the passing of the Climate Change Act in 2008. He suggested that the global reach and universities of a middle-ranking power like the UK make it well-positioned to lead. The group believes that workers within AI firms should decide how the technology is designed and when it is released.

Articles.Title: AI industry workers gather to fight for their rights and regulation

stories.Headline: Sony and Warner sue Anthropic over pirated lyrics used to train Claude
stories.Summary:
Sony Music and Warner Music's publishing arms sued Anthropic in California federal court on August 28, 2026, a filing reported September 1, accusing the company of pirating song lyrics and sheet music to train its Claude AI chatbot. The suit claims Anthropic misused copyrighted song compositions, including hundreds of lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists. The labels say Anthropic downloaded millions of pirated books from LibGen and PiLiMi, including books containing copyrighted lyrics and sheet music. The case names CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann individually. It was filed in the U.S. District Court, Northern District of California.

The labels seek damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed copyright, covering tens of thousands of compositions, and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works. Universal Music Group and Sony Music filed a second copyright lawsuit against Suno on September 18, 2026, in the U.S. District Court, District of Massachusetts, a 45-page complaint targeting Suno's v6 model. The labels claim v6, which Suno said is trained exclusively on licensed music, actually uses their recordings without consent, and that because the new models are partly built on users' outputs derived from former models, they remain in violation. Jason Isbell filed a proposed class action against Suno on August 31, 2026, with David Lowery, Guy Forsyth and Eduardo Calle, on behalf of musicians whose names Suno has accepted as prompts. SOCAN, the Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, filed a statement of claim reported September 15, 2026, citing 150 Suno songs it says are identical or nearly identical to works by Joni Mitchell, The Weeknd, The Tragically Hip and others, seeking $20,000 per work and $10,000,000 total.

Universal Music Group sued DistroKid, in a filing reported September 15, 2026, accusing the distributor of flooding streaming platforms with AI-generated slop and of violating federal copyright laws and Delaware's Deceptive Trade Practices Act. Germany's Federal Court of Justice issued its Metall auf Metall VI decision on September 3, 2026, ruling the disputed use permissible under the pastiche exception for the period from June 7, 2021, when the relevant German provision came into force. The US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit heard arguments on September 25, 2026, in SoundExchange's appeal against Music Choice, and has not yet ruled. SoundExchange says SiriusXM's alleged underpayment now exceeds USD $400 million, a claim SiriusXM denies, and the complaint claimed Music Choice invented its own formula for allocating BES receipts, which the CRB's regulations do not permit. The appeal has put SoundExchange's $3.4 million lawsuit against Sonos on hold.

Music Choice has denied underpaying, arguing that under the rule it owes royalties only on revenue from music it provides exclusively to business customers. Suno is asking a federal judge to dismiss the Isbell lawsuit, arguing that using an artist's name to describe a musical style is protected speech, comparing its technology to a producer asking musicians to create something with more of a Jason Isbell vibe. District Judge Angel Kelley has not ruled on Suno's dismissal request, and the musicians are scheduled to respond by December 1, with Suno's reply due December 15. Putting Jason Isbell into Suno created a song called Paper Bell, described by the AI software as a contemporary Americana singer-songwriter track with fingerpicked acoustic guitar, featuring a male voice imitating Isbell's vocal elements. Warner broke away from the $500-million joint copyright lawsuit originally launched by Warner, Sony and Universal against Suno and has since signed a licensing deal with Suno.

Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and earlier this year over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training, and Anthropic already paid $1.5 billion to resolve a class action from a group of authors. Suno launched v6, its first model trained on licensed music, weeks before the second suit, after partnering with Warner Music Group, BMG and Believe. The original label suit against Suno was filed over two years earlier. The Kraftwerk case is the legal ancestor of basically every sampling lawsuit filed in the United States since, including early cases like Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films.

The SoundExchange dispute with Music Choice is more than seven years old, originally filed years ago. The second UMG and Sony suit against Suno is still in early stages, so no settlement talk yet. Suno has responded to each suit differently, settling with some labels while fighting others in court. SOCAN's lawsuit raises questions about the place of Canadian artists in a music industry increasingly shaped by American tech companies. The articles leave open how Judge Kelley will rule on Suno's dismissal request, how the Second Circuit will decide the SoundExchange appeal, and how the Anthropic, DistroKid and SOCAN cases will proceed.

stories.Headline: Fractal eyes $500 million IPO as India's first AI unicorn
stories.Summary:
Fractal AI is described by Analytics India Magazine as a leader in artificial intelligence solutions, with work spanning sectors that include healthcare and fashion. The outlet's coverage page lists nineteen stories about the company, with the first published on 29 April 2022 and the latest on 24 December 2025. A story dated 24 December 2025 reports that Fractal, called India's first AI unicorn, is eyeing a $500 million initial public offering. Another story from the same day says its Vaidya.ai product outperformed GPT-4 and achieved 83 percent in PG-NEET, a medical examination. A report published on 9 December 2025 says the government will select BharatGen, Fractal and Tech Mahindra in the second phase of the IndiaAI Mission.

Coverage from 3 October 2025 says Fractal's chief executive reflected on what he called the worst mistake of his life after twenty-five years. Earlier stories describe generative AI work on intelligent collections and receivables, dated 9 September 2024, and a visionary approach to transforming the fashion value chain with vision intelligence, dated 1 August 2024. A story dated 26 June 2024 reports that Fractal merged with Eugenie.ai to strengthen AI-powered climate solutions. A story dated 24 May 2024 says AWS and generative AI helped Fractal Analytics reduce call handling time by up to 15 percent. On 26 February 2024, the company introduced Kalaido, described as a new Indic text to image diffusion model.

Coverage dated 16 February 2024 examines how Fractal is leveraging generative AI for insurance. An interview with Chandramauli Chaudhuri, published on 29 April 2022, discusses driving successful AI transformations at the enterprise level. The articles do not say what the reported IPO would involve, what the IndiaAI Mission selection requires, or what terms apply to the merger with Eugenie.ai. They give no further detail on the chief executive's remark beyond the description of the worst mistake of his life after twenty-five years. The page carries no statement of what happens next for the company, and it lists no follow-up dates or plans beyond the stories already published.

stories.Headline: Freshfields analysis asks whether London law can adapt to AI as finance did in 1986
stories.Summary:
Freshfields published an analysis on 21 November 2026 titled Big Bang at 40: London’s Enduring Advantage, which examines how the deregulation of October 1986 transformed London’s financial markets and helped create the international banking and legal powerhouse known today. The analysis asks whether the qualities that built the City’s global dominance can survive another revolution, forty years after the original Big Bang. It identifies artificial intelligence, private capital, geopolitical tensions and changing regulation as forces challenging the City’s established business models. It also says Brexit, immigration policy and international competition threaten London’s ability to attract top talent. Freshfields identifies three enduring advantages that it says underpin London’s position: adaptability, international talent and the strength of English law.

English common law remains central to international finance, according to the analysis, because it provides contractual certainty and sophisticated dispute resolution. Artificial intelligence, however, raises fresh questions about responsibility, liability and whether established legal principles can accommodate new technology. The original Big Bang transformed banking and helped fuel the rise of global law firms, while the next upheaval could transform the lawyers themselves. Freshfields is responsible for the analysis, which was written by Ben Thomson, and the firm frames the central question as whether London’s legal establishment can adapt as successfully as its financial clients did 40 years ago. The analysis does not offer a prediction on that question, and it presents the challenges of AI, private capital, geopolitics and regulation as open issues rather than settled outcomes.

It points readers to the full analysis for the firm’s detailed reasoning. No further commitments or statements from the firm are given in the article. The context is the fortieth anniversary of the October 1986 deregulation, which the analysis credits with transforming London’s financial markets and fueling the rise of global law firms. The article does not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to read the full Freshfields analysis, and it gives no timetable for further work on the issues it raises.

stories.Headline: Greece's labour ministry tables a bill setting first rules on AI and algorithmic management at work
stories.Summary:
Greece's Labour Ministry tabled an AI labour bill in Parliament on Friday 20 November 2026, according to Parliament's records, setting the country's first rules on the use of artificial intelligence and algorithms at work along with new protections for platform workers. Labour and Social Security Minister Niki Kerameus said the bill ensures transparency, introduces human oversight of algorithmic management on digital platforms and sets clear limits on the use of AI. The bill also brings an EU directive on platform work into Greek law, which member states must adopt by 2 December 2026 under the directive's text. Before tabling, the ministry held extensive talks with the national social partners and with workers and businesses in the platform sector, and the final text includes many of their comments, the ministry said.

According to the Labour Ministry, the bill rests on two pillars, the first covering algorithmic management at work by telling workers how decisions that substantially affect their jobs are made and on what criteria, protecting their personal data and requiring human oversight of significant decisions about them. The second pillar covers people who work through digital platforms, seeking to define their employment status correctly so that labour and social security law can apply to them and they can claim their rights, while also making platform services more transparent, tightening enforcement and easing access to justice. The bill creates an Employment Register to record people who work on the platforms, linked to Migration Ministry records so authorities can better record third-country nationals who live and work legally in Greece. Beyond the platform rules, it adds three provisions on insurance cover for children close to adulthood, focused particularly on the move from education to work, makes parental leave and carer's leave easier to access, and gives mothers insured with EDOEAP, the journalists' insurance and health fund, a supplementary pregnancy and maternity benefit from the Public Employment Service (DYPA).

Kerameus said the uncontrolled use of artificial intelligence in the labour market carries risks and that setting rules and safeguards is necessary to protect workers but also the labour market as a whole. She called the bill one more measure to protect workers, service users and businesses, and said it aims to keep the labour market running smoothly. The bill went to public consultation from 5 to 19 November 2026, and Greek City Times reported its planned changes to parental leave and children's insurance at that stage. Parliament's Standing Committee on Social Affairs will now examine the AI labour bill.

Articles.Title: Greece Tables AI Labour Bill to Protect Platform Workers

stories.Headline: SoftBank posts ¥1.12tn quarterly loss as AI bets weigh on shares
stories.Summary:
SoftBank Group shares fell 16 percent to €15.92 on Thursday, bearing the brunt of a broad sell-off in Asian technology stocks, according to ad-hoc-news.de. The trigger, according to broadcaster SBS, was Anthropic's stock market debut, an event that was supposed to validate the sector's sky-high valuations but instead left investors questioning whether returns on hefty artificial intelligence spending can ever justify the price. The drop came against a backdrop of mounting skepticism about AI valuations across the board, and few companies are as exposed to that mood as SoftBank. Its large stake in OpenAI and its holding in Arm make the Japanese conglomerate especially vulnerable to any pullback in AI-related names, Reuters reported.

Masayoshi Son, SoftBank's chairman and chief executive, told investors on Wednesday that he regretted passing up an earlier opportunity to take a position in Anthropic. SoftBank had already committed to OpenAI by the time the Anthropic chance arose, a sequencing decision that now looks costly in more ways than one. For the second quarter of fiscal 2026, SoftBank reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of ¥1.12 trillion, a sharp reversal from the ¥2.50 trillion profit booked in the same period a year earlier. At the half-year level, the group posted a net loss of ¥768.0 billion attributable to the parent company's owners. Buried in those figures is a ¥597.25 billion hit stemming from a reworking of procurement plans for power generation equipment serving US AI data centres, a charge that underscores how quickly the economics of infrastructure build-outs can shift.

Even as losses mount, SoftBank is pressing ahead with fresh commitments. On 9 November, the group joined forces with Grab and PETROS to pledge US$1.85 billion in seed capital for AI infrastructure projects in Malaysia, with SoftBank's own contribution set at US$1 billion. The funding is not unconditional, as it hinges on the projects hitting agreed milestones and on the satisfaction of closing conditions, a staged structure that gives the partners room to walk away if the ventures fail to deliver. For a company nursing billion-dollar losses on one flank while opening its cheque book on another, that caution may be the most telling detail of all.

Articles.Title: SoftBank's AI Bill Comes Due as Anthropic Listing Fails to Calm Investors

stories.headline_source: SoftBank's AI Bill Comes Due as Anthropic Listing Fails to Calm Investors

stories.Headline: Microsoft reports Azure revenue up 48% as free cash flow falls 27%
stories.Summary:
Microsoft shares slipped 2.6% in a broad selloff across technology and AI names, with Reuters reporting that investors are rethinking both the scale of AI expectations and the spending required to meet them. Morgan Stanley's Adam Wood restated an Overweight rating and a $650 price target after conversations with Satya Nadella and Amy Hood at Ignite. RBC Capital's Rishi Jaluria followed a day earlier, keeping a Buy rating and a $640 target. SoftBank Group shares slid 16% to €15.92 on Thursday, bearing the brunt of a broad sell-off in Asian technology stocks. The trigger, according to broadcaster SBS, was Anthropic's stock market debut, which left investors questioning whether returns on hefty AI spending can justify the price.

Currency-adjusted Azure revenue climbed 48% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, ahead of the 45% growth Microsoft had guided for. Capital expenditure came in at $45.2 billion for the quarter, below the company's own forecast, yet free cash flow fell 27% year over year. Management expects capex to exceed $50 billion again in the second quarter of fiscal 2027, and the next earnings report is due January 26, 2027. For the second quarter of fiscal 2026, SoftBank reported a net loss attributable to shareholders of ¥1.12 trillion, a sharp reversal from the ¥2.50 trillion profit booked in the same period a year earlier. At the half-year level, the group posted a net loss of ¥768.0 billion attributable to the parent company's owners, including a ¥597.25 billion hit from a reworking of procurement plans for power generation equipment serving US AI data centres.

Saurabh Dighe, Microsoft's corporate vice president of Azure System & Architecture, said customers need infrastructure built around the workloads that matter to them. Masayoshi Son, SoftBank's chairman and chief executive, told investors on Wednesday that he regretted passing up an earlier opportunity to take a position in Anthropic. SoftBank had already committed to OpenAI by the time the Anthropic chance arose, a sequencing decision the article describes as now looking costly in more ways than one. Microsoft said the Intel collaboration has already delivered up to 2.3 times greater performance and memory flexibility for demanding workloads on Azure M-series v4 virtual machines using CXL memory and Intel Flat Memory Mode in Xeon 6 processors. Microsoft also highlighted up to 2.5 times faster SQL backups on Azure through the first QAT-enabled virtual machines in the cloud.

On Stocktwits, retail sentiment toward CHKP turned bullish, while sentiment toward MSFT and INTL remained bearish. MSFT shares have gained more than 5% year-to-date, CHKP shares have dropped over 18%, and INTL shares have gained over 53% over the same period. MSFT shares traded marginally lower, while INTC shares traded 1.3% lower at the time of writing. Reuters reported that SoftBank's large stake in OpenAI and its holding in Arm make the Japanese conglomerate especially vulnerable to any pullback in AI-related names. Reuters also pointed to hawkish signals from the Federal Reserve as a drag on the market, since persistently high rates tend to reduce the present value investors assign to distant earnings.

The Microsoft and Intel expansion includes a multi-year agreement for Intel Xeon processor supply, covering next-generation server CPUs codenamed Diamond Rapids, Xeon processors with Compute Express Link technology, Intel QuickAssist Technology and confidential computing capabilities. Intel disclosed a multi-year agreement to supply Xeon processors to Microsoft, including the use of Intel's EMIB packaging technology for Microsoft-designed data center chips, covering procurement and manufacturing. Danaher and Microsoft are building AI agents for scientific instruments and laboratory workflows, with first applications at Danaher customers slated for 2026 and further AI-enabled instruments planned for 2027. Check Point expanded its collaboration with Microsoft to deploy its SASE platform on Azure, expected to add 48 Microsoft Azure Points of Presence to Check Point's SASE footprint and incorporate Microsoft Entra for identity-centric Zero Trust security. The deployment is expected to use Microsoft's global network, which connects directly to more than 4,000 internet partners, and Check Point SASE is expected to become available through Microsoft Marketplace in the first half of 2027.

On 9 November, SoftBank joined forces with Grab and PETROS to pledge US$1.85 billion in seed capital for AI infrastructure projects in Malaysia, with SoftBank's own contribution set at US$1 billion. The funding hinges on the projects hitting agreed milestones and on the satisfaction of closing conditions. Demand held firm across small and large customers alike, and no end to capacity constraints is in sight, with Microsoft dividing available compute among Azure, Foundry, its own products and enterprise clients. The models unveiled at Ignite sit at the center of the debate, and the question is whether customers adopt these tools on a paying, recurring basis. Disclosure on customer uptake of the Ignite models would be the clearest signal yet, particularly whether users migrate from trials into paid operation and whether Microsoft can attach incremental revenue to that usage.

stories.Headline: NYC schools chancellor Kamar Samuels says Google refuses an AI-free search option for schools
stories.Summary:
New York City schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels said on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that Google is refusing to offer schools a version of its search engine without artificial intelligence features, which is forcing districts to evaluate other options. New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all weighing alternatives to Google search because of the dispute over AI in classroom search tools. Samuels said Google is trying to give the district an ultimatum by saying schools must either use student generative AI in its search engine or get nothing at all. He said the city is not buying into that binary choice, and he described the disagreement as a reason the district is looking at what else is available.

The concern among school leaders is that AI-generated answers and chatbots could undermine students' critical thinking and interfere with the learning process. Samuels said the district does not want guided learning from a chatbot and wants relearning from a teacher instead. Google says it is giving schools more control over which AI tools they use, but the company says AI features are now deeply integrated into its search engine and that it cannot offer a chatbot-free version. Among the alternatives being considered are Microsoft's Bing and DuckDuckGo, both of which offer options to disable AI-generated answers.

Samuels said New York City has other options available and is continuing discussions with Google despite the disagreement. He said the city will definitely take a look at those options when the time is right. For now, he said the city remains in talks with Google and is seeking greater collaboration, and he said no decision has been made about whether the district will continue using Google's search platform. He also said the city does not plan to change its existing policy on student AI use, noting that parents and teachers love the current policy and that the district will continue along those lines.

stories.Headline: Seoul education chief Chung Keun-sik pushes vocational high schools and essay-based grading as AI reshapes work
stories.Summary:
Superintendent Chung Keun-sik of the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education recently proposed a plan to strengthen career education. He discussed these goals during an interview this month at the National Assembly in Yeouido, Seoul. The plan focuses on nurturing vocational high schools as artificial intelligence reshapes industry work and job structures. Chung argues that students must learn hands-on skills because AI is taking over knowledge processing. He believes direct experience and skill acquisition are becoming more important as AI technology advances.

The office will expand essay-based assessments, raising their share in semester grades to 35 percent by 2027. By 2030, more than 50 percent of regular exams will be converted to the essay format. The office will support teacher training and specialized graders by 2032 and use Chaeum AI for grading. A new five-tier school grading system will apply to the 2028 college admissions cycle for current high school sophomores. This system expands the top tier of students from 4 percent to 10 percent.

Superintendent Chung stated that the perception of college entrance as the ultimate goal of education must change. He argued that getting into Seoul National University does not guarantee a life for a student. Chung believes a child who tests well is different from a smart or fine child. He said the current admissions structure prioritizes university rankings over the actual aptitudes of the students. He noted that students often choose majors to match their scores rather than the work they want.

Parents and students are facing excessive anxiety regarding the new five-tier grading system and admission prospects. Universities are also affected because they must find new ways to distinguish among applicants in the top tier. Chung believes this anxiety is largely a psychological problem and urges a focus on everyday learning. He expressed concern that elementary students relying on digital devices may lack basic reading and writing skills. He suggested a balance between digital education and traditional methods like discussion and reading.

The articles state that a gap exists between college studies and the work people actually do in Korea. The government wants to change local education grants from 20.79 percent of domestic tax revenue to economic growth rates. Superintendents proposed a compromise to keep the tax link but use excess increases for future national investment. The state would cover one-third of the excess decrease if grants fall more than 5 percent. The Seoul office could not accommodate 965.7 billion won in requests, including 676.6 billion won for environments.

The office will continue implementing the phased transition toward essay-based assessments and the new grading system. Chung seeks social consensus before introducing the Alpha Phone to curb student overdependence on smartphones. He continues to push for stable education finances to maintain and improve conditions in schools. The articles leave open how the government will respond to the superintendents' proposed grant funding compromise. They also leave open how the office will define specific Alpha Phone regulations for different grade levels.

stories.Headline: SpaceX plans to lease 47.3 billion dollars in chips for orbital data centers and AI satellites
stories.Summary:
Space Exploration Technologies, known as SPCX, plans to lease 47.3 billion dollars in chips over approximately five years. This agreement requires payments to continue even if the equipment fails, including a 25.2 billion dollar tranche with an 8.259 percent annual yield. The company also acquired Cursor in August through an all-stock deal valued at about 60 billion dollars. Additionally, SPCX raised 85.7 billion dollars during its June IPO after underwriters utilized their overallotment option.

The company will utilize Nvidia Vera CPUs and the Vera Rubin system for its orbital data centers and the first-generation Starmind AI satellite. Anthropic is expected to pay billions of dollars every month to SpaceX for AI computing capacity. Regarding the IPO, banks earned roughly 500 million dollars in fees, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each receiving 20.5 percent. The company's prospectus outlines goals for making humanity multi-planetary, creating artificial general intelligence, and building solar-powered data centers in space.

CEO Elon Musk expressed optimism regarding the Terafab chip project and the expansion of data centers. He mentioned that SpaceX and Tesla are increasingly aligned and might be better together, although he announced no deal. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei praised the services provided by SpaceX but noted that the future infrastructure mix for Anthropic remains uncertain. Meanwhile, Anysphere, the parent company of Cursor, informed Congress that it may phase out Chinese AI models due to geopolitical risks.

Space Exploration Technologies advanced its rocket recovery and reuse capabilities over the most recent weekend. The company continues to integrate advanced hardware to support its ambitious goals for space-based computing. Future developments depend on the successful deployment of the Starmind AI satellite and the orbital data center network. These initiatives aim to expand the reach of artificial intelligence beyond the limits of Earth.

stories.Headline: China uses artificial intelligence to enforce its Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress
stories.Summary:
The People's Republic of China implemented the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress over four months ago. This landmark legislation aims to promote ethnic unity and forge a strong sense of community. The state uses artificial intelligence to enforce these rules through policing, learning, and producing. AI helps the government detect, delete, and report content that undermines ethnic unity. These systems also generate state-approved material and intelligence on people the state watches.

The law requires Mandarin as the basic language of instruction in classrooms. Parents cannot instill ideas not conducive to ethnic unity in the home. Article 31 requires network operators to delete and report information undermining ethnic unity. Article 15 promotes the digitalization of minority languages, while Article 52 mandates alert and reporting systems. Provisions in Articles 16, 19, 24, 61, and 63 also impact ethnic minority identities.

The state is responsible for enforcing these rules through its surveillance infrastructure. Officials aim to achieve the sinicisation of 55 ethnic minorities to adopt mainstream Chinese values. This process seeks to construct one unified national identity for the Chinese people. The government uses AI to monitor communications and shape behaviors across the country. State organs must identify and resolve major risks to maintain national security and stability.

International rights groups and critics view the law as a human rights problem. They argue the goal is han-isation, which assimilates minority identities into the Han majority. Eight UN Special Rapporteurs sent a letter to Beijing in April detailing these concerns. Minority groups are affected by the digitalization of their languages for state policing. Some AI models still write hate speech in Kazakh and Mongolian when asked.

The Cybersecurity Law has prohibited inciting ethnic hatred or discrimination since 2017. The CAC required platforms to police content undermining ethnic unity starting in March 2020. The Criminal Law has criminalized incitement to ethnic hatred for a much longer period. Interim Measures from August 2023 forbid generative AI from promoting ethnic hatred and discrimination. Hangzhou integrated DeepSeek-R1 into its City Brain in February 2025 to process data.

Network operators like Tencent, ByteDance, and Weibo use AI to handle massive censorship duties. AI is integrated into the criminal-justice pipeline, including smart courts and smart prisons. The state continues to build data to help AI understand minority languages better. It remains unclear if this progress will reach the commercial models people use. The articles leave open how AI will fully meet the law's policing demands.

stories.Headline: David Tepper sells Broadcom and AMD stakes to buy Nvidia and Micron shares
stories.Summary:
Billionaire David Tepper of Appaloosa Management reshuffled his artificial intelligence semiconductor positions during the third quarter. The owner of the Carolina Panthers exited his positions in Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices. He used this rotation to buy shares of Micron and Nvidia. Tepper also reduced his stake in Alphabet by nearly half. These moves occurred as he managed his estimated net worth of 28.5 billion dollars.

The rotation involves selling Broadcom and Advanced Micro Devices to buy Nvidia and Micron. Tepper cut his Alphabet stake nearly in half during the third quarter of 2026. He bought Nvidia shares before Jensen Huang stepped down as the company chief executive. Alphabet co-developed Tensor Processing Units with Broadcom to deliver better performance per dollar. These TPUs are used in Alphabet's new TPU 8tx AI system.

Geoffrey Seiler from The Motley Fool believes Tepper made a mistake with these specific trades. Seiler prefers the three stocks Tepper sold over the shares of Nvidia. He argues that Nvidia could face margin compression and a loss of market share. Seiler notes that memory tends to be a commodity with big boom and bust cycles. He warns that Micron is highly exposed to changes in conventional memory prices.

Counterpoint Research projects that custom AI chip shipments will surpass data center GPU shipments in 2028. Bloomberg Intelligence believes TPU sales outside Google Cloud could grow to 135 billion dollars by 2028. Anthropic revealed that its Claude Mythos model can run on AMD GPUs in two to three days. This development affects Nvidia by narrowing its CUDA moat and opening doors for ASICs. Large customers, except Space Exploration Technologies, are developing their own custom chips.

Alphabet developed its TPUs more than a decade ago to create a comprehensive ecosystem. Anthropic is now using these solutions, as is the company known as OpenAI. Advanced Micro Devices recently started shipping Helios systems that combine GPUs, CPUs, and networking. These systems are significantly cheaper than the end to end server racks sold by Nvidia. GF Securities expects the NAND flash memory market to become oversupplied as soon as next year.

Nvidia may face lower profitability even if the company manages to grow its total revenue. The market is moving from the research phase into a global rollout called Act 2. It remains open whether Tepper's rotation into Nvidia and Micron will actually pay off. The articles do not state if Tepper will change his positions again soon. They leave the future performance of the Helios systems and TPU sales as projections.

stories.Headline: India's chief justice says clear AI rules beat a ban for legal education
stories.Summary:
The Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant, said on Saturday, November 21, 2026, that setting clear rules to regulate the use of AI tools would be a better option than a total ban for legal students and the legal profession. He made the statement while delivering the inaugural address at the first annual international conference on legal education, which was convened by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association in Hyderabad. The Chief Justice observed that generative artificial intelligence had unsettled the assumption that an answer sheet reflects the knowledge of a student. He also said that assessment methods should be improved so that written works are supported by oral explanations, and that a law school must ultimately be able to certify with confidence what the students it had produced had learnt.

On legal education in the country, the Chief Justice noted that practical training can strengthen doctrinal teaching only if it is genuine, and that a student learns the strength of law in a supervised moot trial better than in an examination. He said Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, and that such clinical teaching requires trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards. Justice P.S. Narasimha of the Supreme Court said students develop their legal reasoning through repeated drafting of petitions, analysing facts and finding legal solutions on their own. He warned that students who depend on AI tools for legal solutions without undergoing this rigorous training in drafting and legal reasoning might lose the capacity to analyse and fail to distinguish between right and wrong.

Attorney General R. Venkataramani said legal education must respond to the challenges brought about by globalisation, technology and artificial intelligence, and that law schools should evolve into centres of research and innovation while AI tools are used to assist them. He said AI should not be the master but an assistant. P. Sam Koshy, the Acting Chief Justice of the Telangana High Court, said it was high time everyone examined whether the next generation of legal professionals was being prepared merely to understand the law as it existed or was being equipped to shape the laws the future demands. He said the present legal professional cannot be confined to the legal framework of one jurisdiction, and that while learning a domestic law governing a dispute, one should also be aware of its international dimensions. He added that the future of the Commonwealth's legal tradition will not be secured by merely preserving its past, but by its capacity to learn, adapt and evolve without losing its foundational principles.

stories.Headline: Senior advocate Rajshekhar Rao tells law students that judges must stay in the driver's seat of adjudication
stories.Summary:
Senior Advocate Rajshekhar Rao said at the inaugural JusTech National Conclave at Dharmashastra National Law University in Jabalpur that the judge, not artificial intelligence, must remain in the driver's seat of adjudication. He made the remarks on 22 November 2026 at a session on the interplay between artificial intelligence and the future of justice. Rao said this was his first visit to Jabalpur and addressed his remarks largely to the younger lot. He organised the speech around three questions: the potential of AI for access to justice in India, the constitutional and institutional risks of adopting it, and how the legal profession, the judiciary and institutions should respond. He said the question is not whether artificial intelligence will transform the judiciary, which it almost certainly will, but who or what should be in the driver's seat when justice is being administered.

Rao opened with a legal-aid matter he argued as a young lawyer before the late Justice Valmiki Mehta of the Delhi High Court on 23 December 2011, the last working day before the winter break. He appeared for a woman with a minor child who had been evicted from her matrimonial home by her father-in-law, at a time when the Supreme Court was rather more emphatic that a daughter-in-law had no claim to the estate of her in-laws. Moments before his matter was called, Justice Mehta admonished a senior advocate in an earlier item, saying the problem with lawyers was that they do not advise their clients. When Rao rose to say he had a slightly different point to make, the judge replied that he had not made it and pointed him to the child's claim under the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act. The judge asked him to file an affidavit raising additional grounds the same day, admitted the petition, and told the client the law was entirely against her but that this was all he could do to try and give her justice.

Rao said the woman left the house with a settlement in 2023 with a son who is now an engineer looking after his mother, and he described it as the defining aspect of what justice is. He said technology would probably have said no relief because the Supreme Court says this is a daughter-in-law asking for a right in a father-in-law's estate, and would not have taken that additional step forward and found a way to do justice. He said he expected a human presence on the bench at least in our lifetime hopefully and going forward always, a presence that takes an oath under the Constitution as a judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court. He framed the debate as the classic tussle between logic and experience, contrasting Sir Edward Coke's dictum that reason is the life of the law with Oliver Wendell Holmes's view that the life of the law has not been logic but experience. He said the edifice of justice is humanity and therefore technology may assist the administration of justice, improve its efficiency, widen its reach and make it more accessible, but the responsibility for administering justice cannot be outsourced and must remain firmly rooted in the judge and remain human.

Rao said he is not a Luddite or a dinosaur in terms of technological progress and is only asking that the character of the judiciary and its fundamental tenets be preserved while change is embraced. Noting that Madhya Pradesh is known as Hindustan ka dil, he remarked that to do justice you must have a heart. He described technology as an instrument of democratizing justice and said Indian courts embraced technology during the Covid-19 pandemic in a way that made the west look at us and marvel. Referring to Articles 39A, 14 and 21, he said access to justice remains the foundational basis that the constitution guarantees to every citizen and that legal-aid programmes had so far scratched the surface. He said AI had helped translate judgments, prepare pleadings and procedural documents, make legal information accessible to people who cannot navigate legal databases, assist persons with disabilities, and improve filing and procedural efficiency.

Rao cited Odisha, where he said the then Chief Justice set up access points at district courts so that lawyers across the State could appear before the High Court directly. Quoting figures he attributed to the Ministry of Law and Justice in July 2026, he said 817 of Odisha's 845 courts had been equipped with ICT infrastructure and video-conferencing facilities, enabling about 7.61 lakh virtual hearings till June 2026. He called this really the tip of the iceberg and said we have miles to go before we sleep. He cautioned that access to a chatbot is not access to justice and that access to a translated document does not necessarily mean the person has the right translation, since a word misunderstood by the chatbot alters the entire basis of the judgment, which is why there is this whole aspect of hallucination. He said efficiency cannot become a substitute for adjudication and that there is a fundamental distinction between the judge and the machine.

Rao said adjudication is not simply the processing of information but involves the evaluation of competing claims, assessment of evidence, interpretation of legal principles, the application of law to facts, and more importantly the exercise of judicial discretion. He illustrated the point with the opening words of definition clauses, unless the context otherwise requires, which show that the same word can have multiple meanings in the same statute depending upon where it is placed. He said he was not certain that technology at present and in the near future has the ability to make that distinction or to choose between two competing interpretations at a defining moment. He said the legitimacy of judicial power rests not only upon the correctness of the result but upon the process through which that result is reached, and the litigant must have confidence of being heard through a fair process and that the decision is taken by the person conferred with constitutional authority. On bias he said the technology is dependent on the input that it receives and we are still not certain as to what inputs go in, and on opacity he said a judge's experiences define his or her response to a problem and technology is an aid that only helps that experience address a situation more efficiently.

On privacy, Rao described checking in for his flight that day, when the DigiYatra app asked him to consent to eight data points, failing which he would have had to stand in line. He asked whether as a litigant he has the confidence that the information he is feeding in is available only to those that matter and is not going to be misused or used elsewhere, and he pointed to this lingering debate on the right to be forgotten. He referred to recent cautions from the courts on AI misuse, including a Madhya Pradesh High Court order dealing with a hallucinated citation in a counter affidavit filed by the state government, and a Supreme Court ruling delivered two days before the Conclave. He described the draft regulations on the use of AI in courts as one of the most defining moments, because any use of technology must be sanctioned right from the very top and must be clear and consistent so that there is no ambiguity for any lawyer wherever he practises. He said the beauty of our system is that you can be a lawyer enrolled in the bar council of Nagaland and still practise in the highest court in the land, and there must be one standard, which fortunately is now being laid down.

Rao credited the Supreme Court's practice of keeping its judgments on JUDIS as a single official, verifiable database, and noted that a QR code can now be used to verify whether the judgment is authentic or not. He warned young lawyers against over-reliance on devices, asking what they would do if an iPad or computer stopped working, something he said had happened to him two minutes before he came up. He asked whether they could still argue the case, remember the page numbers and fulfil the most solemn obligation that as lawyers we have to assist the judge there to do complete justice. He told students that no matter what technology or tools they use, the buck ultimately does stop with us, and the test is whether one allows AI to become a slave or a master. He said a lawyer who uses AI to identify authorities must read the judgments, warning that an opponent who relies on a summary may miss that one little comma in a document which defines the entire outcome of that case, and he concluded that the lawyer of the future will certainly need technological competence, but technological competence without legal judgment will be a dangerous combination, so safeguards must be built in and accountability held.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase outages and a US flight grounding stem from technical upgrades, not attacks
stories.Summary:
A series of technical failures disrupted American infrastructure and global services starting on Friday, November 14, 2026. Federal aviation authorities ordered a nationwide grounding of planes, while a Microsoft outage affected millions of users worldwide. These events were followed by a widespread outage at United Airlines on Monday afternoon and significant transaction slowdowns at several top United States banks. Other strange occurrences on Friday included a tanker hitting a cruise ship in New Orleans, drones over a British air base, and a bomb discovery in Illinois.

The aviation crisis required a ground stop lasting more than four hours because a technology upgrade overloaded antiquated air traffic control equipment. Microsoft reported that its own service disruption resulted from a network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. Financial instability began when a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase created ripple effects across the broader banking system. United Airlines stated that its Monday technical problems specifically impacted departing flights rather than aircraft already in the air.

Bryan Bedford of the Federal Aviation Administration and representatives from Microsoft both stated that no malicious activity caused these failures. A spokesperson for Chase confirmed that their banking issues were not the result of a cyberattack and that they were working to restore services. While some citizens expressed fear that these events signaled a coordinated attack on the economy, officials maintained that the causes were prosaic. The Federal Aviation Administration indicated that airline schedules should have returned to normal by late Sunday.

Articles.Title: Grounded jets, bank trouble, Microsoft outage, AI chaos make some wonder

stories.Headline: Governors led by Wes Moore propose federal AI oversight while states keep consumer and civil rights rules
stories.Summary:
The National Governors Association published a set of AI principles on Sunday, November 22, 2026, to guide the incoming Congress. This bipartisan effort was led by Maryland Governor Wes Moore and included governors Mike Braun of Indiana, Josh Stein of North Carolina, and Spencer Cox of Utah. The group is asking for a national framework that establishes federal oversight for the most powerful AI models while protecting the authority of state legislatures. They want Washington to manage independent safety reviews and the mandatory reporting of serious security breaches and safety incidents.

This proposal requires that states maintain their own rules regarding consumer protection, the prevention of discrimination, and the impact of AI on employment. Startups providing AI tools for banking, insurance, or hiring would still need to comply with various state laws, including those already passed in Texas, Colorado, and California. This approach contrasts with Executive Order 14365, signed by President Trump on December 11, 2025, which created an AI Litigation Task Force to challenge state laws. The White House also sent a framework to Congress in March that seeks to preempt state laws that impose undue burdens on interstate commerce.

Governor Wes Moore stated that humans must remain in control because artificial intelligence presents both significant opportunities and risks. Governor Spencer Cox added that members of both political parties believe states have a critical role and should work with Congress. The governors aim to reduce regulatory duplication and base all safeguards on evidence of actual risk while allowing smaller firms to compete. They seek to define complementary roles for federal and state governments rather than allowing a single federal rulebook to erase existing state statutes.

The conflict centers on where the line of authority sits between the federal government and the states. Governor Gavin Newsom of California has already pushed for independent safety plans and presented a national framework to Washington this month. While the White House argues that national security concerns necessitate federal preemption, the governors expect this issue to be fought over again in January. No specific Congressional sponsor has been named for the governors' plan, and no official bill text has combined these competing visions.
