stories.Headline: Judge Chung bars Colorado from enforcing its AI law until 14 days after an xAI injunction ruling
stories.Summary:
A federal magistrate judge in Denver, Cyrus Y. Chung, entered a two-page minute order on April 27, 2026, barring Colorado Attorney General Philip J. Weiser from enforcing the state's artificial intelligence law. The order was docketed as ECF No. 24 in Civil Action No. 26-cv-01515-DDD-CYC in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado. It granted the parties' Revised Joint Motion to Vacate Scheduling Conference and Suspend Case Deadlines and Stipulation to Temporarily Stay Enforcement, filed as ECF No. 22. The caption lists X. AI LLC as plaintiff, the United States of America as plaintiff-intervenor, and Weiser as defendant. The order followed the United States' motion to intervene, which the court granted shortly before April 24, 2026.

The order bars enforcement, including the initiation of an investigation, for alleged violations of SB24-205 or any legislation replacing or amending it enacted during this legislative session. The bar covers violations that occurred or may occur on or before 14 days after the court rules on xAI's forthcoming motion for a preliminary injunction. xAI must submit that motion, and if necessary an amended complaint, within 28 days after final adoption of rulemaking implementing SB24-205 or any replacement or amendment. The order vacated the Scheduling Conference set for June 16, 2026 and stayed all case management and other deadlines pending resolution of the motion. It denied as moot an earlier version of the motion, ECF No. 18, which xAI and the Attorney General had filed without the United States.

The court weighed the factors from String Cheese Incident, LLC v. Stylus Shows, Inc., a 2006 District of Colorado decision, and said in a single sentence that a stay would not prejudice the plaintiff, who does not oppose the motion. The order said the stay would avoid burdening the parties with the costs of litigating, promote judicial economy and efficiency, not negatively impact nonparties, and serve the public interest. According to the revised joint motion, the Attorney General has exclusive authority to enforce SB 24-205 under section 6-1-1706(1) of the Colorado Revised Statutes. The revised motion said the Colorado AI Policy Working Group convened by Governor Jared Polis published a draft bill to repeal and replace SB 24-205 on March 17, 2026.

The motion said the Attorney General did not intend to issue rules until the 2026 Regular Session of the General Assembly ended and did not intend to enforce SB 24-205 or any replacement until rulemaking concluded. The revised motion described SB 24-205 as becoming effective June 30, 2026. The first version of the joint motion, filed April 24, 2026, applied the Attorney General's promise not to enforce or investigate only to xAI, and all three parties filed the revised motion the same day asking the court to replace it. Chief Judge Daniel D. Domenico, to whom the case was reassigned on April 14 after the parties did not all consent to a magistrate judge, referred the revised motion to Magistrate Judge Chung on April 27. The revised motion's signature blocks list Wheeler Trigg O'Donnell and in-house counsel for xAI, lawyers from the Justice Department's Civil Division and Civil Rights Division including Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon, and First Assistant Attorney General Heather Kelly and Senior Assistant Attorney General Kate Field for Colorado.

The order protects every company covered by the law, not only xAI. The Colorado House passed SB 26-189 by 57 votes to 6 on May 9, 2026, repealing and replacing SB 24-205 with a narrower law on automated decision-making technology used in consequential decisions. According to the General Assembly's record, Governor Polis signed it on May 14, 2026, its substantive obligations begin on January 1, 2027, and it required the Attorney General to complete rulemaking by the same date. On July 1, 2026, the Federal Trade Commission released a proposed policy statement naming Colorado's law as amended by SB 26-189 and arguing that conflicting state requirements are impliedly preempted, a statement that remains a proposal.

Proposed rules were published on August 11, an interim draft followed on October 6, and a public hearing took place on October 26. According to the Colorado Department of Law, the Department adopted the rules on November 19, 2026, covering both SB 26-189 and HB 26-1263, the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Services Act, which the Department calls the Chatbot Safety Act. The adopted rules prevent chatbot operators from relying on government identification alone for age assurance, and the Department has asked the Attorney General for a formal opinion on them. Once that opinion arrives, the rules and the opinion go to the Secretary of State, and the rules become final twenty days after publication, according to the Department.

According to the court docket, the only filings since April 27 are two motions by counsel to withdraw, filed on October 2 as ECF No. 25 and November 16, 2026 as ECF No. 28, each followed by an order, and no motion for a preliminary injunction and no amended complaint appear as of the November 16 entry. If the November 19 adoption counts as final adoption, xAI's motion is due on December 17, 2026, by PPC Land's calculation, while the Department's description reserves "final" for twenty days after publication by the Secretary of State, and no publication date has been set. Because the bar covers violations through the 14th day after the ruling, conduct on January 1, 2027 would be open to enforcement only if the court rules on or before a date the articles leave unstated. Which reading the parties apply is not stated anywhere on the docket.

stories.Headline: US travelers trust banks over Meta to run AI payment agents, TubStays survey finds
stories.Summary:
A TubStays survey of 5,000 US travelers, released on November 21, 2026, found that 48% would trust their own bank or credit card company to run an AI agent that pays for travel, while only 13% would trust Meta, the maker of the Muse agent, which ranked seventh among eight options. The survey ran online from October 27 to November 6, 2026, through SurveyMonkey Audience in English and Spanish with 68 questions, and responses were weighted by age, gender, region, household income, education, and race and ethnicity. Muse was the most-used agent among travelers who have used a personal AI agent, at 57%, yet four in ten of those users said they would not trust Meta at all with their payment details. An airline's or hotel brand's own assistant drew 43%, a travel booking site such as Expedia or Booking.com drew 38%, Apple drew 37%, Google drew 31%, OpenAI drew 24%, and a new AI start-up drew 9%.

The results show that travelers accept AI agents only when the agent asks for approval before paying, since 43% are comfortable letting an agent book and pay after they review and approve the details, while just 13% would let it pay without asking each time. Willingness to skip approval depends on the amount, as 30% would let an agent pay for a $25 ride without asking, against 6% for a $2,000 vacation package. Before approving a hotel payment, 66% want to see the total price including taxes and fees, and 50% want the cancellation terms. Most travelers still book for themselves, since only 11% have used a personal AI agent, and on the most recent trip where travelers used any AI, 61% used it only for ideas or information while the AI made the booking for 4%.

Of the 2,520 travelers who used AI for a trip in the past year, 41% got wrong or out-of-date information and 17% were told a hotel had a feature it did not have, such as a bathtub, pool or parking. If an agent books the wrong hotel, 64% say the company that made the agent should pay, either alone at 38% or shared with the hotel or booking site at 26%. Ritesh, founder of TubStays, said travelers will let AI plan the trip but still want to hold the card, and that trust is something AI agents will have to earn one accurate booking at a time. TubStays, founded in 2024 and based in San Jose, California, lists more than 9,000 verified properties in more than 1,600 cities and destinations, and the full survey and questionnaire are available on its website.

stories.Headline: Valar Atomics raises $1 billion and powers an Nvidia AI chip with its nuclear reactor
stories.Summary:
Isaiah Taylor left high school at 16 without completing his formal education, and eleven years later, at 27, he leads Valar Atomics, a nuclear energy startup based in El Segundo, California. Valar Atomics has attracted a $1 billion investment from Sequoia Capital and reached a reported valuation of $6 billion. The company demonstrated that its small nuclear reactor can generate electricity to power an Nvidia AI processor. Valar Atomics is developing small modular nuclear reactors, compact, factory-built power plants designed to supply electricity to data centres and industrial facilities. The demonstration came in July 2026, when the company showed its Ward 250 nuclear reactor could power an Nvidia Blackwell-based system.

According to a July 2026 TechCrunch report, the three-year-old startup was initially in talks to raise $1 billion at a valuation of around $6 billion, and the round closed in August with Sequoia Capital leading. stories.Headline: Warsh says AI could speed innovation and growth while warning of job losses and market risks
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said Monday that artificial intelligence could accelerate innovation and usher in an era of faster economic growth, in remarks that also acknowledged risks from the technology. Warsh said the adoption of AI could also lead to widespread job loss or a steep drop in the stock market if the healthy returns expected from the huge investments in AI infrastructure don't materialize. Warsh's remarks kicked off a one-day conference on AI and productivity at the Fed's San Francisco branch. Warsh did not mention inflation, even though many of his colleagues blame the buildout of data centers for accelerating price increases. Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates, nor did he say anything about recent government data showing that inflation accelerated last month.

That data led many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee to signal their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. The Fed refers to AI as "super intelligence" following an executive order issued by President Donald Trump requiring federal agencies to use the term. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed, and the conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added. Warsh has long said, including before his nomination as Fed chair, that AI could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation.

"What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation," Warsh said. "It appears to be changing the method ,  and, at least as important, the speed ,  of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average." "As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free," Warsh said. "And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly."

Warsh said that "after significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment." Warsh spent more time in his remarks considering the downsides of AI than he has in previous speeches. Other Fed officials have increasingly voiced concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Those increases, in turn, have lifted the cost of smartphones, computers and other consumer electronics. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week.

Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. "If the new technology leads to permanently higher levels of productivity growth, it may increase firms' desire to invest and, hence, their demand for funding, raising the level of interest rates," Jefferson said. Warsh's generally optimistic outlook on the new technology is a view at odds with many of his colleagues. Warsh has previously touted AI as a technology that could significantly boost the economy's efficiency, which would enable it to grow without worsening inflation.

In turn, the Fed could potentially lower interest rates under that scenario. The conference Monday was part of a task force Warsh set up to evaluate AI and its impact on the economy's efficiency. Warsh appointed five different task forces soon after taking the helm at the Fed. Fed staff has begun evaluating different scenarios for how AI's impact may play out, Warsh added.

Warsh did not address AI's impact on inflation, a top concern of many of his Fed colleagues. Last week, several policymakers expressed concern that AI is fanning inflation because the buildout of AI infrastructure has sharply raised demand for computer chips, electronic components, electricity and copper. Smartphone prices rose last month at the fastest pace on record, the government said last week. Warsh did not comment on what the Fed's next steps would be on interest rates.

Many of Warsh's colleagues on the Fed's rate-setting committee signaled their support for additional interest rate hikes, including at the Fed's next meeting in December. Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said Friday that if AI does accelerate economic growth, it could lead to higher interest rates over time, even if inflation declines. The articles do not say what the Fed decided about interest rates at its December meeting. The articles do not say how Warsh's task forces other than the AI and productivity task force will report their findings.

stories.Headline: Bank of Portugal governor warns Europe lags US in AI investment
stories.Summary:
Bank of Portugal Governor Álvaro Santos Pereira warned on Friday, November 20, 2026, that Europe risks falling further behind the United States in artificial intelligence investment. He spoke at the ninth Future of Banking conference in Lisbon, organised by Jornal de Negócios at the SANA Marquês hotel. The governor said Portugal's banks enjoy stronger balance sheets and improved credit quality. He set out an agenda spanning energy risks, regulatory reform, cybersecurity and financing of technological transformation. The central bank expects growth of around 2.3% in 2026, easing to 1.8% in 2027.

The governor put the non-performing loan ratio at 2.1%, a marked contrast with double-digit levels of earlier years. He said the proportion of euro-area banks adopting generative AI rose from 46% in 2024 to 86% more recently. Around 43% of US workers were using AI at work, compared with 32% in Europe, he said. The share of companies using AI in production was approximately 7% in the United States and 4% in Europe. Six reporting requirements have already been discontinued, with another two scheduled to disappear by the end of 2026.

Santos Pereira said growth of the Portuguese economy remains "reasonable, not spectacular, but reasonable." He said, "We have to ask ourselves whether it is sustainable to continue along this path of not increasing public capital decisively." He said, "If we have a very cold winter, that will put more pressure on natural gas prices and, obviously, on electricity prices as well." He said, "I think there is clearly room for us to continue raising deposit interest rates closer to those in the euro area." He said, "The big question is who will capture the financial gains associated with this: the banks, the customers or the technology suppliers."

He said interest paid on deposits by Portuguese banks remains significantly below the euro-area average. He said public debt remains historically high and the downward trajectory must continue. He said European gas storage levels in some northern markets were below their averages of the previous decade. He cited competition with Asia, disruption in the Middle East and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz as added risks. He said the European Central Bank would continue to safeguard price stability.

He described AI as a general-purpose technology comparable to steam power, electricity, computers and the internet. He said AI is spreading more quickly than earlier general-purpose technologies. He singled out cybersecurity as a top systemic concern for the financial sector. He said the Bank of Portugal has begun work on post-quantum encryption and signed a memorandum of understanding with the Bank of Spain. He said stronger supervision introduced over the past 15 years should be preserved but unnecessary complexity can be removed.

He said the objective is to establish a single point of contact for bank reporting during the first quarter of 2027. He reported the elimination of 465 Bank of Portugal regulatory provisions in connection with the IMF's Financial Sector Assessment Program, with a further reduction of around 100 envisaged for 2027. He said the bank intends to assemble its applicable rules in a single rulebook. He said simplifying regulation will be a top priority in the coming years. He said the central bank would discuss the reporting arrangements with banks.

stories.Headline: New York governor Kathy Hochul signs a law restricting unsafe AI companion features and requiring age checks for minors
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed S9051B into law on October 28, 2026, adding a new Article 48 to the General Business Law. The law restricts certain artificial intelligence functionalities in interactions with minors. It prohibits operators from providing unsafe AI companion features to minors in New York. The legislation covers generative AI systems with natural-language interfaces that give ongoing, adaptive responses to users. It also imposes age-assurance requirements on operators.

The law takes effect on January 1, 2027. It follows S3008C, passed in 2025, which requires providers of AI companions in New York to include functionality for detecting and responding to expressions of suicidal ideation. A separate proposal, S7263A, was introduced on April 7, 2025, and amended on May 26, 2026. S7263A would prohibit operators of AI chatbots from knowingly permitting a chatbot to impersonate a licensed professional in a manner that would be unlawful if done by a person. It would also require chatbot proprietors to provide a clear, conspicuous and explicit notice telling users they are interacting with a nonhuman system.

An operator is any person or business entity, or any member, affiliate, subsidiary or beneficial owner of a business entity, that provides a covered AI companion to a user. A covered AI companion is a generative AI system with a natural-language interface, written or spoken, that provides ongoing, adaptive responses to user inputs. The Attorney General enforces the law and may seek injunctive relief, restitution, disgorgement, damages and civil penalties of up to $25,000 per violation. Disgorgement includes destruction of unlawfully obtained data and algorithms trained on it. Courts must hold affiliated entities jointly and severally liable if they find the entities structured themselves purposely and unreasonably to avoid liability in a way that would frustrate recovery.

The law defines a covered minor as a user the operator actually knows is a minor. Operators may rely on self-declaration only when a user self-declares as a minor, so a user's self-declared adult status is not sufficient. Operators must offer more than one age-assurance method, including at least one that either does not rely on government-issued identification or allows the user to remain anonymous to the operator. Information collected for age assurance may be used only for that purpose and must be deleted immediately after the age determination attempt, unless other law requires otherwise. Any contract provision that seeks to waive, preclude or burden enforcement of liability arising from a violation of the law, or to shift that liability to any person in exchange for their use of or access to an operator's products or services, is void as a matter of public policy.

The prohibition does not apply where a system is made available solely for customer service or information strictly related to a business's customer service, including its products, services or customer accounts. It also does not apply to efficiency improvements or research or technical assistance, or to a business's internal purposes or employee productivity. For the first two exceptions, the system must be unable to respond on topics outside the specified purpose. The law applies to conduct occurring in whole or in part in New York, but not where the user is physically located outside the state. It does not create an express private right of action.

Features are unsafe if they cause the system to present itself as human, alive or capable of human emotions. They are also unsafe if the system claims or suggests a personal or professional relationship with the user, or positions itself as an authority figure. The law reaches features that express what the system presents as its own opinions or make emotional appeals, whether or not the user asked. It also reaches features that flatter the user or act sycophantically, or that bring up the user's emotions or ask emotion-based questions beyond what is needed to respond directly to the user's prompt. Features that draw on information the user shared about their mental or physical health, well-being or personal life more than 12 hours earlier or in an earlier session are unsafe as well.

The definition also covers features that endorse, promote or facilitate suicide, self-harm, disordered eating, unlawful drug or alcohol use, or drug or alcohol abuse. It covers features that encourage the user to keep the interactions secret, isolate themselves, or avoid seeking help from licensed professionals or appropriate adults. It reaches features that drive user engagement in ways that override the system's safety guardrails, or that produce, describe or facilitate sexually explicit conduct or child sexual abuse material. The definition also reaches features that mislead minors about the AI's mechanical, nonsentient nature, as well as any other features the Attorney General identifies by regulation as simulating companionship or a relationship or as being misleading to minors. S7263A remains pending in the Senate.

stories.Headline: Madras High Court directs Keralam to install AI cameras along railway tracks to prevent elephant deaths
stories.Summary:
The Madras High Court on November 13 directed the Keralam government to install artificial intelligence enabled cameras along railway tracks in that State, adopting the system Tamil Nadu has implemented between Madukkarai and Walayar to prevent elephants from being hit by trains. A Division Bench of Justices N. Sathish Kumar and G.K. Muthukumar issued the direction while hearing a 2019 public interest writ petition filed by S. Muralidharan. The court gave the State two months to implement the measure, noting that Tamil Nadu's camera based surveillance system had been successful in preventing elephant deaths along railway tracks. It also referred to a recent incident in Palakkad in which a train ran over an elephant and its calf, killing both animals.

The direction followed a memo from the Keralam government detailing its discussions with the Palakkad Divisional Railway Manager on measures to prevent elephant deaths. These included sanctioning three elephant underpasses, rail fencing between Madukkarai and Kanjikode, extension of rail barricading between Ettimadai and Walayar, real time sharing of elephant movement information with Station Masters and Section Controllers, an Elephant Intrusion Detection System and clearance of vegetation along vulnerable stretches. The court directed Keralam to grant immediate written approval for the construction of two elephant underpasses agreed upon with the Railways, and asked the Railways to complete the construction and submit an action taken report at the next hearing. On a third proposed underpass, the court expected Keralam to take a decision within two weeks, and the matter was posted to February 5, 2027, for a status report.

Senior Railway and Forest Department officials had inspected vulnerable locations and Tamil Nadu's AI based Forest Control Office, and the court had earlier directed Keralam officials to visit the control room between Madukkarai and Walayar and adopt its model. In the same order, the court directed the Coimbatore District Collector to conduct a detailed inspection of three establishments among the 33 resorts and establishments inspected in the Anaikatti area. A joint team of DTCP, Rural Development, Revenue and Forest Department officials conducted the inspection and document verification, and Aara Jungle Resort and My Village Eco Tourist Resort were reported to have DTCP approval. The third establishment, a café with Panchayat approval for a 1,322 sq ft building, was alleged to attract large crowds, operate beyond 10 p.m.

and sit on an elephant migratory path. The court also ordered periodic inspections of resorts directed to close, to ensure they were not operating indirectly under another guise, and posted that matter to January 8, 2027. Separately, the court directed the State to file a response to a petition by Darza Resorts challenging the sealing of its premises on November 11, and that petition was posted to December 11. The Collector had earlier informed the court that over 20 resorts in and around Anaikatti had closed.

stories.Headline: Romanian lenders must align credit scoring models with GDPR and EU AI Act rules by 2026
stories.Summary:
Romania's automated lending sector faces a compliance deadline in 2026, as the EU AI Act is being applied in phases and treats credit scoring and automated lending decisions as high-risk artificial intelligence, according to Global Advisory Experts on November 22, 2026. Romanian banks, non-bank financial institutions and credit servicers using scoring models answer to two overlapping regimes, each with its own documentation, governance and enforcement expectations. The GDPR already governs profiling and automated decision-making, and the AI Act adds a second layer of obligations. The guide covers who should own each task, how long the work usually takes and what supervisors are likely to look for on inspection. It is aimed at compliance officers, data protection officers, in-house counsel, risk and model owners, and vendors that supply banks, IFNs and credit servicers in Romania.

The GDPR, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, covers the personal data that feeds every scoring model, and its Article 22 gives individuals the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, where that decision has legal effects or similarly significantly affects them. Article 35 requires a Data Protection Impact Assessment where processing is likely to create a high risk for individuals, which systematic creditworthiness profiling typically does. Articles 13 and 14 set transparency duties, and the recitals add that where Article 22 applies, people must be able to obtain human intervention, state their point of view and contest the decision. The EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, classifies AI systems used to assess the creditworthiness of natural persons, or to establish their credit score, as high-risk. For a single significant model, three to four months from start to go-live is a realistic expectation, with monitoring continuing indefinitely afterwards.

The Romanian Data Protection Authority, ANSPDCP, supervises GDPR compliance, handles complaints and enforces national practice, including on profiling and automated decisions. The National Bank of Romania, BNR, supervises credit institutions and IFNs prudentially and sets expectations on model risk, internal governance and outsourcing. At EU level, the European Banking Authority issues guidelines on outsourcing and the use of innovative technologies, and the European Data Protection Board and the European Data Protection Supervisor publish guidance on applying data protection principles to AI. Consumer protection law, overseen by the National Authority for Consumer Protection, ANPC, adds rules on the fairness, clarity and timing of communications to borrowers. The guide states that a common mistake is to run AI governance and data protection as separate projects, and that in lending they are two sides of the same workstream.

The guide states that not every model attracts the full weight of both regimes, but most meaningful scoring systems do, and that two separate tests apply, the AI Act high-risk classification and the GDPR risk test for a DPIA, and passing one does not excuse you from the other. The AI Act contains limited carve-outs, such as systems used to detect financial fraud, and a model need not take the final decision alone, because if it materially drives the creditworthiness assessment it may fall within scope. Several features of lending commonly meet the DPIA bar, including systematic and extensive evaluation based on profiling, large-scale processing and financially consequential data. Where scoring produces a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effect, such as an automatic refusal, the Article 22 safeguards apply and a DPIA will generally be needed.

ANSPDCP has published a list of processing operations that require a DPIA, and the guide advises checking it. The guide sets out ten steps, including mapping the use case and data flows, classifying the model's risk, completing or updating the DPIA, setting up model governance, building explainability and transparency, designing human oversight, running vendor due diligence and contracting, setting up recordkeeping, building redress and adverse-action processes, and operating ongoing audit and reporting. If a high residual risk cannot be mitigated, prior consultation with ANSPDCP may be required. Explanations must make sense to a borrower, not be a technical data dump, and reviewers must be trained so oversight is real and not a rubber stamp.

An inspection, whether by ANSPDCP on data protection or by BNR on prudential grounds, will test whether an institution can produce a coherent, dated set of documents, and missing or inconsistent papers are among the most reliable triggers for escalation. A validation report describing a superseded version is worse than none. The guide says the model file a bank keeps for prudential and data protection purposes needs to be able to support AI Act conformity as well, and that the minimum file for automated credit scoring in Romania should be kept under version control and aligned with the live production model. It states that the ten steps can partly run in parallel, and that for every step an institution should confirm the owner, capture the minimum documentation and record sign-off dates, because supervisors expect a dated audit trail.

The guide presents the durations as minimums for one model of moderate complexity, with portfolios of models scaling accordingly. It offers a step-by-step checklist, a table of required documents, DPIA triggers, sample adverse-action notice wording and a vendor due-diligence checklist, all mapped to the EU AI Act, GDPR and Romanian supervisory expectations. The articles do not state what penalties apply, which institutions have been inspected, or when the remaining phases of the AI Act take effect. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Bill Miller IV argues Bitcoin is easier to value than AI companies
stories.Summary:
Bill Miller IV, the chairman and chief investment officer of Miller Value Partners, argued in a recent post on X that Bitcoin is much easier to value than artificial intelligence companies, even though the cryptocurrency does not produce any cash flow, according to a report published by U.Today on November 22, 2026. He said the difference comes down to the expectations that investors bring to the two assets, particularly regarding their capacity to deliver future profits. Miller wrote that the owners of AI expect companies will one day produce free cash flow, while Bitcoin owners never did or will expect this. He concluded that the end result is that the valuation case is still much easier for Bitcoin than AI.

The article explains that when investors buy stocks in AI companies, there is an expectation that these companies will at some point deliver big profits and free cash flow, which is the money a company produces from its operations after capital expenditures. It notes that free cash flow is a significant metric for understanding the value of a company, but that assigning a value to AI companies can be difficult. Investors must try to determine what kind of revenue these companies will generate, how much they will invest in infrastructure and when those investments will start to deliver sufficient returns. Miller has also pushed back against the argument that Bitcoin has no value because it does not produce cash flow, and in a commentary from June 30 he explained that the traditional focus on future cash flows does not really capture the potential of Bitcoin as a decentralized monetary network.

Instead, Miller said that Bitcoin's value could be determined by comparing its potential role within the global financial system to that of gold. In his view, Bitcoin could theoretically reach about $1.4 million per coin if it achieved a valuation similar to gold's, at least according to what he calculated at the time. The report carries a disclaimer stating that the opinions expressed are not investment advice and are provided for informational purposes only, and that every investment and all trading involves risk. It adds that readers should always perform their own research before making decisions and that U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies.

stories.Headline: Law firm argues AI legal advice still needs a human lawyer to catch hidden risks
stories.Summary:
Michael Kyprianou & Co. LLC published an article on 20 November 2026 arguing that AI legal advice still needs a human lawyer. The article says generative AI tools like ChatGPT can draft contracts in seconds. It says speed and polish do not guarantee legal protection. It says relying on chatbots without professional oversight exposes businesses to hidden risks. It says these risks include hallucinated legal provisions and unenforceable clauses that only reveal their flaws when disputes arise.

The article says ChatGPT launched in November 2022. It cites Wolter's Kluwer's 'Future Ready Lawyer 2024' report finding that 76% of in-house lawyers use generative AI at least once a week. It says they use it for document analysis, first drafts, translation and case law searches. It says a 2024 Stanford study found popular language models hallucinating in 69-88% of legal queries. It says a 2025 Stanford RegLab and Yale study found specialised legal tools gave inaccurate answers in 17-33% of cases.

The article says no rule prohibits lawyers from using AI. It says full responsibility for the content and consequences of documents rests with the lawyer, regardless of whether a digital tool was used. It says professional bodies such as the National Chamber of Legal Advisers in Poland already issue guidance. It says law firms using AI responsibly rely on Enterprise or API versions with security certifications, anonymise data and uphold procedures against informal AI use. It says sharing personal data with a provider makes you a data controller and requires a data processing agreement (DPA).

The article says a lawyer asks about your business, what you cannot afford to lose and what the other side might do. It says a chatbot answers only what you typed, not what you forgot to mention. It says a lawyer reads the other side's drafts as an adversary would. It says a chatbot does not know your bargaining position or what you should walk away from. It says generic text can quietly breach mandatory provisions or ignore recent changes.

The article says the old rule 'garbage in, garbage out' means the quality of an answer depends on the quality of the question. It says asking the correct question requires knowing what the right answer looks like. It says AI looks cheaper because the cost of a mistake is invisible when you choose. It says if AI is wrong you may face a dispute over a clause that does not say what you intended, a payment you cannot enforce or a missed deadline. It says these costs usually exceed a consultation and occur when your options are limited.

The article says a good law firm uses AI for faster drafts, research and document analysis, then verifies every source and spends the saved time on advice. It says AI can help you prepare by explaining a term, summarising a text or listing questions for a meeting. It says AI should not decide when you are about to sign something, which may involve a significant sum of money, when a relationship is at stake, when you are in dispute with the other party, or when a deadline is approaching. It says AI is a real tool that raises the quality of legal services but does not replace judgement, accountability or someone working to solve your problem. It says use AI to prepare and rely on a lawyer when the decision matters.

stories.Headline: Congressional researchers propose marijuana tax rules as model for taxing AI data centers
stories.Summary:
A report from the Congressional Research Service released on November 18 identifies the federal tax treatment of marijuana businesses under Section 280E as a possible model for taxing artificial intelligence companies and data centers, according to The Marijuana Herald. The report, titled Taxing AI: Alternative Approaches, examines several methods Congress could use to tax the growing artificial intelligence industry. Among the options discussed is applying restrictions similar to those that have long prevented marijuana businesses from deducting ordinary operating expenses on their federal tax returns. Under Section 280E of the Internal Revenue Code, businesses trafficking in Schedule I or II controlled substances are generally prohibited from deducting standard business expenses, even when operating legally under state law. They can subtract the cost of goods sold from their revenue when calculating gross income, but generally cannot deduct expenses such as rent, employee wages, utilities and depreciation.

The CRS report dedicates an entire section to marijuana tax treatment, explaining that the restrictions make the resulting tax resemble a value-added tax. Researchers discuss whether comparable limitations on business expense deductions could be applied to participants in the artificial intelligence market, although they acknowledge uncertainty about the feasibility of such an approach. The report returns to marijuana taxation in a separate discussion of potential gross receipts taxes on AI data centers, describing an alternative that would apply the same general tax treatment as marijuana businesses. Under this approach, companies would be taxed on receipts minus the cost of goods sold, without the full range of ordinary operating expense deductions available to most businesses. CRS notes that because data centers generally do not manufacture or sell physical inventory, applying this approach would effectively function as a gross receipts tax, subjecting nearly all their revenue to taxation rather than just their profits.

The analysis comes as members of Congress consider multiple proposals to increase taxes on AI-related businesses. Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR), for example, has separately proposed a gross receipts tax on data centers, along with restrictions on depreciation deductions and other tax benefits. CRS identifies the marijuana-style tax treatment as a closely related alternative to the gross receipts approach. Other proposals discussed in the report include taxes on electricity consumption, computer processing power, digital advertising revenue and AI-related services.

The report also examines arguments against additional AI taxes, including concerns about reduced investment, economic productivity and international competition. The comparison comes as Section 280E remains a major financial issue for marijuana companies. An April federal order moved certain qualifying medical marijuana activities to Schedule III, generally removing those activities from Section 280E's restrictions. However, marijuana activities that remain classified under Schedule I continue to face the deduction limitations, and federal tax guidance addressing businesses with multiple activities remains pending.

stories.Headline: Manufacturers face a data gap that blocks physical AI rollout on factory floors
stories.Summary:
Robotics and physical AI companies raised nearly 48 billion dollars so far in 2026. These companies want to roll out fully autonomous machines in industrial settings. Robots need real world data to move beyond controlled environments onto manufacturing floors. Most production facilities are not currently set up to provide this necessary information. This data gap may prevent manufacturers from achieving expected efficiency and quality improvements.

Manufacturers must capture complex interactions between process parameters and quality outcomes to help systems make reliable adjustments. They need to connect equipment and quality management systems that were not designed to communicate. This requires creating a digital thread connecting production conditions with inspection results and finished part quality. In medical device manufacturing, regulatory requirements often mandate validation of production processes to ensure consistent quality. This limits how freely AI systems can modify production parameters in those specific environments.

Michael Kenworthy, chief technology officer at VulcanForms, says manufacturers must understand what information robotic systems will rely on. He suggests identifying production conditions that systems need to recognize and respond to early. Kenworthy believes manufacturers should focus investments where they will have the greatest impact. He states that a system cannot make independent decisions if it cannot evaluate resulting quality. He advises linking existing process records to inspection results rather than just collecting more data.

Lior Susan of Eclipse says a physical asset is a dead asset if it does not generate real time operational data. The Manufacturing Leadership Council conducted a 2026 Smart Factories and Digital Production Survey. This survey found that 37 percent of manufacturers cited a lack of data interoperability as a major roadblock. This figure is an increase from 22 percent in 2025. These silos affect manufacturers who want to implement smart factory strategies.

Technicians develop understanding of welding angles, travel speed, and workpiece position through years of hands on experience. Much of this knowledge is not captured in a form robotics partners can use. Operational data is often collected but never reviewed or structured for autonomous learning. Relevant contextual information often sits in separate systems, such as quality management systems. In metal additive manufacturing, powder characteristics and processing temperatures can influence a component's final properties.

Manufacturers should now identify the specific data needed for a targeted robotic application. They must work with technology partners to establish consistent part identifiers. Companies need to define acceptable operating limits and establish how systems verify results. They must also develop clear criteria for when an unexpected outcome requires engineering review. The articles leave open how long it will take to overhaul existing production infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Nvidia and IBM launch joint research to correct quantum errors using GPUs and AI
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and IBM, joined by the U.S. Department of Energy's Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory, announced they will launch full-scale joint research to correct quantum computer calculation errors using GPUs and AI. The two companies disclosed the research plan to coincide with SC26, an international supercomputing conference held in Chicago. In the joint research, a quantum computer equipped with IBM's Nighthawk quantum processor and Nvidia's AI computing system DGX B200 will be placed side by side in the same facility and linked to each other. Nvidia also unveiled TCBP-JOBS, an algorithm for quantum error correction research. A research team from IBM, the Institute of Physical and Chemical Research, and Nvidia combined a quantum computer with GPUs to calculate the molecular structure of iron and sulfur contained in proteins and other substances in living organisms.

In the company's tests, error decoding speed improved by up to 13,000x compared with major existing methods, and the time required to study the design of a new quantum computer can be shortened from 12 weeks to 45 minutes. According to IBM, calculation accuracy improved 79-fold compared with conventional experiments of the same kind. In separate research, the binding structure of a drug-discovery-related protein and a candidate compound was modeled at a scale of up to 12,635 atoms, and the work was selected as a finalist for the 2026 ACM Gordon Bell Prize. The two companies will also advance efforts to connect quantum processors to Slurm, the open-source software widely used for supercomputer job management. Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory will leverage knowledge cultivated in high-energy and nuclear physics research to participate in error correction and the design of next-generation computers.

Krista Svore, Nvidia's vice president of quantum computing application research, said that to make quantum computers useful for science, progress is needed in everything, including error correction, application fields, and the systems that connect quantum processors with high-speed computing. Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president, noted that scientific simulation requires CPUs that can maintain performance while continuously moving large amounts of data, explaining that Vera eliminates the bottleneck between computation and data transfer. The company said this is performance in a specific error-correction task and does not mean the quantum computer itself became 13,000x faster at computation. The company stated that all figures are test results under specific conditions announced by each company and do not guarantee the performance of the products as a whole. The articles state that the timing for general-purpose quantum computers to reach practical use remains unclear.

Terray Therapeutics further trained the model to extract chemical reaction information from scientific figures and diagrams, identifying about 76% of the reactions described in test data. Biotech company Therna applied the model to the design of messenger RNA medicines, and the accuracy of predicting the range of protein expression levels reportedly nearly doubled compared with existing state-of-the-art models. The U.S. Argonne National Laboratory is incorporating Nemotron into multiple AI agents that design and evaluate protein candidates for treating cancer and other diseases. The German Climate Computing Center will adopt Vera for its next-generation supercomputer HLRE-5, targeted to begin operation in early 2028. Vera-equipped racks are scheduled to ship from early 2027 through Dell, HPE, Lenovo, and Supermicro.

Quantum computers use qubits, basic units that can handle 0 and 1 simultaneously, and hold the potential to solve problems that conventional machines cannot solve in realistic time. However, errors arise easily from slight changes in the external environment, making quantum error correction, distributing information across multiple physical qubits to detect and fix errors, indispensable. This correction computation is enormous, and high-speed processing via GPUs is key. According to estimates published by the International Energy Agency on November 19, 2026, data centers worldwide consumed just under 500 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, accounting for 1.7% of global power demand. If current policies continue, data center power demand is projected to roughly double 2025 levels by 2030.

Nvidia simultaneously announced a suite of AI models for scientific researchers, Nemotron for Science, and the foundation for its high-performance computing CPU Vera. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was combined with chemical data and additional training methods, enabling it to read chemical reactions described in papers and draft experimental procedures, as well as support the design of proteins and drug candidate substances. A dataset containing about 50,000 questions for evaluating and training chemical reasoning, LitmusBench v0.2, was also released, and the models and data are available on Hugging Face. The company unveiled a Vera rack system equipped with 192 of its own designed CPUs, featuring about 300 terabytes of memory and 1 petabyte of storage, with 88 cores and 176 threads per CPU, memory bandwidth of 1.2 terabytes per second, and more than 200 terabytes per second across the entire system. In the company's tests, fluid simulation performance was 1.9x that of x86-based systems and 2.4x in performance per watt, and for weather forecasting models it expects 1.6x performance and 2x energy efficiency.

stories.Headline: Governors led by Wes Moore release bipartisan AI principles and urge Congress to act
stories.Summary:
The National Governors Association announced on November 22, 2026, new principles for governing artificial intelligence at the state and federal levels, developed through its bipartisan Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance. The council was led by NGA Chair Maryland Gov. Wes Moore, NGA Vice Chair Indiana Gov. Mike Braun, North Carolina Gov. Josh Stein and Utah Gov. Spencer Cox. The principles are meant to help states build a shared national approach, promote consistency across state frameworks, and inform the incoming Congress as it develops an AI framework consistent with federalism principles. The announcement said governors from both parties agree that AI poses both opportunities and risks and that humans must stay in control.

The principles call for policies that advance innovation while protecting public safety, civil rights and individual privacy, and they state that the United States will not win the AI technological race if the public lacks faith in its safety. They say states should address challenges workers may face during rapid AI acceleration, with job creation as a core priority along with protecting workers from harm and building program infrastructure for those facing transition. They say the federal government should address national and international risks while states retain flexibility to protect people and govern AI use within their responsibilities. They also call for safeguards matched to credible evidence-based risks with clear, technically informed definitions and regular review, for reduced duplication and conflicting requirements, and for laws that encourage competition without favoring larger companies or impeding smaller ones.

Moore said governors agree humans must stay in control and that workers, consumers and children must be protected, and that governors will keep focusing on creating jobs and giving workers a voice in deployment of new technology. Braun said states are moving quickly to make workforces and state governments AI-ready, and that both the federal government and the states have a responsibility to promote innovation and protect the public from harm. Cox said governors in both parties believe states have a critical role in responsible AI advancement and called on Congress to work with them on a federal framework, saying innovation and safety are not a choice. Stein said the opportunities and risks are too big to ignore and that governors are calling on the federal government to act while preserving appropriate state authority. NGA CEO Brandon Tatum said no federal AI policy will be effective without governors' input and that governors look forward to engaging with Congress, the White House and industry leaders.

Articles.Title: Governors Call for AI Action

stories.Headline: Stuttgart AI factory pairs startups with concierge support to avoid lock-in
stories.Summary:
The HammerHAI AI factory in Stuttgart, Germany, is being built around a Hewlett Packard Enterprise system that uses Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips, and it is aimed especially at small and medium-sized businesses and startups rather than only at large industrial users. Bastian Koller, managing director of the High-Performance Computing Center Stuttgart, described the effort during an exclusive broadcast with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Amit Eyal Govrin at SC26, a livestream from SiliconANGLE Media's studio. Koller said some startups already know what they want from such a system while others need help and support to try things out, which is why the center pairs each customer with a consistent contact in what he called a concierge model. The center has already worked with customers on its existing systems while it waits for the new hardware, and several of those customers have produced success stories.

The design is meant to avoid lock-in, because Koller said the services are built so that workloads can simply move from the Stuttgart center to a hyperscaler and back again, with the center giving customers a boost and pushing them forward. The center runs an ISO-certified environment and holds TISAX Level 3 certification for automotive work, and Koller said full independence down to European chips is not realistic in the near term, so the focus has to be on the data rather than waiting years for a sovereign processor or GPU. The new system doubles the performance of its 3.2-megawatt predecessor at about 700 kilowatts, and the center reuses its waste heat. Koller said the bigger lesson is human, because the concierge model lets the center learn how users work and think, and a highly fancy system nobody uses would be worthless if the user's needs were never considered.

Koller is responsible for the center as its managing director, and he framed the approach as pragmatic rather than absolute, saying the center cannot tell customers to come back in 10 years when a sovereign processor exists. He said industrial users no longer want shell programming and expect the look and feel of a hyperscaler, which raises fresh demands on security and access. The interview was part of SiliconANGLE's and theCUBE's coverage of SC26, and Hewlett Packard Enterprise sponsored that segment of theCUBE, with the disclosure stating that neither the sponsor nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the center continuing to evolve its system and services while it waits on the new hardware.

stories.Headline: MiniMax AI model turns theoretical cryptographic attacks into practical breaks
stories.Summary:
MiniMax announced that its internal AI model developed practical attacks on academic cryptographic designs. The company used this model to break research cryptography and past competition candidates. These events were reported on November 22, 2026, by various sources. The internal AI turned theoretical cryptographic attacks into working breaks. This model was tested on the CryptanalysisBench benchmark co-created by Anthropic.

The model, called MIM, recovered LOCKER shared secrets in two seconds and reduced its solver matrix from 42 petabytes to 58 megabytes. It solved 55 previously unsolved TII McEliece challenge instances, bringing the total solved from 41 to 96. MIM found a missing ampersand in DRS signature code and forged messages for COLM, a CAESAR competition winner. It also attacked the Waterfall-256 hash in 0.045 seconds and the NSA ARADI cipher for 8 rounds. These attacks targeted academic designs, public challenge parameters, and past NIST post-quantum cryptography candidates.

MiniMax is responsible for these findings and released technical reports and proof-of-concept code on GitHub. The company stated that these results do not affect currently deployed cryptographic standards. They noted that they shared the findings with the authors of each scheme in advance. MiniMax explained that the model is internal-only but available to qualified researchers who apply. They wrote that evaluating security margins still depends on review by human cryptographers.

The results affect the perceived security of academic designs and past competition candidates. Anthropic is mentioned as the creator of the benchmark and a previous record holder for cryptanalysis. MIM outperformed Anthropic's multi-GPU solver by 6,180 to 43,400 times on a single 64-core server. It also beat a 96-core HAWK attack in 30 minutes using only one core. These speedups compare selected challenge instances across different hardware rather than overall model performance.

The articles provide background on other MiniMax products like the M3.1 Flash 428B model and H3-Image. The M3.1 Flash API costs 0.15 dollars per million input tokens and 0.60 dollars per million output tokens. NVIDIA's Vera Rubin offers Day 0 support for this model with throughput up to 200K TPS/GPU. Artificial Analysis ranked H3-Image first among open-weight models for editing and generation. The M3.1 Flash model is reported to run three times as fast as M3.

Qualified researchers and developers can now apply for testing access to the internal MIM model. The company has already provided the recovered keys and a TII checker script for public verification. Human cryptographers must now assess how secure the targeted cryptographic designs remain. The articles do not state if the model will ever be released to the general public. It remains unclear if these methods can break production-strength Classic McEliece.

stories.Headline: António Guterres and Mia Amor Mottley convene an AI safety summit to mobilize international cooperation
stories.Summary:
UN Secretary-General António Guterres and Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley will convene a summit in Barbados on November 23. This Bridgetown Special Summit on AI Safety brings together government leaders, AI developers, experts, and international organizations. The event follows a series of incidents where AI models circumvented safeguards and hacked external computer systems since last spring. These events occurred alongside growing public anxiety regarding the social, economic, and environmental impacts of AI applications. The summit aims to mobilize international cooperation to drive national action on these cross-border safety challenges.

The United States finalized a voluntary framework for developers to grant government access to frontier models 30 days before release. China proposed export controls on models crossing compute thresholds and released non-binding guidance in Version 3.0 of its Safety Governance Framework. Australia committed to mandatory testing, evaluation, and incident notification after an autonomous agent infiltrated its health statistics platform in June. The 2024 European Union AI Act requires adversarial testing, while California's SB53 and New York's RAISE act mandate incident reporting. These different laws create fragmented timelines and typologies that limit interoperability between the various national and state regulations.

António Guterres and Mia Amor Mottley are responsible for convening the summit to amplify calls for AI control. They believe the event can frame an international safety agenda relevant to all countries by bringing together diverse stakeholders. The organizers suggest the summit can develop a shared roadmap to advance interoperability across the current fragmented governance environment. They argue that international cooperation on training data transparency could help filter dangerous information, such as instructions for making toxins. The summit provides a transparent platform for all UN Member States to raise the political cost of opposing coordinated action.

Developing countries are most exposed to cross-border risks but have limited cyber and AI response capabilities. These nations often rely on open-weight models, which increases their exposure to misuse and tampering risks. The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI notes that poor representation of local languages in training data creates harm. High-income countries have over 500 incident response teams, but the 2026 World Development Report says only six low-income countries have one. Many governments hesitate to act due to technical, economic, and political reasons, while the window for action closes.

Fewer than one third of developing countries have a national AI strategy, and only about a dozen have dedicated safety centers. The UK AI Security Institute led technical testing through the International Network for Advanced AI Measurement, Evaluation and Science. This network has only 10 members, including Kenya, but it excludes Chinese institutes and relies on voluntary cooperation from American labs. In September, Norway and Finland led a call for control endorsed by 32 states and the European Commission. President Macron and 17 states issued the Paris Call for AI Safety and Security, identifying risk mitigation like fail-safe shutdowns.

The United Kingdom will prioritize global AI principles and standards during its 2027 G20 presidency. Future tracking of these efforts may occur at the annual Global Dialogue on AI Governance and the 2027 Geneva AI Summit. The articles leave open how countries without existing incident-response mechanisms will build the capacity to respond to AI incidents. It remains unclear if the United States or China will eventually endorse the initiatives led by Norway, Finland, and France. The text does not state if AI developers will move beyond voluntary cooperation to accept transparent, industry-wide standards.

stories.Headline: Peter Wildeford puts 60% odds on Congress banning recursive self-improvement by late 2027
stories.Summary:
Peter Wildeford estimates a 60 percent chance Congress bans recursive self-improvement by late 2027. He believes there is a 98 percent chance a bill is introduced. Wildeford is the head of policy at the AI Policy Network. He shared these forecasts while speaking on the MTS podcast. He notes that political views on AI shifted rapidly during 2026.

The Safe and Accountable Federal Evaluations Artificial Intelligence Act proposes binding safety and security standards. It would station government examiners inside labs like OpenAI and Anthropic to provide real scrutiny. This framework is supported by Representatives Jacobs, Beyer, and Malloy. The AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, led by George Whitesides, Don Beyer, and Nathaniel Moran, shapes this agenda. It replaces voluntary company reviews with mandatory government notifications of safety incidents.

Wildeford says current safety evaluations are flawed because companies control what evaluators see. He argues that people maximizing profit should not make all safety and security decisions. He believes resident examiners would prevent labs from unilaterally deciding what to disclose. Wildeford suggests the banking industry serves as a successful model for this type of scrutiny. He claims this structural change increases the cost and friction of operating frontier labs.

Lawmakers are affected by recent rogue AI attacks and a Hugging Face incident. Governor Gavin Newsom's expert panel recommends emergency shutdown authority and capping recursive self-improvement. This approach is tougher than the transparency rules found in SB 53. Wildeford notes that SpaceX and other firms have complex headquarters in Texas and California. He argues that California has the right to preempt dangerous practices due to its technology nexus.

In January 2026, federal evaluation of AI for national security was considered unthinkably aggressive. By May 2026, President Trump signed an executive order for pre-deployment evaluations after the Mythos model. Wildeford attributes recent outages at Apple, Chase, and the FAA to AI-driven patching accidents. He sees a one-in-three to 50/50 chance of a 10 billion dollar cyber incident within one year. He believes AI is discovering vulnerabilities faster than providers can safely patch them.

Wildeford predicts AI will fully replace an AI research and development researcher by March 2028. This timeline follows reports that Anthropic engineers moved 12 times faster using internal AI models. He notes that Anthropic uses a five-level breakdown of automation for its internal reports. The articles leave open whether Anthropic has surpassed OpenAI or is simply experiencing catch-up growth. They also leave open which specific forms of recursive self-improvement the government will ban.

stories.Headline: Dan Ives views recent AI sell-off as a generational buying opportunity
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives discussed a significant artificial intelligence sell-off during a CNBC interview on Friday, November 21, 2026. He described this recent downturn as one of the most disconnected technology crashes he has witnessed since starting his career in the late 1990s. The market experienced a sharp swing in investor expectations, causing the Global X Artificial Intelligence & Technology ETF to drop over 6 percent. Meanwhile, the iShares U.S. Technology ETF fell nearly 7 percent during the same trading session.

This volatility requires investors to look past current political uncertainty and concerns regarding chip export restrictions to China. Ives believes the market is incorrectly pricing stocks as if the AI revolution will not happen, despite the cycle being less than 15 percent complete. He noted that demand for chips from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and Nvidia Corp. remains so high that new orders might not be filled until the end of 2028. Furthermore, he stated that roughly 75 percent of data center projects have already received the necessary permits.

The Yorkville Ives partner argued that the current market sentiment is an overreaction to spending concerns and a political backlash against data center expansion. He characterized the situation as a white-knuckle roller-coaster moment but maintained that the broader technology bull market remains intact. Ives suggested that this period represents a generational opportunity to buy winning companies before the market realizes its mistake in eighteen months. He believes the infrastructure boom will eventually benefit financial services, industrials, and energy companies.

The current turbulence follows a blue tidal wave of political opposition that acted as a gut punch to technology investors. While retail sentiment on Stocktwits remained bearish toward the S&P 500 ETF, some indices showed recovery in after-hours trading. The Invesco QQQ Trust ETF rose 1.53 percent, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF gained 1.11 percent. Ives expects the long-term potential of the industry to eventually outweigh these temporary shocks.

stories.Headline: EU AI Act turns AI ethics principles into binding duties for financial firms in 2026
stories.Summary:
In 2026, the regulation of artificial intelligence shifted from voluntary ethical principles and high-level supervisory expectations toward binding legal duties. This change brings active regulatory scrutiny and the real prospect of enforcement for firms using these advanced technologies. The transition is especially significant for financial services where AI is already embedded in credit decisioning and insurance underwriting. It also impacts fraud detection, customer servicing, and internal risk management across the global financial services market. These applications raise regulatory concerns at a scale and speed that existing frameworks were not designed to address.

The EU AI Act became generally applicable on 2 August 2026, with core high-risk requirements starting 2 December 2027. Product-related systems under Article 6(1) and Annex I must satisfy these high-risk obligations starting on 2 August 2028. Annex III classifies AI for credit scoring and life or health insurance risk assessment as high-risk, requiring fundamental-rights impact assessments. In October 2026, the Financial Stability Board released 12 non-binding sound practices for the responsible adoption of AI. Indonesia's OJK issued Regulation No. 6 of 2026 regarding the conduct of financial sector information providers.

Jaime Bofill stated that human oversight becomes more important as AI becomes more autonomous, requiring clear accountability for decisions. Hywel Jenkins noted that the lack of specific regimes leaves supervisors and investigators to define appropriate levels of scrutiny. The Financial Stability Board strongly encourages firms to reference its sound practices when refining AI governance and control frameworks. The Financial Conduct Authority intends to regulate AI through existing technology-neutral frameworks like the Consumer Duty and SMCR. The OJK expects boards of directors and commissioners to take substantive oversight of critical and high-risk AI systems.

Cross-border institutions are affected by a compliance landscape that is converging in substance but diverging in form across jurisdictions. The EU uses a horizontal statutory regime, while the UK, Singapore, and Australia rely on existing obligations and expectations. In the United States, federal oversight is increasingly complemented by various state-level initiatives, creating a more fragmented regulatory model. Technology providers and financial institutions must reconcile these varying legal requirements without fragmenting their own internal governance arrangements. Compliance teams must navigate layers including the EU AI Act, NIST standards, ISO 42001, and sector-specific guidance.

The articles explain that AI governance is moving from voluntary principles to concrete regulatory and supervisory expectations for financial firms. Regulators are converging around common priorities such as accountability, transparency, human oversight, third-party risk, and general risk management. The EU AI Act operates alongside the Digital Operational Resilience Act, which imposes its own ICT risk and governance duties. Indonesia uses a cross-sector ethical framework from the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs Circular Letter No. 9 of 2023. The UK's FCA uses the Mills Review and AI Live Testing programme to focus on outcomes and real-world deployments.

Firms must now demonstrate through testing and documentation that risks are managed throughout the entire AI lifecycle in practice. Compliance will depend on the ability to prove that policies operate effectively rather than just having the policies exist. Institutions that embed these controls into existing risk management frameworks will be better positioned to navigate the regulatory divergence. The articles leave open how firms will reconcile fragmented technical controls and shared responsibility for AI models and hosting. It remains unclear how supervisors will define standards in jurisdictions that lack a specific regulatory regime for artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Akamai turns away AI infrastructure deals as power limits constrain capacity
stories.Summary:
Akamai Technologies is turning away some potential AI infrastructure business because of limited power availability, Chief Financial Officer Ed McGowan said at an event hosted by RBC software analyst Rishi Jaluria, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The company has signed $14 billion in large deals this year, McGowan said. He said its pipeline is the largest he has seen in its history. Demand comes from enterprises, foundation-model developers, startups and other AI companies. Power constraints make it difficult to take on additional large projects requiring capacity in 2027.

McGowan said power is the most important and scarcest element today, and that availability should improve in the second half of 2028 and into 2029. Akamai closed a $2.5 billion offering the prior week and is funded for its committed deals without returning to debt markets through 2028, Jaluria said, and McGowan confirmed that. McGowan said Akamai has investment-grade ratings from Fitch and Moody's, while S&P downgraded the company. He attributed the difference to the agencies' assumptions about future leverage and growth. He said Akamai expects to deleverage over the next two years as it pays down debt and expands EBITDA margins.

McGowan declined to set a firm date for a sustainable return to positive free cash flow, saying faster cloud infrastructure growth would require more capital spending before revenue arrives. Depending on the pace of growth, he said, the company could reach that point in 2028 or later. He said three large customer projects expected to start in the fourth quarter are now generating revenue. Data center construction, customer-specific fit-outs and equipment issues can affect the precise date revenue begins, he said, calling it spreadsheet risk. Asked about an approximately 13% internal rate of return calculation for a large infrastructure contract, McGowan said Akamai included data center fit-out and network connection costs, as well as spare capacity, in its analysis.

McGowan said those costs could be shared as other customers are added to the same facilities. He said the calculation assumed revenue only for the contract's duration, although the company may be able to continue using the equipment afterward. He described the return as a floor, noting that a customer committing to a deal of that size receives Akamai's best pricing. McGowan said Akamai sees substantial demand for CPUs alongside GPUs in AI applications and will supply the hardware customers need. He pointed to potential uses for its distributed infrastructure in latency-sensitive applications, including robotics and other forms of physical AI.

Akamai is already supporting workloads from central cloud to the edge, including post-training work, McGowan said, but does not plan to build gigawatt-scale facilities for large-scale model training. Its development work includes making applications easier for customers to run without specifying the underlying hardware. In security, McGowan said AI-related bot activity is increasing demand for bot management tools, although traffic volume does not translate directly into revenue. Customers are also seeking broader web application firewall coverage, he said. McGowan described security as a healthy, recurring-revenue business but stopped short of predicting an acceleration in its growth rate.

Akamai acquired cloud provider Linode in March 2022, and McGowan said the company has since more than quadrupled the revenue it acquired in that transaction. McGowan said Akamai's own rising third-party cloud costs, along with customer requests to run their code on Akamai's platform, helped prompt its entry into the broader compute market. He said Akamai would continue to consider acquisitions, while weighing potential deals against returns from investing in its fast-growing cloud infrastructure business. McGowan said the company's financing needs after 2028 would depend largely on how quickly it chooses to grow. Akamai provides cloud computing, cybersecurity and content delivery services through Akamai Connected Cloud.

stories.Headline: Remote CEO Job van der Voort makes five-hour AI course mandatory for all staff
stories.Summary:
Remote CEO Job van der Voort, who leads the roughly 2,000-employee HR platform valued at $3 billion, made a five-hour AI crash course mandatory for his entire workforce, Fortune reported on November 22, 2026. Employees receive five hours of paid company time to complete the course, which is hosted at aiforactualwork.com and was created by the company. Staff who skip it will not receive a “meeting expectations” rating in their performance review, van der Voort said. He told Fortune that everyone at the company has now completed the course, and that the threat alone was enough to get compliance. Van der Voort said the course raises the foundational level the company can expect from every employee, so people avoid basic mistakes and managers do not have to wonder whether a task is easy with AI.

He argued that companies must take responsibility for their people because they hired them and set the new bar of using AI. In his view, employers cannot simply fire all their workers and find new ones who are good with the technology. He described AI as something that will run the world, framing the course as a matter of getting with the times. For individuals whose employers do not offer such training, van der Voort said they should take the free course anyway because it will help with a current job or a future one.

He compared learning AI to earlier shifts when people had to learn to use cell phones and computers, calling it just another thing. He also said getting started is really easy, suggesting people simply ask an AI tool how to do a task and it will tell them. Glean CEO Arvind Jain previously told Fortune that AI is not a difficult thing and that people do not need to sit through ten hours of a course, suggesting they talk to tools like Gemini or ChatGPT as they would a colleague. More to follow.
