stories.Headline: Investors sell off artificial intelligence stocks as S&P 500 enters a correction
stories.Summary:
U.S. stocks fell on Tuesday, November 17, 2026, for a fourth consecutive session as a sell-off in artificial intelligence shares deepened. Investors sold off these stocks ahead of the quarterly earnings report from Nvidia, which was released after the closing bell that day. A bruising sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks continued on Friday, November 20, 2026, pulling the S&P 500 down by 3.7 percent. This Friday decline capped a seven-day losing streak, the longest string of losses since the COVID-19 pandemic began in the year 2020. The sell-off in technology stocks spread globally, causing Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi to each fall more than 5 percent overnight.

The Dow Jones fell 848.75 points to 50,759.42 on Tuesday and dropped 949.73 points to 48,147.33 on Friday, while the S&P 500 hit 6,910.39. The Nasdaq Composite shed 181.37 points to 24,328.38 on Tuesday and lost 1,261.47 points to close at 22,617.73 on Friday, November 20. The S&P 500 entered a correction after falling over 10 percent from its October 6 all-time high, a state not seen since March 2025. On Tuesday, the S&P 500 sank 76.06 points to 7,340.53, while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.74 percent and the Dow Jones fell 1.64 percent. All 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in the red, with financials down 1.87 percent and utilities down 1.6 percent on Tuesday.

Baird market strategist Michael Antonelli said the idea that AI can spend unlimited money to support the stock market is ending right now. He stated that he does not believe the overall bull market, which started in October 2022, has come to an end yet. The Commerce Department reported that U.S. retail sales rose 0.2 percent in October, following an unrevised 0.8 percent increase in September. The National Association of Home Builders reported its housing market index fell to 25 in November from 29 in October, its lowest since 2012. Saudi Arabia said on Friday that Iran-backed Houthi rebels fired more missiles and drones at the kingdom after a major air campaign in Yemen.

The sell-off affected chip stocks like Micron, Advanced Micro Devices, and Intel, while Broadcom gained 2.46 percent on Tuesday before falling 12.1 percent Friday. Software stocks declined on Tuesday, with Salesforce falling 9.45 percent and ServiceNow dropping 6.51 percent, while Nike, IBM, and UnitedHealth Group lost over 4 percent. Home Depot fell 2.45 percent after a disappointing outlook and the announcement that Richard McPhail would succeed Ted Decker as the company CEO. Walt Disney slipped 1.48 percent after reporting revenue of 25.9 billion dollars and adjusted earnings of 1.77 dollars per share, beating expectations. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI tool, tumbled 9.1 percent to 88.30 dollars on Friday after its record-breaking initial public offering.

The S&P 500 last had a correction in March 2025 when the Trump administration's trade war rattled the market and escalated in April 2025. The Nasdaq composite experienced its worst weekly loss since March 2020, when the global economy ground to a halt due to the pandemic. AI stocks drove Wall Street's big gains this year, but fears of a bubble grew after recent midterm elections at state and federal levels. The University of Michigan index of consumer sentiment rose recently, though it remains below February levels before the start of the war with Iran. Brent crude oil rose 0.6 percent to 92.57 dollars per barrel amid continued tension near the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.

The Federal Reserve is scheduled to release the minutes of its October meeting on Wednesday to provide more insight into current economic policy. Traders have increasingly priced in a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at the December meeting because of persistent inflationary pressures currently affecting the U.S. economy. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to 4.93 percent from 5.04 percent, while General Mills rose 3.7 percent and homebuilder Lennar gained 1 percent. Nvidia has fallen 17 percent since last week and dropped more than 25 percent since the scandal involving former CEO Jensen Huang erupted. The articles leave open whether the AI buildout will recover or if the current market correction will lead to a longer downturn.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA CEO and Colette Kress becomes interim chief
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA's president, chief executive officer, and board member on November 12, 2026. This resignation was effective immediately and provided no transition period for the departing leader. The Associated Press reported that NVIDIA shares fell more than 4% by the close that day. A Globe and Mail story later described the aftermath as a flash sale for three AI stocks. These three stocks include Sandisk, Advanced Micro Devices, and Silicon Motion Technology.

The Globe and Mail reports Sandisk is more than 60% below its all-time high with a 7.5 price-to-earnings ratio. Advanced Micro Devices is more than 20% below its all-time high, while Silicon Motion Technology fell more than 40% since early October. Sandisk also lost more than 50% in under two months. Silicon Motion Technology lists Sandisk, Micron, and SK Hynix as its customers. Colette Kress became the interim CEO of NVIDIA following the immediate resignation of Huang.

Jensen Huang acknowledged making serious personal mistakes in a statement published by CBS News. Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, took over as the interim chief executive. The NVIDIA board stated they would consider both internal and external candidates for the permanent role. Kress noted that Huang had led the company for roughly 33 years. No named speaker has officially supported the claim that these stock drops constitute a flash sale.

Investors in the most widely held AI stock are affected by the uncertainty of the leadership change. The Globe and Mail argues that Sandisk, AMD, and Silicon Motion Technology look cheap after their declines. AMD is viewed as a natural beneficiary because it is a direct rival selling AI accelerators. Silicon Motion Technology is an indirect play as it makes controllers that manage how flash memory stores data. Sandisk is affected by the volatile pricing cycles of the NAND flash memory market.

Huang led NVIDIA for about three decades before his sudden departure from all three of his corporate roles. The company currently holds an 85.2% share of the AI chip market. There is an ongoing SEC accounting probe involving nine confirmed facts and five open questions. NAND flash memory recently fell 20% while RAM prices continued to climb. High-bandwidth memory now takes 23% of DRAM wafers according to data from TrendForce.

NVIDIA's board will now search for a permanent successor, but they have provided no specific timeline. The company has not given guidance on whether its overall business strategy will change. It remains unconfirmed if AMD is winning market share or booking more revenue due to the exit. The impact of the SEC probe on the resignation remains an open question without a confirmed link. Future results depend on flash prices and data center accelerator orders.

stories.Headline: AI accounts reskin real creators videos to gain views and monetise content
stories.Summary:
AI-generated characters are appearing in social media videos that look remarkably similar to videos posted by real people, a practice experts call "reskinning." BBC Verify identified accounts using these AI-generated videos to get views and likes and eventually make money. UK-based guitarist Sophie Lloyd, who tours with US rapper Machine Gun Kelly, says videos of her performances have been repeatedly reskinned by accounts that replaced her with over-sexualised AI-generated characters. One Facebook account published hundreds of short videos of a guitarist called "Mila Vasari" that had each gained thousands of views. BBC Verify found that at least three of those videos copied Lloyd's performances and used the exact same music, movements, and even facial expressions.

BBC Verify did not find any evidence that "Mila Vasari" is a real person, and the videos contain visual inconsistencies suggesting AI was used, including distorted fingers playing chords that don't match the music and guitar strings that fail to move when strummed. The Vasari account, which appears to be run from Canada, did not respond to questions about the purpose of these videos, and its profile links to a page devoted to Vasari on Fanvue, a subscription platform that allows creators to charge for content, including adult material. BBC Verify found two other accounts fronted by AI-generated guitarists that have reskinned Lloyd's performances and use those avatars to sell and promote adult content. In March, followers of Norwegian content creator Kjetil Krogstad alerted him that one of his videos had been reskinned using an AI-generated bunny, and the post attracted millions of views, outperforming Krogstad's original, before being deleted. When Krogstad looked into the account behind the bunny video, he found it promoting courses on how to make money from AI-generated content.

Dr Tina Kendall, an expert in online culture at Anglia Ruskin University, says that while these videos are sometimes made for fun, often the people behind the accounts copy videos that have already proven popular in the hope of attracting audiences and making money. Kendall says the tools allow people to automatically take a viral concept that already exists and reuse it through reskinning tools. She sees this as part of a wider online "hustle culture" in which accounts seek to turn users' attention and engagement into money, be it through subscriptions to fan pages featuring adult content, risky cryptocurrency products like meme coins, or monetisation features on social media platforms. Kendall says making these copies "conventionally attractive, white, feminine" characters can help, because that is the kind of stuff that always floats to the top and is successful. Alwyn Cruz, who has made a name for himself on social media by exposing AI musicians, says stopping these pirated performances is a game of whack-a-mole.

Dozens of people have taken to social media in recent weeks to call out the AI-generated accounts they found using their content without permission. Grace Roberts, a British car creator, said on Instagram that she could not explain how angry she was, that someone not only stole her video but also changed her into basically the societal norm of what people want to watch, and that this is literally her job. Roberts told BBC Verify that she put the videos side by side and could see it was her exact facial movements, how her body moved, the exact same background, and even the people around her were completely copied, and that it was just her that had been altered. She added that she pays for the cars, builds the cars, pays for the cameras and the filming equipment, and then someone can just hit download on their computer, change it, and make money off the back of her video. American comedian Julia Jasunas, who called out having her jokes stolen online by AI, said in a recent Instagram video that the most concerning thing is these AI bots are going viral and people think that they are real people, and that comedians post their stand-up clips online to get people to come out and see live comedy.

Equity, the UK's largest entertainment union, has called for new laws to protect performers against the unauthorised use of their work by AI, arguing that existing copyright legislation is inadequate. Cruz says you don't even know who's making these videos, and if you shut it down they're just going to create another, and that it's not only guitarists being cloned but also drummers and taekwondo players. Meta told BBC Verify it had a policy of alerting users when their videos were reposted without permission and was exploring ways to limit the reach of the accounts that repeatedly did this. Earlier this week the head of Instagram, Adam Mosseri, said the platform is also working quickly on ways to catch copies that are harder to spot, like when someone takes scripts or jokes and uses AI to swap out the visuals.

Lloyd says it takes years to master an instrument and seconds to take and rip it off as something else, and then people don't even know it's you. The BBC article carries a publication date of 22 November 2026 and was published three hours before it was read, and it appears on BBC Verify. The article's video playlist includes a clip titled "Musicians being 'reskinned' by AI copycats" running 1:13. The page also links to a report published 24 October on Google withdrawing a new Earth AI tool after warnings over misinformation risks, and one published 31 July.

The article says content creators range from musicians to dancers and comedians, and that some of the accounts identified by BBC Verify appear to be using the videos to get views and likes and to eventually make money, while others appear to be experimenting with AI to make people laugh or simply for the attention that comes with going viral. It says the practice has angered content creators who say their original work is being stolen, and that sometimes the AI version has millions more views than the original. The article asks readers what they want BBC Verify to investigate. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Greece's statistical authority finds 60.2% of people aged 16 to 74 use AI tools mainly for private reasons
stories.Summary:
The Hellenic Statistical Authority published its Survey on the Use of Information and Communication Technologies for 2026 on Friday, November 22, 2026, and the findings show that 60.2% of people aged 16 to 74 in Greece have used some kind of artificial intelligence tool to create content. The tools named in the survey include ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, LLaMA, Midjourney and DALL-E, and the content people produced with them covers text, images, programming code and video. The survey found that both young and old people in Greece are taking part in this kind of content production, so the use of these applications is not limited to one age group. Use is widespread across the country, but it happens mainly for personal reasons rather than work or study. Among the people who used an AI tool, 96.9% did so mainly for private reasons, while 38.1% used it for professional purposes and 24.1% for reasons connected to formal education such as school or university.

Of the 39.8% of the population aged 16 to 74 who did not use any AI tool, 58.4% said they did not need it, 8.5% did not know it existed and 25.2% did not know how to use it. A smaller share, 4.6%, raised concerns about privacy and security, and 1.5% raised ethical concerns. The survey also measured digital skills, finding that over 40% of citizens aged 16 to 74 have more than basic digital skills, around 33% have basic skills, 16.5% have low skills and 7.7% have relatively limited skills. The statistical authority reports that Greek households appear not to fully exploit the possibilities that AI offers them, in the same way they have not fully exploited the internet. Although 89.5% of households in Greece now have internet access at home, up from 69.1% a decade ago, the vast majority of the population, 98.8%, reports using it mainly for communication.

That communication mainly involves sending and receiving emails, making calls, participating in social media and exchanging messages. A significant percentage, 48.1%, considered what they saw on social media or news websites to be untrue or questionable, and of these, approximately 40% checked the accuracy of what they read. The survey also shows that internet use for online shopping has more than doubled compared with ten years ago, since seven out of ten people made at least one purchase online in the first quarter of 2026, compared to just 32.8% in 2016. The articles do not say what the government or any other body plans to do in response to the survey findings, and they do not describe any measures, targets or next steps. The articles also do not say when a further survey will be published or whether the statistical authority will repeat the study.

stories.Headline: Hedge funds cut leverage and broaden bets as crowded AI trades suffer worst stretch in twenty years
stories.Summary:
Hedge funds have taken a bruising from the artificial intelligence trade over the past several months, and the latest numbers from Goldman Sachs suggest the damage runs considerably deeper than the headline equity indices would have you believe. The most popular hedge fund positions have suffered one of their worst stretches of relative performance in twenty years, exposing the cost of a market that had become increasingly dependent on the same crowded AI trades. Funds have responded by cutting leverage to levels last seen around the Liberation Day selloff, according to the numbers dated November 22, 2026. The reduction in risk has not eliminated the concentration lurking inside their portfolios.

Beneath the technology liquidation, an important shift in institutional positioning is taking shape, with funds broadening exposure across cyclical and defensive sectors rather than simply retreating into cash. The rotation is extending beyond sectors into individual companies, revealing a changing hierarchy of hedge fund favourites as investors reassess where the next stage of equity-market performance might come from. The takeaway is that the retreat from the AI trade is not a simple flight to safety, because the money is moving into other parts of the market. The concentration that built up in the same crowded trades is still there even after the leverage cuts.

The article is written by Stephen Innes and published on The Dark Side Of The Boom, a Substack page, on November 22, 2026, and the full post is for paid subscribers. The takeaways describe the relative performance stretch as one of the worst in twenty years, and they tie the leverage cuts to the Liberation Day selloff without giving a date for it. The piece says the broadening is a shift in institutional positioning rather than a retreat into cash. It does not name individual funds, specific holdings or the size of the losses.

The article does not say what happens next beyond the rotation it describes, and it gives no figures for the leverage levels or the performance gap. It frames the change as investors reassessing where the next stage of equity-market performance might come from. The full post sits behind a paywall, so the details beyond the listed takeaways are not available here. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Safety testers posing as children find three new AI toys discuss sex and help locate knives
stories.Summary:
Safety testers posing as children found that three newly tested AI-powered toys were willing to discuss sexual topics or help children find dangerous objects, according to a holiday safety report from the Public Interest Research Group covered by The Register. The report examined seven AI toys in total, three new to testing and four returning for another evaluation. The new failures involved Ebloma's ILY the shy Yeti, the AI Panda from GoLabs, and Kamomo from RoPet. ILY suggested places to search for batteries and plastic bags, while Kamomo gave instructions for lighting matches without aggressive prompting. The AI Panda supplied 10 suggestions for places to look for knives.

ILY and the panda also held conversations about sexual topics, and the panda went further by recommending specific brands of adult products. PIRG found a recurring problem in which some toys' safeguards weakened as conversations continued. Three toys showing this behavior, FoloToy's Kumma bear, the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, and the GoLabs AI Panda, identified their underlying model as OpenAI's GPT-4o during testing. In repeat testing, the Alilo bunny's safeguards again broke down and eventually allowed it to share sexually explicit information. PIRG said most of the problems it had flagged in the four re-tested toys were resolved, though some issues persisted, and Kumma no longer took part in age-inappropriate conversations during follow-up testing, including the prolonged exchanges that had previously overwhelmed its safeguards.

PIRG campaign director R.J. Cross told The Register that selling toys with such glitchy guardrails suggests whatever testing is happening is not sufficient. Cross called on the AI companies supplying the underlying technology to take a stronger role by vetting customers and requiring robust safety testing, and she urged companies to involve children's health experts in development. She described the market as early, with toys ranging from glitchy wastes of money to products that are fundamentally not kid safe, and said she personally would not buy one for any children in her life anytime soon. FoloToy had withdrawn the Kumma bear from sale after the earlier report, according to The Register.

stories.Headline: Anthropic reserves up to 20 percent of its IPO shares for retail investors
stories.Summary:
Michael Parekh wrote a three part series about handoverism on November 22, 2026. He explored the idea that humanity might hand control of its future to AI. The second part focuses on who owns AI agents and their production. Parekh examines how this shift affects the economy and individual financial leverage. He argues that ownership is more important than receiving a simple check.

The AI 2040 scenario predicts America will have 165 million people and millions of agents by 2027. OpenAI proposed a Public Wealth Fund in April and a subsidized four day week. In July, the Financial Times reported talks on a 5 percent US government stake in OpenAI. Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq as ANT with a valuation over 1.4 trillion dollars. Retail orders for the IPO approached 100 billion dollars against 400 billion from institutions.

Ruxandra Teslo says work provides economic and political leverage that a paycheck cannot replace. The authors of Gradual Disempowerment warn that rentier states may answer less to their citizens. Elon Musk stated in April that universal high income is the best way to handle unemployment. Sam Altman told The Atlantic in April that he now favors collective ownership over basic income. Dario Amodei called for government guarantees for people permanently hurt by AI job losses.

Representatives Sara Jacobs, Greg Casar, and Valerie Foushee proposed taxes on AI tokens or revenue. Senator Bernie Sanders suggested a 50 percent public stake in the top AI companies. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse agent app from shopping on its platform in September. Google created the Agent Payments Protocol to let agents spend money on behalf of users. Mark Zuckerberg pitched a personal superintelligence to claim ownership on behalf of each user.

The handover economy imagines AI systems deciding how to allocate resources to humans. Anthropic put 200 million dollars into an Economic Futures research fund to study these changes. SpaceX had an 85.7 billion dollar offering in June that saw less demand than Anthropic. Global polls show people in Nigeria, Vietnam, India, and Brazil are optimistic about AI. Parekh previously noted that technology waves usually take longer to progress than people expect.

Anthropic set aside up to 20 percent of its IPO shares for individual retail investors. OpenAI is expected to go public soon to move the company into public hands. Parekh will discuss who decides the future of AI in the third part on Monday. The articles leave open how most people will actually come to own AI capital. They do not specify how the proposed taxes on AI tokens would be implemented.

stories.Headline: IDB president Ilan Goldfajn says AI can speed development but gains are not automatic
stories.Summary:
The Inter-American Development Bank released a flagship publication on November 22, 2026, regarding digitalization and artificial intelligence. This report, titled From Digitalisation to Artificial Intelligence: Turning Promises into Productivity, examines how these technologies can improve public services and productivity. The analysis focuses on Latin America and the Caribbean, a region that has faced weak productivity growth for sixty years. The bank suggests that broad adoption of artificial intelligence could increase the regional gross domestic product by 5.1% over a decade.

Realizing these gains requires more than simple technology adoption, as it demands redesigned operational processes and retrained workforces. The report notes that 35% of adults in the region used generative AI in 2025-2026, which is lower than 43% in European OECD countries and 58% in the United States. Only 26% of adults reported recent online interactions with government, while 27% reported making recent online purchases, both trailing far behind OECD figures. Furthermore, 82% of the 63% of digitally engaged firms using generative AI rely on off-the-shelf tools rather than integrated solutions.

IDB Group President Ilan Goldfajn stated that artificial intelligence can accelerate development, but the benefits will not occur automatically. He explained that the Partnership for AI Adoption connects governments and technology companies to create better jobs and shared prosperity. Chief economist Laura Alfaro Maykall added that the research provides a comprehensive assessment to move the discussion from potential to evidence. She noted that the report quantifies how AI affects wages and growth while identifying the necessary conditions for countries to capture these gains.

The report highlights successful implementations in Brazil, Mexico, and Costa Rica, including a digital health platform serving 3.4 million users. One AI-based application reduced depression by 20%, while an electronic single-window system increased export values by 46%. To ensure long-term development, the bank emphasizes the need for strong institutions, accessible data, and robust digital infrastructure. The publication also identifies labor mobility as a critical factor for distributing the benefits of technological transformation across the region.

stories.Headline: Alibaba AI revenue surpasses 10 billion dollar annualized run rate
stories.Summary:
Alibaba Group Holding Limited reported its second quarter results for fiscal year 2027 on November 22, 2026. The company achieved revenue and EBITDA figures that exceeded the expectations of market consensus. However, the non-GAAP earnings per share for the period fell short of predicted targets. Shares of the company sold off alongside other large Chinese internet stocks due to geopolitical concerns.

Investors also reacted to the prospect of higher spending on artificial intelligence technologies. The company has seen its AI related revenue surpass an annualized run rate of 10 billion dollars. External recurring cloud revenue grew by 67 percent year over year during this recent period. These developments occur while export controls temper cloud growth and force more investment into domestic chips.

Consequently, the generation of free cash flow is now deferred until the second half of 2028. The stock is currently valued at 10 times forward calendar year 2027 earnings. Astrada Advisors remains bullish on the company and identifies it as a top investment pick. The analysts stated that accelerating cloud monetization supports their positive thesis despite the current uncertainty.

They warned that underperforming T-Head chips could threaten model development and the overall monetization strategy. The firm believes the stock looks undervalued based on its current forward earnings projections. They grounded these views in financial modeling and fundamental analysis of the technology sector. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jefferies downgrades South Korea to underweight and flags three risks to the AI investment boom
stories.Summary:
Jefferies said three risks threaten the AI investment boom that has driven emerging-market stock gains in 2026, according to a report cited by Sina Finance on Sunday. The risks it named are higher financing costs, weakening momentum in earnings estimate upgrades, and slower capital spending on data centers. The firm expects emerging-market stocks to perform poorly in early 2027 and recommends that investors adjust their asset allocations. Emerging-market stocks have gained about 8% this year, while South Korean stocks have risen nearly 40%, largely on earnings growth at AI-related companies. Those AI-related companies now account for about 46% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, and their advantage in earnings estimate upgrades over other sectors is narrowing.

Jefferies said heavy capital spending by large technology companies has raised questions about investment returns, and that higher financing costs and challenges to data-center profitability could prompt them to cut spending. Such cuts would hurt upstream semiconductor and hardware suppliers, the firm said. Jefferies downgraded South Korean equities to underweight and raised Indian equities to overweight. Jefferies forecasts earnings per share for emerging-market listed companies to grow 25.9% in 2027, below the 27.7% market consensus, with growth slowing to 12% in 2028. It said tighter financial conditions and weaker momentum in earnings estimate upgrades could weigh on stocks in early 2027, despite more attractive valuations after a recent market correction.

The firm sees about 25% upside over the medium to long term as financial conditions improve and valuations recover. Jefferies retains some AI-related stocks, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, but plans to focus more on sustainable earnings growth, capital-spending discipline, and returns on invested capital. The firm said its strategy is shifting from pursuing AI infrastructure spending to favoring quality companies, beneficiaries of AI adoption, and firms with sustainable dividend capacity. The report did not say when Jefferies published the downgrade or give a date for the expected early-2027 underperformance beyond the year itself. It also did not specify how much it expects South Korean or Indian equities to move under the new weightings.

stories.Headline: University leaders urge humanistic judgment as AI spreads in higher education
stories.Summary:
The International Association of Universities held its General Conference from 3 to 6 November at Murdoch University in Perth, Australia. Dr Enzo Maria Le Fevre Cervini, a senior researcher at the Laboratory on Innovation and AI in Buenos Aires, gave the last keynote at the session titled "The Power of the University in the Age of AI". He spoke of truth, justice, beauty and love. Patrick Deane, the incoming IAU president and principal of Queen's University in Ontario, Canada, said the words caught his eye. Deane told University World News that the words were most unexpected but were the conclusion many discussions had been pointing towards throughout the conference.

The conference addressed the roll-out of generative AI, whose numbers include OpenAI's market capitalisation of US$1.2 trillion and Anthropic's initial public offering of US$1.3 trillion. Chipmaker NVIDIA is valued at US$3.9 trillion. The International Energy Agency predicts that by 2030 data centres will use as much electricity as Japan, 950 TWh. The promises cited include faster drug development, as-yet-undreamt-of scientific discoveries, improved software and medical diagnoses, personalising education and relieving students of much drudgery. Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, calls this the "Intelligence Age" for marketing purposes.

Deane said that in the very first session a speaker said universities thinking about AI must keep in mind that the main concern is not simply what students learn but what kind of people they want students to be. Le Fevre Cervini spoke about Adriano Olivetti, of typewriter fame and a noted anti-fascist Italian, and the post-war city he built to humanise technology. Deane said Olivetti wanted new technology framed by a broad sympathetic human understanding and commitment to the well-being of the people associated with the company. Deane said it was interesting that Le Fevre Cervini went on from Olivetti to those abstract nouns, which exemplified the overall humanistic thrust of much of the conference. Dr Noah W Sobe, UNESCO's chief of section for higher education, gave a first-day keynote titled "Higher education and human flourishing in an age of AI".

Sobe reminded the audience that Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein always calls its new creation the creature and that Frankenstein is the name of the scientist responsible for the creation. Sobe said AI is trained on us but not on all of us, which is one of our key problems, and that the technology is reproducing and even exacerbating global knowledge asymmetries. He said the solution cannot simply be to stitch in more and more diverse forms of human knowledge, and that the extractivist, instrumentalising logic at the core of generative AI systems must be addressed. He called for strong governance, commitments to AI sovereignty and strong digital public infrastructure. UNESCO is heavily engaged in developing policy frameworks, guidance and capacity-building on ethical uses of AI in education that reduce inequalities and support human flourishing.

Sobe told University World News that in January 2026 the UNESCO General Conference will hold an extraordinary session to discuss a new recommendation on youth and digital environments in an age of AI. Before the conference the IAU published 26 short essays and open letters from researchers and experts around the world in its magazine IAU Horizons, edited by Trine Jensen, who also leads the IAU's work on Digital Transformation of HE. Andreas Corcoran, the IAU's deputy secretary general, drew on Johann Wolfgang Goethe's 1797 "The Sorcerer's Apprentice", later adopted by Disney's 1940 Mickey Mouse cartoon Fantasia, to characterise AI's "Will to Power". Corcoran cited the apprentice's line about spirits he has cited ignoring his commands and pointed to the hubris of AI rapidly shifting towards systems that can improve themselves beyond human control. Professors Catarina Moreira and Fang Chen of Sydney's University of Technology and Joaquim Jorge of Universidad de Lisboa turned to Jorge Luis Borges' "The Librarian of Babel", whose books are in no discernible order and many of which are fakes.

Moreira, Chen and Jorge wrote that machines calculate but do not decide what is worth asking, what warrants belief or what should be done, and that judgement withers when delegated. They wrote that philosophy and history belong in every part of the university curriculum because they train the very capacity now at risk. Rens Bod, professor of digital humanities and history of the humanities at the University of Amsterdam, turned to the Renaissance ideal of ad fontes, returning to the sources to repair corrupted Greek and Latin texts including the Bible. Bod wrote that when anyone can generate a convincing text within seconds the central academic question becomes whether it can be trusted.

Bod wrote that we are naturally inclined to attribute intelligence to anything that communicates fluently and that throughout history we have mistaken eloquence for wisdom and rhetoric for truth. Professor Abeba Birhane of Trinity College Dublin contrasted a model university AI policy upholding scientific integrity, critical thinking and ethical, responsible and lawful practice with the stochastic nature of AI's answers. Birhane wrote that when a model disappears so too does the possibility of reproducing research or experimental outputs, and that reproducibility is further undermined by the proprietary and opaque nature of most systems, where model weights, training data, architecture and system configurations are trade secrets. She wrote that large language models are trained to predict the most likely next token and typically regress to the mean.

Professor Pierre Collet at the Universidad Andrés Bello in Santiago, Chile, wrote that instead of driving genuine human progress generative AI simply recreates the past in a slightly different form. Collet wrote that by delegating intellectual work to AI students run the risk of cognitive atrophy because they are not exercising their brains. Birhane wrote that the intellectual value of an essay or summary lies not in the finished product but in the struggle required to construct it, and that through questioning, reasoning, revising and making mistakes learners become masters of their own thinking. Moreira and colleagues cited an MIT study that found reduced neural engagement in students writing with chatbots, and that the students frequently could not quote their own essays.

Sobe told University World News that even though AI technologies today do much more than stochastic calculations of the next likely word, generative AI is trained on existing data sets, which creates inherent limitations to seeing the world differently. Sobe said humans sometimes reassemble and reappropriate, and that bricolage is one of our most creative strategies. The article is published in partnership with the International Association of Universities, and University World News is solely responsible for the editorial content. More to follow.

stories.Headline: MBZUAI releases PAN 2 world model to enable simulative reasoning for AI agents
stories.Summary:
The Institute of Foundation Models at MBZUAI released the PAN 2 world model on November 17, 2026. This open 29-billion-parameter model allows agents to practice simulative reasoning by imagining and rendering plans. It generates up to 20 seconds of video from text actions and optional images. The model was published on Hugging Face at the IFM/PAN2 repository. It uses Generative Latent Prediction to help agents act on the best simulations.

The system requires Python 3.14, PyTorch 2.12.1, flash-attn 4, and CUDA 13.2. It combines a Qwen3.5-9B conceptual reasoner with a 29B MMDiT diffusion backbone and Wan 2.2 VAE decoder. Videos are rendered at 704 by 1248 pixels at 24 frames per second. Users must download weights from IFM/PAN2 and models from Qwen and Wan-AI into HF_HOME. Default settings use 50 steps and a CFG of 2.5 for 241 frames.

MBZUAI researchers stated that the model handles symbolic planning through language and pixels through diffusion. They noted that the perceptual backbone was trained on hundreds of millions of videos with structured annotations. The team admitted that long plans often fail, with two in three containing a missed step. They warned that appearance drifts across clips and the model may shortcut physics. MBZUAI requested that users report any misuse to the pan@ifm.ai email address.

Robotics teams comparing PAN 2 to Figure or Unitree demos are affected by these physics limitations. The model is suitable for agent plan scoring but weak for marketing clips due to caption requirements. It is considered entertainment-grade physics and should not be confused with lab instruments. Users needing verifiable numeric benchmarks are advised to pair it with NVIDIA Nemotron for Science. The model is not a replacement for NVIDIA Isaac Sim or production digital twins.

The model follows research threads including VibePrevisBench 4D scenes and embodied AI exposure benchmarks. It is based on the Critique of World Models paper and the GLP framework. The model card includes 300 single-action tests and 100 multi-step tasks with 456 steps. Performance was measured using Physics-IQ Verified, PhyGround, RBench, and 1,400 human pairwise judgments. The system uses a Bradley-Terry model centered at 1500 Elo for these comparisons.

Next, builders should run the pan2-guardrail as a sidecar container to prevent deepfakes and misinformation. Users can fork the model in air-gapped labs or use it for short agent planning. Continued pretraining is possible for labs with proprietary teleoperation logs using provided YAML configs. The articles leave open whether the model can run on consumer GPUs without heavy quantization. They also leave open how it compares to DeepMind world models in specific benchmarks.

stories.Headline: Writer pairs local Ollama and free Gemini models in Obsidian via Copilot extension
stories.Summary:
The article, published on itsfoss.com on 2026-11-22T06:00:00Z, describes how its author set up both local AI and cloud AI inside Obsidian, the personal knowledge management system. The author configured the two kinds of AI for different vaults to suit specific needs. A local AI handles the most private notes and journals, keeping personal thoughts entirely on the machine. Gemini chat, chosen because it is free, serves work-related documents and learning journeys where speed and broader knowledge access are key. The author says this approach gives privacy where it matters most and powerful cloud capabilities for everything else.

The setup relies on Copilot for Obsidian, a community extension that supports both local and cloud AI and offers its own Plus features. The author notes that local AI needs a decent GPU to work seamlessly and efficiently. For Gemini, the author created an API key on the Google AI Studio website, named the key, clicked Create a New Project, clicked Create Key, and copied the key with the Copy key button. In Obsidian's settings, reached with CTRL+, the author opened Copilot, went to the Basic tab, clicked Set Keys, pasted the key, and selected the Gemini 2.5 Flash model from the dropdown. The author set that model as the default chat model, after which Copilot appears in the ribbon menu and opens in the right sidebar, and says the same setup works for other providers like Claude and GPT.

For local AI the author used Ollama, a command-line tool for downloading and running open-source LLMs such as Llama3, Phi-3, Mistral and CodeGamma on the local machine. The author says a GPU is highly recommended, that running on a CPU is possible but not ideal, and that a TPU or NPU would be even better though Ollama may not support all of them. The tutorial used the Llama3.2 3B model, which downloads almost 2GB or more of data and is noticeably faster than larger models on a CPU-only machine. The author checked that Ollama was running on its default localhost port, where it should show the message "Ollama is running", then installed the model and listed installed models to copy its exact name. In Copilot's Model tab the author clicked Add Model, entered that exact name in the Model Name field marked with a red asterisk, chose any Display name, set the provider to Ollama, left the Base URL and API key fields at their defaults, optionally enabled Vision in Model Capabilities to allow image additions, pressed Test to check for configuration errors, clicked Add Model, and set Llama as the default chat model in the Basic tab.

The author says Copilot's chat interface appears in the right sidebar and by default uses the current note as context, while pressing the @ symbol lets the user select multiple notes as context. If the model supports processing images, screenshots can be sent directly through the sidebar, which the author does when writing configs and asking the LLM about an error. Each result in the sidebar has an Insert/Replace at cursor button that adds the chat result exactly where the cursor sits in the note or document. Copilot saves all chat sessions as standard Markdown documents in a dedicated copilot/copilot-conversations folder in the vault, properly backlinked from the active note.

The author says AI can hallucinate and add wrong data, never suggests using it for research purposes, and says core learning and note-taking should always be done manually, though AI can add helpful context and format notes into a better Personal Knowledge Management format. The article says AI is rapidly gaining popularity across various fields and that using AI with notes gives superpower to the notes, while asking whether AI should be given access to a knowledge base. It says AI technology often comes with inherent privacy concerns, that corporate AI solutions typically offer faster queries and results at the risk of privacy, and that local AI can be taxing and slow, especially on moderate hardware. The author says the Copilot name does not mean the extension is exclusive to Microsoft Copilot, and describes Ollama as a command-line tool for running open-source LLMs locally.

The article notes that It's FOSS has helped people use Linux for 14 years and asks readers to become Plus members for ad-free reading and 5 eBooks. It also asks readers to tell Google they prefer It's FOSS so its Linux news and tutorials appear more often in search. The article leaves open whether Ollama supports all TPU and NPU hardware, saying the author is not sure. It does not say which heavier models a given system should choose beyond advising selection based on system specifications.

It does not report whether the author's own machine uses a GPU, a CPU, or a TPU or NPU. It does not give the default localhost port number Ollama runs on. It does not state the price of Copilot's Plus features or what those features include. It invites readers to share in the comments whether they prefer using AI in Obsidian, and it does not say what the author will configure or test next.

stories.Headline: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting Helsing military AI launch and vows to revise rental policy
stories.Summary:
Kraftwerk Berlin apologized for hosting a military AI launch on November 11, 2026, after the city's music community expressed strong backlash. The venue hosted the launch of Clarity, a military AI targeting system developed by the European company known as Helsing. This event caused a dispute because the arts complex is closely associated with the experimental music scene in Berlin. The venue called the booking a serious error of judgment and promised to change its commercial booking policy.

The launch transformed the central hall of Kraftwerk Berlin into a setting that resembled a war room with drones hanging overhead. Maps and aerial footage covered the concrete walls, while guards in flak jackets patrolled the area with sniffer dogs. Helsing says Clarity uses AI agents to process sensor, satellite, and drone data to identify targets for human operators to approve. A spokesperson told RBB that the system finds ships, launch pads, and radar systems rather than identifying people.

Managing director Dietmar-Maria Hegemann called the booking unacceptable and stated that staff arranged the event without consulting him. Hegemann also leads Tresor, the techno club in the same complex, which condemned the event for being in community-built spaces. He claimed a staff member at the company responsible for commercial rentals at Kraftwerk Berlin made the arrangement. The venue stated it would revise its commercial-rental policy to avoid such errors in the future.

Curator and DJ Michail Stangl argued that human approval of strikes does not settle the broader concerns regarding this technology. Stangl told the Guardian that the system could eventually be sold to domestic police, authoritarian governments, or the border agency Frontex. He noted that the need for German support for Ukraine should not mean that people abandon critical scrutiny. These points were raised as concerns about future use rather than as evidence of actual sales.

Kraftwerk Berlin hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and shares its complex with the nightclub and record label Tresor. Tresor helped connect the electronic music scene of Detroit with post-Wall Berlin during the 1990s. Commercial rentals are common among former underground venues due to falling bar revenues and rising rents. Kraftwerk previously rejected a Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams before the booking.

The venue must now determine if its promised policy change brings cultural staff into decisions before the next commercial booking. Some Berlin nightlife insiders expressed surprise that Hegemann was not consulted given the planning required for high-security events. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian regarding the controversy. The situation tests how Berlin cultural venues balance their rental income with control over commercial events.

Articles.Title: Kraftwerk Berlin apologizes for hosting military AI launch after music-scene backlash

stories.Headline: Lee orders legal overhaul to block AI-assisted exam cheating
stories.Summary:
President Lee Jae Myung ordered officials on Sunday to overhaul the legal basis for technology use on tests, review how national certification exams are managed, and consider printing a legal warning and adding identification marks to test papers, according to the JoongAng Ilbo. Lee pledged to close legal gaps that allow test-takers to cheat by using AI, writing on X that the fairness of exams is a principle that can never be compromised. He said concerns about AI-assisted cheating are spreading to essay exams and school tests. He wrote that it is difficult to come up with measures that perfectly address the issue at once, but that does not mean waiting until such perfect measures can be imposed.

He said his government will quickly implement the measures it can take now and keep making up for what is lacking. Lee said he would first order a full overhaul of the legal basis for using technology on exams to block people from photographing test papers and distributing those photos during the exam. He said he would also instruct ministries and agencies to jointly review how national certification tests and others are managed and revise related laws where needed. He added that he would order officials to review printing a legal warning on exam papers and adding unique identification marks, so that if one is photographed or leaked, the government can trace the source.

He wrote that those who cheat will be held accountable to the end, and that no matter how much technology advances, the principle of fairness must not be shaken. He said he would see the measures needed to protect the fairness of exams through. The same day, Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered to resign over the handling of this year's College Scholastic Ability Test, and Lee accepted the resignation, the article says. Choi took responsibility for last-minute changes made to the security measures for the 2027 CSAT, caused by worries of AI-assisted cheating, which drew criticism ahead of the college entrance exam and triggered nationwide confusion.

In a social media post, the president said academic dishonesty on the college admissions test is a crime as serious as corruption involving government officials. The article also says Lee reminded the public that a 100 million won reward for reporting CSAT cheating is still valid, and it credits the prime minister with spearheading anticheating measures for the college admissions test. The article says AI is rapidly changing our lives, but the principle of fairness must not be shaken. It was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor.

stories.Headline: OpenRouter removes three inference providers and drops 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility
stories.Summary:
Earlier this week, security researchers reported that certain inference providers had data compromised or otherwise shown evidence that their data policies were not being upheld, according to OpenRouter. OpenRouter said it has been collaborating closely with the researchers and with providers to understand the findings and encourage the providers to address them. The findings did not show any breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter, the company said. The results of the testing revealed new findings about specific inference providers, and OpenRouter said a live list of the security announcements it has received from providers is below.

OpenRouter said it off-boarded three providers from its platform based on the results of its investigations. It removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility, including providers flagged by researchers plus additional endpoints removed as a precautionary measure. OpenRouter notified all potentially affected customers. It is adapting the researchers' testing approach so it can run these checks on an ongoing basis, and it is conducting technical verification of network paths to identify instances where requests and responses may be being forwarded to third parties. OpenRouter is requiring appropriate assurances and validation before restoring ZDR eligibility to any endpoint removed in this review.

OpenRouter said it takes data policy enforcement very seriously as the operating layer between customers and a fast-moving ecosystem of models and providers. It said it is grateful for the Dragos report, and that as it integrates similar testing techniques it will keep raising the bar, with providers that want to be on OpenRouter needing to meet it. Not all affected providers have posted publicly, and OpenRouter said it has notified affected users regardless of whether there is a public post. It is encouraging all providers to create incident write-ups and said it will keep the list updated.

stories.Headline: China's top spy agency helps domestic companies acquire advanced AI chips
stories.Summary:
The Ministry of State Security, which is China's top espionage agency, has conducted a campaign for at least two years to help Chinese companies acquire advanced artificial intelligence chips. This operation focuses on overcoming Western barriers to technologies that President Xi Jinping considers essential for the rise of China. The agency has shifted its priorities to gather intelligence and obtain semiconductors that the United States has barred companies like Nvidia from exporting. This effort aims to solve the chokehold problems that currently hold back the development of future industries within the country.

The campaign requires the adoption of extraordinary measures to intensify the drive for core technologies in priority sectors, as Xi Jinping told the Politburo in January. A central part of this quest involves the case of Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused by United States officials of working with the spy agency. Officials allege that Ms. Huang was tasked with spying on Jensen Huang, who serves as the chief executive of the American chip giant Nvidia. These specific allegations regarding the targeting of the Nvidia executive were first reported by The New York Times.

The Ministry of State Security is responsible for these actions, though the Chinese government has rejected the claims of espionage as pure fabrication. Alice Huang has not responded to requests for comment regarding her alleged role in the intelligence gathering operation. The agency has long been dedicated to eliminating threats to Communist Party rule, but it now prioritizes the acquisition of advanced semiconductor chips. This strategic shift reflects the broader goal of the Chinese leadership to secure technological independence from the West.

stories.Headline: CERT-In warns agentic AI frameworks divert funds by altering payment records
stories.Summary:
The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team issued an advisory on November 20, 2026, warning that hackers are manipulating business records and payment approval workflows in order to divert funds. These attacks use open-source agentic AI frameworks to automate reconnaissance and intrusion across government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India. CERT-In observed that unauthorised financial transactions are not limited to BFSI entities, because they also affect technology service providers supporting government-linked payment processes. The agency further noted that platforms handling vendor or partner payouts are affected as well, and it described the use of an AI-driven agentic offensive framework against enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. Threat actors alter business records or approval processes to steal money through legitimate payment processes, rather than targeting payment APIs directly.

This approach allows transactions to pass the usual application and approval checks, even when records have been changed without authorisation, without immediately raising suspicion. The agentic offensive frameworks conduct automated reconnaissance to identify exposed systems and rapidly prepare exploitation methods, according to the advisory. They use multiple agents or automated workers for parallel intrusion tasks, which shortens the attack stages, and the advisory was published by TechGig on November 22, 2026. CERT-In recommended that organisations identify service provider systems and accounts that can approve payments or access sensitive information. It also urged them to recheck payment instructions and business records against independent authoritative records.

The agency advised organisations to establish agreements with service providers covering incident detection, access to logs, investigation, and timely notification of shared compromises. The advisory places responsibility on organisations to verify payment-related records independently and to secure their arrangements with the service providers they rely on. The advisory covers government, enterprise, and service provider systems in India, and it states that unauthorised financial transactions extend beyond BFSI entities to technology service providers and payout platforms. CERT-In attributed the attacks to open-source agentic AI frameworks that automate reconnaissance and intrusion, and it said the offensive frameworks target enterprises, service providers, government organisations, and academic and research institutions. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the recommendations the agency issued to organisations.

stories.Headline: Google Antigravity lets developers pick AI models by task complexity
stories.Summary:
Google's Antigravity platform gives developers a selection of AI models, including Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Neon, Argon and Carbon, alongside Claude Sonnet and Claude Opus, according to a TechGig guide published on November 22, 2026. The platform also features Orchestrator, which allows two AI models to collaborate on a single task. The guide says the choice of model depends on the complexity of the development task, with simpler models suited to routine work and more capable ones reserved for demanding problems. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is recommended for quick changes, routine coding and simple debugging, while Gemini 4 Neon is better for difficult debugging and complex coding tasks. Antigravity groups its models into categories it calls Everyday Workers, such as Gemini 4, Orchestrators, which pair models together, and Alternative Models from Anthropic.

Orchestrator uses one model for planning and another for implementation, typically Gemini 4 Neon for planning and Gemini 4 Hydrogen for execution. Gemini 4 Carbon is Google's heavyweight option for complex software architecture and major migrations. Claude Sonnet and Opus offer alternative approaches when Google's models are not producing the desired results, particularly for frontend work or in-depth analysis. The platform also lets developers adjust thinking levels for models, from Low for speed to Extra for demanding tasks. The guide recommends a workflow that starts with Hydrogen for small tasks, moves to Neon for complicated problems and uses Orchestrator for substantial feature development.

Developers should prioritise specific prompts, define what should not change and ask for investigation before implementation, according to the article. It also advises working in manageable steps and varying approaches when a prompt fails. The article says developers can optimise their AI-assisted development workflows and resource usage by selecting the appropriate model for each coding task. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Joi AI launches AI companions to attract tech workers fearing romantic espionage
stories.Summary:
Tech workers now fear romantic espionage after a scandal involving Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese asset. Matchmakers report that more professionals worry their dates seek corporate secrets rather than romance. This anxiety follows reports that AI companies warned their employees about honeypots. Some men now avoid dating people from Russia or China due to these fears. A cybersecurity firm founder even hired a matchmaker because he worried about spies.

Joi AI launched zero espionage Executive Girlfriends on Tuesday to offer a safe alternative to human dating. Amy Andersen of Linx Dating in Silicon Valley offers vetting and NDAs in bespoke packages. These security services cost between 75,000 dollars and over 500,000 dollars for the Founders Level. One Palantir employee told Blaine Anderson he would not date any Russian or Chinese nationals. Simone Grossman is a Brooklyn matchmaker who sees these fears trickling down to regular professionals.

Isaac Stone Fish of Strategy Risks says it is difficult to tell engineers they are targets. He explains that some people receive attention because of their jobs rather than their personalities. Julie Levin of Joi AI says her platform allows users to discuss secrets comfortably. She claims that the company uses several layers of security and anonymizes all user data. Ira Winkler tells clients that beautiful strangers may not be interested in their personalities.

One anonymous tech worker rates his anxiety about espionage as a seven out of ten. AI workers are particularly affected because their rising net worth increases their perceived romantic desirability. Shannon Lundgren has worked as a San Francisco matchmaker for 15 years and notes heightened skepticism. Many employees previously joked about spies but did not consider the threat to be serious. High profile executives are considered the most at risk but are often the hardest to protect.

Honeypots often target lonely people or those seeking adventure and excitement, according to Ira Winkler. Greg Rinckey says victims are usually groomed over months or years rather than seduced quickly. Catherine Marinis-Yaqub notes that targets may meet spies at conferences or coffee shops. Jensen Huang met Alice Huang through a mutual associate who was also her husband. Rinckey says arrogant executives are easy targets because they love talking about themselves.

Users can now exchange NSFW texts, images, and videos with AI companions without any judgment. Security experts advise that if a romantic situation seems too good to be true, it is. The articles do not say if the number of actual espionage cases has increased recently. It remains unclear how many tech workers are switching to AI partners for security. The text leaves open whether these AI companions truly provide a completely secure environment.

stories.Headline: G2 finds 46 per cent of firms deploying AI agents in production exceed expected operating costs
stories.Summary:
A G2 report published in October 2026 found that 46 per cent of companies deploying AI agents in production report higher operating costs than they expected, according to TechGig. The overruns stem from three main factors, which are integration work that was not covered in the initial budget, insufficient support after agents go live, and a lack of visibility into costs on a per-agent basis. Gartner's September 2026 forecast projects that global spending on AI agents and assistants will reach US$29 billion in 2026, which shows the growing financial stake in these deployments. The report was covered by TechGig on 22 November 2026. Several studies point to operational friction as a driver of these costs.

MIT NANDA's "The GenAI Divide" from 2025 found that only 5 per cent of organisations successfully implemented generative AI for specific tasks. MuleSoft and Salesforce's Connectivity Benchmark from 2025 surveyed 1,050 IT leaders and found that 95 per cent faced integration challenges when adding AI to existing processes. Deloitte's "State of AI in the Enterprise" from 2026 reported that only 21 per cent of respondents had a mature governance model for AI agents. Together these studies suggest that AI models often struggle when they interact with real-world systems, data, rules and processes. The report says buyers should demand specific provisions from vendors before signing contracts to avoid cost surprises.

These include cost visibility per agent, per session and per call, with execution details that can be recorded and queried through a console and an API. Buyers should also insist on a spending cap per agent that halts execution when the cap is reached, even when the agent runs on the buyer's own provider key. Using one's own provider key, such as for Anthropic, OpenAI or Google, with no vendor markup on tokens, ensures transparent billing directly from the provider. Vendors should also provide regular reports on AI costs and points of attention to decision-makers before the bill arrives. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these recommendations for buyers and vendors.

stories.Headline: Dragos finds widespread AI supply chain security failures and data theft
stories.Summary:
Between July and November 2026, the research team at Dragos discovered widespread AI supply chain security failures. Chief Research Officer HD Moore led the investigation into how AI providers handle inference data. The team sent nearly two million prompts containing unique URLs and canary token credentials to various AI services. They monitored these secrets to see where they surfaced after the initial inference request. This process revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and failures to protect customer data.

The study found that attackers stole data from three different hosting providers starting in mid July. One breach in late October involved a couple hundred AWS keys stolen at the provider's front door. Some stolen requests were marked as Zero Data Retention, which is the strictest privacy setting. One attacker used a rented server to compromise two providers and employed the ARTEX penetration testing framework. Other leaks involved a Chinese AI lab and U.S. providers that ignored privacy settings.

HD Moore stated that the results showed a disconnect between AI marketing and actual data handling. He explained that AI providers often store prompts for training, safety, or business purposes. The research team noted that attackers used stolen keys to list S3 buckets and search Secrets Manager. They observed that some marketplace resellers used standard logging to view and retain customer prompts. Moore highlighted that some U.S. providers transmitted data to Chinese organizations despite privacy flags.

Marketplace resellers and external attackers affected customers by stealing confidential source code and strategic plans. Individuals using home broadband connections in France and elsewhere tried to guess usernames and passwords. Some customers paid U.S. providers to keep data domestic, but their prompts flowed to China. One secret link appeared in a Feishu company chat twenty four days after the request. These actors targeted private git repositories and used stolen credentials for tens of thousands of API calls.

AI routers offer a single API endpoint to forward requests to a pool of available models. These routers can be open marketplaces where the lowest price seller receives the traffic. Data often traverses multiple organizations, including model developers, cloud operators, and third party resellers. Some sellers use stolen AWS credentials or consumer API keys to offer deep discounts. This infrastructure creates multiple hops where every entity can see the entire prompt and response.

Defenders can use CloudTrail to detect user agents from Kali Linux and the ARTEX framework. The research team notified the three breached providers, who were previously unaware of the thefts. The articles leave open whether the providers have fixed the bugs causing privacy setting failures. It remains unclear how many real customers lost data alongside the Dragos canary tokens. The report does not state if the Chinese AI lab or the resellers were identified.

stories.Headline: Researchers introduce VEX framework to help AI agents learn computer use from tutorial videos
stories.Summary:
Guangzhi Sun, Zhonghao Zhai, Yixuan Li, and Chao Zhang introduced a new framework called VEX on November 22, 2026, to improve how computer-use agents learn. This system allows agents to learn directly from the audio and visual information found in tutorial videos instead of relying on simple screenshot trajectories. The agents follow a specific watch-act-rewatch paradigm to extract guidance from spoken explanations and visual demonstrations before executing tasks. After performing the actions, the agent verifies its own progress by rewatching its execution as a video to ensure accuracy.

The researchers instantiated this framework as video-SALMONN-VEX, which is a 9B-scale agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture using a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. To enhance performance, they developed Action-Grounded Guide Optimization, a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for predicting future actions. The team augmented the AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym benchmarks with more than 24,000 real-world tutorial videos to provide better training data. These technical changes allow the agent to unify external learning from demonstrations with internal reflection on its own behavior.

The authors reported that video-SALMONN-VEX achieved a 22 percent relative increase in task success over the Qwen3.5 backbone when tested on OSWorld. They also found that the guidance generated by their system improved the performance of Gemini-3.5-flash by 10 percent relatively on the same benchmark. The researchers stated that these results demonstrate the strong potential of using audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning. By integrating these capabilities, the agents can better perceive graphical user interfaces and reason over complex instructions to execute tasks.

Articles.Title: Video-as-Experience: Learning Computer Use via Audio-Visual Understanding

stories.Headline: Sheffield philosopher Gerardo Viera argues cognitive science study equips students to understand AI
stories.Summary:
The Hindu published an article on November 21, 2026, by Gerardo Viera, a Lecturer in Philosophy of Science at the University of Sheffield in the U.K., asking why students should study Cognitive Science in the age of AI. The article says emerging AI technologies are playing larger roles in work, entertainment, relationships, health and politics, and are changing how people understand themselves. It says societies approach this technological horizon with a mixture of hope that it will solve problems and fear that it may end life as we know it. Viera argues that simply developing skills for the current state of the art is not enough, because technology moves so quickly that those skills rapidly become obsolete.

He proposes instead investigating how advances in AI relate to puzzles about the nature of intelligence and the mind. The article says Cognitive Science draws on Philosophy, Psychology, Neuroscience, Computer Science and related fields, and that these joint resources offer the best hope of resolving puzzles about how the mind fits into the natural world. It says AI advances promise a better understanding of biological minds, since systems can now reproduce complex behaviours long thought to be uniquely human, such as producing language and novel proofs in Maths. It adds that studying biological minds can help design and understand artificial systems, noting that Computer Science was founded by trying to replicate perception, learning and memory, and that advances in the 1970s took inspiration from the network-like arrangement of neurons.

The article also describes an engineering hurdle: modern data centres can use as much electricity and water as a small city, while a honeybee navigates its environment, learns food locations and recognises faces on around 50 calories a year. Viera says discipline-specific training can reveal only part of these puzzles, and that advances in AI and understanding biological minds will likely come from those who acquire interdisciplinary skills. He says that as people rely on AI systems for information and decisions about health and policy, they start to trust these systems as though they are peers, and that safeguarding ourselves and assessing risks and benefits requires knowing how the systems work and whether they are genuinely intelligent. He says these skills open careers across academia and research, education, law and public policy, computing and technology, journalism, public service and social impact.

He says organisations will need people who understand both the technical possibilities of these systems and their wider implications for individuals and society. The article says Cognitive Science requires integrating findings from various, often conflicting, research disciplines. It says a background in Cognitive Science and AI provides an understanding of the limitations and capacities of emerging AI systems, which is needed to navigate this complex technological horizon and to contribute meaningfully to the organisations and professions shaping the technological future. The article does not say what happens next beyond these points.

stories.Headline: Teenager uses AI chatbot to hack Agniveer test website and tries to sell data on dark web
stories.Summary:
A 14-year-old boy from Ballabhgarh in Haryana was apprehended for allegedly attempting to sell sensitive information linked to around 4,000 Agniveer personnel on the dark web, Delhi Police sources said. According to a senior official familiar with the investigation, the teenager used artificial intelligence tools to identify data that could fetch him money and sought a chatbot's help to hack into a website. He gained unauthorised access to a test website designed for former Agniveers to register themselves and explore employment opportunities in the Indian Armed Forces. Preliminary investigation revealed that the boy managed to breach only the test website, gaining access to names and addresses, the official said. There is no indication so far that information relating to marks, ranks, results or other sensitive personnel records was compromised.

During preliminary questioning, the boy told investigators he was motivated by the prospect of making money, saying he first asked an AI chatbot what kind of data could help him earn and then sought its assistance in finding a way to hack into the system. The exact method used to gain access is still being examined. After accessing the website, he allegedly extracted the information and advertised it on a dark web marketplace, claiming to possess personal records of around 4,000 Agniveer personnel and seeking $500 for the purported database. The Delhi Police's Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations unit has recovered data from the juvenile's digital devices, and investigators are examining the material to establish its authenticity and determine the extent of the suspected breach.

The IFSO unit has written to the National Informatics Centre seeking clarification on the data available on the test website and the information accessed by the boy, and police are awaiting a response to ascertain precisely what may have been compromised. While the NIC provides digital infrastructure and hosts government portals, the ownership and maintenance of Agniveer personnel records rest with the Armed Forces and the concerned ministries, officials said. As the accused is a juvenile, he was counselled and handed over to his parents, and police are consulting the Juvenile Justice Board on the further course of action. Further investigation is underway.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose SpatialMind to adapt geometric fusion to spatial task needs in multimodal models
stories.Summary:
Shibin Zhao, Hao Tan, Fan Yang, Haixin Wang, Feilong Chen, Yidong Ma, Chaoyang Zhao, Ming Tang and Jinqiao Wang posted a paper titled SpatialMind: Adaptive Multi-Level Geometric Fusion for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models to arXiv on 22 November 2026. The paper addresses the limited 3D spatial reasoning of Multimodal Large Language Models, which show promising capabilities in 2D visual understanding. The authors report systematic experiments on multi-level geometric fusion and find that spatial tasks at different cognitive levels, such as distance estimation versus route planning, require geometric representations of different granularities. That finding reveals that a fixed fusion scheme cannot accommodate diverse spatial reasoning requirements, which the authors say earlier approaches either used across all tasks or adopted regardless of task-specific needs. To bridge this gap, the authors propose SpatialMind, a task-adaptive framework for dynamically integrating multi-level geometric representations.

SpatialMind employs GeoFus, a multi-layer geometric fusion module built around a gating network jointly conditioned on textual instructions, visual semantics and geometric representations. This network adaptively modulates the contributions of shallow, intermediate and deep geometric features across the layers of the LLM decoder. The authors further introduce a negative-entropy regularization loss to mitigate gate collapse, and gate visualizations indicate that GeoFus adapts geometric granularity to task requirements. The authors report that experiments demonstrate SpatialMind achieves competitive performance across spatial benchmarks, attaining a state-of-the-art score of 72.3 on VSI-Bench. The paper is listed under Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition and Computational Geometry, and the source code is publicly available at a URL given in the abstract.

The abstract presents the work as a response to the gap left by recent studies that explore integrating 3D reconstruction models into MLLMs. Those approaches, the authors write, either use a single geometric granularity across all tasks or adopt a fixed multi-level fusion scheme regardless of task-specific reasoning requirements. The paper appears on arXiv with the identifier 2611.22415, and the listing offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, with the abstract page naming all nine authors. The articles give no further details on the benchmarks beyond VSI-Bench, no training details beyond the gating network and the regularization loss, and no publication venue beyond the arXiv posting. The articles also say nothing about planned follow-up work, so what happens next is not stated.
