stories.Headline: Mistral opens Singapore science hub and APAC headquarters to build sovereign AI models
stories.Summary:
The French artificial intelligence firm Mistral opened a new science hub and Asia-Pacific headquarters at Asia Square Tower 1 in Singapore on November 20, 2026. This facility aims to create sovereign AI models for robotics, high-tech manufacturing, and the public sector to help organizations keep proprietary technology and sensitive data in-house. To support this expansion, the company intends to increase its regional workforce from approximately 100 to 200 employees by 2027, with most of these new roles based in Singapore. The expansion requires hiring forward-deployed engineers with business acumen and forward-deployed scientists with advanced mathematical training to build unique AI tools. These efforts respond to geopolitical concerns, such as new US rules effective November 19 requiring licenses for certain advanced AI chip exports to Singapore and four other nations.

Mistral also seeks to develop models that reflect Singapore's linguistic diversity and help humanoid robots navigate complex environments. In manufacturing, the technology will be trained on production line images to identify defects and irregularities. Geoff Soon, the vice-president of revenue for Asia-Pacific, stated that governments and enterprises in the region increasingly want to control the technology they depend on for economic competitiveness. Co-founder and chief executive Arthur Mensch explained that the company wants Singapore to be a strategic location for empowering clients to retain ownership of their intelligence. Senior Minister of State Tan Kiat How noted that resilience comes from working with strong partners while building deep local capabilities.

Pee Beng Kong of the Economic Development Board added that this investment reinforces Singapore's position as a hub for frontier AI innovation. The company previously collaborated with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency on Phoenix AI models that reflect local laws regarding race and narcotics. Mistral now plans to establish new partnerships within the Singaporean financial sector, although specific details have not yet been released. This growth occurs as companies fear that overseas decisions could cut off access to essential AI models and the chips that run them. Future developments will focus on creating lasting economic value and industrial competitiveness across the Asia-Pacific region.

stories.Headline: Researchers present MPG-DPO, a method that personalizes LLM alignment using multidimensional user preference data
stories.Summary:
Zhen-Yu Zhang, Jerry Huang, Gang Niu, Takashi Ishida and Masashi Sugiyama posted a paper to arXiv on November 22, 2026 describing a method for personalizing large language model alignment with multidimensional user preference data. The paper is titled Sample-efficient Personalization of Large Language Model Alignment with Multidimensional User Preference Data and carries the identifier 2611.22210. The authors note that preference alignment has become a central tool for aligning large language models with human values and desired behavior. They add that the online variant of preference alignment can advance model capabilities beyond what static data alone offers by repeatedly generating and labeling new responses with human feedback.

The paper states that costly, time-consuming annotations limit the scalability of online preference alignment, which makes sample efficiency essential. Existing methods typically try to improve sample efficiency by expanding coverage of the response space or by selecting pairs with the highest uncertainty for comparison. The authors argue that although these methods are effective, they quantify uncertainty from the perspective of the language model, which may differ from the uncertainty perceived by the user. They give the example that a pair can appear highly uncertain to the model even when past comparisons from the user already imply a clear ordering.

In response, the authors propose multidimensional preference-guided online direct preference optimization, or MPG-DPO, which uses low-cost multidimensional evaluations from automated verifiers on the user's historical comparisons to build a personalized preference cone that guides response selection for online preference alignment. The method first discards responses that are confidently dominated under the estimated user preference, then selects two responses that are competitive under the retained preference cone yet show the strongest unresolved disagreement. Theoretical analysis in the paper shows that, with high probability, the fraction of queries spent on cone-dominated responses vanishes as learning progresses. Experiments across multiple language model families show that MPG-DPO outperforms strong contenders under matched query budgets.

The paper appears on arXiv, which describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share new features directly on the website. arXiv states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have embraced and accepted its values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv is committed to these values and only works with partners that adhere to them. The page also invites ideas for projects that would add value for the arXiv community. The articles do not say what happens next with the method beyond the reported experiments.

stories.Headline: Australia reviews competition laws for AI agent shoppers and surveillance pricing
stories.Summary:
Australia is reviewing its competition laws so they can handle more people using personal artificial intelligence agents to shop, pay and manage money on their behalf, the government said on Nov 21, 2026. Andrew Leigh, assistant minister for productivity, competition, charities and treasury, told reporters in Canberra that the government is doing a whole lot of work to ensure the competition laws keep pace in an AI age. He said more consumers are going to be shopping with AI agents and the government is looking at whether it is important to update the laws there. AI agents are increasingly being designed to shop, make payments and manage money on behalf of users, with retail just one sector among many globally confronting the reality of customers handing over decision-making to agents.

Their growing autonomy is forcing financial institutions to work out how much authority to give them and who is responsible for their actions, the article says. Australians have been shopping online for years, leading to lower footfalls in established retail networks like David Jones, the department store group which has collapsed after almost two centuries in business. Leigh said the government was considering issues such as personalised pricing, also known as surveillance pricing, where different prices can be set for consumers based on their individual data. He cited an example he had heard overseas of people being asked to pay more for a security product because their area was suffering from crime.

Leigh said sometimes that can lead to people paying higher prices, and he stated that the government does not want Australians mucked around by surveillance pricing powered by AI. He said the government wants Australians to get the very best deal in the AI age. The government is also looking at who is responsible for agents' actions as part of its review of whether the laws need updating. The article does not say when the review will finish or what specific changes are being considered.

The article gives no further details on next steps beyond the government's stated work on competition laws and surveillance pricing. It does not name any bill, timeline or enforcement action that would follow from the review. The report was published by The Straits Times on Nov 21, 2026, and was updated the same day. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Asahi CEO Katsuki plans $85mn AI cybersecurity upgrade over three years
stories.Summary:
Japanese beverage maker Asahi Group Holdings is investing 13.5 billion yen, or 85 million dollars, into its cybersecurity infrastructure. This massive financial commitment follows a ransomware attack that occurred in 2025 and disrupted business operations for several months. The company intends to spend this money over a three year period to protect its digital assets. These upgrades are designed to prevent similar security breaches from happening again in the future. The investment requires the company to rebuild its existing systems using advanced artificial intelligence technology.

Asahi Group Holdings will also hire more specialized talent to help detect unauthorized access to its networks. These changes aim to create a more resilient defense against the evolving threats of the digital age. The three year plan focuses on integrating these new tools to ensure long term stability. Chief Executive Officer Atsushi Katsuki detailed the spending plans to address the vulnerabilities exposed by the previous incident.

He explained that the company must modernize its approach to security to safeguard its global operations. The leadership believes that combining AI with expert human talent is the best way to monitor threats. This strategic shift reflects a commitment to protecting the company from further operational disruptions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Optimal Deep Nonparametric Regression with Uniformly Bounded Lipschitz Constants
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on November 22, 2026 by Jiaxin Shi, Ziyuan Chen, Jian Huang and Hansheng Wang sets out a sharp approximation theory for deep ReLU networks held under a split spectral norm product constraint. The authors write that weight norm constraints are widely used to control sensitivity to input perturbations by bounding the Lipschitz constant of neural networks. They add that existing approximation results under fixed bounds on standard norm products are not sufficient to establish optimal statistical rates. Their theoretical result shows that sufficiently smooth Hölder functions can be uniformly approximated to arbitrary accuracy as network depth increases, with the norm-product bound held fixed.

The paper then proposes a penalized least squares estimator for deep nonparametric regression. The authors state that the resulting estimator has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant while still reaching the optimal nonparametric rate up to a logarithmic factor. As applications, they establish optimal prediction rates for two-stage learning and give robustness guarantees under adversarial input perturbations. Numerical studies reported in the abstract show the penalized estimator has well-controlled sensitivity to input perturbations and prediction accuracy comparable to classical deep network methods. The work is listed under machine learning in statistics, machine learning in computer science and statistics theory in mathematics.

The abstract names stability under input perturbations as necessary for deep neural network estimators in many applications involving noisy covariates or estimated features. It presents the fixed norm-product bound as the setting in which earlier approximation results fell short of optimal statistical rates. The authors describe their contribution as a sharp approximation theory together with an estimator that keeps the Lipschitz constant uniformly bounded. The abstract does not give the size of the logarithmic factor, the constants involved or the specific numerical results of the studies.

The paper is identified on arXiv as 2611.23979, and the posting page offers a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source. The abstract does not state where the work has been published or accepted, nor does it give a date for any later version. It also does not say what experiments or applications will follow from the results. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Japan's Noetra AI project faces $5bn cost rise as chip prices and weak yen bite
stories.Summary:
The flagship domestic artificial intelligence initiative in Japan is facing a massive increase in projected expenses. This sovereign project is seeing costs rise by as much as 800 billion yen, which equals approximately 5 billion dollars. The financial pressure on the plan has intensified recently due to the soaring prices of necessary computer chips. A weak yen has further contributed to the rising costs of the technology required for the project. The Noetra initiative now requires a significant amount of additional funding to maintain its current goals.

This sudden cost surge means the Japanese government may be forced to shoulder a much larger financial burden. The project must navigate these economic headwinds to ensure the domestic AI strategy remains viable. These changes are necessary to prop up the initiative against the volatile global semiconductor market. President Hironobu Tamba of Noetra has been speaking about the development of physical artificial intelligence.

He discussed these technological advancements at a government event held in Tokyo on July 16. While the specific response to the cost surge was not detailed, the leadership is managing the project's growth. The government is now evaluating how to cover the multi-billion dollar gap in the budget. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Shachihata launches AI video authentication on X to offset shrinking hanko market
stories.Summary:
A Japanese company that specializes in making traditional carved stamps will launch a new authentication service later this month. Shachihata is moving into the artificial intelligence realm to help users identify videos on X that have been altered. This strategic shift comes as the company seeks new sources of growth to offset its shrinking traditional market. The business is attempting to fight back against the digitalization that is currently devouring the hanko market. The new system requires the use of acoustic watermarks and digital fingerprints to verify the authenticity of video content.

These technical tools will allow users to detect whether a video has been manipulated by artificial intelligence or other editing software. Shachihata is implementing these changes to pivot away from its reliance on physical stamps used for signing documents. The company intends to establish a strong presence in the cybersecurity field by providing these verification tools on the X platform. The leadership at Shachihata is responsible for this transition as they give themselves a mandate to expand their business operations.

They believe that moving into the digital authentication space is necessary because the demand for traditional hanko stamps is declining. By leveraging new technology, the company hopes to protect digital media from the risks associated with deepfakes and altered footage. This move represents a significant departure from their historical focus on physical office supplies and traditional Japanese signing customs. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic plans a Nasdaq IPO to raise over 90 billion dollars for AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Anthropic plans to debut on the Nasdaq stock market this coming Thursday to test investor confidence in the global artificial intelligence boom. The five year old company develops the Claude family of models and expects the initial public offering to generate over 90 billion dollars. Technology companies are committing billions of dollars to the offering despite concerns over financing risks and the sustainability of the investment boom. This arrival occurs during a difficult moment for the sector following a decline in technology shares and a leadership crisis at Nvidia. The company reported a net loss of 104 billion dollars during the first nine months of 2026 but holds 132 billion dollars.

The offering price is expected to be 70 to 78 dollars per share with investments of 26 billion dollars from several major firms. These investors include Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, while Amazon holds a substantial stake. Anthropic has over 900 billion dollars in spending commitments, including 110 billion dollars with Amazon over 10 years and 400 billion dollars elsewhere. It will spend 125 billion to 150 billion dollars on Google chips by 2028 and lease a data centre starting 2027. Amazon also built an 11 billion dollar data centre in Indiana for Anthropic using custom chips, and Google guaranteed 19 billion dollars.

Anthropic stated in its prospectus that it previously underestimated computing requirements, which left the company short of capacity and affected product deployment. Joe Fath of Eclipse called the staggering numbers hard to wrap one's head around, while David Tollen called it smart investing. Subhadeep Chatterjee, a former Google executive, said that everybody knows Anthropic is going to be the future of the Google company. Broadcom provided a financial backstop with a maximum liability of 43 billion dollars to support the rental of artificial intelligence chips. Bank of America, Blackstone, Citigroup and Morgan Stanley offered 63 billion dollars to purchase the racks of chips that Anthropic will rent.

Corey Quinn of Duckbill questioned if the long agreements could remain unchanged, stating that anything past four years is like throwing darts. The Nasdaq fell 5.3 percent in October, which was its worst monthly performance since March 2025, adding pressure to debt heavy providers. Rising interest rates and new United States ballot measures could further restrict the development of new data centres across the entire country. Investors are also concerned by Nvidia, where shares fell 13 percent after chief executive Jensen Huang resigned following reports of extramarital affairs. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive after Huang was linked to a woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence.

The company is committing to infrastructure well in advance because it needs computing power to develop advanced models and expand its services. Cloud providers Amazon, Google and Microsoft account for 31 percent of the contractual obligations listed in the latest official company prospectus. Google is expected to hold an ownership stake of approximately 13 percent following the completion of the initial public offering process. The 10 year agreement with Amazon is twice the length of typical contracts, which has attracted questions about the financial exposure. These investments occur as the broader technology sector faces mounting pressure from indebted cloud infrastructure companies and volatile global stock market trends.

The initial public offering will provide funding for the computing infrastructure needed to operate advanced models and expand the company's current services. The articles leave open whether the long term infrastructure commitments and the 20 year data centre lease will remain financially sustainable. It remains uncertain if the arrangements with cloud providers will be renegotiated before the contracts expire as suggested by some industry experts. The market will see if the 90 billion dollar debut can redefine the scale of technology listings despite the current sector turmoil. Investors must wait to see if the calculated exposure to these staggering costs will result in the predicted future for Google.

stories.Headline: Hideo Kojima warns AI may sap joy of creation while Mamoru Oshii sees no immediate film change
stories.Summary:
Japanese game creator Hideo Kojima and film director Mamoru Oshii discussed the potential effects of artificial intelligence on creative work during a recent event. This conversation took place in Tokyo on November 20, 2026, as part of a celebration for the 150th anniversary of the Nikkei media company. The two leading figures shared their perspectives on how emerging technologies might reshape the boundaries of games and cinema. They examined whether these tools would enhance the artistic process or fundamentally alter the nature of imaginative production. Hideo Kojima warned that while artificial intelligence could be beneficial for business operations, it might sap the joy of creation.

He expressed concern that the widespread use of these tools could make people more passive consumers of entertainment over time. The shift toward automated content might reduce the active engagement and effort typically required to produce meaningful art. This transition could potentially change how audiences interact with stories and how creators approach their craft. The responsibility for navigating these changes lies with the creators and industry leaders who integrate these technologies into their workflows.

Kojima suggested that the efficiency gained through automation might come at the cost of the human spirit in art. Mamoru Oshii offered a different view, stating that he sees no immediate change to the world of film. He believes that in the cinematic arts, the questions surrounding the technology currently outweigh the available answers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Peking University researchers develop AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the School of Advanced Materials at Peking University and other institutions published a study on November 22, 2026. This team of scientists including Qiliang Zhang, Juntao Zhao, and Chuying Ouyang developed an AI-driven cross-scale simulation for lithium batteries. The project received support from the AI for Science Preferred Program and the National Natural Science Foundation of China. These experts worked across several locations including the Shenzhen Graduate School and the Fujian Science and Technology Innovation Laboratory. The new simulation method addresses the high computational costs that often hinder the development of energy storage.

It aims to fix the insufficient dynamic feedback mechanisms that currently limit the accuracy of battery modeling. The research was funded by the Advanced Materials National Science and Technology Major Project under number 2025ZD0618801. Additional financial support came from the National Natural Science Foundation of China through grant number 12426301. This technical approach integrates artificial intelligence to bridge different scales of material behavior. The authors of the study, who include Genming Lai and Zekai Liu, declared that they have no competing financial interests.

They presented their findings in the journal ACS Nano to show how AI can improve battery simulations. The researchers explained that traditional methods are too expensive and lack the necessary feedback for real-time analysis. By using these new tools, they believe the industry can design more efficient lithium batteries more quickly. This work represents a collaboration between Peking University and the Laboratory of Computational Materials Physics. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Over half of Korean workers fear workplace photos could be misused in AI sex crimes, survey finds
stories.Summary:
A survey of 1,000 workers in Korea aged 19 or older found that 53.1 percent worry photos of themselves posted on company intranets or messaging platforms could be used in artificial intelligence-assisted sex crimes, according to results published Sunday by The Korea Times. The survey was commissioned by the labor rights group Workplace Gapjil 119 and carried out by the polling firm Global Research between Aug. 1 and Aug. 7, 2026. Concern was more widespread among women, with 58.2 percent expressing anxiety, compared with 49 percent among male respondents. The poll also asked workers about safeguards at their companies and about the impact of AI on gender inequality in hiring.

Only 11.6 percent of respondents said their employers had rules in place to prevent and respond to AI-related sex crimes, while 48.6 percent said their companies had no such rules. Another 39.8 percent said they did not know whether such rules existed at their workplaces. Asked what measures companies should take, 29.2 percent called for stronger security regulations, and 28.8 percent said employers should establish workplace policies that clearly define digital sex crimes and set zero-tolerance disciplinary standards. The survey also examined how workers view AI's effect on gender inequality in hiring and employment.

Nearly 40 percent of respondents agreed that AI-driven automation could replace jobs in female-dominated occupations first, increasing women's risk of unemployment. Another 36.8 percent said AI-assisted recruitment systems could disadvantage female applicants by learning from male-dominated hiring records. To prevent such discrimination, 42.9 percent called for companies to fully disclose the criteria and details used by AI in evaluating employees. Another 40.4 percent said companies should regularly check AI-backed hiring systems for gender bias and make the findings public.

Kim Ja-yeon, a labor attorney at the civic group, said AI technology is advancing rapidly while digital sex crimes and gender discrimination are penetrating everyday life, and that companies and the government need to take proactive measures to create safe workplaces. The survey report was published by The Korea Times on Nov. 22, 2026, with a publication time of 4:03 p.m. KST, and was written by Lee Hyo-jin. The article presents the findings as a survey showing that more than half of workers in Korea share the concern about misuse of workplace photos.

stories.Headline: SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won calls for universities to teach wisdom over knowledge in the AI-native era
stories.Summary:
Chey Tae-won, chairman of SK Group and of the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies, said at the Tokyo Forum 2026 that universities must build a new educational system suited to the AI-native era. He spoke during the Business Leader session of the forum, held at Yasuda Auditorium at the University of Tokyo in Japan on the 20th and 21st of November 2026. The Tokyo Forum is an event jointly organized by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo, and it has been held annually since 2019. Chey said universities should go beyond teaching knowledge and should focus on cultivating wisdom, and he called for nurturing talent who will steer the direction of change so that the value created by AI can be broadly shared.

Chey defined an AI-native society as a human-centered society in which cyberspace and physical space are fused, and he predicted a society that accepts AI as a naturally given environment rather than merely using it as a tool. He also said that as of now no one has the right answer for how to reach an AI-native society, and he sees education as the starting point for finding that solution. He said AI is new and no one has the answer, so collective intelligence must be pooled to find one, and he added that the answer may turn out to be wrong but that the experience of having designed a system firsthand will become a capability to solve problems when facing real-world challenges. He then introduced SK Group programs to develop talent, support employment, and train data center personnel.

Regarding Aizen, a two-year, non-degree program unveiled last month, Chey explained that it is a model that assigns team projects and lets participants find answers on their own. He said participants will tackle assignments across diverse fields and try out their own designs for solving problems. On collaboration between businesses and universities in the AI era, he said working with people from countries with different cultures, systems, and languages is not easy, but the younger generation strengthened by AI can take on such challenges more readily. He added that it would also be a good approach for companies and universities in Korea and Japan to create and operate joint programs to cultivate AI talent.

Articles.Title: Chey Tae-won, “In the AI-native era, universities should focus on cultivating wisdom rather than knowledge”

stories.Headline: Verónica González Laporte examines Korean society and AI in her novel Peeling
stories.Summary:
Mexican anthropologist and novelist Verónica González Laporte wrote a novel called Peeling about Korean society. She began writing the book in 2020 and completed the work in 2024. The story follows a plastic surgeon named Ji-ho who falls in love with an AI sex doll. Ji-ho faces a family illness and a warning from a shaman during the plot. The author used her personal experiences in Korea to explore beauty, isolation, gender, and shamanism.

The book was originally written in Spanish as K-Beauty before being translated into Korean as Bakpi. It features scenes at Mount Halla and Changdeok Palace, and it mentions the city of Cuernavaca. The plot includes a gay character named Geon-hee and a doll named Seong-mi. González lived in Seoul for over five years with her husband, Bruno Figueroa Fischer, until 2023. The story draws parallels between Latin American women and the haenyeo divers of Jeju Island.

González said she wanted to offer another Korea by looking behind the stage of its polished image. She explained that she aimed to recognize social issues that are difficult to notice because they are familiar. The author stated that younger generations need to recognize patriarchal mechanisms that have been established for many years. She noted that she felt at home on Mount Halla because it resembled her Mexican city. González said that people in different countries are similar even if they do not speak the same language.

The novel explores how gender inequality and women's rights play out within the Korean family structure. Ji-ho's mother represents the vulnerable position of young women and the expectations of their in-laws. The character Geon-hee reflects the social taboos and prejudices regarding homosexuality that the author encountered. The book also examines the contrast between cutting-edge technology and centuries-old beliefs like shamanism. These themes affect the characters as they navigate the tension between fantasy and reality.

Inspiration came from a visit to a dermatology clinic during the COVID-19 pandemic for facial redness. González read reports about bodies in plastic bags in China and a man suing for a sex doll. She observed that Korean brands often have similar windows and colors, creating a sense of visual uniformity. Her background as an anthropologist included studying male shamans in northern Mexico before seeing female mudang. She noticed that Korea is a highly organized society that sometimes lacks fantasy in its decorations.

A Spanish-language edition of the novel is currently in preparation for publication. The author recently visited Seoul and noted that the orange taxis she remembered had disappeared. The text describes how the novel reveals shared values that transcend borders through its various characters. The articles do not state when the Spanish edition will be released to the public. They leave open whether the book will be translated into other languages beyond Spanish and Korean.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Mythos model finds thousands of flaws, driving a global patching surge that causes outages
stories.Summary:
Microsoft patched 3,554 security flaws in the two and a half months before a major November outage. This surge in patching followed the March 2026 release of the Anthropic Mythos model to select firms. The model scanned code for bugs and found hundreds of vulnerabilities, some dormant for decades. These rapid fixes caused outages for Microsoft Outlook, Apple, Workday, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase, and US air traffic control. The NSA also suffered a classified messaging system outage last week due to a PHP programming language upgrade.

The industry found over 100,000 confirmed vulnerabilities this year, more than double the 48,000 found in 2025. New Zealand health sectors faced Microsoft disruptions in January in the upper North Island, July in Waikato, and November. The NCSC recorded 4,673 incident reports and 23.8 million dollars in losses for 2025/26, down from 5,995 and 26.9 million. The Reserve Bank names concentration risk in shared AI, software, and cloud providers as a financial stability concern. Its Operational Resilience Standard will not take effect until 2028.

US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the NSA outage was a fix and not an attack. Retired General Paul Nakasone stated that the current situation of frequent outages is a new normal. Twenty chief executive Joe Lin described a collision between the speed of discovery and the ability to address flaws. US Representative Jim Himes warned that the pace of patching could cause more frequent outages. Health NZ director James Allison insisted disruption was minimal because of satellite phone and Starlink contingencies.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs said all available evidence suggests the recent outage events are not connected. Azul CTO Gil Tene believes AI-driven patch velocity is already causing major incidents. Filigran CEO Samuel Hassine argues updates are pushed onto systems that cannot take much change. Cogent IT expert Tony Grasso criticized the move to the cloud over servers for creating single points of failure. Unions want hospital IT treated as life saving clinical care rather than relying solely on Microsoft.

The acceleration of vulnerabilities began in March 2026 when Anthropic shared its Mythos model with security firms. Most firms moved to the cloud because it was sold as a cheaper and more secure option. The NCSC warns that malicious actors may gain frontier lab AI capabilities by early 2027. This would allow attacks to unfold faster than businesses can detect or respond to them. The RBNZ and FMA are currently urging firms to get the basics right.

Mitiga field CISO Brian Contos recommends using tested rollback procedures, monitoring, and staged rollouts. Business leaders should map vendors under critical functions and build offline fallbacks for processes that cannot stop. Firms are encouraged to ask suppliers how they reverse and stage their updates. The articles leave open how SMEs will handle the risk before the 2028 rules arrive. It remains unclear if the health sector will reduce its reliance on Microsoft.

stories.Headline: Microsoft study finds Copilot offers lowest monthly AI costs across everyday and advanced users
stories.Summary:
Microsoft released research, conducted with GigaOm and published on November 21, 2026, that compares the total cost of ownership of three leading AI tools: Microsoft Copilot, ChatGPT Enterprise and Claude Enterprise. The study tested multiple scenarios across two categories of users, everyday users who handle routine tasks such as searching for information, preparing for meetings, analyzing data and creating content, and advanced users who manage complex multi-step workflows. Over the month evaluated, the research simulated tasks for both groups and found that Copilot consistently offered the lowest monthly costs. For everyday users, Copilot's monthly subscription stands at $30, compared with $205 for Claude and $81 for ChatGPT, making it more than six times cheaper than its most expensive counterpart. For advanced users, Copilot costs $96 per month, compared with $299 for Claude and $149 for ChatGPT, meaning competitor costs run more than three times higher.

The study also examined output quality, with evaluators assessing accuracy, relevance and completeness, and it found that quality across Copilot, ChatGPT and Claude remained broadly comparable even though pricing varies dramatically. According to the research, Copilot's lower pricing comes from three main elements: everyday AI tasks included in the user subscription, which prevents additional fees; a Work IQ feature that provides context-sensitive assistance by drawing on data within the Microsoft ecosystem; and an Auto function that dynamically selects appropriate models and effort levels for the task at hand. The article notes that the study assumes certain usage patterns and that costs could vary depending on the types of tasks performed and negotiated pricing, so some firms may need their own evaluations. GigaOm invites organizations to use its methodology in their own environments for tailored insights.

The research was released by Microsoft in collaboration with GigaOm, and the article was written by David Wilson for Small Business Trends. The article states that the findings suggest small businesses can use a comprehensive AI solution without breaking the bank and without sacrificing work standards for cost savings. It also cautions that as businesses ramp up their use of AI, costs can scale up if not managed proactively, making budgeting and cost oversight crucial for firms that want to scale efficiently. The article says the findings emphasize that costs are one facet of a broader strategy and that embracing an efficient AI solution could provide a competitive edge. It directs readers to the full GigaOm report for further details and insights from the research.

Articles.Title: Study Reveals Microsoft Copilot Offers Lowest AI Costs for Users - Small Business Trends

stories.Headline: Anthropic introduces a novel governance framework as Nvidia faces a leadership crisis and share slump
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia in November 2026 after news of his extramarital affairs broke. He had a relationship with an Nvidia executive and a woman US authorities believed was a Chinese spy. Huang misrepresented the nature of the relationship with the alleged spy to senior Nvidia officials. The spy was linked to Megaspeed, a major Nvidia chip buyer in Singapore with Chinese ties. These events led to a significant slump in Nvidia shares and a supply shock for technology.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses for advanced AI chips for Chinese data centers providing remote computing. Licenses are also required for exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to diversion risks. Nvidia shares fell 22.9 per cent last week and 38.7 per cent since the spy scandal began. The S&P 500 dropped 8.8 per cent and the Nasdaq 100 fell 11.8 per cent in that period. Nvidia reported robust third-quarter numbers and strong revenue guidance for 2027 despite the share price slump.

Nvidia stated it is not considering inviting Jensen Huang back to the company. The company's founders at Anthropic wrote a letter to investors about the potential for AI to boost productivity. They warned that AI could inflict immense harm on humanity and has large positive and negative externalities. They said these externalities are in tension with the incentives of for-profit companies and standard governance structures. The founders stated they expect to make mistakes and learn from others as they evolve.

Investors, technology sector luminaries, and Nvidia employees are calling for the return of Jensen Huang. Some investors may be appalled by the multiple share classes introduced by Anthropic for its listing. Holders of Class A shares will face dilution from the ongoing issue and conversion of Class N shares. The US government was alarmed by Huang's ties to a spy linked to a Chinese company. The wider AI ecosystem has seen weakened confidence following the exit of the Nvidia chief executive.

Anthropic was formed as a public benefit corporation to weigh shareholder interests against its public benefit mission. It reached a US$1.5 trillion valuation within six years, while Nvidia hit US$1 trillion in 2023. Anthropic uses five share classes, with Class F and Class T holding most of the control. A single Class F share gives seven co-founders 50.1 per cent voting power over the company. The Long-Term Benefit Trust holds the Class T share and appoints four of seven board members.

Anthropic will issue Class E shares to non-founder employees to give them a say on some governance matters. Class A and Class N shares hold all economic benefits, but Class N shares have no voting rights. Anthropic plans to contribute 2 per cent of equity to its fund for every 50 per cent price increase. Market regulators and governance experts must now consider how to effectively check seemingly indispensable corporate leaders. The articles leave open whether Anthropic's novel governance framework can successfully improve upon standard corporate practices.

Articles.Title: Nvidia’s slump, Anthropic’s listing turn spotlight on Big AI’s need for new governance frameworks

stories.Headline: Voyager 1 becomes first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth after 49 years of travel
stories.Summary:
NASA announced that its Voyager 1 probe reached one light-day from Earth at 2:16 a.m. PST, 5:16 a.m. EST, on Nov. 18, 2026, after more than 49 years of constant travel. The spacecraft is now about 16.1 billion miles, or 25.9 billion kilometers, from Earth. Voyager team members at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, early Thursday.

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman praised the mission in a post on X. Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, and light travels at about 186,000 miles, or 299,000 kilometers, a second in a vacuum. A light-year is 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers. Sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. Signals traveling at the speed of light now take approximately 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and another 24 hours to return.

Voyager 1 travels about 38,000 mph, or 61,155 kph. Joe Westlake, director of the Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington, said traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is much more than a distant traveler. He said the mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets. He said it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the Sun. Dave Gallagher, JPL director, said the crossing is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery.

Gallagher said the milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today. Ray Jayawardhana, president of Caltech, said that nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. He said its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades. Jayawardhana said Voyager captures something profound about the human spirit and may never be known where its journey will ultimately lead. Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL, said the Voyagers are revolutionizing understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere.

Spilker said one big surprise is the extent to which the Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL, said the team listens to Voyager 1 every day and sends commands to the spacecraft weekly. Dodd said it just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to, and that one day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars. The team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, and the spacecraft is sending a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth.

Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone and continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Communication is managed by the agency's Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world. Voyager 1 is the farthest human-made object from Earth and the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. It was the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere, the boundary where influences from outside our solar system are stronger than those from the Sun.

Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons, Thebe and Metis, and at Saturn it found five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring. Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment and were the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn and the first to return high-resolution imagery. Voyager 2 went on to study Neptune and Uranus, and both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun's magnetic field across vast distances. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space, and Voyager 2 crossed the boundary in 2018.

Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives, a move not without risk, to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. The generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity, and with the plutonium supply continually depleting, both probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. The probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.

stories.Headline: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang mocks Apple days after praising its partnership on Muse Spark Open
stories.Summary:
Meta AI Lab head Alexandr Wang mocked Apple on X on November 22, 2026. He responded to a rumor that Apple is building an AI agent like Meta's Muse. Wang called the company a corposlop that would unleash another butthole on the public. This dig happened days after he complimented Apple and CEO John Ternus. He had previously thanked them for a partnership announced last month.

The partnership involves the Muse Spark Open, which Meta calls the most powerful US open-weight AI model. This model runs locally on two or four connected Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework. These specific computers are powered by Apple's M5 Ultra chips. The model is free to download with a license for commercial use. It is also available through developer tools and cloud providers.

Alexandr Wang told Axios that he was excited for mommy and daddy to be playing nice. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg also posted a rare public thanks note to Apple on X. He stated that the model runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to Apple. John Ternus replied that it is amazing to run such a model efficiently from a desk. Ternus added that Mac Studio keeps pushing the boundaries of on-device AI.

Wang has often made fun of Google Gemini on the platform formerly known as Twitter. This latest target is the iPhone maker, which has spent years trading barbs with Meta. The two companies have openly criticized each other regarding the future of computing and privacy. Wang acknowledged that the two firms will continue to compete in some areas. He believes this competition does not have to prevent them from working together.

Meta and Apple have a history of public conflict over various technology and privacy issues. Muse Spark Open is an open-weights model, allowing developers to customize it and understand its work. Meta claims this specific model is the most powerful open-weight AI developed in the United States. The collaboration allows the model to run on Apple hardware. This marks a shift from their previous pattern of trading public insults.

Wang stated that the companies want to partner where it makes sense to do so. The articles do not say if Apple will actually build the rumored AI agent. It is unclear if the partnership will expand beyond the Muse Spark Open model. The text does not mention other specific projects between the two tech giants. No further details are provided regarding the long term nature of this collaboration.

stories.Headline: Meta lifts 2026 AI infrastructure spending to as much as $145B
stories.Summary:
Meta Platforms narrowed its 2026 capital spending guidance to a range of $135 billion to $145 billion, with the bulk of the money aimed at artificial intelligence infrastructure, according to an update that arrived with the company's third-quarter 2026 earnings report on October 21, 2026. The new range tightens an earlier forecast of $130 billion to $145 billion, so the top end stayed put while the floor rose. The spending covers the full AI stack, which means data centers, chips, networking products, and the systems needed to train Meta's Llama AI models. Meta's capital expenditures in 2025 came in at approximately $72 billion, and the 2026 guidance puts the company on track to roughly double that figure in a single year.

The company says its AI work is already improving content recommendations, ad impressions, and revenue per ad, and the numbers in the report back that up. Third-quarter 2026 revenue reached $64.6 billion, a 26% increase from the same quarter a year earlier, and advertising accounted for $63.06 billion of that total. Ad impressions rose 10% year over year, while the average price per ad climbed 14%, and Meta's family of apps averaged 3.64 billion daily active users in the quarter. Free cash flow in the third quarter of 2026 came in at negative $2.12 billion, and Meta plans to introduce a new class of non-voting Class C stock while looking to raise up to $95 billion through equity offerings to fund its AI ambitions.

Mark Zuckerberg founded Facebook in his Harvard dorm room in 2004, and two decades later the company is pouring tens of billions into chips and server farms. Zuckerberg and his team increasingly view AI as the critical lever for refining ad tools and deepening engagement on platforms like Facebook and Instagram, according to the report. The non-voting stock structure lets Meta bring in fresh capital without weakening Zuckerberg's control over the company. The article does not say what happens next beyond the planned equity offerings and the stock class.

Articles.Title: Meta Platforms commits up to $145B to AI as its ad machine keeps paying off

stories.Headline: LeBron James sues PlayVision over AI app using his likeness and Bron name
stories.Summary:
LeBron James sued the makers of an AI sports-betting app on Tuesday, saying they deliberately violated his publicity rights and trademarks by calling it "Bron" and using artificially generated images of him in their marketing. The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in New York, according to the Associated Press. James is a Philadelphia 76ers star and NBA superstar. The app's developer is PlayVision Inc., which is based in California. The app is called "Bron."

The complaint asks the court to block the makers from using James' name, to give up any money they've already made and to award damages, including fair market value for the use of his name as well as punitive damages. James' lawyers sent a cease-and-desist letter on Nov. 5, after which the startup removed the ad from its X and Instagram accounts. The company took the ad down, but not before it had been reposted and viewed about 1 million times, the lawsuit said. The ad attracted about one million views on X within a day, according to the lawsuit. The marketing campaign this month featured an image of a person resembling James, down to his tattoos, voice and No. 23 jersey, sitting in a locker room and scrolling through the app.

James' attorneys called it "a willful, bad-faith tactic" to use the player's fame, likeness and nickname to promote "a new and unknown product." The lawsuit states that "Defendants did not care that they had engaged in illegal conduct to gain notoriety for their previously unknown app." It says they "intentionally created the false impression that Mr. James endorsed and was affiliated with their Bron App, in an effort to drive downloads and paid subscriptions." Gupta responded to the attorneys' demand on social media by writing that the app would get a new name, but no new name had been adopted by the time the lawsuit was filed. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

Messages sent by The Associated Press through the app's website and to email addresses for its founders seeking comment were not immediately returned Tuesday. The lawsuit notes that James typically commands tens of millions of dollars for such endorsement deals and that he already has an exclusive deal with the prediction market platform Polymarket. It alleges that the app's marketing was especially harmful in part because it showed the AI-generated James scrolling through bets involving NBA players. The lawsuit said "The integrity of NBA competition -- and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play -- is of paramount importance to the league, its players, and its fans." It added that "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app's developer, PlayVision Inc., was launched by chief executive Anish Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby in 2025, with backing from the startup accelerator Y Combinator, as a program that would use artificial intelligence to analyze game and practice footage for sports teams and fans. This year, the company released its "Bron" app, which it says does not take direct wagers but charges a subscription fee for services such as bet tracking and odds comparisons. Bron is described in Apple's App Store as a "sports analytics and betting research app with live odds comparisons, data-backed picks, player and team trends, a multi-leg Slip and bet tracking." The listing says it does not accept wagers. PlayVision participated in Y Combinator's fall 2025 batch.

James is seeking damages and a court order preventing the defendants from using his name, image, likeness, and voice, as well as the Bron name. The lawsuit claims the founders calculated that the publicity would outweigh any potential legal consequences, effectively treating the alleged violation of James' rights as a marketing expense. It argues that James' endorsements are "uniquely valuable," adding, "That is why defendants decided to steal it for themselves." However, the ad remained available through third-party reposts, and the company had not changed the app's name as of the lawsuit's filing. Gupta wrote on social media this week that the new name will be announced Wednesday.

stories.Headline: Vietnam urges schools to teach national identity through Vietnamese and AI
stories.Summary:
Báo Thanh niên published an article on 21/11/2026 about educating national identity in the age of AI, carried by Vietnam.vn at 02:14:48Z. The article states that artificial intelligence is changing the way people learn, communicate, and acquire knowledge and culture. It states that English is promoted as a second language in schools, and that education about national identity faces new demands. It states that educating about national identity not only preserves traditional values but also helps the younger generation develop independent and creative thinking based on Vietnamese culture. It states that this helps the younger generation confidently integrate into the global community.

The article states that AI can translate multiple languages, explain cultural differences, and create texts, music, and paintings. It states that technology is increasingly bridging language and geographical gaps, enabling people to access a global wealth of knowledge. It states that national identity is present not only in the traditional ao dai dress, folk songs, festivals, or glorious historical accounts, but also in the Vietnamese language, historical memory, manners, community spirit, compassion, and aspirations for nation-building. It states that identity is not an immutable system of values but continues to develop through reception, creation, and adaptation to the times. It states that schools must help students understand the meaning of tradition, apply positive values to their lives, and be creative based on national culture.

The article states that education in national identity cannot simply stop at imparting knowledge, memorizing historical events, or organizing formal cultural activities. It states that uncreative preservation can lead to the stagnation of tradition, and that embracing the new while forgetting one's roots can cause people to lose their cultural anchor. It states that identity education needs to combine both requirements, helping young people understand where they come from while equipping them with the capacity to dialogue, learn, and contribute to the world. It states that Vietnamese is the foundation and English is the bridge, and that developing foreign languages must go hand in hand with strengthening Vietnamese language proficiency and understanding of national culture. It states that Vietnamese is not only a means of communication but also an environment for shaping thinking, preserving cultural memories, and expressing the Vietnamese soul.

The article states that the ability to use Vietnamese accurately, reason logically, and express independent thoughts is a crucial foundation for lifelong learning. It states that English helps learners access scientific and technological knowledge and human culture, expand cooperation, and introduce Vietnam to the world. It states that the two languages are not opposed but complement each other. It states that the history of Hue National High School from 1896 to 1945 offers a thought-provoking perspective, and that within the French educational environment, with French as the dominant language, the school still contributed to training many generations of patriotic students.

It states that these students included Ho Chi Minh, Tran Phu, Ha Huy Tap, Le Duan, Pham Van Dong, and Vo Nguyen Giap, along with intellectuals and artists such as Dang Thai Mai, Xuan Dieu, Huy Can, Te Hanh, Nguyen Van Thuong, and Tran Hoan, and prominent scientists such as Ta Quang Buu, Ton That Tung, Dang Van Ngu, and Hoang Tuy. The article states that this demonstrates that embracing external knowledge does not equate to losing national identity. It states that language is a tool, knowledge is a resource, while patriotism, character, and social responsibility are formed through the interaction of education, family, living environment, and each individual's awareness. It states that in the age of AI the goal is not just to train people who are proficient in foreign languages, but to cultivate citizens with a strong cultural foundation, independent thinking, the ability to engage in equal dialogue with the world, and the capacity to apply human knowledge to develop the country.

It states that AI necessitates a revolution in the way national identity is taught, and that students can use technology to explore local history, digitize heritage, learn about folklore, compare cultures, and introduce Vietnamese values in multiple languages. It states that in literature classes students can use AI to compare English translations with the original Vietnamese texts, identifying cultural nuances that are difficult to convey between the two languages. The article states that AI can also compose poetry, prose, and music, and pose questions about the differences between machine-generated products and human creations. It states that the Hue City High School Literature Olympiad exam for the 2026-2027 school year raises the issue of creating literary works in the AI era, by placing Xuan Dieu's poem "Going by Boat" alongside poems created by ChatGPT that also write about time.

It states that in history class students can utilize digital resources, verify information, and create products that introduce the nation's history, and that interdisciplinary projects open up opportunities to build online museums, make films about heritage, and create cultural products aimed at an international audience. It states that it is crucial that AI becomes a tool to support critical thinking, not a means to replace human learning, and that copying AI's answers may provide information but does not necessarily lead to deep understanding. It states that schools need to help students learn to ask questions, verify information, identify biases, evaluate products, and take responsibility for their creations. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Educating about national identity in the age of AI. - Vietnam.vn

It also gives no paraphrased remarks from officials or others. The article's claims are presented as the writer's own analysis of Swift's work.

The context is a commentary piece, not a news report, so there is no sequence of events to follow. The article looks back to Swift's writing to comment on present-day concerns about AI. It does not say what happens next or describe any response to the piece. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Agar Capital stays cautious on AI stocks despite Nvidia earnings growth
stories.Summary:
On November 20th, Nvidia lost nearly 14% in a single session, the very week it announced 103% growth in quarterly revenue, according to an article by Agar Capital published on Seeking Alpha on November 22, 2026. The S&P 500 officially entered a correction, while the Nasdaq 100 was approaching bear-market levels despite exceptionally strong corporate earnings. It also says AI financing arrangements and hyperscaler capital expenditure raise legitimate concerns about future earnings. The author remains constructive on the medium-term outlook but prefers to preserve capital and wait for more favorable entry levels.

The article says CTA selling, leveraged ETF rebalancing, and deteriorating liquidity could extend the decline even as valuations become increasingly attractive. It states that the author's sell ratings reflect near-term downside risks, not a belief that the AI revolution or the secular bull case has ended. stories.Headline: SK chair Chey Tae-won proposes joint Korea-Japan AI talent program at Tokyo forum
stories.Summary:
SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won called for Korean and Japanese universities and businesses to jointly develop artificial intelligence talent, speaking at Tokyo Forum 2026 on Saturday. He said education systems and universities need a fundamental redesign for an AI-native society rather than minor curriculum changes. The two-day forum was co-hosted by the Chey Institute for Advanced Studies and the University of Tokyo and began Friday. Its theme was AI as a Transformative Technology: Humanity, Knowledge and Civilization. Chey joined NTT Group Chairman Jun Sawada, Taejae University President Yeom Jae-ho and Sophia University President Miki Sugimura in a discussion moderated by University of Tokyo President Teruo Fujii.

Chey said an AI-native society is not one that simply uses AI but one that accepts AI as an inherent part of its environment. He said new governance and systems are needed because society as a whole, including the current university system, must be designed differently. He called for AI-native universities with entirely new designs and governance structures, adding that minor changes to existing curricula would not be enough. He stressed the importance of collective intelligence, saying even unsuccessful attempts to design new systems could help young people develop problem-solving skills.

He cited SK's initiatives in talent development, employment support and data center workforce training, highlighting AIGEN, a two-year non-degree program launched last month that encourages participants to find solutions through team projects. Asked how companies and universities could cooperate on AI talent, Chey proposed a joint program involving Korean and Japanese institutions. He said there are many opportunities not only between countries but also between companies and universities. He said such a program could create internship and employment opportunities in both countries while nurturing social innovators capable of addressing societal challenges.

In a video welcoming address on Friday, he stressed developing talent capable of guiding change in the AI era. He said people need to ask themselves what problems they want to solve with AI, what new value they want to create and what kind of society they want to build, urging universities to move beyond teaching knowledge and focus on cultivating wisdom. The forum brought together global experts, including French government AI envoy Anne Bouverot and Sakana AI co-founder Ren Ito. The article was published on Nov 22, 2026, and updated the same day.

stories.Headline: Whistleblower alleges a candidate used a calculator to pass a North Chungcheong teacher appointment test
stories.Summary:
An anonymous individual identified as A recently reported that a candidate used a calculator during the Chungbuk teacher appointment test for the 2025 school year. This person claimed that the candidate managed to solve every question on the examination using the device and eventually passed the test. The incident allegedly occurred despite the presence of two supervisors who were tasked with monitoring the examinees in the classroom. Other candidates reportedly informed the supervisor about the calculator use during a break, but the official allegedly ignored the claim.

The situation requires a serious review of the supervision systems used for teacher appointment examinations to prevent future misconduct. This specific case involved the 2025 school year appointment test in North Chungcheong Province where a candidate allegedly cheated. The whistleblower A noted that the supervision was rough because only a few people take this particular test. There are growing concerns that the current management is insufficient to stop candidates from using prohibited electronic devices. This incident has sparked a wider debate about the integrity of professional examinations for educators.

The anonymous author A is responsible for bringing these allegations to light through an online community post on November 22. This person criticized the supervisors for neglecting their duties and claiming they did not see the calculator being used. According to A, the central supervision office stated that the candidate could not be caught because the test had already ended. The whistleblower expressed deep doubt that cheating will be properly prevented in the next appointment test cycle. This individual linked the failure of the supervisors to a general lack of rigor in the testing process.

The controversy comes at a time when the public is buzzing over the use of artificial intelligence glasses to cheat on the CSAT and other professional tests. Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin has reportedly been confused over the specific measures needed to prevent such high-tech cheating. The report suggests that if basic tools like calculators are not caught, more advanced AI technology will pose an even greater threat. There is currently no information regarding official disciplinary actions taken against the candidate or the supervisors involved. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Burger King Korea sells its AI-advertised Chocolate Whopper dessert burger in Seoul
stories.Summary:
Burger King launched the Chocolate Whopper in South Korea, a dessert burger made with brownies, chocolate, and cream cheese mousse, according to Merca 2.0. The product went on sale Thursday, November 19, exclusively at the Flame Ground location in Seongsu, Seoul, the article said. Burger King Korea introduced the item through an advertising campaign that used artificial intelligence, and after releasing AI-generated images and videos, the company published a follow-up announcement confirming the Chocolate Whopper was neither a joke nor a fictional product. Each burger is handmade, only a limited number are available each day, and customers can purchase just one. The Chocolate Whopper is a dessert-inspired take on Burger King's signature burger, designed to preserve its familiar appearance while replacing traditional ingredients with sweet treats.

Instead of beef, it features a chocolate brownie patty, traditional vegetables are replaced with gummies and chocolate pieces, and savory sauces give way to chocolate and raspberry sauces. According to Burger King Korea's official social media posts, the ingredients include chocolate fudge buns, chocolate sauce, dark chocolate shavings, strawberry gummies, milk jelly rings, crunchy chocolate discs, brownies, raspberry sauce, and cream cheese mousse. The Chocolate Whopper costs 9,800 South Korean won per burger, according to Burger King's launch information reported by South Korean media outlets, and each burger is made fresh and available daily starting at 11:00 a.m. while supplies last.

The brand also limits purchases to one per customer and requires the dessert to be consumed on-site, with takeout and delivery not available. In its follow-up announcement, the brand clarified that the product was neither an April Fools' joke nor an AI hallucination, but an actual item it planned to sell. The company released promotional content created with artificial intelligence, explicitly disclosing the use of the technology in its official Instagram posts, and Burger King Korea later confirmed that the Chocolate Whopper was real and would be available at one of its locations. As part of this marketing strategy, the company used technology commonly associated with generating synthetic images to promote a food product it later confirmed was real.

The campaign also illustrates how artificial intelligence can be incorporated into marketing communications, not necessarily to develop a product itself, but to shape its visual presentation and spark consumer curiosity. So far, Burger King has only announced the Chocolate Whopper's availability at Flame Ground Seongsu, its flagship location in South Korea. Burger King's Chocolate Whopper is an example of how a brand can use artificial intelligence to turn an advertising concept into a real consumer experience. What began as a burger that seemed to exist only in AI-generated images has become an actual product available to customers in South Korea.

stories.Headline: AI builds a $75 Thanksgiving menu for six in Houston that rings up at $64.31 at Kroger
stories.Summary:
KPRC 2 News reporter Joy Addison, working with photojournalist Michael Lemons, gave artificial intelligence a challenge to build a Thanksgiving shopping list for six people in Houston with a budget of just $75, and the station published the results on November 21, 2026. The menu had to include a turkey, traditional sides and dessert, and the suggested list included a whole turkey, mashed potatoes, stuffing, green bean casserole, corn, cranberry sauce, dinner rolls and pumpkin pie. AI estimated the cost at $61.75, including a $10 cushion for extra expenses, which would leave $13.25 for anything else the family might need. The station then took the list to Kroger and put together an online cart, and the subtotal came to $64.31, still under budget with $10.69 left to spare. The cart also showed a promotion offering $5 off when shoppers spend $36 on eligible items, but another $26.02 in qualifying products would need to be added to unlock the deal.

Shoppers told the station that grocery prices are hard to ignore, with one saying the prices are pretty much off the charts, and pointing to a McCormick chicken gravy packet that used to cost about $1.99 and was now priced at $3.27. That shopper still believed feeding six people Thanksgiving dinner for $75 is doable, saying the strategy is to look for sales, shop around and take advantage of grocery store specials, and added that using AI for a shopping list had never occurred to them before but might be something to look into. Emily Taylor was not as convinced about the $75 challenge, answering simply no when asked if she thought she could feed six people for that amount. Taylor said sharing the cost with family and friends can help make holiday meals more affordable, and recommended coupons and apps for the right grocery stores as always helpful.

The test showed that AI can help take some of the guesswork out of holiday shopping by giving a menu, organizing the grocery list and helping set a spending target, and the Kroger online cart came in at $64.31, just $2.56 more than AI's estimated spending of $61.75. The station noted that prices and availability can vary and that digital coupons often come with requirements, so shoppers still need to compare prices and make sure they are getting enough food for everyone at the table. With a little planning, some smart shopping and help from technology, keeping Thanksgiving dinner within budget may be more manageable than you think, according to the report. The bottom line, the station said, is that AI won't do the grocery shopping for you, but it might help you make a plan before you hit the aisles.

stories.Headline: Senate and House urged to pass No Fakes Act banning nonconsensual A.I. replicas of voices and likenesses
stories.Summary:
Three years ago Tom Hanks posted a warning to his millions of fans after a dental plan ran an A.I.-generated ad featuring a younger version of the actor, and he had nothing to do with it. It is not just celebrities who are being impersonated by A.I., because voice actors who were paid a few hundred bucks for recordings they were told were for internal research later found clones of their voices for sale online. A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements. Whether all this is legal is right now an open question, but the opinion article argues it should not be. The article says Hollywood does not need America's leaders to devise a new concept for new circumstances, and that they need to extend and enforce the rules that already exist.

The use of Americans' faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short, that you need to get permission and you need to pay for the use. That principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century, and whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person's voice or likeness, famous or not. The bill was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and there is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year. It is one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support, and the article says the Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature.

That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era, according to the piece. The writer comes to this issue not as a policymaker but as a practitioner who runs a global talent agency, and part of that job is helping clients license their likenesses and performances, sometimes to A.I. companies. The writer says the agency regularly negotiates those deals and that the bill pending in Congress delivers what the industry needs and what will protect all Americans. Some A.I. companies already follow many of its measures voluntarily, the article states. The article does not say what happens next beyond the push to pass the bill before the end of the year.

stories.Headline: Dubai government deploys over 90 AI applications across 20 entities and releases state of AI report
stories.Summary:
The government of Dubai activated more than 90 artificial intelligence applications across 20 different government entities on November 21, 2026. This large scale deployment represents a significant push to integrate advanced technology into the daily operations of the city's public administration. The initiative aims to modernize how the government functions by utilizing automated systems to handle various administrative tasks. These tools were rolled out simultaneously to ensure a consistent digital transformation across multiple sectors of the local government.

This technological shift requires the integration of smart software into the existing infrastructure of 20 separate government bodies to improve efficiency. The deployment involves the use of over 90 specific AI applications designed to streamline public services and internal government workflows. By implementing these tools, the city intends to change how citizens interact with state services through faster and more accurate digital processing. The state of AI report released alongside this announcement details the specific requirements and the current status of these digital implementations.

Officials from the Dubai government are responsible for this rollout and they stated that the move is part of a broader strategy for innovation. They explained that the goal is to enhance the overall quality of life for residents by making government services more accessible and responsive. The leadership emphasized that adopting these technologies is essential for maintaining the city's position as a global hub for future technology. They believe that the successful integration of these applications will set a new standard for governance in the region.

This deployment follows a series of agreements between the Dubai Immigration and Future Foundation to promote the growth of artificial intelligence and modern technology. The broader context involves a city wide effort to embrace digital transformation and improve the standard of living for all citizens. Future steps will likely involve expanding these AI capabilities to more departments as the government evaluates the performance of the initial 90 applications. The city continues to invest in innovative projects to ensure its infrastructure remains competitive on an international scale.
