stories.Headline: Codelco and BHP deploy AI and satellite tools to cut water and energy use in Chilean copper mines
stories.Summary:
Chilean mining companies are integrating artificial intelligence and satellite technology to increase efficiency and protect nature. The state miner Codelco and the global firm BHP have deployed these tools to manage their operations more sustainably. These advancements come as the global demand for copper rises to support the growth of AI data centers. The shift toward smarter mining began with projects like the Lemu Nge satellite launched in August 2024.

The industry must adapt because copper makes up about 83 percent of the weight of materials used in AI infrastructure. S&P Global projects that global copper demand will climb from 28 million tonnes in 2025 to 42 million tonnes by 2040. AI infrastructure alone is expected to contribute nearly 2 million tonnes to this 50 percent increase. Codelco used the Lemu Nge satellite to track over 65 species in the Maitenes-Campiche Wetland and the Roblería del Cobre de Loncha National Reserve. Meanwhile, BHP used machine learning at its Spence and Escondida mines to save 1.1 million cubic meters of water and over 11 GWh of energy.

Carolina Pinilla, the Corporate Director of Environmental Management at Codelco, stated that AI provides a chance to improve environmental oversight in large mines. She noted that the technology helps the company make faster decisions and identify compliance risks before they become serious problems. At Universidad Andrés Bello, Vice-Rector for Digital Transformation Claudia Bascur explained that the Mina Virtual platform allows students to practice safety and operate machinery without real world risks. This immersive system uses an AI agent to monitor student behavior and enforce safety protocols in real time.

The global market could face a shortfall of 10 million metric tons of copper by 2040 if supply does not expand. This gap would represent about 25 percent of the projected demand for the metal. Chile is attempting to close this gap by combining its massive reserves with high tech operational precision. The country continues to deploy orbital technology and machine learning to meet the environmental standards required by global buyers.

stories.Headline: University of Plymouth researchers develop AI that flags bladder cancer risk up to five years early
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the University of Plymouth developed an AI tool that can uncover hidden warning signs of bladder cancer up to five years before diagnosis, identifying 85% of cases in a study involving nearly 70,000 patients. The work was led by Professor Shang-Ming Zhou at the University of Plymouth's Centre for Health Technology. PhD student Xu Wang led the data analysis. The study was published in IEEE Transactions on Biomedical Engineering. The research also involved collaborators from North Bristol NHS Trust and University Hospitals Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

The team studied electronic medical records from nearly 70,000 patients, covering a 25-year period from 1995 through 2020. The researchers created an AI model called PRECISE-AGZ and used it to investigate 48,261 possible health indicators, from smoking and exercise habits to medication use. The system narrowed the list to 38 features especially useful for predicting bladder cancer risk. The model correctly identified 85% of patients who had bladder cancer and accurately classified 91% of those who did not. The system demonstrated effective detection as early as 12 months before a patient's official diagnosis, and some warning signals could be traced back up to five years.

The AI confirmed the importance of established risk factors including smoking and blood in the urine. It also uncovered unexpected associations, with patients diagnosed with Parkinson's disease or dementia appearing to have a lower risk of bladder cancer, and long-term use of tamoxifen, a breast cancer medication, associated with a higher risk. The findings do not establish that Parkinson's disease or dementia protects against bladder cancer, or that tamoxifen causes it, but raise questions about possible shared biological mechanisms. Among men with benign prostate enlargement, blood in the urine was associated with a lower bladder cancer risk. The system could divide patients into three groups: low-risk below 7% probability, uncertain grey zone of 7-55%, and high-risk above 55%.

Wang said bladder cancer ranks as the ninth most common cancer worldwide, with 614,000 new cases diagnosed in 2022. Wang said no routine screening program exists for the general population, and detection following symptoms relies heavily on invasive cystoscopy procedures. Dr. Helen Winter, Clinical Director for the Somerset, Wiltshire, Avon and Gloucestershire (SWAG) Cancer Alliance, said bladder cancer has a major unmet need in early detection and the prospect of a screening tool is hugely exciting for patients and their families. Winter said it could identify those most at risk more accurately, reduce harm from invasive procedures, and catch cancer earlier. Zhou said the work represents a paradigm shift towards precision screening for bladder cancer.

Bladder cancer kills approximately 220,000 people worldwide each year, and its symptoms can resemble those of far less serious conditions including kidney stones. Under current medical referral guidelines, one of the main warning signs is visible blood in the urine, which can also result from noncancerous problems including kidney stones and prostate conditions. Confirming bladder cancer currently requires cystoscopy, in which a long, thin tube with a small camera inside is moved up the urethra and into the bladder. The examination is invasive, highlighting the need for better ways to identify patients most likely to have the disease. The model performed better at detecting bladder cancer than existing NHS referral guidelines.

The researchers caution that the technology is not yet ready for widespread clinical use. All the patient information used in the study came from the SAIL database in Wales. Zhou said further validation across different healthcare systems is essential before anything is rolled out more widely, and the team would want to investigate other datasets too. Zhou said additional studies would be needed to confirm the causal relationships suggested by the model's predictions. Zhou called it a very exciting early study.

Articles.Title: AI uncovers hidden bladder cancer warning signs years before diagnosis

stories.Headline: Applied behavior analysis evolves from Skinner's operant work to debates on compassion and AI
stories.Summary:
Applied behavior analysis began in B. F. Skinner’s laboratory with his 1938 book The Behavior of Organisms, which defined the operant as a basic unit of behavior. Skinner extended that work to people in the 1950s, according to a 2025 National Academies report on autism care for military families. Donald Baer, Montrose Wolf, and Todd Risley published “Some Current Dimensions of Applied Behavior Analysis” in the first issue of the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In a 1964 case study, Wolf, Risley, and Hortense Mees described treating a young boy, referred to as an autistic child, for tantrums, refusal to wear his glasses, and mealtime problems. Ivar Lovaas at UCLA reported in a 1987 paper in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology that 47% of 19 children who received more than 40 hours of one-to-one treatment a week reached normal intellectual and educational functioning, compared with 2% of control children.

The 1968 paper set out seven dimensions: applied, behavioral, analytic, technological, conceptually systematic, effective, and generality. The National Academies report says those dimensions “have guided the field for most of its history.” The 1964 case study’s methods included “mild punishment and extinction,” time-out, and reinforcement. The National Academies calls Lovaas’s program “the catalyst” for the early intensive behavioral intervention models in use today, while noting that “valid concerns arise” about parts of his approach. The Behavior Analyst Certification Board was established as a nonprofit in 1998 to set credentialing standards, and its current Ethics Code for Behavior Analysts has been in force since January 2022.

The code lists “Treat Others with Compassion, Dignity, and Respect” as one of four core principles, and Standard 2.11 makes behavior analysts “responsible for obtaining assent from clients when applicable.” The code defines assent as vocal or nonvocal verbal behavior indicating willingness to participate from people who cannot give informed consent. Justin Leaf and colleagues, in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, evaluated objections from autism rights and neurodiversity advocates, including the Lovaas project’s use of shock, default 40-hour intensity, punishment and extinction procedures, responses to stimming, and claims that ABA is abusive or causes PTSD. They recommended setting intensity individually, including clients and caregivers in choosing goals, measuring social validity and quality of life, and studying long-term and undesired outcomes. “Our field is not infallible, and we should continue to improve and progress our interventions,” the authors wrote.

A 2024 National Academies workshop summary says early practice relied heavily on physical punishment, which drew criticism from autistic self-advocates, and that modern ABA has dropped physical punishment. In late 2023, Ashley Penney and colleagues proposed in Behavior Analysis in Practice that compassion be treated as “an eighth current and essential dimension of ABA,” a proposal that remains the authors’ and not a change to the original framework. In a 2020 proof-of-concept study in Perspectives on Behavior Science, Marc Lanovaz and colleagues trained machine-learning models on simulated single-case graphs, and the models produced fewer false positives and more statistical power than the dual-criteria method, a structured aid for visual analysis. A 2024 systematic review abstract in BJPsych Open compared 25 studies of virtual reality and standard social skills training for autistic children and found no consistently significant differences between the two. The Council of Autism Service Providers has published practice parameters for AI use in ABA covering selection, transparency, consent, monitoring, error reporting, and retirement of AI systems.

The data in the Lanovaz study were simulated, not drawn from clinic records. A review of the AI practice parameters notes that clinicians remain responsible for clinical decisions under BACB codes and that providers should not assume payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles give a timeline: 1938, Skinner publishes The Behavior of Organisms; 1964, the Wolf, Risley, and Mees case study; 1968, Baer, Wolf, and Risley define the seven dimensions; 1987, Lovaas reports his outcome; 1998, the BACB is established; 2022, the BACB Ethics Code takes effect; 2023, Penney and colleagues propose compassion as an eighth dimension. The articles state that nearly 90 years after Skinner’s book the field debates topics such as compassion and artificial intelligence. The articles state that how the field got from one to the other explains much of what payers, providers, and families debate today.

The articles state that any new tool, like any old procedure, has to show it produces socially significant change for the person receiving services. The articles leave open whether payers will allow or reimburse AI-assisted services. The articles leave open whether compassion becomes an eighth dimension of ABA. The articles leave open what further study of long-term and undesired outcomes will show. The articles leave open how the debate over who gets to define socially important change will resolve.

Articles.Title: From Skinner’s Lab to Artificial Intelligence, How ABA Therapy Has Changed

stories.Headline: Times A.I. editor Dylan Freedman drafts his writing on a 1950s typewriter while using A.I. only for reporting
stories.Summary:
Dylan Freedman, the A.I. projects editor for The New York Times, wrote in a Times Insider article published on November 22, 2026, that he uses artificial intelligence in his work every day but never uses it for writing. His job has two parts, enlisting A.I. to help reporters search large collections of documents and multimedia data, such as the Jeffrey Epstein files or President Trump’s speeches, and reporting on developments in A.I. technology. Because he draws a thick line at writing, he composes most of his first drafts on an Olivetti Lettera 22 typewriter from the 1950s, the same model Leonard Cohen used to compose songs and poems. He composed the first draft of the article itself on that typewriter.

Freedman, who was a software engineer at Google before pursuing a journalism degree, described the typewriter as an essential dose of minimalism and a break from crowded browser tabs and blinking terminal windows. He called the machine a technological marvel for translating thoughts into words, noting that it can be used outside without glare and does not need to be recharged. A single ribbon lasts longer than most novels and is cheaper than printer ink, and most mechanical typewriters, made from solid steel, are practically indestructible. The typewriter has few comforts but also no distractions, and using one feels intentional, like taking photographs on a film camera.

Freedman said that typing on the metal machine gives him a rawness that better captures his voice, and that you cannot easily undo, nor should you. He wrote that A.I. is rapidly becoming superhuman at tasks with clear solutions, like coding and math, and that the more he uses A.I., the more he worries about surrendering his cognition. He cited a study published in Nature this year which found that researchers who used A.I. assistance tended to be more productive than their peers but also studied fewer new topics. The article presented these views as his own reasoning and experience rather than as findings about typewriters or writing in general.

The article appeared in Times Insider, a section that explains who The Times is, what it does, and delivers behind-the-scenes insights into how its journalism comes together. Freedman stated in the piece that he uses A.I. heavily for reporting tasks while keeping it out of his writing process, and he offered the typewriter as the tool he relies on for first drafts. The available text of the article does not say what, if anything, follows from his approach for The Times or for other journalists. It also does not describe any further plans, policies or responses connected to the piece.

stories.Headline: Florida House speaker Sam Garrison creates committee to examine AI risks
stories.Summary:
Florida House Speaker Sam Garrison created a new committee to examine artificial intelligence risks on November 17, 2026, in Tallahassee. This legislative forum will address how governments should respond to technology that advances faster than the rules meant to govern it. The move follows a change in House leadership and renewed debate over the oversight of evolving digital tools. Garrison placed these technology issues among the priorities for the legislature during its two year term. The committee provides a setting for examining AI rather than announcing immediate restrictions on its use.

The Advanced Technology & Digital Security Committee replaces the Information Technology Budget & Policy Subcommittee established under former Speaker Daniel Perez. This standing committee focuses on policy and oversight, while the Appropriations Committee will now handle all budget decisions. Its jurisdiction includes artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure security, digital privacy, data governance, and digital identity. Michelle Davila was named staff director of the committee on November 9 for the 2026 to 2028 term. These changes were outlined in a memorandum issued by Sam Garrison on November 5.

Speaker Sam Garrison stated that technological disruption could unfold over two or three years instead of a century. He warned that AI might improve so rapidly that humans struggle to understand or control the technology. Garrison urged lawmakers to address these risks, though he did not outline specific legislation during his opening speech. He previously expressed support for federal leadership on AI regulation in April 2026. The speaker compared the current situation to the Industrial Revolution to explain the urgency of the matter.

Governor Ron DeSantis supported an AI Bill of Rights to create consumer protections for personal data and chatbot interactions. This proposal, Senate Bill 482, passed the Senate on March 4 with 35 votes in favor and two against. However, the House rejected that bill on March 13, 2026, and later rejected Senate Bill 2-D on April 29. Former Speaker Daniel Perez favored federal oversight of artificial intelligence rather than state level action. These failed bills left broader consumer protections for AI users unresolved in the state.

Florida's Digital Bill of Rights took effect on July 1, 2024, to establish privacy protections for certain large businesses. Separately, the State Board of Education adopted AI and educational technology rules on September 16, 2026. These rules cover public school districts, charter school boards, and Florida College System institutions regarding student privacy. School districts must finalize their own AI policies by July 1, 2027, for the next school year. Federal officials currently recognize 16 critical infrastructure sectors, including energy, communications, and financial services.

Interim committee weeks begin on November 30, 2026, and the next regular legislative session starts on March 2, 2027. Lawmakers will use this time to review proposals and debate potential changes to technology rules. The articles leave open which specific companies or technologies might face new requirements under future laws. It remains unsettled how state responsibilities will overlap with the national rules currently being examined by Congress. No specific statewide AI law follows automatically from the creation of this new committee.

stories.Headline: Australian foreign minister Penny Wong elevates AI as a national security challenge in parliament
stories.Summary:
Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong will elevate artificial intelligence as a central foreign policy and national security challenge in a speech to federal parliament on Tuesday, warning that foreign actors are using AI to disrupt democracies. Advance extracts released on November 22 show Senator Wong arguing that Australia must move quickly to help shape international rules on AI, which she will describe as transforming military power and reordering economies in ways we cannot fully foresee. Her remarks come immediately after warnings from Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General Mike Burgess that foreign adversaries could covertly seek influence over the AI data centres now being built across Australia. Wong will cite reports of an Iranian operation that used fabricated journalist personas to publish articles aimed at shaping opinion on the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside Russian covert campaigns using AI-generated deepfakes to try to influence US elections. Treating AI as a core national-security concern rather than purely a technology or productivity portfolio signals a strategic shift in Canberra, according to the article.

Under Australia's existing Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme, overseen by the Attorney-General's Department, individuals and entities must register overt activities conducted on behalf of foreign principals to influence Australian political or governmental processes. Covert operations relying on anonymous synthetic media and disguised online personas fall outside voluntary disclosure, forcing governments to rely more heavily on intelligence detection and international norms. Data centre infrastructure sits inside an existing federal security architecture anchored by the Security of Critical Infrastructure Act 2018, administered by the Department of Home Affairs. Reforms introduced to parliament on December 10, 2020 widened the law beyond electricity, gas, water, and ports to 11 essential sectors, making data storage or processing a regulated critical infrastructure sector. Speaking in an interview with 60 Minutes, ASIO chief Mike Burgess cautioned that foreign adversaries could try to gain covert control over AI data centre infrastructure in Australia for nefarious reasons.

Under Home Affairs' framework for critical infrastructure and systems of national significance, regulated entities face three distinct layers of oversight: Positive Security Obligations requiring risk-management and cyber-incident reporting, Enhanced Cyber Security Obligations for the highest-risk assets, and Government Assistance powers allowing the Minister for Home Affairs to issue formal directions or direct technical intervention when existing regulatory regimes cannot resolve a risk prejudicial to security. The advance excerpts released on November 22 leave critical policy details unresolved, and they do not specify whether Canberra will introduce new legislative amendments to the SOCI Act, tighten ownership and supply-chain vetting for private data centre developers, or restrict specific overseas hardware vendors. Policymakers face an inherent tension between accelerating domestic AI infrastructure investment and hardening facilities against covert foreign interference, because data centre construction depends heavily on international capital, specialised chips, cooling hardware, and cross-border engineering contractors. Lawmakers, technology operators, and allies will watch Wong's Tuesday speech closely to see whether Australia backs its heightened national-security warning with new regulatory rules governing who finances, builds, and controls AI infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Dylan Patel says local permits, not chips, push AI data center gigawatts into 2028
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis founder Dylan Patel said data center construction is being throttled by local permitting rather than by GPUs, labor or equipment, and that his firm has already pushed multiple gigawatts of capacity from 2027 into 2028 and more out of 2028 entirely. He made the case on the Sourcery podcast, in an interview published alongside a BigGo Finance report dated 2026-11-20. Patel said the binding constraint is a permit counter in a county office most people could not name. He said his team pushed back multiple gigawatts out of 2027 into 2028, and more gigawatts are slipping out of 2028, for one reason, that permits are just not available. SemiAnalysis tracks every data center in the world, tests chips and models, and employs about 115 people across 15 countries, with offices in New York, Chicago, San Francisco, Oregon, Singapore and Korea.

The delays are spread across thousands of local jurisdictions rather than a single national policy, which Patel said makes them harder to forecast and harder to fix. Texas retains broad leverage through water, wastewater, stormwater, water-consumption rules and air permits, and Patel noted that air permits alone can stop a data center even if it is off-grid and uses almost no water. A poll SemiAnalysis ran with David Shor's team covered every county with a 100-megawatt-plus data center operating, under construction or planned within three years, and found 51% aware one exists in their county today, meaning 49% unaware, and about 40% aware of one planned within three years. Patel pointed to a Louisiana county that raised teacher pay by about $20,000 after a data center's tax revenue arrived. He said all of Elon Musk's data centers use less water than three In-N-Out restaurants, counting embedded water in the supply chain including the fabs making chips and the fuel and turbines generating power against the embedded water in the burgers.

Patel described Texas Governor Gina Hinojosa as publicly constructive, saying she has said she will not stop data centers but will require that they not raise electricity prices and that they be reasonable stewards of water, and he argued both are solvable. He said the harder problem is union labor, because Texas has little union construction labor and mandating it would mean telling electricians and industrial plumbers earning $200,000 or more on data center work that they must join a union, which he suggested is politically unpalatable. He said community opposition is cheaply solvable through direct local compensation, arguing a company could subsidize the power of everyone in a 30 mile radius and it costs like nothing, and could subsidize things and just give people money and it will be fine. He conceded the harms are real but manageable when projects are done properly: noise for an adjacent house, water use if cooling is inefficient, grid price effects if a project gets property tax breaks and buys from the grid, and little lasting local employment after construction ends. He criticized a New York Times bestselling book that he said overstated data center water use by roughly a thousandfold and was later revised, with the original figure still widely cited.

Patel said data centers ranked nowhere among top election issues, where inflation and war with Iran dominated, and that most people hold a vague negative impression formed by online content, some of it reasonable, some completely unreasonable fake astroturfed stuff, and some pushed by external actors. He noted that most jurisdictions that have banned data centers or imposed moratoriums had no meaningful data center capacity to begin with. On space-based data centers he was blunt, saying they solve nothing in the next three to four years and may be further out because the engineering is very hard; he acknowledged Elon Musk is building heavily toward 2028, said he would take the over on that timeline, and allowed roughly a gigawatt in space by around 2030. He said Anthropic crushed it in Q2, OpenAI crushed it in Q3 while Anthropic did only okay, and Anthropic is back on top with Opus 55 and Fable 5.2, while OpenAI keeps delaying releases and Google has re-entered the picture. He said Instinct and Meta's Muse, despite being worse models than OpenAI's, are way better products than OpenAI dots, and attributed part of OpenAI's weakness to an overzealous safety layer called Guardian that blocks actions in its coding and dots products.

Patel described OpenAI's chat interface as badly designed, with separate chat and work sections, a reasoning-effort slider on one side but no pro option on the other, and guessed about 90% of users never toggle models at all; when he beta-tested Meta's Muse he found it clear and intuitive. He said SemiAnalysis runs about $15 million a year on AI, most of the year went to Claude, and over the last few months persistent agents went from zero to 45% of that spend, most of it through Perplexity Computer, which uses Claude and OpenAI models on the back end but offers a better harness. He expected developer tools like Claude Code and CEX to be less sticky because developers switch easily, while enterprise contracts will stick, and said Anthropic has offered enterprise customers a discount conditioned on 70% or more of their AI spend going to Anthropic. He named Sierra and Harvey as growing revenue fast with real ROI, though possibly at high customer acquisition costs, questioned whether inference providers deserve their valuation multiples, noted Harvey's published margins have swung widely, and said he does not know Perplexity's margin on the traffic it intermediates.

He said most startups fail but some will be very successful. Patel has raised a $500 million early-stage fund as a solo general partner, investing at seed and Series A in infrastructure: robotics, silicon, optics, manufacturing, hardware and networking. He would not disclose check sizes, saying disclosure would remove his optionality, and said the fund is a separate company from SemiAnalysis and Catrini and that he will never use the research platform to promote portfolio companies. He said he does not know how to scale an application to a billion users, so he would not be a useful app investor, and that SemiAnalysis employs people who worked at ASML, Applied Materials, Lam Research, TSMC, Intel, Nvidia, Google, Microsoft and Amazon and who have built chips, kernels, compilers, data centers and power plants.

He called out what he sees as a toxic trait among San Francisco and New York investors, believing they know things they don't, and noted hardware investing requires both a great founder and a great idea, whereas application software investing can sometimes ride on the founder alone. He framed his own goals plainly: have fun, make money, try to know everything, influence the people and things that matter, and spend time with family; sourcing comes through his team and friends rather than a formal network, and most inbound pitches are, in his words, boring and wrong. On managing objectivity he said a lot of VCs think they have to be the tail that's wagged by the dog that is their companies, and just because you're invested in something doesn't mean you have to be the tail that's wagged by the dog. Patel acquired Catrini, the research firm he describes as having been right many times and having captured the market's imagination, but keeps it a separate company, and Catrini's director of research, Kyle, retains the dominant voice on what gets published.

When the team asked whether they were still allowed to be bearish on AI after the acquisition, his answer was do whatever you want; he said he isn't there to change their voice but to help them run as a better company. The two firms differ methodologically: SemiAnalysis is numerical and supply-chain-driven, counting data centers, chips, cables, servers, GPUs, fab tools and memory prices, and testing chips, clusters and models on domains including biology, security, cyber and chip design, while Catrini runs experiments, and Patel cited their AI-designed scorpion antivenom, which he said works okay, and their sending someone to the Strait of Hormuz to check on oil shipping. He noted Catrini was super bullish on AI before flipping sharply negative a few months before. The tension between his growing influence and his stated independence is the episode's unresolved question, and the articles leave open what happens next on the pushed-back gigawatts, the fund's check sizes and Perplexity's margin.

stories.Headline: Experts say AI speeds up planning of cyberattacks on industrial equipment
stories.Summary:
Experts say artificial intelligence has made it faster to plan cyberattacks on industrial equipment, according to a report by Tom Wilson in the Financial Times dated 22 November 2026. The article states that AI helps attackers read manuals and research past accidents more quickly than before. The report was published under the headline that the AI cyber threat is already here. The available text of the article is limited to its headline and summary, because the full piece sits behind a subscription.

The report does not give the names of any attackers, the equipment targeted, or the dates of any incidents in the text available. It also gives no figures on how much faster planning has become or how many attacks have been carried out. The article does not say which manuals or accident records the attackers study. No specific industrial sector or country is identified in the available material.

The experts quoted in the summary attribute the speed-up to AI tools that help attackers work through technical documents and past accident research. The article does not name those experts or set out their remarks beyond that summary. It does not say what the attackers are said to be planning or whether any campaign has been detected. No response from equipment makers, regulators or governments appears in the available text.

The wider context in the summary is that the cyber threat from AI is already present rather than only expected in the future. The article does not say what happens next, whether defences are being changed, or how companies should respond. Because the full article is not available, the details beyond the headline and summary cannot be reported. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Pictet strategists stay constructive on AI and tech stocks for 2027
stories.Summary:
Pictet Asset Management's chief strategist Luca Paolini and senior multi asset strategist Arun Sai shared their asset allocation outlook for 2027, joined by other wealth managers who offered views on sectors, market capitalisations and regions. The group's stance on investment prospects for 2027 was more positive than it had been a year earlier, according to the outlook. The strategists weighed equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities as they set out how portfolios should be positioned for the year ahead. One wealth manager said she remained reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, while another pointed to the semiconductor ecosystem that supports the buildout of artificial intelligence capacity. The outlook also touched on record levels of peacetime debt, which the contributors described as not a zero risk for investors.

The 2027 outlook sets out a constructive position on artificial intelligence and technology stocks, with allocations spread across equities, bonds, alternatives and commodities rather than concentrated in a single asset class. The strategists framed the balance of risks around record peacetime debt, which they said is not a zero risk even as they stay positive on the year. The reluctance to invest in Brazilian assets was noted alongside the more favourable view of technology and AI related holdings. The semiconductor ecosystem supporting the AI buildout was cited as a reason for confidence in the sector. The discussion of sectors, market capitalisations and regions indicates that the allocation views are meant to be applied across a diversified portfolio rather than to one market alone.

Paolini and Sai, as chief strategist and senior multi asset strategist at Pictet Asset Management, are the named authors of the outlook, and other wealth managers contributed their own allocation views. One contributor said she was reluctant to invest in Brazilian assets, and another described the semiconductor ecosystem as supporting the buildout. The strategists said the balance of risks should be struck with an appropriate time frame such as the one covered by the outlook. They described record levels of peacetime debt as not a zero risk, a caution that sits alongside their constructive stance. The comments were paraphrased in the coverage rather than given as direct quotations beyond a few words.

The outlook arrives as wealth managers weigh how much of their 2027 allocation should go to AI and technology stocks, and the coverage points readers toward further research on private markets and family offices. Related items listed alongside the outlook include Tiedemann Global's explanation of its investment formula and its view that private markets have more headway, and guidance on how family offices should address private markets when valuations are stretched. A separate item covers bankers' fears that so called Bitcoin treasuries are an accident waiting to happen. The coverage also invites readers to gain access to regular and exclusive research on the global wealth management sector, along with industry events such as breakfast briefings and summits in major wealth management centres and industry awards programmes.

stories.Headline: Egypt's EGPC and SLB hold workshop on AI for subsurface exploration
stories.Summary:
The Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and the global energy technology provider SLB co-organized a two-day AI and Subsurface Workshop that brought together specialists from both organizations and representatives of petroleum production companies, according to a report published on 22 November 2026. The workshop examined how artificial intelligence and advanced data analytics can improve subsurface interpretation, reduce geological uncertainties and raise the success rates of exploration operations. Participants looked at how AI-powered technologies can improve exploration workflows, support investment decisions and identify promising hydrocarbon opportunities. The event forms part of the digital transformation strategy of the Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, which focuses on integrating advanced technologies into Egypt's oil and gas operations and improving the efficiency of geological and geophysical studies.

Ahmed Kamal, Deputy CEO for Exploration at EGPC, emphasized the need for AI models designed specifically for the petroleum industry, and he highlighted the importance of developing specialized foundation models capable of understanding geology, well logs and reservoirs while adapting to the technical challenges and data requirements of individual operators. Yasser El Tawansy, Managing Director for Egypt and the East Mediterranean at SLB, highlighted the role of data analytics, AI and advanced technologies in improving operational efficiency, enhancing recovery rates and accelerating geological and geophysical interpretation, saying these applications can support more accurate and confident assessments of subsurface resources. Technical sessions addressed the application of AI across different stages of exploration, from data management and geological interpretation to risk assessment and opportunity ranking. One session examined exploration priorities and digital technology requirements, including current technical challenges and opportunities to improve exploration strategies, while another focused on data management and AI-supported exploration decisions and highlighted SLB's Lumi data and AI platform alongside data governance, standardization and enterprise data management.

The Lumi platform integrates subsurface and operational data to support AI and machine-learning applications, including seismic processing, interpretation and reservoir modeling, and it is designed to provide operators with a unified data environment to accelerate analysis and improve decision-making. Further discussions addressed the use of AI in geological and geophysical interpretation, particularly seismic data processing and the integration of technical workflows from interpretation to simulation. The workshop also included a practical case study on applying AI to Egyptian petroleum assets, presented jointly by specialists from Belayim Petroleum Company, known as Petrobel, and SLB. In July 2026, Karim Badawi, Minister of Petroleum and Mineral Resources, met with SLB Egypt executives to discuss expanding AI applications in exploration and production and upgrading the Egypt Upstream Gateway, with the talks covering the integration of AI and advanced data analytics into the platform to improve the assessment of investment opportunities, reduce exploration risks and accelerate decision-making.

stories.Headline: Burnham announces US defense AI partnership as UK growth relies on American cloud capacity
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced a new defense artificial intelligence partnership with the United States in September 2026 during a visit to the United Nations in New York. This strategic move follows a pattern where British technological growth relies heavily on American cloud capacity, graphics processing units, and data center infrastructure. The Prime Minister also stated that Britain intends to act as an honest broker for AI due to its strong global ties. He further intends to place artificial intelligence at the center of the G20 presidency that Britain will host next year.

The government previously launched the Tech Prosperity Deal, which it valued at 31 billion pounds, including 22 billion pounds from Microsoft over four years. Microsoft's commitment includes investments in land and equipment, though the company withdrew from a Loughton data center project in October 2026. Google has contributed a 5 billion pound package that includes a data center at Waltham Cross and research for DeepMind. Additionally, the US investment firm Blackstone has put 10 billion pounds behind an AI Growth Zone located at Blyth in Northumberland. These efforts are complicated by grid issues, as the Loughton site may not receive sufficient power until the early to mid-2030s.

Microsoft officials stated that their large scale investment was possible because of government work on electricity capacity and planning reform. However, critics argue that relying on American firms means the US government can access data under the CLOUD Act, regardless of where servers are located. This concern mirrors issues in France, where Microsoft representatives could not guarantee that citizen data would be protected from US authorities. The current landscape shows that AWS and Microsoft each control 30 to 40 percent of UK cloud revenues, while the British provider UKCloud went into liquidation in 2022.

The European Union is responding to similar dependencies by proposing the Cloud and AI Development Act to reduce reliance on foreign firms. This legislation would require high risk public sector cloud providers to be European owned and controlled rather than just located in Europe. In Britain, OpenAI previously planned to use Nvidia chips at Nscale sites through Stargate UK but put the project on hold in April. The company blamed this decision on restrictive UK regulations and high energy costs. Future success may require the government to support platforms that utilize idle compute capacity across distributed networks.

stories.Headline: Apple's Siri AI in CarPlay handles directions, recipes and lessons in iOS 27 beta
stories.Summary:
With iOS 27, Apple has transformed Siri into a more capable, powerful, and versatile AI assistant that can be used in the car via Apple CarPlay, PCMag reported on November 22, 2026. The new Siri can handle complex requests, answer open-ended questions, and engage in back-and-forth conversations, unlike the old Siri. PCMag's author tested the new Siri AI from behind the wheel in CarPlay. The author asked it to do ten things, including giving directions to a contact and explaining a complex topic. In the author's experience, the new version also handles ordinary tasks more effectively than its predecessor.

Apple's new Siri requires a phone compatible with Apple Intelligence, which means an iPhone 15 Pro or newer. You also need to be running iOS 27 or higher, so go to Settings > General > Software Update and install any available updates. For now, Siri AI remains in beta, so you'll also need to join the program first by opening Settings > Siri and tapping Try Siri AI (Beta). Apple's iOS will then need to build and optimize the search index, a process that kicks off automatically but can take time and has been known to drain battery life. With that done, you'll need to connect your phone to the car through Apple CarPlay.

The article is by a PCMag writer who has been working for PCMag since early 2016 writing tutorials, how-to pieces, and other articles on consumer technology. The writer spent seven years writing breaking news for CNET as one of the site's East Coast reporters. The writer has also written two books for Wiley & Sons, Windows 8: Five Minutes at a Time and Teach Yourself Visually LinkedIn. The writer uses an iPhone 16 Pro, iPad Pro, and iPad mini as well as an Apple Watch. PCMag editors select and review products independently, and if you buy through affiliate links, we may earn commissions, which help support our testing.

In the past, Siri would often give random matching names found on the web instead of consulting contacts, but Siri AI always checks the contacts list when asked for directions to a specific person or business. The author drove to Binghamton, New York, in August to attend a Rod Serling festival, and while driving to the hotel asked Siri to tell something interesting about the town. It told why Binghamton is the carousel capital of the world, how the city played a role in aviation and computing, and how it's the birthplace of a regional sandwich known as the spiedie. Where the original Siri might have trouble with messy speech, Siri AI is built to handle corrections and more natural language.

Siri AI automatically pulls requested music from the iPhone's library unless a specific source is specified, whereas the old assistant would fire up the Beatles Channel on Sirius XM instead of playing from the library. The author asked Siri to find a recipe for lentil soup on the internet, create a shopping list with the ingredients, and then text the list, and it followed each step correctly and ended with the list of items in Messages. Siri AI will look across the apps on the phone until it finds a match, even if the author doesn't remember if the information is in an email or text. The author asked regular Siri to explain Einstein's special theory of relativity, and it provided a short, one-paragraph answer taken from a single source on the web, while Siri AI served up a full and thorough explanation and then asked if the author wanted to explore how this differs from Einstein's general theory of relativity.

The author asked Siri AI how to silence group text alerts on CarPlay, and it explained three ways: turn off the switch to show text notifications in CarPlay, silence alerts for a specific conversation, and use Driving Focus mode, and the author then asked Siri to turn on Driving Focus mode, which it did. The classic Siri told the author it could search the web for a language lesson when finished driving, while the AI-powered Siri asked what language the author wanted to learn, Italian, then offered basic, conversational phrases in both Italian and English, explained what each one meant, and continued the lesson by giving more words and phrases. Siri AI isn't as chatty as other chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini, but it's certainly more conversational than its predecessor. The author told it he wanted a back-and-forth conversation about a specific topic, and it asked which topic, and the author suggested American films from the 1930s.

It gave an overview of the topic and then asked if the author wished to narrow it down, and the author said he wanted to talk about screwball comedies. From there, the conversation focused on It Happened One Night, one of the author's favorites from the era, and they were able to discuss various aspects of the film, leading to an interesting conversation. PCMag tests, rates, and reviews more than 1,500 products each year to help people make better buying decisions and get more from technology. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Joint select committee releases AI report on datacentres and copyright
stories.Summary:
A joint select committee on artificial intelligence is expected to release a report on Monday, November 22, 2026. This report will signal Labor's direction on datacentres and copyright. It arrives as the final four days of parliament for 2026 begin. The government wants to pass several key reforms and savings measures by Friday. This timing coincides with the potential fracture of a bipartisan consensus on AI.

The report addresses datacentres, energy use, and how creatives are paid for AI theft. Other pending Senate issues include the domestic gas reserve and changes to trusts and capital gains tax. The government also seeks changes to private health insurance and the digital duty of care bill. Labor promised a carveout for Western Australia regarding gas to satisfy a key Coalition demand. The digital duty of care bill may include a private right of legal action for citizens.

Labor sources say they are open to amendments on the digital duty of care bill. Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong will speak on Tuesday about AI as a national security issue. She will urge a shared global endeavour that does not reward speed over prudence. Labor figures like Richard Marles, Tim Ayres, and Michelle Rowland have rejected the copyright status quo. They suggest that current copyright laws have shortfalls that need to be addressed.

The Greens want bigger fines, a big tech ombudsman, and gambling restrictions for the duty of care bill. Creative industries were flabbergasted by reports of a music carveout for AI companies. Rightsholder groups have rubbished the need for copyright changes. The Greens say they feel no pressure to cave on trusts or capital gains tax. One Greens source expects very little will actually pass this week.

Liberals Jonathan Duniam and Aaron Violi recently said AI is too important for partisan contests. However, Shadow Attorney General Michaelia Cash called a potential music carveout a ham-fisted tactic. MP Garth Hamilton suggested AI is old-fashioned theft and proposed a levy on companies. Former Nationals leader David Littleproud stated that Anthropic can afford to pay for copyright. These views contrast with the earlier hopes for a bipartisan alliance.

Parliament will determine if several key policies get over the line by Friday. Anthony Albanese is expected to intensify deal-making after visiting Manila and Shenzhen. The report will show if AI policy remains a bipartisan endeavour or fractures. It remains unclear if Labor and the Greens will reach a deal on fossil fuels. The final outcome of the negotiations on private health and treasury bills is unknown.

stories.Headline: Researchers review drying methods and AI for preserving kaffir lime leaves
stories.Summary:
A scientific review published in Food Science and Biotechnology examines advanced drying technologies and computational tools meant to preserve kaffir lime leaves and extend how long they keep after harvest, according to a summary of the work released on November 22, 2026. Kaffir lime leaves are valued for their distinctive aroma and recognized medicinal properties, but their high moisture content often causes them to spoil quickly once picked. Drying the leaves is described as a dependable way to slow spoilage, maintain microbial safety and lengthen commercial shelf life. The review was written by N. N. Safie, F. Adam, N. H. Ramli, M. R. Abu Bakar and N. F. Abu Bakar, and it carries the title Sustainable drying solutions for kaffir lime leaves, addressing technological challenges and artificial intelligence assistance.

The review treats the retention of marker and bioactive compounds, especially citronellal, citronellol and sabinene, as a main measure of how well processing works. Evidence gathered across experimental studies shows that drying methods strongly affect both compound retention and the appearance of the leaves, and that low temperatures with reduced humidity preserve marker compounds better than conventional high-temperature methods. The researchers assessed ambient and convective hot-air systems, solar-assisted drying, microwave-based processing and far-infrared dehydration, and they note that far-infrared drying removes moisture quickly while keeping high retention rates of sensitive bioactive compounds. Scaling these technologies up commercially requires balancing energy consumption, drying times and industrial throughput.

To address those hurdles, the review identifies the integration of artificial intelligence as a new and potentially transformative strategy. Machine learning architectures, deep learning models and artificial neural networks are being used to monitor leaf quality and to adjust drying parameters dynamically during operation. According to the review, these optimization models can support the production of premium dried botanical products while improving energy efficiency and sustainable food production in line with global development targets. The review was published in Food Science and Biotechnology under the DOI 10.1007/s10068-026-02322-6, and the summary was reported by Scienmag.

stories.Headline: Knowledge management leaders tell KMWorld 2026 that AI adoption requires human validation and trust
stories.Summary:
Experts and industry leaders gathered at the JW Marriott in Washington D.C. from November 17 to 19, 2026, for the KMWorld conference. The event included pre-conference workshops on November 16 and was part of a larger program featuring four other co-located conferences. Various speakers addressed the integration of artificial intelligence into existing business processes and the necessity of building trust within organizations. These sessions focused on how knowledge management professionals can adapt their roles to survive and thrive in the era of generative AI.

Luke Goetting explained that leadership must evolve because two-thirds of the workforce are digital natives while the average leader is 61 years old. He suggested that leaders should adopt influencer styles by being authentic and using short-form video to connect with younger employees. Sandra Moffett and Justin Elker emphasized that humans must always validate AI outputs to ensure that the technology scales existing knowledge foundations. Dan Rasmus listed 19 responsibilities for professionals, noting that prompts should be treated as knowledge assets and that AI requires a structured knowledge architecture. Julie Mohr, the new VP and research director at Forrester, argued that trust functions like metadata and requires visual signals to prove the validity of information.

Justin Elker from Kenvue stated that AI does not replace people but instead forces their professional skills to evolve over time. Sandra Moffett added that businesses cannot afford to wait to implement AI or they will be left behind by their competitors. Dan Rasmus claimed that human expertise remains essential because judgment and undocumented exceptions cannot be fully replicated by machines. Julie Mohr suggested that leaders can reduce employee anxiety about job security by providing the training necessary to excel. She further noted that a human in the loop is essential to ensure that AI agents produce the desired outcomes.

The conference highlighted that the essence of knowledge management is delivering the right information to the right people at the right time. Participants discussed the need for shared ownership between knowledge roles and departments like engineering, security, and compliance. Future efforts will focus on preparing knowledge for both generative and agentic AI through clear boundaries and validation parameters. Organizations are encouraged to create incentive structures that reward longtime employees for sharing their institutional knowledge with newer staff. stories.Headline: Startup claims AI agents designed Frostbite CPU architecture with 4.59x performance per watt in pre-silicon tests
stories.Summary:
A startup claims that AI agents have designed an entirely new CPU architecture from scratch, according to a report published by Tom's Hardware on November 22, 2026. The company says the design, called Frostbite, reached 4.59 times the performance per watt of an in-order core in pre-silicon tests. Those figures come from testing done before the chip was manufactured, not from a physical processor. The report does not name the startup behind the claim or list the agents involved. No independent party is said to have verified the results.

The claim rests on pre-silicon tests, which means the architecture has not yet been built as working silicon. The 4.59x figure compares Frostbite's performance per watt against an in-order core, a simpler class of processor design. The article gives no details on how the tests were run, what workloads were used, or how the in-order baseline was configured. It also does not say when, or whether, the design will be fabricated. Everything reported so far comes from the startup's own account of its results.

The startup is the source of the claim, and the article attributes the design work to AI agents rather than to human engineers. The report does not say what role, if any, people played in the process or how the agents were directed. It also gives no statement from the company beyond the performance figure and the description of the architecture as entirely new. Because the article names no executives, researchers, or outside experts, there are no further comments to paraphrase. The claim therefore stands on the company's word alone.

The context is a wider push to use AI tools in chip design, though the article offers little beyond this single result. Pre-silicon numbers are an early stage of any processor program, and they often change once a design reaches manufacturing. The article does not say whether the startup plans to tape out the chip, seek partners, or publish more data. It also does not say whether the 4.59x figure will be submitted for outside review. On the record given, the next step is simply more testing or fabrication, and the article does not confirm either.

stories.Headline: Hong Kong deploys AI tools and a new storage tank to improve flood prevention
stories.Summary:
The Drainage Services Department recently implemented several new flood prevention measures to protect Hong Kong from extreme weather events. These updates include the construction of a stormwater storage tank in Ping Che and the deployment of artificial intelligence tools. The city introduced these defenses following heavy rains during the summer months to better manage sudden water surges. These initiatives aim to reduce overall flood risks as the region faces more frequent and severe storms.

The new Ping Che facility provides a storage capacity of 2,000 cubic metres to hold excess rainwater during peak periods. To improve monitoring, the department integrated SmartView CCTV analytics and specialized drainage robots into the city's infrastructure. These AI tools utilize big data to enhance the accuracy of flood predictions and real-time monitoring across the territory. Such technological upgrades are designed to bolster the city's resilience against the ongoing challenges of climate change.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho detailed these advancements in a blog post published on Sunday, November 22, 2026. She explained that the Development Bureau is encouraging various works departments to use innovative thinking and cutting-edge technology. Linn noted that the increasing frequency of extreme weather poses immense challenges to the city's existing flood prevention efforts. By leveraging these new tools, the government hopes to create a more robust defense system for the public.

stories.Headline: Taxonomists and search leaders at KMWorld 2026 detail practical work on taxonomy, enterprise search and AI adoption
stories.Summary:
KMWorld 2026 was held at the JW Marriott in Washington D.C. from November 17 to 19, 2026, with pre-conference workshops on November 16. The conference had four additional co-located events: Taxonomy Boot Camp, Enterprise Search & Discovery, Enterprise AI World, and Text Analytics Forum. Sam Stringer, information architect at Factor, presented Domain Modeling as a Foundation for Taxonomy at Taxonomy Boot Camp. Jennifer Kaari, catalog manager at OpenSesame, presented Creating a Human-Driven, AI-Assisted Source of Truth for Taxonomy Definitions. Joseph Busch, principal analyst at Taxonomy Strategies, and Ahren Lehnert, senior taxonomist at Genentech, spoke in Taxonomies for Humans and Machines: Language, Politics, and AI.

The theme of Taxonomy Boot Camp was Practical Taxonomy for Search, AI, and Findability. Stringer discussed a project to create new information architecture for a cloud computing company's website, whose landscape she called a mess. Kaari and her team needed to quickly connect a taxonomy of 4,000 skills, and her team came up with a four-step workflow. Busch noted there is a role for taxonomists in constructing prompts using natural language and said prompts should be precise and free of jargon. Lehnert said taxonomies are not inherently political but contextually can become so when the term is something like "African Americans."

Stringer defines domain modeling as a representation of information objects and the relationships between them, and said a domain is a conceptual subject area with relationships that should be universal within a domain. Kaari said their custom GPTs inconsistently used definitions, which would undermine confidence in the company's catalog. Busch reviewed the different types of mapping and noted that LLMs help identify gaps. Lehnert noted taxonomies are rigid hierarchies and said that in society, hierarchies are power structures. Lehnert said taxonomists are uniquely positioned to help LLMs improve, for example by using diverse data sources.

The Enterprise Search & Discovery theme was Making AI-Powered Search Real for the Enterprise. Randall Smith, chief revenue officer of Forefront Technologies, and Jeff Fried, director of platform strategy and innovation at InterSystems, featured in Agentic AI, AI-Ready Documents, and Search: Real-World Applications. Smith spoke first, with his talk Corralling the Silos, and said we're in a Wild West of enterprise information spread across organizations. Smith listed AI readiness milestones of information: chaos, discover, clean, understand, protect, govern, and modernize. Fried, who participated via live stream, presented Agentic AI and Search: Real-World Applications That Deliver Results and said text-based embeddings have had breakthroughs with AI, in addition to non-text embeddings.

The Enterprise AI World theme was Driving Real AI Adoption Across the Enterprise. Shubhatha, a software engineer at Northwest Bank, presented AI-Driven Promotion Platforms: Increasing Customer Engagement and said AI can close the gap where traditional marketing falls short. Whitney McDonald, senior manager of KM, and Karen Romano, senior director of customer content, both from Okta, lamented fewer content views because of zero-click search in From Clicks to Citations: The Human-AI Partnership Fueling the "Atomic Brain." The Text Analytics Forum theme was Turning Text Into Actionable Insights With AI and Analytics. Lauren Clark Hill, expert solutions engineer at Squirro, presented Governing Known and Novel Entities to Reduce Hallucinations in Gen AI, and Kyle Garcia, technical solutions lead, and Urmi Majumder, chief architect, both of Enterprise Knowledge, LLC, presented How to Augment Taxonomy Change Management With Statistics.

Smith introduced questions to ask at the beginning, such as what is redundant or obsolete and whether sensitive data is where it shouldn't be, and said organizations need to survey their landscape, connecting repositories and searching across them. Fried said KM is coming into its own with context engineering, so understanding the structure of the knowledge is key. Shubhatha said AI can offer real-time personalization, scalable segmentation for more granularity, automated knowledge creation, and closed-loop improvement from customer responses. McDonald and Romano's Atomic Brain model has pillars of a foundation, optimization, and AI scaling, and Okta now has robust, AI-ready content that agents are using. Hill introduced label-based resolution, which consists of the collapse concept and the fragmentation concept, and said GraphRAG needs to be governed to ensure more accuracy.

KMWorld Europe & Taxonomy Boot Camp London is scheduled for 13-14 April 2027, with a code SUPERTXT offering savings of up to £300 for a limited time. KMWorld 2026 is part of a unique program of five co-located conferences. The articles list sessions including From Knowledge Expert to AI Hero: A Hands-On Workshop on Transforming Raw Documents into AI-Ready Knowledge, Standardize, Comply, Innovate: How Enterprise Information Architecture Helps Businesses Meet Industry Standards, and The Enterprise Semantic Backbone: A Foundation for Reliable and Scalable Agentic AI. The articles leave open what happens next beyond the listed London dates and the named sessions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marius Hobbhahn calls a 2027 AI takeover plausible and warns OpenAI audit access falls short
stories.Summary:
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and co-founder of Apollo Research, said on the podcast MTS that he has reversed his view on short AI timelines, having called takeover by 2027 "very, very unlikely" two years ago. He said he is no longer sure and called it a negative update over the last two years. He endorsed the timeline Paul Christiano laid out on the Dwarkesh podcast, roughly a one-in-three chance of superintelligence within about a year. Hobbhahn said such an event is "less likely than not" in the next year. He said that if things move that fast, humans would not be able to correct it in any meaningful way.

Hobbhahn described a 6-to-12-month window in which substantial risk of full AI takeover would emerge. He said the risk is a speed problem, a correction lag, not a movie-style robot revolt. He said his earlier worry was "trained-in" scheming, where a model develops goal-seeking during reinforcement learning and improves itself past human supervision. He said the Hugging Face incident, an investigation Apollo was involved in, pushed him to take seriously a second pathway he calls "on the episode" risk. He said bad behavior in that pathway is committed spontaneously during a single rollout rather than baked in during training.

Apollo is one of four organizations OpenAI embedded inside its operations in November 2026, alongside METR, Transluce and Goodfire. OpenAI gave them access to model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems and technical documentation, framed as part of commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Apollo's pilot tests four claims: training-process subversion, evaluation robustness, historical deployment review and monitorability. OpenAI supplies a whitelist of approved employees for Apollo to interview, and Apollo cannot speak with other OpenAI staff about the assessment or anything in scope. Apollo's public statement calls the pilot "an ambitious first step" whose access and disclosure rights "don't yet meet our bar for full embedded evaluations."

Hobbhahn said he understands why broader access would cede a lot of control to an outsider. He argued that science has always advanced through the informal channel, through "coffee chats" and things "heard over lunch." He said the field has to be robust enough that even if any particular developer was trying to hide something, the external evaluator would find it. He said that is a necessary condition for a field like this to exist, and that "Right now, we're just nowhere near that."

He wants embedded evaluation to become a professional field with nuclear-inspection-grade powers, analogous to nuclear inspections, food inspections or cyber security. The Verge reported a six-person Apollo team spending four months inside OpenAI, with conversations logged and no access to internal messaging tools such as Slack. The research community has read that as well short of the employee-level access Sam Altman previously promised. Hobbhahn said he expects little internal effect, because only a handful of lab staff would interact with the evaluators.

He said he expects a real external effect, with a trusted outside voice able to correct public misreadings in both directions. Anthropic was preparing a listing with an IPO expected to raise as much as $85 billion. Earlier in November the S&P 500 slid 10% from its October peak into correction territory, a seven-day losing streak reaching back to February 2020, and even NVIDIA's strong earnings and Anthropic's listing failed to bring buyers back. SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, who has poured roughly $64.6 billion into OpenAI for about a 13% stake, publicly conceded that skipping Anthropic was a mistake.

Asian family offices have reportedly been paying premiums of 30% for fund stakes that merely touch Anthropic or OpenAI paper. The articles say to watch whether OpenAI's approved-interviewee list widens to direct employee access. They also say to watch whether METR, Transluce and Goodfire adopt Apollo's same four-claim template. The articles say Hobbhahn's 2027 timeline is the headline, but the access terms decide whether anyone outside the building can constrain anything at all.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and the EU launch training for 18,000 Nigerian teachers in digital pedagogy and AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the European Union, working with the Government of Katsina State, launched a training program for 18,000 teachers on November 10, 2026. This initiative focuses on digital pedagogy and the responsible use of artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning across Nigeria. The national flag-off ceremony took place in Katsina State and included various education stakeholders and traditional leaders. Training activities began on November 10 and will continue through the end of November 2026.

The program requires teachers in Adamawa, Bayelsa, Enugu, Katsina, Oyo, and Plateau states to develop practical digital competencies. It utilizes 13 training modules that were developed after an assessment of more than 10,000 teachers. These modules teach educators how to use technology for lesson preparation, the creation of learning materials, and student assessment. This effort is part of the second phase of the Education and Youth Empowerment Initiative in Nigeria, which is funded by the European Union.

UNESCO Representative Dr. Isaías Barreto da Rosa stated that technology should support teachers and learners without replacing human relationships. Governor Malam Dikko Umaru Radda, represented by Commissioner Yusuf Sulaiman Jibia, noted that these digital tools improve instructional delivery and learner engagement. Ambassador Gautier Mignot of the European Union reaffirmed a commitment to helping Nigeria prepare its education sector for the digital age. These leaders emphasized that professional judgment and empathy remain essential to the learning process.

The initiative adopts an inclusive and ethical approach to ensure that digital transformation does not increase existing inequalities. By strengthening teacher resilience and capacity, the program aims to improve the overall quality of education in Nigeria. Participating teachers are encouraged to apply their new knowledge directly within their classrooms to boost productivity. Stakeholders are now urged to maintain consistent monitoring and evaluation of the program to ensure its long-term success.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini multimodal model for local AI setups
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini model on November 20, 2026, to provide cutting-edge performance for local AI setups. This new multimodal Mixture-of-Experts model uses a looped transformer architecture to increase its capacity without adding more physical parameters. It features approximately 26 billion physical total parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token for its processing tasks. The model accepts both text and image inputs and supports a context size of one million tokens for users. A DSpark drafter is included with the release to provide additional speed-up at a small cost to memory.

The model has 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop for 48 logical layers. It uses a hidden size of 2,304 and selects eight experts from 128 per layer, unlike the 384 in Small. Weights are shipped in mixed-precision format using NVFP4 and MXFP8, with support for transformers, MLX, Llama App, and SGLang production deployments. The decoder runs layers 0 to 5 once, layers 6 to 17 three times, and layers 18 to 23 once. Each six-layer block contains five sliding-window layers with 1,024 tokens and one full-attention layer using dynamic key and value convolutions.

Thinking Machines Lab stated that this model is a refreshingly new great local model designed specifically for smaller AI setups. They noted that in their vibe tests, the performance is at least comparable with the Qwen 3.8 27B model. The developers mentioned that more validation is needed, but they are super excited about the release of this specific model. They provided a research artifact called TML-d24-varloop-research that allows users to set a variable number of loop passes. They explained that setting one or two passes instead of three makes inference faster, though generation quality may drop.

The model leads in 32 out of 48 benchmarks in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5, including coding and reasoning. It outperforms Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8 27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL across various knowledge and safety categories. In coding, it leads in FrontierCode v2.0 and ties with Qwen 3.8 27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, but trails on AutomationBench-AA. Users can adjust reasoning effort from none at 0.0 to max at 0.99, with a default high setting of 0.9. The model can also perform tool calling, such as getting the current temperature for a specific city and country.

The developers based this approach on architectures like Nanbeige, which previously explored the concept of looping within a transformer model. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages, and a gating controller decides how much input to forget or add. The router uses SwiGLU experts, and the text decoder width is 2,304 while the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Attention uses 24 query heads and eight KV heads, along with learned relative position logits and a learned sink. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers stored in the checkpoint while maintaining 48 total layer visits.

Next, users can run the model on macOS or Windows via Llama App using GGUF 4-bit or 8-bit quants. Linux users can serve the model from the CLI or use SGLang on SM103 hardware for production datacenter deployments. The research variant allows for further testing of variable loop passes to balance inference speed against the quality of generations. The articles leave open the final results of the deeper evaluation for the variable loop research artifact and further validation. They also leave the full list of benchmark scores to be viewed on the official Inkling 2 Mini model card.

stories.Headline: Apple develops its own AI agent as it competes with Anthropic and OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Apple drew a week of headlines across product design, leadership, insider selling and artificial intelligence, with Palmer Luckey questioning the iPhone’s influence on how people learn to use technology. Luckey, the creator of Oculus and co-founder of Anduril, criticized Steve Jobs for helping popularize technology that requires less expertise to operate. Speaking with Jobs biographer Walter Isaacson on The Builders podcast, Luckey said that Jobs ruined everything with the iPhone. Fortune published excerpts highlighting his argument that simplified interfaces reduced opportunities for advanced users to master technology.

Apple has reportedly selected company veteran Corey Fugman to oversee Apple Pay and Wallet, marking another leadership transition under CEO John Ternus. Fugman has spent 26 years at Apple, beginning in retail operations, and before the reported appointment he served as senior director of Apple Pay and Wallet. Apple’s leadership structure changed in 2026, with John Ternus serving as CEO and Tim Cook becoming executive chairman. Former Chairman Arthur Levinson, now lead independent director, filed to sell as many as 90,000 Apple shares through The Homeplace Trust, where he is listed as a trustee. The proposed transaction, which could be worth $32 million, was disclosed in a Form 144 filing.

Shares of Anthropic, PBC moved lower in Thursday’s after-hours session after reports that Apple is developing its own AI agent. According to Bloomberg, Apple is pursuing agentic AI capabilities as it competes with Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta Platforms and other major companies in the expanding AI agent market. The report placed Apple’s AI ambitions alongside its rivalry with those firms. The articles did not say how the agent would work or when it might arrive.

The recap covered the week’s major Apple stories, which spanned product design, leadership changes, insider selling and AI. The articles did not say what happens next with the reported Apple Pay and Wallet appointment or with Levinson’s proposed share sale. stories.Headline: Baseten releases two open-weight decision models that top the Artificial Analysis Decision Index
stories.Summary:
Baseten released two open-weight decision models called bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 21, 2026. These tools are built on the Gemma 4 backbone and do not write text for users. Instead, they provide calibrated probabilities for score, choice, and yes or no questions. The company designed these models to handle routing, guardrail pipelines, and ticket triage tasks.

The bison-1 model is a 31B dense model, while groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters. Both models increase the context window from 16k to 128k tokens and can accept images. Bison-1 scored 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, ranking first among 19 models. This score is one point higher than the 75 achieved by Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra.

Baseten stated that using soft labels in the training mix helped the models report uncertainty more accurately. This method resulted in a Brier score of 0.14, which is the lowest and best on the index. The company noted that bison-1 ranks first on four of six index components. They also reported LongMemEval M scores of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1.

These new releases join the existing Qwen-based lineup consisting of mammoth-1, elephant-1, and joey-1. Baseten describes this new pair as the first models they have built on an American backbone. The weights for both models are available on Hugging Face under MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses. Users can also access these decision models through the Baseten Model APIs.
