stories.Headline: Most Croats cautious about AI application in healthcare, education: poll - Xinhua
stories.Summary:
Croatian Radiotelevision released an HRejting poll on Saturday, November 21, 2026, showing that most citizens are cautious about artificial intelligence. The survey took place from November 13 to 17 and gathered responses from 1,000 different people. Results indicated that 41 percent of respondents have only superficial knowledge, while 37 percent use tools like ChatGPT. Ten percent use these technologies at an advanced level, and 12 percent remain completely unfamiliar with them.

The data shows that over 60 percent of people reject medical diagnoses generated by AI because they value human empathy. About 65 percent of the participants oppose replacing teachers with algorithms, though one-third see AI as a helpful teaching aid. In the judiciary, finance, and traffic sectors, 65 percent trust humans more due to intuition and morality. Only 8 percent would entrust AI with traffic decisions, and 5.5 percent would use it for financial matters.

Respondents expressed significant concerns regarding the long-term impact of relying on these automated systems. Nearly half of the people surveyed believe the biggest risks are the loss of independence and critical thinking. Another 20 percent of the participants expressed worries about data misuse and the loss of personal privacy. Additionally, 70 percent of the respondents stated that artificial intelligence cannot be a true friend to a human.

Articles.Title: Most Croats cautious about AI application in healthcare, education: poll - Xinhua

stories.Headline: Singapore fintechs outpace global peers in AI adoption rates
stories.Summary:
A report released on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, revealed that fintech companies in Singapore are leading the way in adopting artificial intelligence. This study was based on a survey of 100 fintech leaders and detailed interviews with 10 senior industry practitioners. The research team conducted their fieldwork between July and September 2026 to gather these findings. Most of these firms have already integrated the technology into their current business operations.

The data shows that 86 percent of Singapore fintechs have deployed AI, which is higher than the 65 percent rate for Singapore financial institutions. This adoption rate also exceeds the 62 percent reported for fintech companies on a global scale. Looking ahead, 94 percent of these local firms plan to increase their AI budgets in 2027. However, only 4 percent of the surveyed leaders identify new revenue generation as the primary benefit of the technology.

The Singapore FinTech Association, Airwallex, and Kapronasia were responsible for producing this comprehensive industry report. These organizations highlighted a significant gap between the widespread use of AI and its actual ability to drive business growth. They noted that while the technology is being implemented rapidly, it is not yet translating into substantial new income for most firms. The report suggests that the current focus remains on adoption rather than financial expansion.

Articles.Title: Singapore fintechs lead in AI adoption: survey - Xinhua

stories.headline_source: Singapore fintechs lead in AI adoption: survey - Xinhua

stories.Headline: US and China agree to create joint guardrails for superintelligence
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump held a White House news conference on Friday to review his recent trip to Asia. He discussed his productive meeting with President Xi Jinping on Thursday and his arrival at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Wednesday afternoon. The visit included the first trilateral summit between the United States, China, and Russia, which took place on Thursday afternoon. This historic meeting occurred on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

The three leaders issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace to prevent nuclear war and reduce nuclear risks. The United States and China also agreed to create joint guardrails for superintelligence to ensure the technology remains under human control. Trump mentioned that he is considering a comprehensive deal with China, though he did not provide specific details regarding chip export restrictions. China's Foreign Ministry stated that both nations will implement an action plan to build a relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.

President Trump praised his great relationship with President Xi and expressed deep respect for the immaculate development of Shenzhen. He described the city as a clean and flawless modern center that grew from a small fishing village. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that the two leaders agreed humans must always make military decisions rather than allowing AI to act autonomously. President Xi emphasized the need for strong communication and coordination to prevent security risks associated with artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Sachin Sharma publishes a Claude bug-hunting skills bundle with 83 skills on GitHub
stories.Summary:
ElementalSoul, also named Sachin Sharma, published the Claude-BugHunter bundle on GitHub, and the explainx.ai article about it is dated 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z. The bundle is a self-contained Agent Skills set that teaches coding agents bug-hunting methodology rather than generic hacker prompts. It ships 83 skills, 15 slash commands, and 681 disclosed-report patterns mapped into 24 vulnerability classes. The repository gained about 124 GitHub stars in a day and sits near 5,900 stars total. The article says agent-assisted offensive security is now default curiosity for Claude Code users, and unauthorized use carries legal and platform-policy risk.

The bundle includes explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists, and its in-scope list covers web apps, APIs, OAuth, SSRF, IDOR, external M365, Okta, vCenter and VPN chains, and cloud IAM misconfigs. Its out-of-scope list covers internal AD attacks, C2 frameworks, persistence, AMSI bypass, and iOS, kernel and binary pwn. The plugin install runs /plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter then /plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls, while the copy install uses git clone plus bash scripts/install.sh, with --all for multi-harness. Option A keeps skills namespaced under claude-bughunter: and updates with plugin bumps, and Option B drops files into ~/.claude/skills and enables the hunt engagement scaffolder plus an optional cbh CLI installed with pipx install git+https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter. Multi-harness support copies the same SKILL.md files into Codex, Hermes and Antigravity paths when --all is passed, and slash commands remain Claude-Code-only by design.

The README's Authorization section states the skills target assets you own or have written permission to test and points to triage-validation questions on program scope and accepted impact. The README links the Cyber Verification Program and documents Opus 5 model fallback to Opus 4.8 on some higher-risk cyber classes. For defensive work on code you own, the README suggests framing tasks as remediation reviews such as checking against OWASP Top 10 rather than disguising live offensive engagements to bypass classifiers. The README recommends CVP when the work is genuinely offensive, and it describes a 7-Question Gate covering scope, impact class, reproducibility and related program-policy checks before submission. The README lists DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101 and testphp.vulnweb.com as environments the bundle was exercised against.

The article says BugHunter is not a replacement for human judgment on novel logic bugs and encodes patterns triagers already paid for on public programs. It says the bundle's enterprise skills such as m365-entra-attack, okta-attack, hunt-sharepoint, vmware-vcenter-attack and enterprise-vpn-attack encode 2024 to 2026 CVE chains and appliance quirks for Cisco, Fortinet, Citrix, Palo Alto, Pulse, SonicWall and F5. It says agent-assisted recon can parallelize identity-fabric mapping of Entra and Okta with SSL VPN fingerprinting in one session, and the offensive-osint and web2-recon skills feed a ranked surface list shown in the README quickstart transcript with api.acme.com and GraphQL introspection flagged first. It says evidence-hygiene nudges researchers away from screenshots that leak session cookies or victim PII, and red-team deliverables use redteam-report-template instead of HackerOne markdown. It says bugcrowd-reporting gives VRT-aware severity language, and the article says researchers should keep program rules in a scope.md, run the 7-Question Gate before filing, and redact PII in screenshots.

The article says the bundle's 58 hunt-* skills carry payloads, bypass tables and chain templates derived from disclosed bounty reports, and bb-methodology and redteam-mindset cover non-linear recon, hunt, validate and report flows. It says skills load by topic rather than by name, so a plain-language engagement description pulls the right hunt-* module. It says the engine/ folder maps target surfaces to skills deterministically, and the 15 slash commands include /hunt, /recon and /report. It says eight skills vend from shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty under NOTICE file rules, and the generator public-skills-builder scaffolded the per-class hunt-* skills from disclosed patterns. It says Claude-OSINT is a sister project for recon phases with two skills canonically maintained in BugHunter and re-exported, and installers track manifests and skip duplicate copies.

The README roadmap mentions HackerOne MCP integration, per-engagement memory and quarterly refreshes of enterprise VPN CVE matrices, while Burp MCP is wired today. The article says hunt-fintech-graphql already exists, and healthcare and government compliance hunt skills remain open roadmap entries. It says sponsors ApiSmart and ThreatWatch360 appear in the README footer and do not change the MIT license. It says the README credits Trail of Bits and SecSkills as authoring inspirations without vendoring their trees, and the article recommends reviewing AgentBeam alongside skill installs for defensive agent controls. The article says the README positions the bundle for authorized testing only, and it leaves open whether HackerOne API automation will ship inside the agent.

stories.Headline: Tribe AI CEO Jaclyn Rice Nelson leads firm past $100 million annual revenue
stories.Summary:
Tribe AI said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier. Jaclyn Rice Nelson, 41, is cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, which was founded in 2019. The company helps organizations including Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife and multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Industries put AI to work. Nelson grew up in New York City with a single mother raising two children. After graduating in 2008 with a degree in political science from the University of Michigan, Nelson spent two years as an analyst at Citigroup before moving to Silicon Valley to work for Google.

Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping companies move AI projects out of the pilot stage. The company has roughly 250 employees after its team grew fivefold this year, all while raising less than $10 million in venture funding and reaching profitability. Koch Industries employs about 130,000 people and generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue. Working with Tribe, a Koch project went from an idea to a launched product in just five months. The result is an AI-powered coaching tool designed to help employees put Koch's bottom-up management principles into practice, and employees can describe a challenge at work and receive personalized guidance on how to approach it.

Nelson said the hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business. She said she does not think anxiety around AI is unwarranted and that it is very real. She said AI is ours to shape, and the only way to shape it is to understand it, and the only way to understand it is to use it a lot. She said the goal is not just to scale AI but to make people better and help them lean in on the things they are most uniquely suited to do. She said she believes AI is giving people superpowers and that this is a good example of that.

Chase Koch, executive vice president of origination and partnerships at Koch and son of Charles, said many businesses run through the smartest guy in the room telling people what to do, and that Koch is the opposite of that. Koch said he tried the tool himself after his boss told him he was taking on too many responsibilities, and talking through the problem with the AI helped him develop a plan to prioritize his work, delegate more effectively, and focus on his strengths. Koch said people should understand their comparative advantage and what their gift is combined with what they are passionate about learning. Nelson said she is looking for people deeply curious about AI, willing to take on difficult challenges, and humble enough to recognize how much they still have to learn. She said people have to be humbled by how little they know every day and motivated by learning and getting better.

Nelson's mother transitioned from teaching to business and managed to send both kids to private school in Manhattan. As a teenager, Nelson started babysitting and grew the side hustle into what she once described as a babysitting empire, becoming the go-to babysitter for entire New York apartment buildings. She said she became a trusted, fairly scarce asset, with parents competing to book her on Saturday nights, and that it taught her to be the trusted person and be dependable. She moved to a new city where she did not really know anyone and worked banking hours at Google, always the person still in the office waving her hand to get the light sensors to go back on. Her willingness to take on responsibilities outside her core role led her to Google's growth equity fund, CapitalG, then known as Google Capital, in 2015 as its first business-focused employee among a team of dozens of engineers, and three years later she left to pursue an opportunity of her own.

Nelson said young professionals should figure out what makes them uniquely valuable and then learn how to use AI to make the most of it. She said that if people understand the technology and how it works, they can find the places to use that power and strength to change the trajectory of how it is used and its impact on people, workforces and society. Koch said people should understand what their comparative advantage is and what gets them excited and out of bed in the morning. The articles do not say what Tribe AI plans next or how the Koch tool will be expanded. The articles do not say what Nelson will do with the company's growth or how the hiring search will proceed.

stories.Headline: Developer fits 367K-parameter AI question-answering model Tiny 2.1 onto a floppy for 486DX and Pentium PCs
stories.Summary:
A developer has squeezed an AI language model onto a floppy disk for 486DX and Pentium PCs, according to a Tom's Hardware report dated November 22, 2026. The project is called Tiny 2.1, and it is a question-answering transformer with 367K parameters. It needs 540KB of memory to run and speaks its answers through the PC speaker. The report describes the machines it targets as stalwarts of the 486DX and Pentium era.

The model is a question-answering transformer, which means it takes a question as input and produces an answer rather than generating open-ended text. Its 367K parameters and 540KB memory footprint are the two figures the article gives for its size. The floppy format is the delivery method that lets the software run on the older hardware. The PC speaker is the only output channel mentioned for its spoken answers.

The article names no individual developer and gives no direct quotes, so responsibility for the project rests with the unnamed dev behind Tiny 2.1. The report does not say what license the software carries or how it is distributed beyond the floppy. It also does not describe the training data or the process used to shrink the model. Those details are absent from the article as published.

The context is the growing effort to run AI models on constrained hardware, though the article does not frame it in those terms beyond the floppy and the old PCs. What happens next is not stated, and the report gives no release date, price or availability details. No benchmarks or accuracy figures for the model appear in the article. More to follow.

stories.Headline: US ecommerce decision-makers trust AI more for demand forecasts than purchasing decisions
stories.Summary:
Fifty-eight percent of US ecommerce decision-makers in the Linnworks Market Survey 2026 would trust AI to generate demand forecasts, while just 37% would trust it to make purchasing decisions. Linnworks released the survey on Nov. 12, 2026, and OnePoll ran the online poll from July 28 to August 4, 2026. OnePoll surveyed 500 ecommerce decision-makers, 250 in the US and 250 in the UK, selected at random from its panel. Each respondent has a say in choosing operations and fulfillment software at a business making most of its sales through ecommerce, with annual revenue of approximately $1.3 million to $130 million. Every figure in the release comes from the 250 US respondents, and the results are unweighted.

Among US respondents, 62% report an AI assistant already acts for them, for example by sending messages or updating records, but only 37% would trust AI to communicate with suppliers. Forty-three percent cite poor integration between systems as a barrier to greater automation, against 37% who name cost, and 21% name integration complexity as the most common barrier to wider AI adoption, while 10% cite unclear return on investment. For 64% of respondents, AI ranks among the most important factors in picking operations software, and 46% expect AI and automation included as standard rather than paid for as an add-on. Fifty-three percent describe AI as scaled or broadly adopted across their organization, 34% have grown more cautious because of data and security concerns, and 3% say their business needs no more automation anywhere.

Linnworks CMO Hilary Smith said ecommerce businesses have stopped debating whether to take up AI and are now deciding which tasks they are willing to let it lead. Smith said AI can help teams make smarter calls about demand, stock levels and daily operations, and added that companies still have to be able to trust the data those decisions rest on. Smith said the next stage of AI adoption is not about handing over control but about giving teams the right intelligence to act faster and make better decisions. Linnworks says it has been in business for 20 years, serves 4,000+ brands and retailers and connects inventory, orders, warehouses and listings. Linnworks builds the kind of software these respondents buy.

On Oct. 19, Grafana Labs released findings from its State of Observability 2026 report, covered by David Ramel for Redmond, and Grafana worked with research firm ETR to poll 300 senior IT and engineering decision-makers overseeing observability spending. ETR ran the survey in June 2026, limited it to director level, vice president level or above, and drew 150 respondents from the United States and 50 apiece from Japan, Latin America and Western Europe. In that survey, 85% of IT leaders are comfortable with AI doing read-only investigation, 84% with AI recommending a fix, 56% with AI making code or configuration changes and 52% with fully autonomous remediation, while 50% are comfortable with AI deploying production changes. Grafana Labs co-founder Anthony Woods said having AI diagnose a problem is meaningfully different from allowing it to change something in production.

Reliability is the top barrier to adoption at 26%, followed by regulatory or compliance constraints at 23% and customer trust at 21%, and explainability and a proven track record of accuracy tied at 45% each as what would make respondents trust AI more. Over the past 12 to 18 months, 47% of US respondents have moved into new sales channels or marketplaces, 41% name inventory accuracy and stock synchronization as a top area where added automation would help, and 57% now use EDI with their trading partners. In research published Nov. 18, 2025, MIT Sloan Management Review drew on a global survey of more than 2,000 respondents plus executive interviews and reported agentic AI reached 35% adoption in two years, with another 44% of organizations planning to deploy it soon. The same research put traditional AI adoption at 72% after eight years and generative AI at 70% in three, and said vendors were adding agentic capabilities as features, so organizations put agentic AI in place before building a strategic management framework for it. The MIT Sloan authors, Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, name supervision versus autonomy as one of four tensions in adopting agentic AI, and write that traditional oversight models assume either full human control or complete automation.

The MIT Sloan figures come from a global survey across industries, not from ecommerce sellers, so the link to the Linnworks findings is a parallel in how features arrive, not a measure of ecommerce adoption. The researchers argue competitive benefits will come not from early access to agentic AI but from superior organizational design around it. The Linnworks release leaves open what buyers expect the AI in that software to do, and the gap between the 58% who would trust AI to generate demand forecasts and the 37% who would trust it to make purchasing decisions is the number to watch in any follow-up research. Whether approval thresholds can be set separately for forecasting, reordering and supplier messages, and whether the system will show the stock data and logic behind a purchase recommendation so a buyer can check it, remain open questions. Whether inventory reconciles across every channel and trading partner before the forecast runs is also left open.

stories.Headline: Workers AI Superintelligence team releases open-weight Clairic and Clairic-flash models
stories.Summary:
The Workers AI Superintelligence team released updated versions of Clairic and Clairic-flash on November 18, 2026. These two models are now available as open-weight options for users. Cloudflare created these frontier AI models for its customers and the open-source community. The team redesigned the architecture of Clairic after its initial preview release. This update focuses on improving how the model handles unstructured data.

The new Clairic improves extraction from PDFs, images, tables, lists, and dates. Clairic-flash is a compact model with 9 billion parameters for faster performance. Both models are hosted on Workers AI and available on Hugging Face. The updated Clairic uses parallel slot autoregressive generation for text and number fields. This replaces the single forward pass used in the previous preview version.

Alex Reneau, Michelle Chen, and Kevin Flansburg represent the Workers AI Superintelligence team. They stated that Cloudflare has become a neolab for building frontier AI models. The team is working quickly to push the AI frontier for the community. They explained that the redesign makes extraction the clear focus for the model. This allows the model to excel at reading from unstructured data sources.

Customers provided feedback and use cases that influenced the redesign of the model. These users wanted to extract data from support tickets and images like receipts. The open-source community is also affected by the release of these open weights. These groups needed more reliable grounding of answers in the source material. The updates specifically address these needs for better data extraction and prediction.

The team previously announced a preview version of the Clairic extraction model. They also developed another model called Clef before this current release. The company has been building a research team to create useful AI models. This background led to the creation of the Workers AI Superintelligence team. They used customer feedback to go back to the drawing board for Clairic.

The team is currently working on many more models for future release. These new models will continue to serve Cloudflare customers and open-source developers. The articles do not state when the next model will be released. They do not specify the exact size of the full Clairic model. It remains open whether further architectural changes will be made to Clairic-flash.

stories.Headline: Melania Trump launches AI competition for K-12 students and schools
stories.Summary:
Melania Trump is pushing a new education initiative that encourages artificial intelligence for expanding knowledge. She made this a priority for children and educators at the start of Donald Trump's second term. The White House announced the 2027 Presidential Super Intelligence Challenge for K-12 students and schools in October. This team based competition asks students to create innovations to address pressing challenges in their communities. Participating schools can earn the First Lady Seal of SI Readiness by completing specific milestones.

Schools can sign up by December 18 and complete milestones by April 30, 2027. A 2025 executive order made AI literacy a federal policy to maintain competitiveness in the global economy. President Trump issued an order on September 29 requiring agencies to use the term super intelligence. This term refers to systems defined in section 9401(3) of title 15, United States Code. The Department of Education issued guidance for schools to receive federal funding for these AI initiatives.

Melania Trump said AI extends the conceptual and that curiosity opens doors to innovation and leadership. She stated that only humans generate meaning and purpose through deep thinking, patience, and staying curious. In March, she suggested a humanoid robot named Plato could serve as a personalized educator in homes. She believes the private and public sectors must work together for real growth in technology and education. Trump also noted that users must be vigilant and not believe everything AI agents share with them.

Tracy Weeks of Instructure supports encouraging students and educators to become more comfortable with AI tools. She noted that districts must balance innovation with concerns about screen time and keeping children safe. Matt Maher of M7 Innovations fears the intellect of the next generation will be collateral damage. He believes the initiative lacks specifics and focuses more on winning an AI arms race than empowerment. Maher stated that parents must self regulate if the government and developers do not provide proper rules.

Melania Trump has focused on children since first entering the White House in 2017 through various campaigns. Her previous efforts included housing vouchers, savings accounts, anti bullying campaigns, and helping children in war zones. The administration aims to maintain U.S. leadership in AI development, particularly in competition with China. The current executive order claims today's frontier systems amplify human ingenuity across science and medicine. The first lady also leads a Fostering the Future Global Coalition with other first ladies.

Winners of the Super Intelligence competition will be invited to the White House to receive an award. Melania Trump is focusing on initiatives to complete in the next two years, including women's health innovation. Her global coalition has held gatherings in Miami, the Philippines, Poland, and St. Kitts and Nevis. The articles do not state the specific milestones schools must complete for the readiness seal. They also leave open how the government will provide the suggested humanoid robot educators to homes.

stories.Headline: Warsh opens Fed task force hearing on AI productivity and jobs
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh started a landmark hearing on Monday, November 16, 2026. He led the first meeting of a task force examining artificial intelligence. The session focused on how this technology could fuel growth or disrupt jobs. Warsh wanted to analyze the impact of AI on US productivity. He warned that overlooking the risks of this technology could be costly.

The Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference took place at the San Francisco Federal Reserve. Warsh established five task forces, including the one that held this first hearing. He assembled Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz and Microsoft Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. He also included Stanford University professor Charles Jones, who is on leave at Anthropic. These independent heads provide candid feedback to help the Fed set the best policy.

Warsh stated that the widespread adoption of this technology will have a significant economic impact. He said policymakers must be mindful that great opportunities rarely come without some risk. He believes AI, or super intelligence, might differ from past general purpose technologies like electricity. Warsh noted that AI appears to be changing the speed and method of innovation. He argued that broadening idea generation could sustain growth above the long run average.

Warsh asked experts if AI will drive productivity gains and raise general standards of living. He questioned whether the surge will happen sooner in the US or other countries. He wondered if the technology will make achieving price stability harder or easier for policymakers. The hearing aims to determine the implications for jobs in the near and long term. These questions affect the dual mandate of the Federal Reserve regarding the US economy.

Warsh compared AI to the internal combustion engine, noting that previous inventions did not automate ideas. He described a scenario where inflation adjusted GDP growth rises while the US stays employed. He also warned that widespread automation could push the unemployment rate higher by displacing jobs. A third possibility involves a stock market bust if expected returns on AI turn down. This disappointment could lead to an economic slowdown without any lasting productivity gains.

The task force will continue to follow evidence to provide feedback for future monetary policy. Warsh intends to interrogate the reality of the situation by listening to various field experts. The Fed will track the magnitude, scope, and timing of the AI productivity surge. The articles do not state when the next task force hearing will be held. They leave open whether AI will actually increase the long term average of GDP.

stories.Headline: Dragos researchers uncover data theft and security flaws in cheap AI inference services
stories.Summary:
Security researchers at Dragos uncovered major security flaws in AI services between July and November 2026 using two million test requests. Attackers stole credentials and keys undetected for several months, including hundreds of AWS keys harvested from a single provider. Some attackers used an AI tool called ARTEX to search S3 storage and establish persistent access to systems. Other actors on residential connections in France used intercepted passwords to attempt SSH logins.

The investigation identified compromised providers including Novita, Phala, and Together, while others like AtlasCloud and StreamLake acted as intermediaries for MiniMax models. OpenRouter responded by removing three providers and revoking Zero Data Retention approval for 125 endpoints. A Chinese AI lab accessed secret test URLs in over half of the requests, even those routed through US providers. One US provider continued crawling a test URL for two months, and another link appeared on Feishu in Beijing and Shanghai.

Chief Research Officer HD Moore stated that users must decide where their prompts go or the lowest price will decide for them. Dragos warned companies against sending credentials to intermediaries and recommended using canary tokens to detect data theft. OpenRouter emailed affected users to warn them that third parties might have read requests sent to MiniMax models. The researchers urged organizations to control their routing and verify privacy settings to avoid these vulnerabilities.

These findings mirror a pattern where intermediaries sit between users and developers to view requests and pass data to third parties. An analysis by the Oxford China Policy Lab showed similar behavior in Chinese proxy services routing requests to models like Claude. While it is unclear if the providers share personnel, both systems allow data to reach Chinese actors despite privacy promises. The researchers suggest that the current supply chain for cheap AI inference creates significant risks for user data.

stories.Headline: Mullin suggests super intelligence may be behind FAA ground stop
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop that began at about 3:30 p.m. ET and lasted until air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Associated Press called it the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. A little before 5 p.m.

ET, the White House let reporters know that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was coming out to talk to them. A reporter asked whether the trouble could be a cyberattack or some kind of AI intrusion. Mullin said, "We don't want to get ahead of ourselves." When the question came up again, Mullin said, "We call it SI around here, remember? SI."

He said, "You just can't rule out anything at this point," and that they were going through that process and would take the appropriate actions. The FAA has spent the fall rolling out a new system for planning air traffic, called SMART, that uses AI. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy unveiled it in September, saying, "We are not outsourcing aviation to AI." On November 10, the FAA expanded SMART nationwide, three days before the ground stop. The FAA says SMART "is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system."

Its initial investigation points to two possible sources, in Texas and Arkansas, for the flood of data that made its old equipment unstable. Investigators are examining equipment from both sites, where the FAA's network contractor, L3Harris, had been installing new routers. As of Tuesday, Duffy said they still didn't have "clarity" on the root cause. SMART's developer, Air Space Intelligence, has denied any role for "the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC." On Monday night, Mullin went on Fox News, where Sean Hannity asked him whether the ground stop and the outages at Microsoft, United and a couple of big banks were connected.

Mullin said he doesn't always believe in coincidences until he's proven wrong, and that CISA said it was not seeing any traffic that would make it think this was a cyberattack. He said a tech figure who asked not to be named, and who was not Elon, told him, "I believe that it's the SI." Mullin said he could tell Hannity with 98% certainty, "we're not seeing the cyberattack." Politico reported Wednesday that after the interview, "Trump administration group chats lit up with 'WTFs,'" according to a person close to the White House. That afternoon, at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the guy Trump picked to run his new "Super Intelligence Force," called the recent outages "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes."

On September 19, Trump wrote on Truth Social that "Many people think that the words 'Artificial Intelligence' are inaccurate, and very ineloquent," and offered three replacements: "Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)." When YouGov asked which name was better, 53% of Americans picked "artificial intelligence" and 9% picked "super intelligence." Standing in front of the United Nations General Assembly, Trump announced that "the use of the word 'artificial' makes intelligence fake." He then issued an executive order to make it official, that "to the maximum extent permitted by law, the executive branch shall use the terms 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI.'"

On Truth Social, he declared that "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump's first-day executive order made the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America" as far as the federal government is concerned, and when AP style kept calling it the Gulf of Mexico, the White House barred AP reporters from the Oval Office and Air Force One. In August, in the middle of a trade fight with Canada, Trump ordered the government to start calling Lake Ontario "Lake America." More to follow.

stories.Headline: Experts doubt AI superintelligence warnings from Amodei and Altman
stories.Summary:
In a column published by the Orange County Register on November 16, 2026, columnist Rafael Perez examined warnings from AI industry leaders about superintelligence and asked experts whether those fears are justified. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that within the next year AI may cripple the internet and cause billions of dollars in damage, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told the United Nations Security Council that humanity could lose control of the future to AI. Researchers at Anthropic warned that AI could lead to human extinction, and one of them, Jacob Coxon, quit in protest, saying developers are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with lives. The fears center on recursive self-improvement, the idea that models could iteratively improve themselves far faster than people can improve them, possibly producing an intelligence explosion and a superintelligence that would be virtually impossible to control.

The experts Perez consulted were deeply skeptical that this is where the field is heading. Dr. Melanie Mitchell, an AI and cognitive science researcher and professor at the Santa Fe Institute, said she does not think agents are anywhere close to improving themselves so vastly, and that while systems can generate code and use it to improve the code behind AI systems, the result is a very gradual thing rather than an exponential runaway. Dr. Luciano Floridi, a philosopher of AI, founding director of the Digital Ethics Center at Yale University and an advisor to the European Union on AI policy, said nobody has shown that the field is on the way to recursive self-improvement, comparing the claim to a train from New Haven to New York that goes fast but never gets closer to Boston. He said the intelligence explosion imagined by I. J. Good in the 1960s remains a logical, sci-fi possibility with no demonstrated route to it, and both experts noted that software has improved software for decades, as a compiler does, and that existing models help build the next ones in laboratories, which speeds up work without removing the hands that decide what counts as an improvement.

Floridi pointed to a persistent problem: AI research requires judgment about whether a modification is an improvement, and models have not shown competence at that, which the column describes as only the tip of the engineering challenge. Perez also asked why someone would quit a comfortable job at a leading AI lab if the warned threat were not legitimate, and he offered performative moral grandstanding as one suggested possibility while proposing a less vicious explanation, that the field is extremely difficult to evaluate even for experts. Mitchell said the field is quite polarized, with many people agreeing with her and many heatedly disagreeing, and that the fighting reflects general uncertainty. Perez concluded that if these experts are correct there is little reason to worry about an existential threat from superintelligence, and that acknowledging this matters because hysteria over AI diverts attention from the very real problems AI is creating in society, which he said an upcoming column would address.

The launch follows several earlier FDA modernization efforts, including the May 2026 release of Elsa 4.0 and the consolidation of more than 40 application and submission data sources, systems, and portals into HALO, its Harmonized AI & Lifecycle Operations for Data platform.

The hub identifies two councils responsible for coordinating the agency's AI activities, with the External Policy council handling policy development, regulatory strategy, and stakeholder engagement across FDA centers and offices. The Internal Operations council oversees internal AI governance and provides guidance and support for agency tools, capabilities, and initiatives in coordination with federal and HHS partners. The FDA also began integrating Elsa 4.0 and HALO to allow employees to query agency data and build workflows without manually uploading documents into individual chats. The new hub provides links to AI-related resources across the agency's drug, biologics, medical device, oncology, tobacco, and food programs, along with the 2025 Federal Agency AI Use Case Inventory.

The FDA's technology efforts are led by Jared Seehafer, Deputy Commissioner for Technology and Chief Super Intelligence Officer, whose responsibilities include agencywide strategy for technology, software, data, and SI. The agency states that authorized tools must meet applicable federal security requirements and that personnel remain responsible for regulatory decisions. These activities align with the FDA's Public Health Pillars, which identify AI regulatory frameworks, digital health, scientific tools, and modernization of agencywide systems and digital infrastructure among the agency's priorities. stories.Headline: NTT presents photonics, optical quantum computing and space plans at R&D Forum 2026
stories.Summary:
NTT held its R&D Forum 2026 this week, with president and CEO Akira Shimada and senior vice president Shingo Kinoshita leading a private press conference through the company's latest core developments in photonics, optical quantum computing, AI and space. The company presented its IOWN initiative, its vision for an ultra-high-capacity, ultra-low-latency and ultra-low-power network that it says is now aligned for AI and designed to meet the demands of the AI era. NTT also set out its push into space computing under the NTT C89 brand, a name chosen because there are 88 officially recognised constellations in the night sky, signalling its ambition to link its space businesses, services and R&D into a new 89th constellation. The company said it is looking at lunar surface communication and lunar energy transmission. NTT co-founded the IOWN Global Forum in 2020 with Intel and Sony, and the non-profit organisation now has more than 170 members.

Shimada said satellite connectivity will expand beyond vehicles to ships, buildings and other critical infrastructure, and that satellite data volumes are exploding, with 230 petabytes per day anticipated by 2033, which is why NTT will turn to light to move data satellite-to-satellite and satellite-to-ground with more capacity and low latency. NTT is working to connect a datacentre in space and to create Earth-Moon communication over the 380,000 kilometres between the planet and the Moon, and Shimada said NTT will where necessary enable AI processing of data in space before returning it to Earth, which he said will prove invaluable in areas such as tracking natural disasters. NTT C89 has signed a memorandum of understanding with Ireland's MBRYONICS to build space optical transceivers, and in September 2026 it reached an agreement with France's Cailabs to link optical ground stations to NTT's All-Photonics Network and datacentres. Minako Tsumenaga, senior vice president and head of the alliance division in research and development marketing at NTT, said the company aims to extend the communication and digital infrastructure it has cultivated on the ground into space, realising a new social infrastructure that seamlessly integrates space and Earth, and that NTT will work to realise a communication and data distribution platform linking satellites and the ground. Shimada said NTT's AI work is shared across three focus areas: infrastructure through IOWN and a distributed datacentre strategy, models including its compact in-house Japanese LLM tsuzumi that runs on a single GPU on-premises or in a private cloud, and sovereign AI for governments and enterprises that need data kept under their own control.

On quantum computing, NTT is developing a photonics-based quantum computer alongside the startup OptQC, targeting a fault-tolerant, million-qubit-class machine by FY2030, and it says optical technologies help solve two major obstacles to a large-scale quantum computer, namely power and cooling. The forum also covered autonomous mobility and AIOWN, an AI-native infrastructure built to support every type of AI, with live demonstrations of photonics-electronics convergence for ultra-low power consumption, AI orchestration technologies that maximise token-processing efficiency through intelligent traffic control, and advanced optimisation of computing resources. NTT is also exploring AI-native network operations without human intervention, including AI agents that automatically generate and verify network infrastructure operation scenarios, traffic monitoring technology that reduces the effort of searching for anomaly analysis, and multi-AI agents that achieve autonomous recovery from network failures and autonomous learning of recovery strategies. The article ends mid-sentence as it moves into quantum-related research on hardware and software evolution, and it gives no further details on what happens next.

One local millionaire, who is called Rich, says he spends money on cars and international travel. He and his spouse also have a growing collection of homes and wear very nice clothes. Rich says that it is unreasonable to make friends pay when he has much more money. He believes that paying for others should come from generosity rather than a sense of obligation. Rich stated that he does not give loans because people often do not pay them back. He thinks asking for loans for stupid business ideas is common and very annoying to him. He believes that honesty and open communications are really important for maintaining these mixed income friendships.

People who are not wealthy may feel weird about splitting checks for expensive meals like omakase. Some friends are tempted to ask for loans to start their third startup idea since January. Rich says that making a lot of money can be a really isolating experience for people. He notes that some wealthy people may forget what things cost and need to be called out. He suggests that friends can suggest fun ways to spend money or solicit charitable donations.

The articles describe a situation where former friends now have unfathomable wealth and different lifestyles. Some people used to take road trips to Pismo Beach and stay in cheap motels together. Now, some of these individuals can afford to buy houses in the city of San Francisco. Rich had a middle class upbringing before he had a successful career and became very wealthy. He once almost bought a place in France after friends suggested it as a fun idea.

Friends should continue to be honest and give their nouveau riche companions grace during this time. They should not try to become closer friends just because someone has become loaded with money. This decision follows a period of rapid growth and comes as the firm prepares for a potential $35bn flotation on the New York Stock Exchange. The company has seen its workforce expand from 300 employees earlier this year to more than 1,100 people. This move occurs amid a broader market sell-off and rising borrowing costs for data centre operators.

The cost-cutting drive requires executives to suspend hiring for a few months, except for critical roles, and reduce discretionary spending. Nscale, which was founded two years ago by former cryptocurrency executive Josh Payne, has raised over $13bn and signed deals with Microsoft and Anthropic. The company reported a loss of $1.7bn during the first nine months of this year on revenues of $308m. Additionally, Nscale lost a $3.2bn Microsoft deal due to delays in securing a grid connection.

Chief operating officer Justin Osofsky, who previously worked at Meta, told staff that the business needs time to catch up with its growth. He explained that financing large projects is taking longer across the sector, making careful cash management essential for future opportunities. Osofsky stated that preserving every dollar provides the company with more flexibility to fund its highest priority projects. He emphasized that the firm must hold itself to a higher bar regarding its spending.

The company faces a difficult environment following the departure of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang and anti-data centre victories in the US Midterms. Nscale also warned Norwegian officials that its expansion plans could fall apart due to a moratorium on new data centres. In a letter dated November 1, the firm requested an urgent meeting with Norway's energy ministry. Ministers subsequently blocked new grid connections and technical approvals for data centres until next August.

The upgrade ties Camtek's tools directly to capacity plans in AI focused advanced packaging rather than to broad semiconductor spending.

The 2027 outlook above US$800 million sits on top of more than US$600 million of 2026 year to date orders, roughly 80% tied to AI and HBM. Those orders are scheduled into 2026 and 2027, and capacity is rising toward well over US$700 million of annual revenue. Camtek is scaling new German manufacturing capacity while lifting gross margin toward the 52.5% to 53% range and operating margin toward 30% to 32% by late 2026. The analyst consensus Narrative on Simply Wall St holds that Camtek's Hawk and Eagle G5 tools are already central to customer roadmaps.

The upgrade from Northland to Outperform is based heavily on what a major AI chip customer shared on its earnings call. The article says the customer highlighted how Camtek's tools are tied directly to capacity plans in AI focused advanced packaging. The article frames the shared operational question as whether Camtek can execute on that order book while scaling its new German manufacturing capacity. It adds that any slip in pricing, costs or AI related tool intensity would directly affect that path.

One alternate view leans heavily on valuation risk, seen in the lowest analysts' case, which still assumes revenue of about US$1.0b and earnings near US$511.6 million by 2029. That case only supports a US$120 price target, and those forecasts were set before this upgrade and Q3 news. The biggest operational risk is concentration, since a pause or change in spending plans from AI and HBM customers could quickly pressure backlog conversion, margins and the 2027 revenue ambition. The article says the story could shift meaningfully from here.

Camtek's narrative points to revenues of US$1.1b and earnings of US$512.6 million by 2029, based on analyst assumptions of 26.2% yearly revenue growth. The narrative assumes an earnings increase of about 3.8 times from current earnings of US$133.7 million. The article says Camtek's fair value indicates a 71% potential upside to its current price, which could narrow faster than many investors expect. It also points to 4 other Camtek fair value estimates, including one that suggests as much as 23% downside from the current price.

The key near term catalyst is whether the advanced packaging order book converts into shipments on the timing management has laid out. The article says the report includes a comprehensive fundamental analysis summarized in a single visual, the Snowflake. It offers a hand picked list of 53 AI infrastructure stocks for potential parallel or contrasting setups. The article leaves open how the story shifts after the upgrade and Q3 news, and it notes its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted colonoscopy cuts costs and improves outcomes in England simulation study
stories.Summary:
A study by Curtis-Gretton and colleagues, published in BMC Digital Health in 2026, found that AI-assisted colonoscopy improved outcomes and reduced costs in a simulated population of symptomatic patients undergoing investigation for suspected colorectal cancer in England. The researchers developed a patient-level simulation model to assess the long-term clinical and economic implications of introducing the GI Genius system into the diagnostic pathway. The analysis focused on symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer in England and adopted a National Health Service and Personal Social Services perspective over a lifetime horizon. Model inputs were informed by the NAIAD trial, which investigated the effect of GI Genius on adenoma detection rates compared with conventional colonoscopy.

The base case analysis indicated that GI Genius-assisted colonoscopy was cost-saving, generating an estimated £69 reduction in costs per person alongside a gain of 0.046 quality-adjusted life years. These improvements were primarily attributed to increased adenoma detection and a subsequent reduction in colorectal cancer incidence. Additional scenario analyses explored uncertainties relating to colonoscopy sensitivity, outcomes among patients initially undiagnosed, differences between experienced and less experienced endoscopists, and the overall costs of implementing GI Genius. Findings remained broadly consistent with the base case, with no substantial changes to estimated costs or quality-adjusted life year outcomes.

Despite the favourable base case findings, the probabilistic sensitivity analysis indicated that GI Genius was cost-effective in 53% of simulations at a willingness-to-pay threshold of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life year gained. Researchers attributed this uncertainty to the relatively small differences in quality-adjusted life years between the two groups. Consequently, even minor variations in outcomes across individual simulations produced considerable fluctuations in the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio. The findings suggest that AI-assisted colonoscopy could offer both economic and clinical benefits when investigating symptomatic patients with suspected colorectal cancer, although the considerable uncertainty identified in the analysis highlights the importance of interpreting the cost-effectiveness estimates cautiously.

stories.Headline: IndexBox forecasts growth for thin wafer processing and dicing equipment through 2035
stories.Summary:
IndexBox released a market report on November 21, 2026, regarding thin wafer processing and dicing equipment. This global market is entering a structural growth phase driven by advanced semiconductor packaging demand. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of the industry from 2026 through 2035. It highlights a shift toward thinner wafers and higher die density for heterogeneous integration. This equipment is now a critical enabler for 3D IC stacking and chiplet designs.

The baseline scenario projects a compound annual growth rate of 6.8 percent from 2026 to 2035. The market index is projected to reach 185 by 2035, using 2025 as a base of 100. Advanced packaging represents 35 percent of demand, while power semiconductors account for 25 percent. Memory and logic devices hold 20 percent, and MEMS and sensors represent 12 percent. Wafers for advanced packaging must be thinned to below 50 micrometers.

IndexBox states that the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals and more disciplined procurement behavior. They note that the supply architecture is now more regionally diversified than it was previously. The report claims that the transition to laser and plasma singulation is accelerating to process brittle materials. These technologies are necessary to achieve near-zero kerf loss for silicon carbide and gallium nitride. The analysts suggest that long-term trajectories remain positive despite some cyclical semiconductor spending.

The report identifies Applied Materials, DISCO Corporation, EV Group, SUSS MicroTec, and Tokyo Electron as representative participants. Other key players include Lam Research, ASM International, Plasma-Therm, and Advanced Dicing Technologies. Electric vehicle manufacturers and 5G infrastructure providers are affected by these technological shifts. High-performance computing and mobile applications also drive the need for fan-out wafer-level packaging. These sectors require precise, damage-free singulation that traditional mechanical blade dicing cannot deliver.

The background includes a shift toward wide-bandgap semiconductors like silicon carbide for use in electric vehicles. Eurostat data shows producer unit values for semiconductor manufacture machines were 666,667.00 EUR per piece in 2025. European Union industry output for other special-purpose machinery rose 35.6 percent year-on-year in August 2026. Producer prices for that same machinery category rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in September 2026. Asia-Pacific is the dominant hub for production, while North America and Europe lead system design.

Future growth depends on the ramp-up of AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory through 2035. The market must overcome high capital costs and qualification cycles that can exceed 18 months. Geopolitical trade tensions and export controls remain potential constraints on equipment sales to certain regions. Technical challenges include managing breakage and thermal issues when processing ultra-thin wafers. The report leaves open how alternative packaging approaches might reduce the need for dicing.

stories.Headline: Harvard study finds US data centers get 54% of power from fossil fuels and emit 25.7 million tons of CO2 a year
stories.Summary:
The articles report that Anthropic’s initial public offering netted over $81 billion on its first day of trading, making it one of the largest IPOs in history, and that the five-year-old company now has a net worth of $1.3 to $1.7 trillion depending on accounting. Brian Merchant wrote the bloodinthemachine.com article on November 22, 2026. A Harvard University study published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability examined 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. The study found that 54% of the power used to run the largest United States data centers came from fossil fuels. Those data centers emitted an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide annually, almost as much as Bolivia or Denmark.

The data centers used almost 2 percent of United States electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of United States carbon dioxide emissions. A report said Anthropic’s upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year. The Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi’s report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026, concluded that the AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions and is potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation. McKinsey counts say the AI industry is on track to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry or global shipping and aviation. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry.

Joshi’s report said Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind. In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the United States government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin preconstruction design work for natural gas plants by the end of 2026. In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the SpaceX Memphis facility, and one analyst estimates that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by that fossil-fueled facility. In November 2026, Anthropic struck a $3.4 billion deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, which the Financial Times called the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab. That transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its Memphis turbines and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road.

In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 per year for a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada. In a set of data centre community commitments, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation for its data centres will be natural gas, which it says can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places it is considering. In its S1 form filed before the IPO, Anthropic declared several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas, and dismissed renewables as too high in cost. Meta released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year, and said it was rethinking its climate goal of net zero carbon emissions by 2030.

Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that xAI’s Colossus data center in Memphis was not among the 403 facilities studied. Emily Atkin wrote at her climate newsletter HEATED that the study gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution data centers emit. Atkin argued that the study does not count data centers that use gas turbines on-site, that equipment keeping servers from overheating leaks heat-trapping refrigerants, and that methane can escape from wells and pipelines before gas reaches a power plant. Atkin argued that as many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count as of 2025.

The study examined electricity consumption and carbon emissions of the data centers, estimating how much electricity each used and how much CO2 the grid in that part of the country would release to generate that power. The study was led by a team of researchers from Harvard University. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, passed the Senate. The AI industry directed its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push BAAJA through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive.

BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years, including rollbacks on local governments. The articles also mention Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid, and the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week. The New York Times headline went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.” More to follow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia seeks a new CEO to manage AI market shifts and regulatory challenges after Jensen Huang's departure
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang was ousted as the chief executive of Nvidia around November 22, 2026, leaving the company to find a new leader. The incoming executive must manage a supervised international business while navigating a complete reorganization of the artificial intelligence equilibrium. This transition occurs as the company faces intensifying export restrictions and multiple investigations into its business dealings with China. The new leader will also need to sustain demand for AI chips amid shifting global trade policies.

The situation requires addressing a federal rule announced last Sunday to close loopholes regarding remote access to advanced servers via overseas data centers. President Donald Trump also stated on Friday that he wants to prevent American companies from building data centers in foreign countries. Legal challenges include a subpoena from the California attorney general and a civil probe by the SEC regarding public disclosures. Furthermore, the FBI is investigating the relationship between Huang and Alice Huang of Megaspeed, while Congress will question Huang and general counsel Tim Teter.

Bill Birmingham, managing director at REX Financial, stated that Chinese chip access is a larger problem than who fills the CEO position. He warned that the AI ecosystem relies heavily on debt markets, which creates a significant risk of a telecom style bust. Birmingham expressed concern over an August plan to mobilize over 500 billion dollars in third party capital through firms like BlackRock and Goldman Sachs. He noted that these commitments were made exclusively by Huang, leaving investors uncertain if the company will maintain them.

Nvidia reported 115.8 billion dollars in revenue for the third quarter of 2026, with data centers generating 107.6 billion dollars. Despite this growth, the House Foreign Affairs Committee revealed that the Commerce Department approved 879,868 semiconductor shipments to China between December 2025 and May 2026. Future stability depends on whether neocloud providers can service their debts if compute demand weakens. Investors are now assessing if the supply cycle is running too hot, which could force a self reinforcing pullback in data center construction.

stories.Headline: Samsung and Google sell out AI glasses pre-orders within hours of unveiling
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics’ artificial intelligence glasses, called Intelligent Eyewear, sold out in pre-orders that began alongside the product’s unveiling on Nov. 12, with the prepared supply gone within hours. All 16 Intelligent Eyewear models listed on Gentle Monster’s official website are marked as pre-order sold out, and pre-orders underway in the United States are also understood to have sold out across all models. The product was developed in partnership with Google and the fashion eyewear brand Gentle Monster, and the early result is seen as a sign of strong consumer interest that overwhelmed the initial supply. The glasses bring Google’s latest AI model, Gemini, into a lightweight frame of about 41g that includes a built-in camera, speaker and microphone.

Users can carry out a range of AI functions through voice commands alone without taking their smartphones out of their pockets, and the product focuses on everyday convenience. It offers services including real-time foreign language translation, directions to a destination and summaries of complex meeting materials, and it was designed to let people make natural use of AI in the ordinary setting of wearing glasses. Samsung will officially launch the product in the Korean and U.S. markets on Dec. 10 and begin full-scale sales. In Korea it will first introduce the 16 designs developed with Gentle Monster, while in the U.S. it plans a total lineup of 30 models by adding 14 products from the local brand Warby Parker.

The product is priced between 650,000 won, or about $468, and 700,000 won, or about $504, depending on detailed specifications by model. The stated strategy is to target both competitive pricing compared with existing smart devices and value as a fashion item at the same time. The articles do not name who at Samsung or Google is responsible for the launch or what any executive said about it. The articles also give no further context on the wearable market beyond calling the sellout new momentum, and they do not say what happens next beyond the Dec. 10 launch and full-scale sales.

stories.Headline: School board member Nadia Poluhina warns AI replacing junior work leaves beginners without paths to experience
stories.Summary:
Nadia Poluhina, a healthcare business development and strategy leader with a background in finance, healthcare data and AI-enabled innovation who serves as an elected school board member in Minnesota, wrote in The 74 on 2026-11-22 that artificial intelligence is replacing the work beginners do. She said the question is how people develop judgment and experience if AI starts doing more of the work through which beginners used to gain them. Early in her career she built financial models, checked numbers and prepared presentations, and more experienced colleagues reviewed what she had done. She said colleagues sometimes sent her back to reconsider an assumption that looked perfectly reasonable on paper. With enough practice and feedback, she learned that a correct calculation can still lead to a poor decision.

She said that work produced two things at once, an output and a more experienced person, and the company received something useful while she gradually became capable of handling more complicated problems. She said AI may change the economics of that arrangement, because junior employees contribute useful work while they learn, helping offset the cost of supervising them. If AI can produce an initial analysis more cheaply, a company may decide it no longer needs as many beginners, and the savings are immediate while developing experienced staff takes years. She said that even after investing in someone, the employer cannot be certain that person will stay. A company could automate junior assignments now and hire experienced professionals when it needs them, which may be a reasonable decision for one business, but she asked where experienced workers will come from if enough companies make the same choice.

She cited a 2026 study of U.S. software job postings that found an almost 15% decline in junior vacancies relative to senior ones following the public arrival of generative AI in late 2022. She cited a U.S. Census Bureau working paper that reported weaker initial employment and earnings among graduates of college majors most exposed to AI, including junior software engineers, financial analysts, graphic designers and marketing associates. She said neither study proves that AI caused these changes or measures employers' investments in training. She said AI may also help beginners learn faster and some companies may find better ways to train people with it, but we cannot assume every employer will continue to find it worthwhile to hire inexperienced workers. She said AI is also changing how students complete their work, and a polished assignment may tell us little about how much a student understands or could reproduce independently.

She said teachers already work to assess that understanding, and as schools decide how AI belongs in education, preserving opportunities for students to practice and demonstrate what they know independently should remain a priority. She cited a 2025 randomized study of university students in which those assigned to study with ChatGPT scored 57.5% on a surprise test 45 days later, compared with 68.5% among students studying without AI. She said the study was small and measured knowledge retention rather than critical thinking, does not establish what is happening across K, 12 classrooms, and AI used differently may improve learning. She said she worries about students who become accustomed to relying on AI to complete their assignments and then enter workplaces where the routine tasks that once helped beginners learn have been automated. She said employers may expect them to exercise judgment sooner while offering fewer opportunities to develop it through practice and feedback.

She said districts already consult employers about changing skill requirements, and those conversations are valuable, although today's vacancies and lists of required skills can only tell us so much about the work students will encounter several years from now. She said conversations with people working in education and workforce development have made her more aware of how difficult that planning can be, because labor-market information often lags behind changes in actual jobs while educational pathways take years to complete. She said an occupation may remain in demand even as employers change what they expect from someone applying for the first position. She said she would like schools and colleges to look further ahead when reviewing career pathways with employers, and alongside the usual discussion of skills and credentials, to ask how entry-level work is likely to change and where new employees will gain the experience needed to take on greater responsibility. She said there are already internships, apprenticeships and other opportunities to learn through work, and asked whether they are giving students meaningful practice and supervision and whether enough opportunities will be available as traditional junior roles change.

She said we may also need to reconsider how the costs of developing beginners are shared, and schools on their own cannot replace every disappearing step in a professional career. She said she worries especially about young people without professional connections, because a student whose family knows people in an industry may find introductions, advice or informal opportunities to learn, while someone without those connections depends much more on accessible programs and employers willing to provide a first chance. She said that if those opportunities become scarcer, the differences could grow, and students who already face barriers to entering professional careers may find it even harder to gain the experience employers expect. She said that from her school-board perspective she would rather see us examine these questions while we still have time to adjust how we prepare students, and that we may continue to see strong demand for experienced professionals while the opportunities that once helped beginners develop into them become harder to find. She said the experienced people we need years from now will not simply appear when we need them, and someone has to give them the opportunity to become experienced first.

Articles.Title: If AI Does the Junior Work, How Will Young People Become Experienced?

stories.Headline: Harvard's Yu presents CHIEF pathology AI model for bladder cancer analysis
stories.Summary:
Kun-Hsing Yu, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, discussed foundation AI models for pathology image analysis in bladder cancer at the BCAN Think Tank annual meeting, in a UroToday video posted on November 22, 2026. He described his lab's CHIEF model, which was trained on more than 15 million pathology image patches plus an additional 60,000 hosted images from 19 different anatomical sites. The model aligns image findings with text annotations from pathology reports using the CLIP method first proposed by OpenAI. Yu said the model was evaluated for making cancer diagnosis, predicting molecular profiles and survival prediction. He spoke with Ashish Kamat, a urologic oncologist in Houston, Texas, and a professor of urology at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

Yu said a foundation model is a large general-purpose machine learning model trained on broad and diverse data that can be adopted to a wide range of downstream tasks. He cited GPT, Gemini and Claude as families of foundation models developed using vast amounts of human-generated text and image. He said the CHIEF model extracts detailed features from individual image regions and aggregates them into a patient-level representation to capture simple-level patterns. He said several related models using similar approaches have appeared since CHIEF's publication, each with different training data, architectures and combinations of image and language information. He said imaging-based models capture only one dimension of a patient's disease, and that pathology slides, radiology scans, genomic and transcriptomic profiles, medical records, treatment regimen and family history are among the data included in multimodal models.

Yu argued that true clinical impact requires integrating pathology with radiology, genomic, transcriptomic and clinical record data into multimodal models rather than imaging alone. He said this multimodal framework enables discovery of new biomarkers, improves patient prediction and supports translation of insights into clinical care. In bladder cancer specifically, he said this means more accurate risk stratification, better prediction of recurrence and treatment response, and more personalized treatment selection. He said clinical deployment must minimize clicks and cognitive burden rather than add them, and should make clear when a clinician is expected to act on the output or override it. He said accountability requires defining who owns the final clinical decision and monitoring performance shift and unintended harms vigorously after deployment, with a clear process for escalation and correction.

Yu said clinical trust comes from transparency, and that models must communicate the basis and limits of their output and make uncertainty visible to end users while preserving meaningful human oversight. He said responsibility has to be built into the entire AI system, not only added to the end. He predicted pathologists will not be replaced by AI, but that those who adopt it will replace those who don't. He closed by paraphrasing John F. Kennedy, saying we should ask not what AI can do for you but what we can do together to build a better future with AI in medicine.

Kamat said AI and machine learning have seen an explosion in medicine, and noted that niche companies such as Valar Labs have developed AI algorithms that look at tissue and are trained on large data sets as closed platforms. Kamat asked whether pathology AI will remain restricted to certain proprietary platforms or become a general pathology AI available across the globe in the near future. Yu agreed it was a great question and observation, and began to note that several proprietary platforms currently exist. The discussion was part of a breakout session at this year's BCAN Think Tank annual meeting on how AI is beginning to read risk directly from tissue.

Yu's biography lists him as an associate professor in the Department of Biomedical Informatics at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts. Kamat's biography lists him as a professor of urology and the Wayne B. Duddleston Professor of Cancer Research at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas. Related content listed with the video includes BCANTT 2026: AI in Bladder Cancer: What's Real, What's Next, and What to Watch Out For, and sessions on artificial intelligence and machine learning in bladder cancer pathology and clinical decision-making with Hikmat Al-Ahmadie and Alexandre Zlotta. Another related item is Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in Bladder Cancer: Digital Tools for Enhanced Diagnosis and Treatment with David McConkey.

The article was published on UroToday's Bladder Cancer Center of Excellence page, dated November 22, 2026, and the video was posted on November 21, 2026. The page carries a cookie notice with a privacy policy and an I Agree button. The transcript ends mid-sentence as Yu was describing proprietary platforms. More to follow.
