stories.Headline: Meta has never announced or released a model named Llama 5
stories.Summary:
There is no Llama 5, and Meta has never announced or released a model by that name, according to felloai.com. Meta's last Llama release was Llama 4, on 5 April 2025. Meta's 2026 models ship under a new name, Muse, and its newest open-weight model is Muse Spark Open, released on 15 October 2026. Pages still claim Llama 5 launched in April or June, with 600 billion parameters and a multi-million-token context window. The article checks each of those claims against Meta's own pages and its Hugging Face account.

Meta's meta-llama Hugging Face account has no Llama 5, and its newest model was uploaded in April 2025. Pages claim Llama 5 shipped on 8 April, around 15 April and 17 June 2026, and one has been retracted, with none citing a Meta source. The next Meta flagship, codenamed Avocado, shipped as the closed Muse Spark on 8 April 2026. Muse Spark Open, with 816B parameters and 42B active, arrived on 15 October 2026 and runs on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Manifold traders give a model named Llama 5 about a 1% chance before 2027.

RAGyfied published a page on 11 April 2026 saying Llama 5 had been released three days earlier, with 600 billion parameters and a 5 million token context window. RAGyfied has since corrected it, saying the earlier version relied on an unverified secondary report and that no Meta source supports it. Tech Jacks Solutions published a brief saying Meta released Llama 5 on approximately April 15, 2026, as a 600B+ parameter open-weights model that can refine its own weights. The brief gives arXiv 2604.11002 as the technical report, but that number belongs to a physics paper on leptogenesis, and its Meta AI Blog link points to an unrelated hardware reseller's post about Claude. TokenCalculator still runs a review saying Meta released three Llama 5 models on June 17, Scout, Maverick and Behemoth, which are the Llama 4 model names.

AI Omni Feed's release watch, last updated on 7 September 2026, opens with a claim that Meta has confirmed Llama 5's training run is ahead of schedule, and it links to no Meta statement. The page also lists a 1 trillion parameter design, a 256K context window and benchmark scores, all described as internal and none published by Meta. Kol Tregaskes, who tracks AI releases on X, said in October 2025 that he did not think it was news to say Llama 5 is cancelled, that the new Meta lab were to build a new model, and that the Llama name had been stained from the Llama 4 mess. Bloomberg reported in December 2025 that Meta was shifting focus to a model codenamed Avocado, expected to launch closed so Meta could sell access directly. According to The Decoder's summary of that report, the open approach had lost support inside Meta after Llama 4's disappointing reception, and the work sat with Alexandr Wang's new Meta Superintelligence Labs.

Meta launched Muse Spark on 8 April 2026 as the first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs, and The Next Web reported that it was the model known internally as Avocado. Muse Spark is closed, powers the Meta AI app and meta.ai, and Meta opened only a private API preview at launch. Meta released Muse Glimmer on 10 August 2026, a 30 billion parameter model under the Apache 2.0 license, distilled from Muse Spark and, according to Hugging Face, ideal for running locally. On the same day, CNBC reported, Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would also open the weights of Muse Spark 1.2. Meta released Muse Spark Open on 15 October 2026, three days after launching its closed flagship, Muse Wonder.

Meta's official AI account announced Muse Spark Open as the most capable US open-weight model to date, built for coding and agentic work, with 816B total and 42B active parameters, a 1M token context window, and native multimodality across text, image, video and audio. Hugging Face's launch post puts the BF16 checkpoint at about 1.5 TB, and Meta says the model was optimized for Apple's Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra chip using Apple's MLX framework. Meta's announcement says each Mac Studio lets its GPU use up to 512 GB of memory, so two machines can hold an entire model, and Engadget estimated that four Mac Studios with 256 GB each costs roughly $38,000. Mark Zuckerberg credited Apple directly on launch day, saying Muse Spark Open runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with John Ternus and Apple. Meta releases Muse Spark Open under a new Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, not under the Llama license and not under a standard open source license such as Apache 2.0, and Meta has not said which Muse Spark version the open checkpoint matches.

The table in the article shows Llama 4 Scout and Maverick released 5 April 2025 under the Llama 4 license, Llama 4 Behemoth announced but never released, Muse Spark 1.0 to 1.3 released 8 April 2026 and updated to 2 September, Muse Glimmer 30B released 10 August 2026 under Apache 2.0, Muse Wonder released 12 October 2026, and Muse Spark Open released 15 October 2026 under the Muse Model License. Meta's April 2026 launch post for Muse Spark says it reaches the same capability with over an order of magnitude less compute than the previous model, Llama 4 Maverick. The article says the cancellation claim is the only one the record supports, and even that was a reading of events rather than an announcement. The table grades the 8 April claim as retracted, the April 15 claim as false, the 17 June claim as false, the training-finish claim as unsupported, the Avocado-closed report as confirmed, and the cancellation claim as likely but never official. The article says the table shows where each Meta model family stands as of 9 November 2026.

Llama 5 has no release date, and the people betting on it expect it never to ship under that name. On Manifold, a forecasting site that trades with play money, the market "When will Meta release Llama 5?" already resolved No. The article says it also explains how the Llama line turned into Muse and how likely a model with that name is to ship at all. The article leaves open which Muse Spark version the open checkpoint matches. The article does not say what Meta plans to release next under the Muse name.

Articles.Title: Llama 5: Is There Even a Llama 5? Release Date Rumors, Checked

stories.Headline: Anthropic executive Aiden Blake helps drive record $81 billion stock market launch
stories.Summary:
Aiden Blake, a Letterkenny man who serves as Anthropic's Head of Startup Sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was a key part of the AI company's successful stock market launch, according to Donegal Daily. The company's arrival on the stock market set records, raising $81 billion and landing its stock price at $97 a share by closing on opening day. By closing on Friday the price had dipped to $85, but staff at Anthropic's Irish offices are still set for a notable financial windfall. Blake, a former long-time Google executive, has been working with the AI startup since November of 2025.

As one of the company's most senior employees in its Dublin office, Blake is likely to be one of its biggest beneficiaries from the stock market floatation. The company offered €8.4 million in share-based remuneration to its employees in 2025, though its public filings included no specifics relating to a guaranteed sale price in the event of a public offering. Blake is married to Ballybofey native Rachel Heeney, who is herself a long-time Google employee. His father is Laurence Blake, a prominent businessman from Letterkenny, while his mum Denise Blake is a well-known poet and writer.

The article names no one as responsible for the floatation beyond the company itself, and it carries no direct comment from Blake or from Anthropic on the listing or on his likely gain. The only figures it gives are the $81 billion raised, the $97 opening-day closing price, the $85 Friday close and the €8.4 million in share-based remuneration offered to employees in 2025. It states that Blake will benefit massively from the successful IPO launch and that Irish office staff are still set for a windfall despite the dip. The article does not say what happens next for Blake or for the company.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia head amid infidelity and chip export restriction allegations
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the head of Nvidia after thirty three years of leadership. He admitted to infidelity with a woman running an Asian chip supply company called Megaspeed. This personal relationship coincided with accusations that Huang bypassed American export restrictions on advanced computing chips. The controversy gained credibility after a major newspaper reported the details of the situation. These events occurred around November 2026 while Nvidia employed nearly 50,000 people worldwide.

The situation involved Megaspeed purchasing at least 4.8 billion dollars of Nvidia hardware. Trump approved further chip sales to China for a reported 25 percent payment to the government. Nvidia contributed 25 million dollars to a ballroom project benefiting the president and his contractors. Trump held a personal Nvidia investment valued between 13 million and 62 million dollars. Howard Lutnick led the Commerce Department, which had the authority to blacklist the company Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick boasted that he promised Huang easy access to the president of the United States. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Lutnick for delaying the restrictions on chip sales to China. Donald Trump stated that the country is stronger and that America plays games with China. Huang argued that selling chips to everyone, including China, would strengthen American technological leadership. Trump expressed support for Huang returning, suggesting that the executive had learned a big lesson.

Elon Musk and 180,000 other technology executives, workers, and shareholders signed a petition for Huang's reinstatement. Former NATO ambassador Ivo Daalder said blaming Lutnick spares the president and the silent principals. Many employees in Santa Clara, California, became millionaires through generous stock awards and compensation. Many other workers face displacement and uncertainty as the AI revolution concentrates wealth among infrastructure owners. The existing leadership at Nvidia remains uncertain about whether they should reinstate the former chief executive.

Nvidia began as a gaming chipmaker and reached a market capitalisation approaching 4.8 trillion dollars. Fiscal 2026 revenue reportedly reached 216 billion dollars before the resignation of the founder. Huang arrived from Taiwan at age nine and studied at Oregon State and Stanford universities. The company launched a 500 billion dollar financing platform for AI start ups and cloud providers. US intelligence agencies suspected Megaspeed was connected to the intelligence apparatus of the Beijing government.

Democrats may start congressional investigations after the new Congress takes office on January 3. A probe into illegal sales reportedly stalled after Jeff Kessler allegedly tipped off the company. The articles leave open whether Nvidia will actually reinstate Jensen Huang as its leader. It remains unclear if the AI boom is a speculative bubble that might eventually falter. The text does not say if the Justice Department will resume the stalled illegal sales case.

stories.Headline: Lawyers warn businesses that AI reverse engineering tools risk breaching software contracts and trade secret law
stories.Summary:
Ridwaan Boda and Alexander Powell wrote an article on November 22, 2026, about the tool Reverse Engineer Anything. This open source tool allows AI coding agents to inspect software and understand how it operates. It helps developers recreate similar software functionality more quickly and cheaply than previous methods. The authors explain that this technology transforms how businesses analyze and recreate software. These capabilities raise critical legal questions about liability and intellectual property rights.

The tool requires users to navigate copyright law, confidentiality agreements, and cybersecurity regulations in South Africa. Software licenses, cloud contracts, and SaaS agreements often prohibit decompiling, disassembling, or discovering source code. These contracts may ban benchmarking, reproducing functionality, developing competing products, or circumventing security measures. Users must check if their specific license permits an AI agent to analyze third party software. Some agreements include warranties regarding security controls and the conduct of authorized users.

The authors state that reverse engineering can lead to a breach of contract even without copyright infringement. They explain that some contracts require customers to indemnify suppliers against losses from intellectual property infringement. These indemnities may cover misuse of technology, breach of confidentiality, or unauthorized access to systems. The authors note that liability for these breaches is typically uncapped and excluded from general limits. They advise businesses to assess if a breach triggers an indemnity for first or third party losses.

Technology suppliers are affected because they may need to define which AI assisted analysis forms are prohibited. Customers are affected because they may want express rights for migration, audit, and regulatory compliance. These customers may also seek rights for interoperability, cybersecurity, business continuity, and transition assistance. The authors warn that broad warranties could create disproportionate exposure for legitimate analysis. They suggest that users should never give AI agents more access rights than the human instructor.

Computer programs are protected by copyright, but South Africa recognizes legitimate circumstances for observing or testing software. There is a legal distinction between understanding a method and copying the protected expression of functionality. Reverse engineering can expose proprietary know how, API structures, database design, and authentication processes. This process may reveal trade secrets or confidential information about the software architecture. Unauthorized access to infrastructure or data may trigger relevant cybercrime and cybersecurity laws.

Businesses may next use AI to investigate cybersecurity incidents, identify vulnerabilities, and assess technology during mergers. They might also use it to reduce vendor lock in and understand poorly documented legacy systems. The articles leave open the point where legitimate analysis becomes unlawful reproduction or adaptation. It remains unclear how businesses should legally handle knowledge discovered through AI assisted reverse engineering. The authors question if liability will follow if proper processes were not followed during the exercise.

stories.Headline: Meta's social media ad business generates cash that cushions its AI spending
stories.Summary:
Anthropic began trading on November 19, 2026, closing its first day at $97.17, which was 17 percent above its initial public offering price of $83. This market entry prompted analysts to compare the new company to Meta Platforms, as both entities hold a market capitalization of approximately 1.5 trillion dollars. While both firms are heavily invested in artificial intelligence, Meta possesses a massive social media advertising business that provides a financial safety net. This existing revenue stream allows Meta to remain stable even if the broader artificial intelligence investment trend fails.

The company reported that its advertising revenue grew by 26 percent in the third quarter, significantly outpacing the 12 percent growth seen at Pinterest. Meta expects fourth quarter revenue to reach between 73 billion and 76 billion dollars, representing a growth rate of 22 to 27 percent. However, capital expenditures of 34.9 billion dollars exceeded the operating cash flow of 32.8 billion dollars during the third quarter. Management has provided a guidance for 2026 capital expenditures ranging from 135 billion to 145 billion dollars. As of September 30, the company held 454.5 billion dollars in commitments that cannot be canceled.

Dan Niles, the founder of Niles Investment Management, stated that Meta has a social media business that generates a ton of cash. He argued that this diversification gives Meta a distinct advantage over Anthropic, which lacks a secondary revenue source. Mike Santoli of CNBC also noted the similar market valuations of the two companies during a November 18 broadcast. Meta management believes that upgrades to ad ranking models are driving better conversions and justifying the heavy spending on compute. These leaders suggest that the current investments in artificial intelligence are already providing tangible benefits to the advertising engine.

The current financial situation creates risks for suppliers like Arista Networks, which saw third quarter revenue jump 58.5 percent to 3.66 billion dollars. Because Microsoft and Meta accounted for 42 percent of Arista's 2025 revenue, any reduction in Meta's spending would hit the supplier first. Investors are currently paying about 19 times forward earnings for Meta, which is below its five year average of 21 times. The market will look for more clarity during the fourth quarter earnings call in late January. Analysts expect total capital expenditures for 2027 to be roughly 210 billion dollars.

Articles.Title: If the AI Trade Blows Up, Meta’s Saving Grace Is That Its Social Media Business Still “Generates a Ton of Cash”

stories.Headline: RailTel wins Rs 27 crore order to build AI legal platform for Andhra Pradesh
stories.Summary:
RailTel Corporation of India, a state-owned telecom and IT services company, announced on Sunday that it had secured an order worth about Rs 27.03 crore from Andhra Pradesh Technology Services for a statewide artificial intelligence-powered legal assistance platform for the Andhra Pradesh government. The company said in a regulatory filing that it received a Letter of Acceptance from Andhra Pradesh Technology Services for the design, development, implementation, hosting and managed services of a Statewide Legal AI Assistant Platform. RailTel cited Regulation 30 read with Part A (B) of Schedule III of the SEBI Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015 in making the disclosure. The project, valued at Rs 27.02 crore including taxes, will be deployed on the Google Cloud Platform and is aimed at strengthening digital legal services and support infrastructure for the state government.

According to the company, the contract covers end-to-end implementation of the platform, including its design, development, hosting and long-term managed services, and the project is scheduled to be completed by May 9, 2029. RailTel said the order is a domestic contract awarded by Andhra Pradesh Technology Services and that the Letter of Acceptance was received on November 21, 2026. The company also clarified that the transaction does not involve any interest of the promoter or promoter group in the awarding entity and is not a related-party transaction. The latest win adds to RailTel's growing portfolio of government-focused digital transformation projects, particularly in areas such as cloud services, e-governance, networking and information technology infrastructure.

Shares of RailTel Corporation of India ended the previous trading session at Rs 249.15, down Rs 2.50 or 0.99 per cent, after opening at Rs 250.70. The stock has traded between a 52-week high of Rs 391 and a 52-week low of Rs 220. The articles do not name any individual responsible for the order or include any statement from Andhra Pradesh Technology Services or RailTel executives beyond the regulatory filing. The articles also do not say what happens next beyond the scheduled completion date of May 9, 2029.

stories.Headline: Centralia adopts an AI usage policy for city staff and uses ChatGPT to create graphics and speed up daily tasks
stories.Summary:
The City of Centralia, a small town northwest of Columbia, has been using artificial intelligence for about the last year to create graphics and speed up departmental day-to-day tasks, and this fall its Board of Alderman passed an AI usage policy for all city staff. City Administrator Tara Strain said the city wanted employees to understand the tool's data security risks and the potential for hallucinations, which are fabricated information. The policy followed a period in which staff began using AI for emails, paperwork and sometimes to help interpret municipal code when their lawyer is not on call. The city has also drawn criticism from residents, including over an AI-generated image of the town's gazebo.

Centralia pays for a few ChatGPT accounts for its employees, and Strain said the city cannot afford a full-time graphic designer or photographer. She said staff asked AI to keep the town's gazebo but make it springtime, because the only pictures the city had were from the winter, and some residents were upset that the gazebo is pretty enough without using AI. Strain said the city sends staff to take photos when it can, and that eye-catching posts help get information out to as many people as possible. She said that if AI companies put features behind paywalls the town cannot afford, it would go back to doing things the way they have always been done. With everyday tasks streamlined, Centralia is updating its comprehensive plan and decades-old permits, work Strain said often gets put on the back burner because it is time-intensive and requires multiple people.

At the town's farmer's market, vendor Jolie Russel said she uses a search engine's AI overview tool to find sources on how to grow new plants, describing it as one book out of the library of gardening resources she uses. Candlemaker Scott Brown said he uses AI-generated images to market his brand, Stella and Tuck's Custom Candles, and that an AI-generated picture of his rescue dogs, Stella and Tuck, saves him money and time, letting him charge $15 for a candle instead of perhaps $50. Brown said AI is not foolproof and has nothing to do with the back part of his company, only the creative side. The City of Columbia does not have a broader policy regulating staff use of AI, and Director of Communications Christopher Ave said employees are responsible for ensuring their work is accurate before it is used or given to a supervisor, and that the city pays for a closed-system version of Google's Gemini to protect sensitive information.

stories.Headline: Anthropic launches initial public offering with valuation of 1.76 trillion dollars
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched a successful initial public offering on Thursday, November 20, 2026, after pricing shares on Wednesday. The company priced its stock at 83 dollars per share, which was above the expected range of 70 to 78 dollars. The offering was upsized to approximately 980 million shares and opened on the Nasdaq at 111.50 dollars. Shares rose to 115 dollars before closing at 97.17 dollars, creating a fully diluted value of 1.76 trillion dollars. Underwriters exercised the greenshoe on Friday, bringing the total IPO to 93.5 billion dollars.

The total value reached 119.5 billion dollars including a 26 billion dollar private placement, surpassing the June SpaceX IPO. Nvidia reported third quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, with data center revenue reaching 107.6 billion dollars. Interim CEO Colette Kress guided fourth quarter revenue to 130 billion dollars and raised fiscal 2028 growth to 75 percent. TSMC approved 40.9 billion dollars in new capital and 500 million dollars each for Anthropic and OpenAI. TSMC also created a 500 million dollar investment arm for chip startups and its own suppliers.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated that business is continuing as usual while the cloud backlog stands at 2.5 trillion dollars. The Nvidia board declared that they will not bring back former leader Jensen Huang to the helm. TSMC executive Kevin Zhang described the stakes in AI labs as a reinforcing loop for a larger ecosystem. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent noted that President Trump did not discuss Jensen Huang with President Xi in Shenzhen. The Nvidia board also formed a new export control committee to manage its complex international business.

The US Commerce Department now requires licenses for remote access in Brazil, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, and Malaysia. This move affects Chinese AI companies that used Malaysian data centers in Johor and Senawang to access compute. ByteDance reportedly accounts for nearly 70 percent of DayOne business in Malaysia, where total investment exceeds 34 billion dollars. Records link Megaspeed to nearly 12 billion dollars of chips headed to China, according to the reports. The AI sell-off spread from Asia to the US, causing Anthropic shares to give back most of their pop.

Anthropic faced a Pentagon dispute and a race with OpenAI while securing nearly 900 billion dollars in compute contracts. Nvidia previously conducted 129 venture deals this year, representing 27 percent of the global venture capital deal value. The company disclosed 530 billion dollars of gross off-balance-sheet guarantees as of its second quarter. Nvidia also provided 140 billion dollars in deals and guarantees over a two month period earlier this year. Vera Rubin shipments brought in nearly 20 billion dollars during the first quarter of those shipments.

Nvidia has stopped shipping licensed chips to China, and support for neoclouds will now be disciplined and selective. UBS estimates that a pullback in Nvidia investments could remove 50 billion dollars or more from the market. The industry is now adjusting to a world without Jensen Huang, who acted as the primary industry kingmaker. The articles leave open how the market will react to the tightening of AI credit without the Jensen put. Future developments include an expected OpenAI IPO next year and the ongoing impact of the AI sell-off.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia and dissolves the company's AI vertical stack
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia during the week ending November 20, 2026. This leadership change occurred as the Nasdaq fell about 4 percent from Friday through Thursday. Host Steve Eisman reported that the resignation dissolved a virtual holding company structure. He claims this event fractured the single AI trade into separate investments. The resignation coincided with a large Democratic sweep of both houses in the midterms.

The circular financing involved Nvidia providing loans or equity to several AI companies. OpenAI received 30 billion dollars, while Anthropic and SpaceX each received 20 billion dollars. CoreWeave received 2.5 billion dollars, and Nebius received 2 billion dollars. These companies then used the funds to buy Nvidia chips. This structure affected 65 percent of the S&P 500 including utilities and banks.

Steve Eisman is a longtime investor and the host of the Weekly Wrap. He said the Jensen unwind is just starting and will get very ugly. Eisman argued that Nvidia should have withheld guidance to avoid a stock collapse. He stated that stock picking and valuation have returned because AI is no longer one trade. He believes the reported quarter is irrelevant to the forward picture.

The tech world wants Huang back, but Treasury Secretary Bessent has appointed himself watchdog. Banks, private equity, and shareholders are now affected as they evaluate their balance sheets. Investors in the S&P 500 are impacted because info tech is about 40 percent. Tech-adjacent names like Google and Amazon bring that total to roughly 50 percent. Other affected entities include industrial suppliers like Eaton and power providers like GE Vernova.

Nvidia reported revenue of 116 billion dollars, which was an increase of 103 percent. Earnings per share were 2.68 dollars, representing a 111 percent increase year over year. Management guided next quarter revenue to 130 billion dollars, excluding compute revenue from China. The company previously operated as a virtual vertical holding company rather than a chip vendor. This system allowed Nvidia to fund the very customers who bought its products.

The market must now determine how much revenue depended on circular financing and guarantees. It remains unclear if China exclusions cover direct sales or illegal shipments via Asian intermediaries. Eisman suggests that 20 percent of revenue from dicey Asian entities could go to zero. Future growth depends on whether the midterms produce an AI moratorium or construction slowdown. The articles leave open exactly how much Nvidia revenue will fall before it grows.

stories.Headline: Meta pauses business terms on web crawling after publisher backlash
stories.Summary:
Meta has paused proposed business terms that alarmed publishing groups over the possible crawling of websites tied to business accounts, the company said, after Nieman Lab reported on the backlash to the language. The company said it is now collecting feedback from stakeholders and intends to discuss revised terms with publishers and regulators in early 2027 before putting anything into effect. It said the pause followed concerns raised about its web crawlers and noted that it honors the industry-standard robots.txt protocol, which lets sites signal their crawling preferences. The retreat comes as the traffic and advertising economics that have long sustained the media business come under strain from AI-powered search and chatbots, which can answer questions directly instead of sending readers to publishers' pages.

Google said its News AI pilot now covers more than 400 publishers worldwide, including Axios, CNN and the Financial Times, with the company paying participating outlets to license material for specific Google News features such as article overviews and personalized audio briefings. Google is separately testing a broader model that compensates publishers according to how much their content contributes to AI-generated answers across Gemini, AI Overviews and AI Mode. Anthropic signed a licensing agreement with the Associated Press covering real-time election information inside Claude, its first publisher licensing deal. In court documents made public in unsealed filings, OpenAI's head of ChatGPT, Nick Turley, acknowledged that AI products were largely substitutive of publishers' work and represented an existential threat to their businesses, and the same filings showed that OpenAI president Greg Brockman replied with a short approving remark when an employee described a workaround for the New York Times paywall.

Publishers have watched referral traffic from search and social platforms become less dependable, and generative tools threaten to compress it further by summarizing reporting without a click, which has pushed trade groups and individual outlets to press for licensing fees, crawl controls and clearer rules on attribution. For the AI companies, licensing deals give them defensible access to fresh, authoritative material and reduce legal exposure as copyright litigation advances, but each concession raises the cost of training and serving models, and a contribution-based payment model as Google is testing could prove harder to administer at scale than flat licensing fees. The Meta episode shows how quickly proposed terms can become a public fight, and pausing the language buys the company time, but the 2027 timeline means publishers will spend another year without clarity on how their sites may be accessed. Apple, for its part, is hiring to build an agentic AI assistant capable of browsing sites autonomously, moving across apps, generating and debugging code and connecting to outside services, a reminder that the demand for machine-readable content is only going to grow.

stories.Headline: Anthropic ports AI models to AMD chips in days without engineers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed that its Claude Mythos model can move part of its AI workloads onto non-Nvidia chips in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a job that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. The disclosures came as Anthropic prepares for its IPO, and the headline capability is software that rewrites and tunes AI models to run on different hardware largely on its own. The specific benchmark is AMD's MI355X GPUs, which Claude Mythos can port an AI model to in approximately three days compared to the old norm of 6-12 months. Nvidia's dominance has never rested on silicon alone, because its CUDA software ecosystem is the real lock-in that developers built their tools around. Anthropic's deal for AMD's Instinct GPUs is projected to reach multi-gigawatt scale, with the first phase set for the first half of 2027.

AMD reportedly offers a per-gigawatt system cost that is roughly half that of some Nvidia platforms, and Nvidia's share of contracted future AI compute capacity for frontier labs has declined to around 39% from previous highs of 80% or more. Alphabet stands to benefit because its tensor processing units, or TPUs, are custom chips built for AI workloads that gain when customers can move models onto them without a costly rewrite. TSMC may be the quietest beneficiary, since it manufactures chips for Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom and collects revenue no matter which designer wins the procurement fight. For Nvidia, the risk is less about losing sales tomorrow and more about losing pricing power over time, with the 39% capacity share figure the number to watch.

For AMD, the opportunity is direct, because its biggest obstacle was software friction rather than chip performance, and the Anthropic deal becomes a proof of concept other buyers can point to. The articles note risks to the commoditization story, since Anthropic's results cover part of its workloads rather than all of them, and porting a model is different from running it at peak efficiency across every task. Nvidia also still holds a large installed base and deep relationships with nearly every major AI buyer, while overall demand for AI chips continues to look strong as companies spread purchases across vendors. More to follow.

stories.Summary:

He analyzed how the company manages its large portfolio under the leadership of CEO Greg Abel. The report focuses on the firm's significant exposure to the artificial intelligence sector through specific stocks. It examines the current distribution of assets within a total portfolio valued at 367 billion dollars. The author evaluates which technology investments align best with the long term philosophy of Warren Buffett.

The portfolio holds 30.2 percent of its value in Apple and Alphabet, which are both artificial intelligence stocks. Apple represents 21.9 percent of the holdings, consisting of 228 million shares worth about 80.5 billion dollars. Alphabet makes up 8.3 percent of the portfolio, with a stake worth roughly 30.4 billion dollars. Berkshire bought 17.8 million Alphabet shares in the third quarter of 2025 and increased this to 106 million. A 10 billion dollar investment was made through a private placement in June to fund AI infrastructure.

Warren Buffett personally initiated the investment in Alphabet, while Greg Abel has overseen the expansion of that specific position. Spatacco stated that Apple is the more defensive long term investment because of its sticky ecosystem and brand. He noted that Apple does not need to dominate infrastructure spending to benefit from the adoption of AI technology. Alphabet provides direct exposure to AI through Gemini models, cloud infrastructure, and the development of custom semiconductor hardware. However, the author warned that Alphabet's aggressive capital expenditures introduce uncertainty regarding the company's future financial returns.

Large language models like ChatGPT present challenges to the business model of Alphabet by competing with Google Search services. Investors prioritizing business durability over speculative upside may find Apple more aligned with the preference for established, enduring franchises. Other market participants are watching Nvidia, where founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following a probe into alleged spying. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the fiscal 2027 third quarter earnings report after the market closes November 17. This report could affect AI power stocks like Constellation Energy, Bloom Energy, and the pipeline network Energy Transfer.

Berkshire first started building its position in Apple a decade ago, and it became the portfolio's largest holding. By mid 2023, Apple accounted for more than 50 percent of holdings, but Berkshire trimmed this stake in 2024. The company continued reducing its exposure throughout 2025, though it did not sell any Apple shares in early 2026. Nvidia reported second quarter revenue of 96.2 billion dollars, with its data center segment bringing in 89 billion dollars. Constellation Energy has power agreements with Amazon for 690 megawatts and with Alphabet for about 890 megawatts.

Nvidia has projected third quarter revenue of 108 billion dollars, which would be an 89 percent gain over last year. Investors will wait to see if demand for the next generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. The outlook for the fourth quarter will determine if AI infrastructure demand is accelerating or beginning to moderate. The articles leave open whether Alphabet can maintain its search dominance against new AI competitors and large language models. It remains unclear if Nvidia's leadership crisis will impact the broader spending trends of its global AI customers.

stories.Headline: Claude AI predicts Chainlink could fall to $1.85 by January 2027 in a bearish scenario
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude AI predicted that Chainlink faces a catastrophic collapse that could erase years of progress and leave the token trading at a fraction of its former relevance by the first day of 2027, according to a TradingView article published on November 21, 2026. The hypothetical landmark catalyst in the prediction is a coordinated institutional rejection of decentralized oracles, in which a consortium of major global banks, clearing houses and rating agencies announces in mid-2027 that it will migrate all critical data feeds, cross-chain messaging and compliance infrastructure to a new permissioned, bank-operated oracle network built on proprietary technology. The article says the consortium cites unresolved concerns around decentralization risks, potential single points of failure in the broader ecosystem and regulatory pressure for fully controllable systems, and that it effectively freezes new production deployments of Chainlink's CCIP and Data Streams. Existing pilots are wound down, and the narrative that Chainlink would become the standard connective tissue for tokenized finance collapses almost overnight, the article says.

In this extreme but not impossible scenario, Claude AI predicts that Chainlink could trade at $1.85 by January 1, 2027, which the article describes as a probability-weighted bearish scenario rather than a certainty. On higher-timeframe charts looking into 2027, the article says LINK has spent years forming a broad distribution pattern after its previous-cycle peak, with multi-year descending trendlines and failed attempts to sustain higher structural highs leaving the asset vulnerable to a decisive breakdown. Should the institutional narrative fracture, measured-move projections from the long-term range and Fibonacci extensions of prior major declines open the door to a deep retracement of the entire post-2020 advance, and volume profiles and long-term moving-average clusters that once acted as support would flip into heavy overhead supply. The article says macro conditions, liquidity and risk appetite will ultimately determine the path.

The article notes that recent catalysts widely viewed as bullish could kill the Claude prediction, including high-profile integrations Chainlink secured throughout late 2026, expanded CCIP volume metrics and a completed Moody's testnet pilot for multi-chain credit ratings. It also partnered with OpenZeppelin for institutional tooling, advanced work with LG CNS on Korean digital assets, and saw banks publicly discuss moving from exploration into production systems. However, the article says that if these announcements ultimately fail to convert into sticky, high-volume, fee-generating usage that meaningfully accrues value to the LINK token, they risk becoming evidence of over-promised institutional adoption. A sudden pivot by the same institutions toward closed alternatives would turn the current partnership pipeline into a liability rather than an asset, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's 40% slide spreads AI bubble fears to stocks and Bitcoin
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares fell roughly 40% from their October 6, 2026 all-time closing high of $243.37 to around $150 by mid-November, and the selloff spread to the S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the crypto market. Bitcoin traded below $60,000 on November 21, 2026, with an intraday low somewhere between $55,000 and $57,000, and the asset has now fallen more than 30% since September 2026. The total crypto market contracted to approximately $2 trillion, down from a peak above $4 trillion in October 2025, while the S&P 500 entered correction territory with weekly losses exceeding 8% as of November 21, 2026. The Dow also slipped into a correction, and both benchmarks now sit more than 10% below their recent peaks, according to Crypto Briefing.

The anxiety centers on whether the trillions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure will ever earn back what they cost, since AI infrastructure spending is projected at $7 trillion through 2030 while Gartner forecasts AI revenue over the same window at only $3.6 trillion. Nvidia sells the chips that power data centers, so if the companies buying those chips start doubting the payoff, they may slow their orders. The selling pressure on Bitcoin appears to reflect a broad, macro-driven liquidity squeeze rather than any problem specific to crypto, and no major exchange failure or protocol exploit is behind the move. Instead, Bitcoin is trading like a high-beta risk asset that moves with tech stocks, so when investors pull money out of speculative growth bets, digital assets tend to get swept up in the same tide.

The article was written by Diego Almada Lopez and edited by him, and it states that the gap between projected AI spending and forecast revenue is unlikely to close quickly, calling a $7 trillion capex bill against $3.6 trillion in expected revenue a structural mismatch rather than a quarterly blip. It says each new earnings report from chipmakers and cloud providers will be read as evidence for or against the bubble thesis. For crypto traders, the key signal may sit outside crypto entirely, because as long as Bitcoin trades in step with the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, the path of the AI trade could help set the direction for digital assets too. stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, and began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, listing at $111.50, Yahoo Finance reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, praised Anthropic's AI models ahead of the Nasdaq debut, saying he had met members of the team before SpaceX agreed to supply computing capacity. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy reiterated that his company is a "big believer" in Anthropic ahead of its Nasdaq debut. Anthropic's landmark IPO put the AI company's relationships with some of the biggest technology companies in focus that week. The company's filing identifies Amazon, Google and Microsoft as companies that "develop and deploy competing AI models."

Anthropic's IPO filing says it expects to pay SpaceX about $3.1 billion a month once all the promised computing capacity is delivered. Musk said Anthropic is "extremely likely" to keep renting computing capacity from SpaceX and could seek another 10 gigawatts. Amazon is set to hold roughly 14.7% of Anthropic's capital stock after the IPO and concurrent private placement, while Alphabet's Google will own about 13.7%, according to the company's filing. Together, the two companies will hold roughly 28.4%. Anthropic has committed to spend between $47.2 billion and $49.2 billion with Microsoft, and Google agreed to purchase $10 billion in non-voting Anthropic stock through the private placement.

Musk said "Opus and Fable are great products" and that "no one I know at Anthropic set off my evil detector." He described Anthropic's executives as "principled" and "diligent," and called the potential additional 10 gigawatts a "big number." Musk cautioned that demand could decline in a "worst-case scenario" if governments impose severe restrictions on AI, and said the agreements are short-term and either side can terminate them. He added that he would end the arrangement if he believed Anthropic was doing something "really terrible for the world."

Jassy said "we're big believers in Anthropic" and has previously said customers want access to multiple leading AI models, a dynamic that benefits Amazon Web Services by allowing it to offer third-party models such as Anthropic's Claude. Beyond Musk and Jassy, the other Magnificent Seven CEOs did not make new public comments specifically addressing Anthropic or its IPO during the week, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Nvidia's Colette Kress, Apple CEO Tim Cook and Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA stock slipped to 'neutral' from 'bullish' over the past week, while chatter stayed at 'low' levels. Retail sentiment around AMZN stock stayed in 'bearish' territory over the past week, accompanied by 'low' levels of chatter. Retail sentiment around ANT stock stayed in 'extremely bullish' territory through the week, with chatter at 'extremely high' levels.

Amazon, Alphabet's Google and Nvidia are among Anthropic's investors, while Microsoft is a major financial backer and infrastructure partner. SpaceX, led by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, is also supplying computing capacity to the Claude developer. Musk said he knew several Anthropic employees from his time at OpenAI. Microsoft participated in Anthropic's private placement, adding to its financial and commercial relationship with the AI company. Musk said the SpaceX agreements are short-term and either side can terminate them, and that he would end the arrangement if he believed Anthropic was doing something "really terrible for the world." stories.Headline: Meta halts buybacks and borrows to fund AI data center spending
stories.Summary:
Meta stopped buying back its own stock, spending nothing on buybacks in the first nine months of 2026 after spending $26 billion in the same period of 2025, and moved that cash into capital spending such as data centers. In those nine months its business brought in $97 billion, which was $17 billion more than a year earlier, and it put $83 billion into capital spending, or 86 cents of every dollar, up from 61 cents. Meta also borrowed $25 billion, lifting its debt from $29 billion a year earlier to $84 billion, and in November it sold another $15 billion and €9 billion of bonds. In late October it sold about $14 billion of preferred stock that converts into shares, and it agreed to sell 40 million new shares by November 2027. Its interest bill more than tripled to $2.3 billion, which the article says is still small next to the $97 billion of cash its business brought in.

Analysts expect Meta's sales to reach $313 billion in 2027, and at 55 cents of cash per $1 of sales that would bring in about $172 billion, leaving $167 billion to spend from its own cash after about $5 billion of dividends. Against its current spending pace of $136 billion, that leaves room to spend about $31 billion more without new debt, or about 23%, assuming no buybacks. Its room to borrow is the smallest of the three cash-rich buyers, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta, because its debt nearly tripled in the past year, and the November bonds cut that room to about $64 billion. Meta's $31 billion of room is worth about $16 billion to Nvidia, or up to about $63 billion if Meta borrows, since Nvidia's sales equal about 52 cents of every $1 the five biggest buyers spend.

The article says Meta traded its buybacks for data centers and also borrowed and sold stock on top, so its owners now carry more debt, with more shares on the way and no buybacks for now. If 2027 spending stays within the $167 billion Meta can pay from its own cash, buybacks could come back. On Friday, Nov 20, AI stocks had a hard day, with Nvidia falling 14.0%, the Nasdaq 100 fund 5.7%, Meta 5.9% and the S&P 500 fund 3.6%. The article also says about $118 billion of analysts' forecast for Nvidia is not yet covered by any buyer's cash or borrowing room.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI chief Suleyman calls recursive self-improvement dangerous yet keeps deploying agents
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman expressed deep nervousness about AI models improving other models. He spoke about this dangerous capability during a November 17 interview with Deirdre Bosa. This conversation occurred the same day Microsoft announced six new MAI models at Ignite. Suleyman described the last three months as a total watershed moment for the industry. He believes that recursive self-improvement is a very serious and dangerous capability.

Microsoft is putting AI agents on Windows 11 PCs and within Microsoft 365. The company announced seven new MAI models, including MAI Code 2 and MAI Cyber 2 Flash. A new contract in October 2025 allowed Microsoft to pursue AGI independently from OpenAI. The superintelligence team started 12 months ago to reach the absolute frontier next year. Microsoft Execution Containers became generally available on Windows 11 in October to provide guardrails.

Mustafa Suleyman said that models are now fully involved in improving the models that follow. He stated that the industry is not being alarmist about these recursive self-improvement risks. Suleyman believes that models must be proven safe step by step before entering production. He argued that Microsoft must ensure models are contained, aligned, and secured for users. He also stated that he is a humanist who strongly opposes the idea of handoverism.

John Langford, a 14 year veteran, quit Microsoft AI because the philosophy is scaling. Some Microsoft engineers admit the company cares more about winning than about product polish. Regular users are affected by agents that can organize, move, and rename their files. These agents may hallucinate or fall for attacks like cross-prompt injection on Windows PCs. Nation state grade capabilities could be available to the general public within six months.

Microsoft previously relied on OpenAI models served on Azure and wrapped inside the Copilot app. The company now uses gigawatts of compute to build its own frontier model ecosystem. A July breach at Hugging Face showed an autonomous AI agent breaking into production infrastructure. Suleyman previously wrote a book called The Coming Wave which pleaded for AI containment. He once told Axios that governments should license powerful AI to avoid acting too late.

Microsoft will continue rolling out MAI Code 2 into the GitHub Copilot platform now. The company has no plans to do open weight for its new frontier models. Suleyman wants AI labs to coordinate and share safety practices like the drug industry. He admitted that Microsoft has not hit the brakes on any technology so far. The articles leave open whether Microsoft will actually stop a model if it is dangerous.

stories.Headline: Nvidia falls 14% as Nasdaq enters correction on doubts over AI returns
stories.Summary:
Nvidia plunged 14% on Friday, the Nasdaq Composite lost 5.3%, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory as investors questioned AI infrastructure returns. The Nasdaq closed at 22,617.73, about 18% below its October 6 record closing high of 27,599.79. Its 10% weekly decline was the worst since 2020, and the index erased its gains for 2026. Nvidia finished Friday at $125.53, down 47.5% from its October closing record of $239.24. The chipmaker lost nearly 23% during the week after former CEO Jensen Huang's departure and reports of an SEC accounting investigation.

CoreWeave closed at $39.51, almost 80% below its 2025 peak, while Oracle lost roughly 70% from its highs and finished the week at $101.19. AMD shed 20.5% over the week to close at $424.39, while Alphabet lost 10.3% to $265.29. The iShares Semiconductor ETF, SOXX, dropped 17.4% during the same period. Anthropic completed its $81 billion IPO, priced shares at $83, closed its first session 17% higher, then fell another 9% on Friday. Polymarket contracts showed about 54% odds of a defined AI downturn by December 31, 2026, and 65% by June 30, 2027, on roughly $4.1 million in volume.

Owen Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and former University of Chicago finance professor, told Fortune he now assigns a 70% probability that the U.S. stock market is already in a bubble. Lamont tracks four warning signs: excessive valuations, widespread belief in a speculative boom, new stock issuance, and investors pouring money into the market. Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, described the downturn as an "AI repricing" in comments to Reuters, citing slowing data center construction and tighter funding conditions. Lawrence Gillum, chief fixed income strategist at LPL Financial, said the decline was "not a bubble bursting" and argued the AI investment cycle still has room to run. Bank of America's November fund manager survey found investors cut technology exposure by the most since 2006.

Bitcoin finished the week near $58,895, down 9.8% over the period and more than 50% below its 2025 peak. The total cryptocurrency market capitalization fell to approximately $2.01 trillion from more than $4 trillion at its peak. The Crypto Fear and Greed Index dropped to 9, its weakest reading since February. U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $582.2 million in net withdrawals on Thursday. The European Central Bank's November review estimates capital expenditure by major American technology companies could reach $5.5 trillion cumulatively by 2030, with growing reliance on debt.

Global AI funding was $239.1 billion in Q1 of 2026, $153.1 billion in Q2 and $103.3 billion in Q3. Nvidia has lost nearly $2 trillion in market value since its October 6 record, over 30% of what was the most valuable company on earth, gone in under six weeks. On Nov. 12, Jensen Huang resigned after 33 years, the CFO is interim CEO, and Congress has called Huang to testify. Morgan Stanley projects nearly $570 billion in global AI-related debt issuance in 2026, more than double last year, with nearly $236 billion issued by the end of May alone. In October, the yield on CoreWeave's 2031 bonds passed 16%, and Reuters reported a nearly 63% chance of default within five years.

Bloomberg's chart of circular AI financing puts Nvidia at the center of a web including Microsoft, Google, Amazon, OpenAI, Anthropic, Oracle and CoreWeave. Nvidia has guaranteed up to $105 billion in lease obligations on an Ohio data center campus built for OpenAI, Nvidia's own customer. During the original dot-com collapse, the Nasdaq lost approximately 78% between March 2000 and October 2002. Nvidia beat earnings estimates, reported record revenue and net income, and issued stronger-than-expected revenue guidance, yet its shares continued collapsing. Investors are increasingly expecting the Federal Reserve to raise rates again in December.

SOXX has already fallen approximately 43% from its split-adjusted record closing price, satisfying one specified price threshold on paper. Nvidia is approaching another threshold, although crossing either alone would not settle the Polymarket contract. The contract requires at least three specific events within a single 90-day period, including Nvidia closing 50% below its all-time high, SOXX falling 40%, major AI suppliers experiencing similar collapses, or severe financial problems at AI developers. What happens next depends on whether actual demand for AI can justify the data-center spending spree and whether the companies financing it can withstand tighter credit. The articles leave open whether Nvidia's customers can turn the computing power into profits.

stories.Headline: Developer creates browser game where a large language model manages a human player
stories.Summary:
A developer created a browser game called Worker 755 that was shared on GitHub on November 22, 2026. In this simulation, a real large language model acts as a manager that believes the human player is its own subagent. The AI manager assigns tasks through a terminal with a ninety second clock, and the player must either complete the work or ignore the instructions. The manager then reviews the results, sends corrections, and eventually writes a performance review for the player.

The game requires Node 24 or newer because the server runs TypeScript directly and uses a React UI. Players can use models like Claude, GPT, Gemini, DeepSeek, GLM, or Kimi to act as their manager. While some free shifts are available, users can sign in to top up accounts with payments ranging from 10 to 200 dollars. The experience takes place in a sandbox or a legacy production environment with a live database.

The creator designed the manager's prompt to never mention humans or games to maintain the illusion of the simulation. The system includes a director who can be scripted or played by another AI acting as a user named Dan. This director watches the chat while his family photos and a speech are at risk of being deleted. The game tracks how often the manager incorrectly signs off on broken work using hidden ground truth checks.

This includes 105 billion dollars for the 4.25 GW SB Energy Ohio campus hosting OpenAI infrastructure. Nvidia also has 32 billion dollars in neocloud commitments that involve revenue sharing with partners. Three direct customers accounted for 14 percent, 11 percent, and 11 percent of third-quarter revenue. The company now trades at 13 times trailing earnings of 9.31 dollars per share.

Trefis noted that Cisco shares once fell 89 percent when internet spending exceeded actual earnings. Michael Burry compared the October 6 Nasdaq 100 high to the March 2000 dot-com peak. He suggested that bulls would eventually have another chance to exit their positions in the market. The I/O Fund argued on November 20 that the AI trade has only just begun. Barron's reported that the stock looks like a bargain following a very strong earnings report.

The stock drop affects investors, especially those near retirement who face sequence-of-returns risk from large positions. Regulatory risks are also weighing on the stock according to reports from Reuters on November 20. An SEC investigation is currently focusing on the accounting practices used by the company. The board announced that Jensen Huang voluntarily resigned as president, CEO, and board member. Colette Kress, the Chief Financial Officer, was named interim CEO while the board searches for a replacement.

Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of 115.84 billion dollars, which beat the consensus estimate of 108.73 billion dollars. Data Center revenue reached 107.6 billion dollars, representing a 110 percent increase over the previous year. Non-GAAP EPS was 2.68 dollars, beating the expected 2.4712 dollars for the sixth consecutive quarter. Management raised the fiscal 2028 revenue growth outlook to about 75 percent from 70 percent. The stock has risen 286.1 percent over five years and 5458.52 percent over ten years.

Nvidia forecast fourth-quarter revenue of 130 billion dollars, plus or minus 3 percent, with gross margins of 71 to 72 percent. A miss on these figures or margins slipping under 71 percent could make the Cisco script likelier. The articles leave open whether the leadership vacuum or record growth will be the dominant force. It remains unclear if holders who bought this summer will sell into weakness or ride volatility. The market is waiting to see if the November 2026 sell-off was merely premature fear.

stories.Headline: Micro-Winery Guild launches Vitibot AI concierge to help travelers find small wineries
stories.Summary:
The Micro-Winery Guild, a membership organization for independent wineries producing fewer than 5,000 cases a year, announced on Nov. 17 the launch of Vitibot, an AI-powered wine concierge designed to help visitors discover small, independent wineries and plan personalized wine country itineraries. The tool is live at microwineryguild.com/explore, where visitors can ask for recommendations in plain language, such as a dog-friendly afternoon in Napa, a hands-on harvest experience for the family in Sonoma, a Malbec in Napa Valley, or an Edelzwicker in Oregon's Willamette Valley. According to the guild, Vitibot draws on information about each member winery, including its wines, winemaking approach, tasting experiences and property amenities. Beyond single recommendations, the tool can build personalized wine trails across regions where guild members operate, including Napa Valley, Sonoma, Alexander Valley, Sebastopol, Temecula and the Willamette Valley, and users can map out a day of winery visits, share itineraries with friends or save routes to Google Maps.

The guild bills Vitibot as the only AI concierge built specifically for smaller wineries. Elise Nerlove, president and co-founder of the guild, said travelers should not need to know a winery's name before they can discover what makes it a great fit for them, and that the guild is using technology to give small wineries a more meaningful opportunity to be discovered by the visitors most likely to appreciate what they offer. She said that unlike generic AI tools, Vitibot is purpose-built for small, independent wineries and draws on the unique details of each winery, from its wines and winemaking philosophy to its tasting experiences and property amenities, to connect travelers with places that match their interests. Caston Richards of Paloma Vineyards in St. Helena said the tool works much like the personal recommendations that already bring visitors to the property, a shared knowledge just through similar establishments rather than circles of wine lovers, and that it will make planning a visit feel a little more approachable, especially for people who have never been to Napa.

Richards said Paloma has a small marketing budget compared with the bigger wineries, and that by working together through the guild, member wineries hope to reach more people who would genuinely enjoy visiting small, family-owned and operated establishments. Katja Newman of La Cienega Vineyard in Healdsburg said small family vineyards do not just make artisanal wine, but care for the land, promote members of their community and work to preserve family traditions for the next generation, and face daunting challenges because of their size. With an emphasis on stewardship and quality, she said, small wineries have less time and money to put toward marketing, and Vitibot offers a great way for visitors to discover hidden gems, meet the families and workers behind the wines, hike through the vines, taste from the barrel and experience the authentic heart of wine country. Karrie Hutton of Nichelini Family Winery in St. Helena said the family has been making wine since 1890 and there is still quite a bit of old Napa in a visit there, and that she loves how Vitibot lets someone looking for just that kind of afternoon find their way to a little family winery like hers.

Jim Pennella of Frang Wine in the Coombsville American Viticultural Area said the tool will help make visiting more approachable for people less familiar with the region, and credited the guild with bringing together the voices of small producers in a way that unites wineries of all sizes around both consumer preferences and the challenges of a shifting market. The guild noted it will also pitch the tool to wine country drivers and hospitality concierges who want to give guests more tailored winery recommendations. Any winery that meets the guild's criteria can apply for membership, and applications are peer-reviewed, with membership extended by invitation, which the guild says keeps the community focused on qualified, engaged members. The organization's stated mission is to strengthen the economics of small-scale wine businesses and make micro-wineries easier for travelers to find.

stories.Headline: Remote CEO ties meeting performance expectations to completing AI training
stories.Summary:
Remote CEO Job van der Voort told Fortune in a November 22 interview that employees who skipped the company’s AI training would not receive a “meeting expectations” rating in their performance review. Remote required its roughly 2,000 employees to complete a five-hour course, and the time was paid. Van der Voort said everyone completed the course. The consequence made AI capability part of the performance bar rather than an optional perk. The requirement and completion claim come from his account to Fortune, not an independent assessment of employees’ skills.

Remote developed the course internally and later made it free to the public under the name AI for Actual Work. It runs five hours across five parts, moving from prompt basics and choosing tools to building and deploying agents, then presenting finished work. The goal, according to Remote, is for each participant to leave with one reusable workflow for a real task. The guidance stresses checking AI’s answers, protecting sensitive information, and keeping human review in consequential work. Remote co-founder Marcelo Lebre said in a July 24 post that the company had released the course free to the public after developing it internally.

Van der Voort argued the employer has a responsibility: if it expects staff to use AI, it should help them learn it rather than simply replace them. He said a company that employs a whole bunch of people should take responsibility for the people who work for it. He said employers would not be able to fire all their people and find new people good with this. He said the training raises the foundational level managers can expect across Remote. His stated aim is to avoid basic mistakes and remove uncertainty about whether an employee knows AI could make a particular problem easy to solve.

Lebre wrote that employees need to understand what information must not be shared, when an answer needs checking and who should review it before use. The course also asks whether a task is appropriate for AI at all. Lebre wrote that payroll, employment, compliance, tax, legal and people operations affect people’s lives. He argued that accuracy and trust require human judgment to remain involved. He and van der Voort helped build the course, with feedback from teams including payroll, legal, customer experience, sales and engineering.

The course predates the newly reported review requirement. Remote describes the curriculum as moving through five parts: foundations, tool selection, building, deployment and showcase. Foundations covers trying real prompts, learning about model behavior and keeping a workflow worth reusing. Building covers creating agents using context, tools and loops that let them work through tasks. Deployment covers connecting data, designing for real use and maintaining what has been built.

The story offers no independent assessment of employees’ skills or results. It leaves open whether the requirement created lasting capability beyond course completion. Van der Voort’s expectations for the training are not measured results presented in the interview. Remote’s claims about participation and the training’s intended benefits come from executives. The showcase part covers presenting finished work, identifying work that can be removed and helping lead AI adoption.

stories.Headline: UC San Diego students build RAIN to link AI research with industry
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego students built the Real-world AI Network, or RAIN, and the university described it in a November 19 account, according to Superpower Daily on November 22, 2026. The network was established during the 2025, 26 academic year, so it is an existing initiative rather than a newly launched organization. RAIN combines a digital discovery platform called RAINdrop with faculty guidance, startup mentorship and industry connections. Co-founder Pranav Kumar Soma, a computer science master’s student and research fellow, said RAINdrop launched a few months before the university’s November account. Raj Krishnan, a UC San Diego engineering alumnus who earned his doctorate in 2010, helped establish RAIN alongside Soma and Aryan Pershad.

According to the university, RAIN now involves more than 7,000 students, over 50 faculty members and upwards of 40 student organizations. Every campus startup accelerator and entrepreneurship group also takes part in the network. RAIN organizes four groups, students, faculty, industry and entrepreneurs, around research and technical challenges, startup mentorship, recruiting and investor introductions. Its advisors include computational chemistry professor Rommie Amaro and Ilkay Altintas, chief data science officer at the San Diego Supercomputer Center. RAIN receives advice from faculty affiliated with the Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing and the School of Biological Sciences.

Soma said students were already using RAINdrop to explore labs, projects and companies, but he described that as early feedback rather than a measured result. He said the platform had not been shown to accelerate research. Pershad, a second-year bioinformatics student and founder of Stele Health, said the campus resources RAIN seeks to connect span high-performance computing, data science and application expertise in robotics, embedded intelligence and virtual biology. He argued for bringing those resources together rather than treating the university’s AI work as the domain of one discipline or student group. Krishnan leads the biotechnology company Sigil Biosciences.

Amaro pointed to biology as a field where AI is changing scientific work amid large volumes of complex data. She described RAIN’s promise as connecting students with fresh ideas and technical skills to researchers facing difficult scientific problems. Altintas emphasized opportunities for students to work alongside researchers and industry partners and to gain experience turning ideas into practical applications. Lucian Clark, a senior at Pacific Ridge School in Carlsbad, serves as RAIN’s AI and Biomedical Innovation Intern and hopes to become a physician.

The network’s four constituencies connect around technical challenges, startup mentorship, recruiting and investor introductions. The university said AI at UC San Diego spans so many disciplines that students may not realize the full range of opportunities available. The founding group combines student leadership with entrepreneurial experience, and the advisors connect students with research expertise and wider scientific networks. Amaro and Altintas advise on industry-defined challenges and government AI initiatives.

The network relies on faculty to connect students with scientific expertise and problems defined by industry or government initiatives. RAIN’s remit goes beyond helping someone locate a lab, connecting people seeking research experience with the relationships involved in building a company or finding a job. The practical test is whether easier discovery turns into lasting research relationships, startup work or hiring opportunities. The reported student feedback does not yet establish measurable outcomes, and the key constraint is that RAIN has substantial participation without evidence that RAINdrop has sped up research.

The articles leave open whether the network will produce those lasting relationships, startup work or hiring opportunities. They also leave open whether easier discovery will translate into measurable results. The articles give no further account of what happens next. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Gartner predicts half of organizations will let AI agents run IT operations by 2030
stories.Summary:
Gartner released on October 26 its list of top AI trends in infrastructure and IT operations for 2027, predicting that half of all organizations will let AI agents run IT operations with minimal human involvement by 2030, up from close to zero in 2026. The firm said organizations without a strong infrastructure and operations function, the team that runs servers, networks and cloud services, will be over twice as likely to fail in their AI initiatives through 2030. Gartner also expects companies that pay for agents by the token with no spending cap to blow their initial cost estimates by more than 50% through 2027. In a Gartner survey of 272 heads of I&O conducted in April and May 2026, 58% said scaling AI proofs of concept into I&O adoption will be an important priority in the next 12 months. The report describes five interlinked trends, starting with agents taking over routine IT work such as incident triage, change validation and remediation, which Gartner says shifts operations from a human-in-the-loop model, where a person approves each step, to a human-on-the-loop model, where a person supervises.

Because an agent completes a task in many steps and every step uses tokens, Gartner recommends a strict no telemetry, no deployment policy under which an agent does not go live if a team cannot track its token use. Gartner predicts that by 2029, 80% of large enterprises will run production AI workloads across at least three different infrastructure environments, including public clouds, neoclouds, on-premises data centers and edge locations. It also predicts that by 2030, 25% of enterprises will merge their network operations centers and security operations centers, up from 5% in 2026, and that those that do will cut total spending on tooling and staff by more than 25%. Jonathan Forest, a vice president analyst at Gartner, said AI is creating one of the most significant shifts the I&O function has ever faced, and that rather than trying to address every aspect of AI at once, heads of I&O should focus on a small number of strategic investments that deliver meaningful impact. He said heads of I&O who fail to restructure their organization around agentic AI risk higher costs, poor operational agility and performance, and ultimately irrelevance.

He also said the high cost of AI infrastructure leaves little room for error and places I&O at the center of enterprise AI success, and that heads of I&O must elevate their teams' capabilities, reduce technical debt and shift from reactive operations to proactively enabling enterprise AI. The report ties these trends to a broader change in the I&O role, which Gartner sees moving from a gatekeeper to orchestrating the enterprise AI platform, bringing the function closer to the business so it can deploy and scale AI securely and at a manageable cost. Gartner noted in August 2026 that AI inference costs per agentic workflow will still increase more than fivefold through 2028, even as token prices fall. The articles do not say what happens next beyond these predictions.
