stories.Headline: Historians of technology call recent US tech outages routine failures in innovation cycles
stories.Summary:
A nationwide ground stop halted all flights across the United States, customers found themselves unable to conduct transactions at America’s largest bank, Microsoft Outlook went down, Apple services became inaccessible, and even the National Security Agency’s classified email system went offline, according to a New York Times report published on November 21, 2026. The article, written by William J. Broad, describes a spate of recent tech outages that annoyed and puzzled many people across the country. Some officials linked the failures to routine tech upgrades, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested that a cause might be the global rush to build defenses against A.I. hackers. No public evidence suggested that cyberattacks had caused any of the failures, the report stated.

Historians of technology call such mishaps mundane, arguing that disasters in complex systems are inevitable parts of innovation’s boom-bust cycles. In ages past, the report says, advancements often came with the loss of thousands of lives, citing steamboat explosions at the dawn of the industrial age, the Hindenburg disaster in the early years of commercial flight, and the Apollo 1 fire near the start of the space age. From this view, the recent outages are simply part of the learning curve and are blessedly bloodless. Because inventors tend to work at the cutting edge of physics, materials science and human understanding, significant failures and trial and error are the main way they uncover the hidden flaws behind their bright ideas, according to the article.

Historians tend to agree that cycles of progress and failure have been part and parcel in the creation of steam power, electrical grids, airplanes, chemicals, medicine, rocketry and computers, the report states. The article presents this pattern as a paradox of advancement, in which the same drive that produces new tools also produces the failures that reveal their hidden flaws. The piece was published under a headline asking whether a new era of A.I.-driven chaos might just be progress, and it frames the recent outages within that longer history. The report does not say what specific fixes or changes, if any, followed the ground stop, the bank outage, the Outlook disruption, the Apple service failure or the NSA email outage.

The article names William J. Broad as the author and gives November 21, 2026, as the publication date, and it attributes the historical view to historians of technology rather than to any single named expert. It records Marco Rubio’s suggestion about defenses against A.I. hackers while noting that no public evidence tied the failures to cyberattacks. The report does not identify the largest bank, the operators of the affected services, or any agency response beyond the NSA system going offline. It ends its available text with the historians’ broad agreement on cycles of progress and failure, and it offers no further account of what happens next.

Articles.Title: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.

stories.headline_source: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.

stories.Headline: Researchers link hospital support and job crafting to positive AI attitudes in nurses
stories.Summary:
Xuan Cui, Haihong Li, Min Shi, and Ting Zhao conducted a cross-sectional investigation among clinical nurses in China. The researchers published their findings in Frontiers in Medicine by November 21, 2026. They studied how hospital backing and self-initiated professional modifications connect with technology reception. The team analyzed responses from 305 clinical nurses at a tertiary grade A general hospital. Their work focused on the link between organizational support, job crafting, and artificial intelligence attitudes.

The study required data from 305 nurses at a Chinese tertiary grade A general hospital between April and June 2026. It used the Perceived Organizational Support Scale revised by Li, the Nurse Job Crafting Scale translated by Cao, and the Attitudes towards AI Application at Work scale. The researchers followed Institutional Review Board approval reference LW-20260402001-01 and used the Wenjuanxing digital survey platform. Participants included 280 females and 25 males, with 135 nurses aged 30 to under 40 years. Educational levels ranged from one doctoral credential to 255 bachelor degrees and 36 technical college diplomas.

The authors stated that proactive job crafting accounts for 60.8 percent of the association between organizational support and positive AI attitudes. They explained that organizational support theory suggests employees reciprocate employer value with constructive attitudes and innovative behaviors. The researchers noted that job crafting involves task, relational, and cognitive modifications to optimize job demands and resources. They emphasized that their cross-sectional design reflects statistical associations rather than proven causal effects. The team argued that identifying workplace conditions can alleviate anxieties and encourage proactive technological adoption.

A systematic review of 37 studies with 10,000 participants showed nurses feel guarded optimism and unease regarding algorithmic transparency. A qualitative synthesis across five nations identified concerns about professional displacement, clinical autonomy, and workloads from poorly integrated interfaces. Nurses are affected because they are the largest cadre of direct patient care providers and critical to implementation. These professionals expressed fears regarding ethical liability, deskilling, and the loss of patient-centered human connection. Many nurses reported ambivalence and cautious sentiment across the healthcare workforce.

AI is expanding through clinical inpatient and outpatient settings for decision support, documentation, risk warning, shift scheduling, and patient education. A meta-analysis of 23,451 nurses across 18 countries linked perceived support to lower burnout and reduced resignation intentions. A study of 472 Jordanian nurses connected structural organizational backing to sustained electronic health record utilization. Earlier Chinese investigations identified job crafting as a conduit between institutional backing and innovative behaviors or well-being. The authors observed that scholarship rarely examined job crafting as an explicit mediator for artificial intelligence acceptance.

The researchers suggest that longitudinal follow-up trials are necessary to prove causal effects. Future efforts may focus on the 75.7 percent of nurses who have not attended formal training. The articles leave open how to improve the 45.9 percent institutional device availability rate. They do not specify how to resolve the identified fears of professional displacement or ethical liability. The text does not detail specific policy changes needed to increase organizational support.

Articles.Title: Job Crafting Links Hospital Support to Favorable AI Attitudes in Nurses

stories.Headline: Roberto Riggio models distributed AI pipelines with a dual plane orchestration framework
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Roberto Riggio formulated a mathematical model and algorithmic framework to orchestrate distributed artificial intelligence workloads across converged connect-compute networks. The work was published in the Journal of Network and Systems Management by researcher Roberto Riggio. The investigation addresses deployment of complex multi-stage machine learning pipelines across heterogeneous physical substrates spanning end-user devices, near-edge servers, far-edge clusters, and centralized clouds. The central architectural contribution formalizes Artificial Intelligence Functions as modular and independently deployable software components encapsulating individual stages of a machine learning workflow. The framework establishes an explicit functional split separating an inference-focused data plane from a parameter-focused control plane.

The architecture treats Artificial Intelligence Functions as first-class orchestratable building blocks, each encapsulating an individual pipeline stage from lightweight sensor filtering and video anonymization to neural network inference and federated averaging. Every unit exposes four operational interfaces, with the northbound interface if1 providing an application-level configuration entry point for runtime parameters such as loaded model architectures, inference batch sizes, and telemetry reporting intervals. The westbound mechanisms divide into the if3 interface for the machine learning data plane and the if2 interface for the machine learning control plane, which exchanges model parameters, gradient updates, distilled representations, and distribution statistics. The data plane carries ordered, high-bandwidth, latency-critical inference traffic demanding strict sub-hundred-millisecond latencies with strictly acyclic dependency flow. The control plane carries episodic bulk transmissions of model state dispatched at intervals ranging from seconds to hours, accommodating latencies up to several seconds, often forming cyclic or hub-and-spoke topologies.

The author notes that split inference, wherein intermediate activations of a single partitioned model are transmitted between nodes, is classified under the data plane because intermediate activations represent continuous request-specific payloads that strictly gate execution progress. The paper formalizes the global mapping challenge as an Integer Linear Programming model aimed at minimizing cumulative placement cost while satisfying capacity, mapping uniqueness, semantic anchoring, latency, and multi-commodity flow conservation constraints. The formulation ensures each virtual function is mapped to exactly one substrate node, each physical node hosts at most one function from a given request, and cumulative resource demands never exceed available physical capacities. Hardware acceleration constraints enforce that functions requiring graphical processing units are mapped exclusively to acceleration-equipped substrate nodes, while anchoring constraints bind specific functions to fixed physical endpoints such as physical cameras or localized radio controllers. The author developed a two-phase greedy heuristic termed AIFG-H that decouples node placement from link routing, sorting functions in topological order along the acyclic data plane graph and mapping data plane links along latency-shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm while routing control plane links along hop-shortest paths.

Experimental evaluations across multiple substrate topologies demonstrated that the greedy heuristic achieves near-optimal resource placement costs while decreasing algorithmic computation times by three to four orders of magnitude compared to standard integer linear programming solutions. The evaluation framework benchmarked the algorithms across nine experimental scenarios combining three Waxman random substrate sizes, small with 20 nodes, medium with 50 nodes, and large with 100 nodes, with three request complexity tiers ranging from simple graphs of three to five functions to complex graphs of eight to twelve functions. Experiments evaluated 500 problem instances per scenario on server hardware equipped with an Intel Xeon Gold processor and 256 gigabytes of memory. The greedy heuristic was compared against exact solutions computed with IBM CPLEX version 22.1 under a 3600-second execution limit, as well as three comparative baseline algorithms: an acceleration-extended service function chaining heuristic designated SFC-ACC, a node-ranking virtual network embedding algorithm termed VNE-NR, and an adapted composite edge application algorithm known as CEA.

To isolate the specific impact of the control and data plane split, an ablated heuristic variant termed AIFG-H-uni was evaluated, wherein link differentiation was disabled. The study positions its technical motivation within the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence workloads across sectors such as automated mobility, healthcare, industrial automation, and immersive entertainment. These emerging applications integrate interdependent functional stages encompassing data acquisition, feature extraction, real-time inference, and centralized model consolidation. While fifth-generation mobile networks provide programmable connectivity fabrics through features like network slicing, multi-access edge computing, and disaggregated radio access, orchestrating non-monolithic machine learning pipelines across these fabrics remains challenging.

Traditional orchestration architectures rooted in virtual network function and service function chain placement fail to capture the dual nature of modern artificial intelligence tasks, typically modeling service requests as chains or directed acyclic graphs carrying a single class of uniform inter-component traffic. Consequently, standard frameworks cannot effectively reconcile the latency-critical streaming demands of live inference execution with the high-bandwidth, latency-tolerant bulk transfers required for centralized retraining, federated model parameter aggregation, drift-triggered updates, or canary rollouts. The publication details two representative industrial use cases, the first examining a pedestrian crossing warning system designed to detect approaching vehicles and trigger acoustic or visual alarms in real time. The corresponding application graph connects five functions: a camera-anchored video ingestion unit, an obfuscation component that blurs faces and license plates for privacy compliance, a hardware-accelerated feature extraction unit running object detection, an actuation interface controlling physical crossing signals, and a cloud-hosted consolidation engine managing federated learning updates.

The second use case targets adaptive video streaming using the MPEG Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP protocol, in which telemetry functions interface with an Open Radio Access Network Near-Real-Time Radio Access Network Intelligent Controller via the A1 interface to monitor physical channel conditions. Co-located bitrate prediction models process radio measurements to forecast client throughput, directing proactive chunk selection at a central media server while cloud-based update functions push revised model weights downstream over control plane links. The framework represents application requirements as an Artificial Intelligence Forwarding Graph, defined as a directed multigraph where vertices denote individual functions and edges represent typed virtual links constructed over typed triples to accommodate parallel edges connecting the same pair of functions. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Rep. Nathaniel Moran co-founds House AI caucus to balance safety and innovation
stories.Summary:
Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas co-founded a new House AI caucus on November 21, 2026. This legislative group aims to address the rapid growth of artificial intelligence within the United States government. The representative believes that Congress must act quickly to manage the evolving landscape of this technology. He intends to lead efforts that balance safety with the need for technical progress.

The initiative requires the creation of specific safeguards to mitigate the potential risks associated with artificial intelligence. These measures must be carefully designed so they do not stifle innovation or slow down domestic development. Representative Moran argues that overly strict regulations could allow China to gain a significant competitive advantage. He believes the United States must maintain its leadership in the global technology sector.

Representative Moran is responsible for championing this balanced approach to legislative oversight of artificial intelligence. He stated that the government should protect the public without hindering the growth of new tools. The congressman emphasized that the goal is to secure the nation while fostering a pro-innovation environment. He believes that strategic oversight will prevent risks without sacrificing the speed of American discovery.

Articles.Title: Rep. Moran co-founds House AI caucus, says safeguards should not stifle innovation

stories.headline_source: Rep. Moran co-founds House AI caucus, says safeguards should not stifle innovation

stories.Headline: DARPA awards New Mexico State University $600,000 to develop verified AI reasoning architectures
stories.Summary:
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency awarded a research grant to New Mexico State University on November 20, 2026. This funding supports the development of verified neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence architectures for safety-critical defense engineering. The agency provided 600,000 dollars for this specific research effort over a two-year period. Computer scientists at the university will pair machine learning pattern recognition with formal logical proofs. This work falls under the Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering program.

The project, called Project SPARTA, involves New Mexico State University, Arizona State University, and the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Professor Son Tran and Assistant Professor Stylianos Vasileiou lead the effort at New Mexico State University. Professor Chitta Baral directs the Arizona State University group, while Professors Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno lead the Nebraska team. The program requires native algorithmic compositionality instead of using post-hoc validation filters on large models. It utilizes splitting-based logic programming, polynomially-bounded automated reasoning, and tensorized adaptation interfaces.

Principal investigator Son Tran stated that integrating these AI branches provides machine learning speed with verifiability. He noted that reasoning proofs offer strong logical explainability and computational tractability for practical engineering. Tran emphasized that computational tractability is the make-or-break criterion for real-time deployment in industrial systems. The goal is to replace unverified statistical guesses with rigorous logical guarantees. This approach ensures that mathematical proofs execute within deterministic processing budgets.

Superpower Daily reported that this initiative represents fundamental basic science rather than a commercial product. The outlet noted the challenge of scaling formal verification across complex systems beyond laboratory benchmarks. Defense contractors building unmanned aerial systems or radar signal processors are affected by these outputs. These contractors could eventually integrate reusable verification libraries into safety-critical firmware. University research offices must also manage subawards and export controls like ITAR and EAR.

Deep neural networks rely on correlation rather than deduction, which creates vulnerabilities in safety-critical domains. Failures can occur in flight control software, aerospace trajectory synthesis, autonomous naval navigation, and power grid automation. DARPA's Defense Sciences Office identified the current serial configuration of AI safety as fundamentally brittle. The CLARA program was solicited as a Disruption Opportunity to fast-track high-risk basic research. McAllister and Quinn noted that these opportunities challenge prevailing commercial assumptions.

During the first twelve months, teams will establish theoretical formalisms and engineer prototype mapping modules. The second year involves integrating algorithms into a unified open-source toolchain for rigorous benchmarking. Researchers will measure verification runtime, proof validity, and model generalization using DARPA-supplied engineering challenges. The articles leave open whether formal verification can remain scalable across arbitrary complex systems. They do not state if the project will meet all its technical milestones.

Articles.Title: DARPA Grants NMSU $600K for Verified AI Reasoning

stories.headline_source: DARPA Grants NMSU $600K for Verified AI Reasoning

stories.Headline: Researchers find data infrastructure gaps limit AI use in ESG financial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers Miehleketo Mathebula, Abiodun Modupe, Vukosi Marivate, and Elda Du Toit conducted a systematic literature review. They published their investigation in the journal Discover Artificial Intelligence by November 21, 2026. The study assessed how artificial intelligence is applied across environmental, social, and governance financial intelligence. They examined 70 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2017 and 2025. The authors wanted to find the cause of operational limitations in sustainable finance analytics.

The review requires moving past proprietary data dependencies and incompatible metadata schemas. It identifies gaps in unstandardised disclosure environments across the Global Reporting Initiative and Sustainability Accounting Standards Board. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures also creates inconsistent reporting structures. Researchers used IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and MDPI databases starting January 7, 2026. They analyzed 1,623 candidate records before narrowing the final corpus to 70 articles.

The authors stated that computational model architectures have significantly outpaced the required data infrastructures. They argued that principal constraints arise from institutional disparities rather than algorithmic complexity. The researchers urged the community to stop treating commercial ESG ratings as objective ground-truth labels. They also said that post-hoc explainability cannot compensate for unverified data provenance. They claimed technological interventions cannot fix absent semantic crosswalks.

The study affects the research community and those using high-stakes financial environments. It notes that African institutions contributed only eight studies compared to larger volumes from Asia, Europe, and North America. South Africa produced 11 documents but showed very low global integration. The review found that most tasks were executed in isolation on curated benchmark corpora. These tasks rarely demonstrated integration with live compliance verification or supervisory auditing pipelines.

The background shows a shift from traditional machine learning to generative language modeling. Traditional machine learning appeared 40 times, while deep learning appeared 36 times. Natural language processing had 26 implementations, and general large language models had 15. The review used a six-criterion appraisal framework to score studies up to ten points. This process involved two independent reviewers who achieved a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.82.

Next, the authors propose a conceptual architecture for preprocessing, semantic standardisation, and governance oversight. They illustrated this using a South African report prepared under the King IV governance code. The articles leave this architecture as an unvalidated design blueprint rather than a deployed solution. Future progress requires concerted global investments in open-access benchmark datasets. The researchers leave the actual deployment of these software solutions open.

Articles.Title: Data Infrastructure Gaps Limit Artificial Intelligence in ESG Financial Intelligence Review

stories.Headline: University of California signs $1.2 million annual OpenAI deal to bring ChatGPT to campuses
stories.Summary:
The University of California signed a systemwide agreement with OpenAI worth $1.2 million a year to give students access to ChatGPT and other artificial intelligence tools, the New York Post reported on November 21, 2026. The partnership, which expands on a 2024 campus-by-campus arrangement, will bring ChatGPT Edu and the coding tool Codex to UC campuses in the coming weeks. The deal covers basic AI models, while individual campuses and users may buy access to more advanced versions at discounted rates. UC President James B. Milliken announced the agreement in a letter to faculty.

Milliken said the purchase would ensure equitable access to widely used tools while providing stronger data protections and lower costs, and he stressed that the agreement sets no new academic policies and does not require students or professors to use the technology. The commitment reportedly caught members of UC's Academic Senate off guard, and faculty leaders raised concerns late last month that administrators had not sufficiently consulted educators. Academic Senate Chair Susannah Scott said it is unwise to give students universal access to a tool capable of performing the academic work required to earn a degree without first addressing faculty concerns about curriculum, teaching and academic integrity. A UC spokesperson pushed back on claims that faculty were left out, telling EdSource that the senate had been consulted and that its feedback was thoughtful and helpful.

Greg Leazer, an associate professor of information studies at UCLA, told the Los Angeles Times that ChatGPT reduces learning and substitutes homogenized slop in place of the productive struggle of careful reading, discussion and writing. The criticism comes amid broader concerns about declining academic skills, including reports of college instructors having to teach students basic math. UC Berkeley mathematics professor Richard Borcherds, who made headlines last month for no longer grading homework because of AI, said he now bases grades mainly on in-person exams with no electronic devices allowed, adding that online exams are now a waste of time because several students just use AI to answer the questions. Supporters have argued the partnership gives all students access to tools that wealthier classmates can already afford, while some educators told the Post they feel AI is being shoved down their throats.

Articles.Title: California colleges strike major AI deal as educators rage at machine learning: ‘Homogenized slop’

stories.headline_source: California colleges strike major AI deal as educators rage at machine learning: ‘Homogenized slop’

stories.Headline: Researchers argue clinicians must critically assess AI outputs to ensure safe clinical use
stories.Summary:
A perspective published in the journal Discover Artificial Intelligence on November 21, 2026, by researchers Ryan W. Hunton, Tama The and Jonathan Ilgen argues that the safe clinical use of artificial intelligence may depend less on how well a model performs and more on whether clinicians can evaluate what it produces. Large language models are increasingly used in clinical settings to support reasoning and decision-making, and early studies suggest they perform strongly on medical knowledge and reasoning tasks with the potential to reduce medical errors. However, the authors note that emerging evidence highlights significant safety concerns, because AI outputs can contain clinically significant management errors that are not readily apparent to users. This leaves open the central question of how to integrate these tools into practice in a way that consistently improves patient outcomes.

The authors argue that AI-assisted reasoning must be examined as an unfolding sequence of decisions rather than an isolated single moment, beginning with the initial choice of whether to consult AI for a given clinical question. The process then moves through deciding how to engage with the tool, how to interpret its output, and finally whether to act on the guidance in a clinical case, and each stage introduces distinct points of vulnerability and potential failure. Clinicians face risks that include inappropriate tool selection, providing incomplete or biased inputs, showing overconfidence in fluent responses, and failing to recognize underlying errors or appreciate clinical nuance. These vulnerabilities are shaped by the same clinician factors that govern clinical reasoning more broadly, such as medical experience, clinical workload and how providers handle uncertainty in practice.

The authors conclude that safe clinical implementation depends not merely on advancing model quality but on cultivating the clinician's ability to critically assess model responses. They say preparing clinicians to identify when algorithmic outputs must be questioned, verified or entirely set aside will be crucial as automated reasoning tools become more deeply embedded in routine patient care. Recognizing that AI-clinician collaboration functions as a continuous process reveals key opportunities for targeted medical training, according to the analysis. The article was published with the DOI 10.1007/s44163-026-02851-3.

Articles.Title: Clinical Safety with Artificial Intelligence Depends on Clinicians Questioning Model Outputs

stories.headline_source: Clinical Safety with Artificial Intelligence Depends on Clinicians Questioning Model Outputs

stories.Headline: Review finds deep learning aids forensic dentistry but needs human oversight
stories.Summary:
A scoping review published in BMC Medical Imaging on the applications of artificial intelligence in dental imaging and forensic odontology has concluded that deep learning models reach high diagnostic accuracy while methodological limits mean the tools should assist rather than replace specialists. The review was written by Gurbet Alev Oztas Sahiner and Bengisu Karatas, who set out to map how artificial intelligence is used across the main forensic tasks of dental age estimation, biological sex estimation, human identification and tooth classification. The authors also examined recent multimodal artificial intelligence applications in forensic dentistry and described current diagnostic performance, existing methodological limitations and directions for future investigation. The work was carried out under the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, and the researchers searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Google Scholar for relevant studies published from January 2022 to December 2025. The search strategy combined keywords related to the main topic with explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria to identify original research across the field, and the review included original studies evaluating machine learning, deep learning, hybrid models and multimodal large language models applied to forensic dentistry.

Two independent reviewers performed duplicate study selection, data extraction and formal methodological quality assessment using the QUADAS-AI tool, and because the selected literature showed pronounced methodological heterogeneity the authors conducted a narrative synthesis rather than a quantitative statistical meta-analysis. A total of twenty articles met all the predefined criteria for inclusion, and among the analyzed applications dental age estimation was the most widely studied forensic problem. Human identification was the second most common subject of study, followed in descending frequency by biological sex estimation and tooth classification. Deep learning architectures based on convolutional neural networks demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy across various dental imaging modalities, and the evaluated networks performed effectively on panoramic radiographs, cone-beam computed tomography images, intraoral scans and cephalometric radiographs. These results show that deep learning systems can process the diverse two-dimensional and three-dimensional radiographic records commonly used in dental forensic investigations.

Despite the positive diagnostic results, the evidence base revealed notable methodological weaknesses, and the researchers emphasized that the existing literature was limited by retrospective study designs, reliance on patient-specific sample sets, a widespread lack of external validation and high methodological heterogeneity. The authors therefore stress that although artificial intelligence offers strong potential to improve standardization, efficiency and objectivity in forensic analysis, it must presently function solely as a decision-support aid with human oversight. The review notes that growing interest in artificial intelligence stems from improved objectivity, efficiency and repeatability in forensic analysis, and the authors conclude that automated algorithms should currently serve as decision-support tools with humans remaining in the loop. The article was published with the DOI 10.1186/s12880-026-03073-w, and the news report on the review was written by Blake Davidson and dated November 21, 2026. The articles do not say what further research or validation the authors propose beyond their call for future investigation, and they give no timetable for clinical adoption of the reviewed tools.

Articles.Title: Scoping Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Accuracy and Gaps in Forensic Odontology

stories.headline_source: Scoping Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Accuracy and Gaps in Forensic Odontology

stories.Headline: Researchers track a surge in artificial intelligence studies for pulmonary embolism
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a bibliometric analysis on November 21, 2026, to track global trends in artificial intelligence for pulmonary embolism. The study examined 590 scientific publications indexed in the Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection databases. These investigators used specialized software packages including CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and R software to analyze academic literature. The research focused on papers published between 2006 and 2025 to map the evolution of the field.

The analysis shows that scholarly output grew slowly until 2017, when only 62 articles represented 10.5 percent of the total. Production surged from 2018 onward, with 375 articles or 63.6 percent published between 2023 and 2025. This network includes 3,844 authors and 1,377 institutions across 63 countries, with the United States and China being the most prolific. The United States produced 257 articles with 9,791 citations, while China contributed 117 articles with 1,320 citations.

T. Xiong, K. Abulimiti, Y. Zhang, and L. Shi stated that theoretical development has outpaced practical healthcare implementation. They noted that current research focuses heavily on image-based detection rather than validated clinical decision support tools. The authors argued that existing models lack proven clinical effectiveness or verified improvements in patient outcomes. They suggested that future progress requires prospective, multicentre studies featuring rigorous external validation and multidisciplinary collaboration.

This research is driven by the global health burden of pulmonary embolism, which causes significant cardiovascular morbidity and death. The authors observed that the landscape of diagnosis, risk stratification, and prognostication had never been systematically mapped. Recent trends show a surge in interest regarding prediction and risk factors within peer-reviewed investigations. Future efforts must address fundamental methodological shortcomings to move these artificial intelligence systems into routine clinical care.

Articles.Title: Bibliometric Review Tracks Surge in Pulmonary Embolism Artificial Intelligence Studies

stories.headline_source: Bibliometric Review Tracks Surge in Pulmonary Embolism Artificial Intelligence Studies

stories.Headline: David Fincher defends AI use in new film as critics decry visible flaws
stories.Summary:
Critics and fans began complaining on X this past Thursday about the heavy use of artificial intelligence in David Fincher's new movie. The film, titled The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, has faced backlash following early screenings of the studio production. Patrick Tomasso, a filmmaker and critic on YouTube, claimed the movie is overshadowed by some of the most blatant AI use he has ever seen. Another user who claims to work in visual effects described the amount of AI in the film as astounding to an absurd degree.

The technology reportedly causes faces to change mid scene, creates goofy physics, and results in the garbling of fine lines. Tomasso noted that full body performance swaps and AI signs are visible, and the trailer shows people holding reins for horses that are actually behind them. This project follows a report from Bloomberg in March stating that Fincher used AI post production tools from InterPositive, a company owned by Ben Affleck. Fincher also previously used generative AI to clean up the composition of shots for a new 4K restoration of his 1995 film, Se7en.

David Fincher defended the use of these tools in a timely interview with the Los Angeles Times. He stated that he is not a Luddite and questioned why filmmakers should stop iterating on an art form that is only a hundred years old. Fincher argued that since the technology exists, there is no reason why filmmakers should not use it to their advantage. He compared the evolution of cinema to the thousands of years humans have spent painting to justify the adoption of new tools.

Fincher was previously known for his meticulous attention to detail in classics like Fight Club and The Social Network. He had earned praise for using invisible visual effects to create refined images without the audience noticing any alterations. Some observers suggest that the smooth sheen of AI imagery is a natural extension of his lifelong preoccupation with correcting flaws. It remains to be seen how the general public will react to these technical choices upon the wide release of the film.

Articles.Title: David Fincher’s New Movie Is Apparently Stuffed With AI

stories.headline_source: David Fincher’s New Movie Is Apparently Stuffed With AI

stories.Headline: Six FLORetina-ICOOR 2026 courses follow AI through retinal imaging, trials, atrophy care and robotic surgery
stories.Summary:
The FLORetina International Congress on OCT Angiography, En Face OCT, and Advances in OCT (FLORetina-ICOOR) will run December 3 to 6 at the Fortezza da Basso in Florence, the articles state. The course listings published so far include 2 courses tagged AI and 4 more under an AI and robotics heading. Six instructional courses at this year's congress follow artificial intelligence through retinal imaging, drug development, geographic atrophy care, and robotic surgery. At last year's meeting, much of the discussion was about what algorithms could do. The 2026 courses spend more time on how to use AI tools in practice, including how to validate them, put them into clinic workflows, build them into trial endpoints, and explain them to patients.

The course "Pearls and Pitfalls of Artificial Intelligence for Retinal Research and Practice" is co-chaired by Daniela Ferrara, MD, PhD, FASRS, and Usha Chakravarthy, MD, PhD, and co-moderated by Giovanni Staurenghi, MD. Stela Vujosevic, MD, PhD, FEBO, will speak on OCT-based algorithms and Daniel Ting, MD, PhD, on color fundus photography. Pearse Keane, MD, FRCOphth, will discuss oculomics, the use of retinal imaging as a window to systemic health. Valeria De Filippis, MD, PhD, will cover AI-based mining of electronic medical records, and Nadia Waheed will address AI in retinal research and clinical trials. Lajos Csincsik will discuss validation approaches for clinical imaging algorithms, and the course description names multimodal and agentic AI as emerging approaches.

A second Ferrara-led course, co-chaired with Waheed, is titled "Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Trials in Retinal Diseases: From Imaging Biomarkers to Digital Twins." Its description says AI is becoming a mandatory technology in drug development for retinal diseases. The talks include imaging biomarkers as trial endpoints (Waheed), treatment response prediction in exudative macular disease (Virginia Mares, MD, MSc, PhD), and GA progression prediction (Oliver Leingang, PhD). Ferrara will present on AI-enabled digital twins, Hrvoje Bogunovic, PhD, on external control arms and real-world data, and Marion Munk, MD, PhD, on the move toward fully digital, in silico trials. According to the organizers, digital twins could make synthetic control arms possible, especially in early-phase trials, and barriers include data standards, governance, cybersecurity, and regulatory frameworks they describe as outdated.

Anat Loewenstein, MD, MHA, who discussed home OCT monitoring at FLORetina 2025, will cover AI-enabled home OCT monitoring in clinical trials. That talk comes as home-based platforms such as Notal Vision's SCANLY, which received FDA De Novo authorization in 2024, move into research use. SAIVO was founded in May 2025 and ran its first course at FLORetina last year. Its 2026 symposium, "Implementing AI in retina and posterior segment diseases: triumphs and challenges," is again moderated by founding members Munk and Quan Dong Nguyen. Mario Romano, MD, PhD, will discuss lessons from Vision Code 2026, and Niranjan Manoharan, MD, will present an imaging-integrated prescreening pipeline for GA trial recruitment.

Roomasa Channa, MD, will describe putting an automated GA area algorithm into clinical workflows, and Rita Wolf, MD, will report on validation and outcomes of autonomous AI-based retinopathy screening in children. Talks cover AI quantification of hyperreflective vitreous particles in uveitis, human-in-the-loop triage of choroidal lesions for possible melanoma on ultra-widefield imaging, and foundation models for external-eye imaging in oculoplastics. The symposium closes with Mary K. Daly, MD, "Informed Consent for AI in an Epistemic Void." "AI in Clinical Practice: A Practical Patient-Centered Roadmap for Geographic Atrophy Management," organized by Roy Schwartz, MD, and Caroline Baumal, MD, follows the GA care pathway in 5 steps. The steps are differential diagnosis against genetic mimics (Dinah Zur, MD), AI-based risk stratification (Gregor Reiter, MD, MSc, PhD), measuring and monitoring from baseline to treatment response (Aude Ambresin, MD, PhD), functional monitoring (Baumal), and predicting individual patient trajectories (Schwartz).

Omer Trivizki, MD, MBA, closes the course with a look at future needs, and the organizers promise live demonstrations and real-world cases. The United States now has 2 approved GA therapies, but specialists have pointed out that AI-driven imaging analysis for GA has not been cleared for routine US clinical practice, while some such tools are already used in Europe. Ophthalmology Times has also reported on investigational AI tools, such as functional OCT, that aim to estimate retinal sensitivity from structural scans, and those tools have not yet been cleared by regulators. "Artificial Intelligence in Vitreoretinal Surgery: A crash course," organized by Rodrigo Anguita Henriquez, MD, and Martin Zinkernagel, MD, PhD, is written for surgeons who say they lack practical AI training. It starts with the basics of machine learning and neural networks (Philippe Valmaggia, MD) and asks whether no-code AI is ready for clinicians (Lorenzo Ferro Desideri, MD).

It then covers proliferative diabetic retinopathy (Aude Couturier, MD), predictive modeling (Zinkernagel), and real-time computer vision for intraoperative guidance, presented by congress president Stanislao Rizzo, MD. Anguita Henriquez, MD, MBBS ends with "From generative to agentic AI: the road to surgical intelligence." "Robotics, AI and the Future of Eye Surgery," organized by Jean-Pierre Hubschman, MD, may be the most forward-looking session of the meeting. Fanny Nerinckx, MD, will present first-in-human experience with the Luca robotic system.

In 2024, Luca was used to perform 7 vitrectomies at Ghent University Hospital in Belgium, and the company reported no device-related adverse events. Nerinckx has said the platform operates with 20 times less tremor than a human hand. Other speakers include Marc de Smet, MD, CM, PhD, BSc(hon), FARVO, FRCSC, FRCOphth, FEBOphth, FMH, on moving robotic platforms from the lab to the operating room, Khalid Al Sabti on building a new robotic system, Rodolfo Mastropasqua, MD, PhD, FEBO, on intraoperative OCT and robotic automation, and Aya Barzelay Wollman, MD, PhD, on machine learning in robotic instruments. Steven Schwartz will address barriers to adoption.

The course ends with a panel whose title asks the question many surgeons and administrators will have: "Is robotic eye surgery ready, and who will pay for it?" Across all 6 courses, the faculty seem less interested in whether AI works than in what it takes to deploy it responsibly. That means validation across devices and populations, workflow integration, regulatory pathways, reimbursement, and patient consent. Ophthalmology Times will be on site in Florence to cover the AI sessions and the rest of the FLORetina-ICOOR 2026 program.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania consumer advocate joins seven states to urge PJM to delay December auction
stories.Summary:
The PA Environment Digest Blog published a roundup on Saturday, November 21, 2026, of A.I. and data center articles from the previous two weeks, covering November 16 to 23. The roundup's first announcement reports that Pennsylvania Consumer Advocate Darryl Lawrence joined advocates in seven other PJM states and the independent PJM market monitor. They urged PJM to delay its December generation auction to avoid billions in added costs to consumers. The roundup also reports that Spotlight PA said the Consumer Advocate filed a complaint against PPL Electric aimed at forcing A.I. data centers to pay their fair share. The roundup states that Spotlight PA reported utility customers who shop for energy suppliers pay more, and the PUC agrees the numbers raise concerns.

The roundup states that the PUC approved a 3.5% natural gas delivery base rate increase for National Fuel Gas. It reports that DEP received U.S. DOE approval to launch a $258 million program providing rebates on appliances and building retrofits to reduce home energy bills. It states that legislators and environmental leaders unveiled a 100-day blueprint to lower electricity bills, rein in data centers and expand clean energy. The roundup reports that DEP says about 25 data center projects are in some stage of permitting in Pennsylvania, and none have signed a consent order saying they will comply with GRID standards under the Governor's executive order. It states that Marcellus Drilling News reported on the status of 27 Pennsylvania data centers in the permitting process and their sources of power.

The roundup states that Gov. Shapiro said new PJM governance rules ensure the electric grid will continue to be held captive by what he called greedy corporate interests. It reports that the North American Electric Reliability Corp. winter outlook said extreme winter weather conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls due to data center demands and impacts on natural gas distribution systems. It states that the independent PJM market monitor warned of another $5 to $10 billion in electricity grid costs on consumers by data centers after delayed PJM market reforms. It reports that PJM Interconnection proposed a one-year process for speeding generation connections, and that PJM said the plan would cut generation and transmission service interconnections for large loads to one year. It states that PJM proposed new rules to protect grid reliability as A.I. data center demand grows.

The roundup reports that the Scranton Times said Olyphant Boro Council approved a $101 million A.I. data center settlement over the objections of more than 200 people at the meeting amid heavy police presence. It states that the Scranton Times editorial said the approval without real public input was a bad night for the democratic process and appalling. It reports that the Olyphant police chief said public threats over the approval will result in arrest, and that they have been overwhelmed with threats, many online. It states that continued opposition by Mid Valley School District holds up Olyphant's $101 million A.I. data center settlement. It reports that Lackawanna County rescinded the tax abatement on the proposed Olyphant A.I. data center site after the council approved the settlement.

The roundup states that the Morning Call reported a proposed 2.1 GW A.I. data center in Upper Mount Bethel Twp. would create what was called an infrastructure problem of biblical proportions in Northampton County. It reports that PennLive said a second major A.I. data center proposal is moving forward in Swatara Twp. despite utility and pollution concerns from neighbors in Dauphin County, and that no hearings were held on the proposals. It states that PennLive reported a $120.3 million community benefits agreement from an A.I. data center developer promises Swatara Twp.

and Dauphin County, and the township held no hearings or comment period on the agreements. It reports that PennLive said a proposed A.I. data center complex in Monroe Twp., Cumberland County, is now dead after strong public opposition. It states that the Pittsburgh Business Times reported the first two of seven natural gas electric generation turbines were set up at the Homer City A.I. data center and power plant complex in Indiana County. The roundup states that DEP was reminded to hold a meeting and hearing on November 23 on the proposed Project Atlas A.I. data center in South Whitehall Twp., Lehigh County.

It reports that DEP posted 38 pages of permit-related notices in the November 14 PA Bulletin and 45 pages in the November 21 PA Bulletin. It states that DEP was reminded to hold a November 18 hearing on the Mid-Atlantic Transmission Line water quality permit in Pike County and a November 20 hearing on the PPL water quality permit for the Stanton Summit Transmission Line Project in Lackawanna County. It reports that the Scranton Times said DEP would hold a hearing that day in Scranton on the PPL Electric Transmission Line Project in Lackawanna and Luzerne counties. It states that the roundup lists Pennsylvania data center hearings and meetings from Physicians for Social Responsibility PA.

stories.Headline: ServiceNow raises year-end AI contract value target to $1.7 billion
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow, Inc. (NYSE:NOW) was named the tenth stock on Insider Monkey's list of 10 Oversold Stocks With 50%+ Upside Potential, in an article published on November 22, 2026. Faheem Tahir wrote the article for Insider Monkey, which Yahoo Finance republished. The article said ServiceNow earned the place after a 37.69% monthly decline. It said the median analyst target implied 76.70% upside as of November 20. The article asked whether the selloff could offer a second opportunity.

The article said third-quarter subscription revenue reached $3.99 billion, growing 20.5% in constant currency. It said ServiceNow raised its year-end AI annual contract value target to $1.7 billion, from $1 billion at the start of 2026. It said these are contracted sales commitments, not revenue already recognized. It said renewals remained at 98%, while AI net new annual contract value increased 65%. It said ServiceNow trades at approximately 18.5 times estimated 2027 earnings, with consensus projecting roughly 21% EPS growth.

On October 29, RBC maintained its Outperform rating but lowered its target to $165 from $176. RBC noted the disconnect between management's bullish AI commentary and the results and outlook. The article said accelerating paid usage and stronger contracted revenue growth would help close that gap. It said stronger AI adoption must produce enough incremental business to sustain overall growth. It said the valuation becomes more compelling if AI adoption translates into durable earnings expansion.

According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward. Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations. Bank of America's November fund manager survey found nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting. More than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months.

The article said the AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward. It said investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns. It said rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook. It said strong demand alone cannot eliminate the financial risks associated with rapid expansion. It said falling share prices can widen implied returns without necessarily improving fundamentals.

The article said the correction may offer another entry point for investors who missed the initial rally. It said the challenge is distinguishing companies whose growth prospects remain intact from those whose valuations have further to fall. It said ServiceNow's role in automating enterprise workflows with AI earns it a place on the list. It said the business benefits when companies move beyond experimenting with AI and start paying to automate everyday work. It said certain AI infrastructure stocks offer far stronger long-term potential at a much more attractive entry point.

stories.Headline: DOE science chief Gil denies Genesis AI takes 10% from Office of Science research
stories.Summary:
On 20 November 2026, DOE Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil rejected a report that the Genesis Mission AI initiative is paid for partly by taking 10% from the Office of Science’s traditional research budgets. He said this in an interview with AIP’s FYI, speaking with science policy reporter Clare Zhang one year after the White House announced the Genesis Mission. The mission is a DOE-led effort to use AI to double scientific productivity within a decade. Zhang asked Gil about a report in Science that DOE funds Genesis in part by taking 10% from the Office of Science’s traditional research budgets. Gil called that “a total, in my view, mischaracterization of how we’re doing this.”

Gil said each program office began with a science question and that no project was funded unless the science criteria were met. He said “This is not about taking money from High Energy Physics and giving it to ASCR (Advanced Scientific Computing Research) to do SI,” using DOE’s shorthand for superintelligence. He said “I don’t accept the formulation of the 10% thing.” Asked whether Genesis grants are a subset of Office of Science research grants rather than separate, he answered “For sure. We’re not moving any money around.”

Gil’s letter to the research community, published by DOE on 12 November 2026, and the AIP interview give figures that are DOE’s own and are presented as Gil states them. Office of Science funding is at an all-time high of $8.4 billion, according to the Gil letter and the AIP interview. The Office of Science national laboratories’ operating budget is a record $9.8 billion, and laboratory personnel number 28,445, both per the Gil letter and the AIP interview. The Genesis first cohort is 297 teams across 369 institutions in all 50 states, and the first call received over 5,000 proposals, both per the Gil letter. There are 33 National Science and Technology Challenges with over 15 federal agencies, per the Gil letter.

Gil also said the response to the open call was the largest in DOE’s history. In a White House announcement of 22 July 2026, Energy Secretary Chris Wright reported 278 projects selected and more than $5 billion in federal commitments from more than 15 agencies, and the 297-team figure in Gil’s November letter is the later count. Asked about the $300 million, Gil said “I think the overall investments that are going to be required will be larger than that.” He added that the dialogue with appropriators is “very positive” and that “they are the ones that have the responsibility to figure out what is the right level of investment.”

His stated top priority for year two is for Congress to take ownership of Genesis in a bipartisan way and codify it in legislation. Asked how to distinguish enthusiasm for Genesis from a general wish for reliable federal research funding at a time of widespread uncertainty, Gil said he could speak only to his own area of responsibility and pointed to the budget, laboratory budget and employment figures, which he called all-time highs, saying “I’m not saying it’s all easy and roses” and acknowledging that advances in computing “create a lot of anxiety.” The Genesis Mission was launched by an executive order signed in November 2025, and CASRAI has covered it since, including an August 2026 report on the first project selections and a Genesis Mission guide explaining eligibility and how funding works. The Office of Science’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research program, which Gil named in his answer, is one of its research programs.

In mid-November, DOE’s Lux system at Oak Ridge debuted on the TOP500 list, which Gil cited as an example of the platform effort. The Senate Appropriations Committee released its Energy and Water Development bill and explanatory statement on 12 November 2026, and according to AIP’s report of 13 November, the Senate proposal would raise the Office of Science budget by about 1% to $8.52 billion, including $120 million in previously appropriated funds, while the House bill would set it at $8.525 billion. AIP also reports that the Senate explanatory statement recommends using up to $300 million within the office’s budget for Genesis Mission research. The next dated milestone is 11 December 2026, when the current continuing resolution expires, according to AIP, and a lapse would begin on 12 December if Congress does not act.

Congress has to reconcile the Senate and House Energy and Water bills, including the Genesis language. Gil also said DOE would decide in early January who will pursue the goal of building a fault-tolerant quantum machine by 2028, a competition that is part of the same effort. The articles leave open how a renewal or continuation will be handled in fiscal 2027 and whether a Genesis-scoped call is expected to be the route. They also leave open whether the Senate and House figures and the Genesis language will survive reconciliation.

Articles.Title: DOE’s Genesis AI push: Gil disputes report of 10% cut to Office of Science research budgets - CASRAI

stories.Headline: Greens senator David Shoebridge pushes for binding Fair Work Act rules on workplace AI
stories.Summary:
The Greens have attacked the Albanese Government's draft guide on artificial intelligence in the workplace as voluntary and unenforceable, and the party says it will push for a legal duty to consult, human review of significant AI decisions and penalties for employers. The government released the guide on 12 November 2026, and the Greens call it a draft, non-binding document that employers are free to ignore. The party says big corporations had a hand in drafting it, while employees exposed to job cuts, AI monitoring and automated rostering have been left without enforceable protections. Greens AI spokesperson Senator David Shoebridge said the government's approach would leave workers without a remedy, and he named QANTAS, Canva, NAB and ANZ as large employers that had fired Australian workers as part of offshoring and an AI rollout.

Senator Shoebridge said that when the government talks about asking employers nicely to consult staff, what it is really saying is that a worker who loses their job to an algorithm will have no legal recourse at all. He said bosses looking to slash wages with AI won't be stopped by an optional best practice guide, and that it is clear the time for optional guidelines has passed. He said Australians need enforceable protections against AI surveillance at work, automated hiring and firing decisions, and bosses using algorithms to monitor and discipline staff. He also said that passing on AI's gains to workers through higher pay and reduced working hours needs to be written into law instead of left to the goodwill of employers.

Senator Barbara Pocock, the Greens spokesperson for finance, workplace and employment, said workers were losing their jobs to AI, or AI washing. She set out the legislative change the party is seeking, saying the Greens want to amend the Fair Work Act to have the power to regulate the use of AI in Australian workplaces and to ensure that employers have a duty to protect employees against the harmful impacts of AI. The proposals come from a party outside government, and the Greens' statement did not include draft legislation or a timetable for the proposed Fair Work Act amendments. The party wants employers placed under a legal obligation to consult, workers given the ability to have significant AI decisions about their employment reviewed by a human, and employers who breach the rules made liable to penalties.

stories.Headline: AI tools expose software flaws faster than teams can safely patch them, Nadella says
stories.Summary:
During November 2026, a series of massive technical failures disabled Microsoft email, Apple services, and Chase payments, while also halting all FAA departures and crashing the NSA internal network. Senator Josh Hawley questioned if these simultaneous events were a coincidence, but intelligence and law enforcement officials informed Congress that they found no evidence of an external attack. Investigators determined that each outage had a separate origin, including a bug shipped by Microsoft in July, a contractor installing a new router for the FAA, and internal updates at Apple, Chase, and the NSA. The current instability requires a faster patching cycle because AI tools are discovering security holes more quickly than they can be safely fixed. On November 17, the startup Calif used OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber model to find Java4Shell, a critical flaw in Java used by the government and 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies.

This followed a previous discovery by Calif in PHP, which powers roughly 70 percent of websites, and Microsoft fixed a record 1,413 vulnerabilities in October alone. The FBI also warned on November 13 that hackers are using an open-source AI tool called ARTEX to gain administrator access in under three hours. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained that while AI helps find and fix bugs, the resulting rush to patch creates instability in production systems. He noted that critical bank patches that once took a week to test must now be deployed instantly because flaws are exploited in the wild. Calif CEO Thai Duong believes the Java4Shell flaw will threaten systems that fail to update for the next five to 10 years.

The UK AI Security Institute reports that open-weight models without safeguards are trailing advanced cyber models by only four to seven months. The industry is now racing to secure critical software before AI can be weaponized by attackers. Anthropic's Project Glasswing is working toward this goal and discovered over 10,000 high or critical severity bugs during its first month of operation. Experts expect more emergency patches and system flare-ups as AI continues to uncover vulnerabilities in Windows, iOS, and Chrome. This process will likely worsen before it improves as the tools for finding flaws become more widespread.

stories.Headline: Taiwan, China and South Korea implement measures to stabilize stock markets after AI selloff
stories.Summary:
Taiwan, China, and South Korea announced measures to support financial markets on November 22, 2026. These actions followed a brutal week for global stocks caused by a rout in the artificial intelligence trade. The selloff battered sentiment across the region after a period of extreme volatility. This market crash affected several major Asian economies heavily reliant on technology. The downturn occurred during a period of significant global financial instability.

Taiwan's Financial Regulatory Commission banned short-selling below the previous day's close and raised minimum margins to 150 percent from 130 percent. South Korea announced a market support fund and temporary easing of corporate share buyback restrictions on Sunday. China's Shanghai and Shenzhen Stock Exchanges adjusted the financing margin ratio for investors to 80 percent from 100 percent. These changes followed the KOSPI sliding over 5 percent on Friday and plunging nearly 47 percent from June. China's indexes hit their lowest levels since June and July 2025.

Taiwan's Financial Regulatory Commission issued a statement on Saturday regarding the situation. The commission noted that stocks had continued to fluctuate sharply in recent days. They claimed these five specific measures were necessary to maintain the order and stability of the securities market. The commission acted after the benchmark index saw its worst weekly performance since August 1990. These officials sought to stem the bleeding caused by the AI wipeout.

The AI trade affected Taiwan and South Korea because they house the world's biggest contract chipmakers and semiconductor equipment manufacturers. Investors worried about massive debt-fueled financing for AI infrastructure and uncertain returns on billions of dollars spent. A sweeping Democratic victory in the U.S. midterm elections created regulatory concerns for data centers. Wall Street suffered its worst weekly performance since April 2025, pushing the S&P 500 into correction territory. These events caused a massive wipeout of value for technology stocks.

The AI trade faced pressure before the week began due to financing and regulatory fears. Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings, but a governance crisis led to the shock departure of chief executive Jensen Huang. Anthropic had a record-breaking initial public offering that popped in its market debut. However, the IPO did not address the wider worries plaguing the artificial intelligence trade. These combined factors triggered a sharp decline in global semiconductor and AI stocks.

The Asian governments have now implemented emergency measures to stabilize their respective stock markets. South Korea is currently preparing its market support fund to prevent further plunges. China's regulatory commission has already approved the new financing margin ratios for its investors. The articles do not state if these measures will successfully stop the current market slide. It remains open whether the AI trade can recover from this governance and regulatory crisis.

Articles.Title: Asian countries take steps to aid stock markets after AI rout

stories.Headline: OpenAI strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol safeguards, cutting reasoning extraction attack success from 54.0% to 0.2%
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a post on November 20, 2026 titled "Combatting adversarial distillation," describing how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation and how it strengthened protections for its models' protected reasoning. Adversarial distillation is when an actor uses a frontier model's outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities. OpenAI said it combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated extraction attempts. OpenAI said it strengthened defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, the average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

OpenAI said its updated safeguards align more closely with those it uses for biology and cybersecurity. OpenAI said it places particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting protected reasoning, the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. OpenAI said these traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. OpenAI described a September disclosure of attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. OpenAI said it strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user's encrypted reasoning.

OpenAI said that with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol it ties a model's protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. OpenAI said that as new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning, and that if an earlier message is rewritten, its API drops the reasoning that followed it. OpenAI said it also prevents older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol's protected reasoning. OpenAI said that when its systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract its models' reasoning, it investigates the accounts responsible. OpenAI said that when it identifies violations, it enforces against the network of accounts, consistent with its policies and terms of service.

OpenAI said that through investigations of each campaign it generates insights that allow it to upgrade its defenses to better detect similar activity. OpenAI said it shares indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. OpenAI said its consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering its models. OpenAI said it works closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. OpenAI said sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

OpenAI said distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another, for example another model's answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. OpenAI said that beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks, because a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. OpenAI said the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, where a model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them. OpenAI said that in an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, it used the content normally visible to users, final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions, as its baseline for distillation. OpenAI said it started each training run from the same pretrained student model and created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks.

OpenAI said each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. OpenAI said it evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. OpenAI said that after supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. OpenAI said that after reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. OpenAI said its cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under its usage policies.

OpenAI said that across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. OpenAI said it will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. OpenAI said it defends against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of its safeguard stack, with model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls at the request level and patterns in request-level and account-level signals at the campaign level. OpenAI said attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing its safeguards.

OpenAI said its adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. OpenAI said adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. OpenAI said it uses input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments, applying to both streaming and non-streaming responses. OpenAI said tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool's arguments without including it in its final answer, and output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

OpenAI said that in static evaluations it replays a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning, and in adaptive evaluations automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds. OpenAI said black-box testing gives testers the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. OpenAI said that in its adaptive black-box evaluation it tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. OpenAI said that on GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type, and both rates were substantially lower than on GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards.

OpenAI said it is now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT-6 Astra as well. OpenAI said it has seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on its platform this year. OpenAI said it shared initial findings from those campaigns. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Combatting adversarial distillation - OpenAI

stories.headline_source: Combatting adversarial distillation

stories.Headline: New York judge weighs order that Kalshi says could shut its exchange nationwide
stories.Summary:
New York Attorney General Letitia James sued the prediction market Kalshi in July, claiming the company operates an illegal gambling business. US District Judge Vernon Broderick sent this lawsuit back to state court on Thursday, November 19, after finding the federal court lacked jurisdiction. On Friday, November 20, US District Judge Lorna Schofield denied a request from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission to stop the state court from ruling. Justice Melissa Crane has now scheduled a hearing for Monday at 11:30 a.m. ET to consider a temporary restraining order.

The attorney general seeks an order to stop Kalshi from offering sports contracts without a license from the New York State Gaming Commission. This legal action targets betting on New York college teams and sports wagering by individuals under 21 years of age. The proposed order covers contracts on sports, culture, elections, and other events offered within or from New York. The lawsuit also seeks the forfeiture of profits, restitution, and various penalties against the company. Kalshi reports having 1.2 million users in New York, an annualized trading volume of $178 billion, and a $22 billion valuation.

Kalshi attorney Sean Murphy and CFTC attorney Andrew Weisberg stated that the order could force the liquidation of all positions and shut down operations nationwide. They argue that because Kalshi is based in New York, any order covering contracts offered from the state would affect all customers. Attorney General representative Kate Rhodes Janofsky told the federal court that there is no evidence of market disruption. Kalshi spokesperson Elisabeth Diana said the company wants to reach a resolution with the Governor and the Attorney General.

The CFTC has sued 12 states, including New York, arguing that federal derivatives law overrides state gambling laws. Recently, a federal appeals court ruled that Kalshi cannot stop Maryland from regulating its sports contracts. Additionally, the Senate passed the DEATH BETS Act to ban contracts regarding war and death. The company continues to fight the New York order to avoid a total exchange shutdown.

Articles.Title: Kalshi fights a New York restraining order it says could shut its exchange nationwide - MLQ.ai
