Robo.ai revenue from June through October surpassed $380 million based on management accounts, with a full-year target of up to $600 million.

Roadzen's Rohan Malhotra said the next milestone over the next year is to get to cash flow breakeven. Robo.ai's Adrian Wong described the company as a UAE-based diversified technology company serving critical infrastructure industries, with Quantum Core Capital acquired in June and now fully integrated. PureCipher's Wendy Chin began building the company's security and safety technology four years ago, before the launch of ChatGPT. American Fusion's Brent Nelson said an independent third-party reviewer recently completed an on-site evaluation of the Texatron fusion engine, with draft highlights looking good so far. Nelson said American Fusion has 10 to 11 data center proposals outstanding, with a combined value he puts in the billions of dollars.

Vince Caruso, Co-Founder and CEO of New to The Street, said Show #781 is about AI growing up. Malhotra said Roadzen's insurer, car maker and fleet clients are adopting AI very rapidly, with an acceleration on almost all aspects of the business. Wong said Robo.ai's Neurovia AI unit has completed validation and is now integrating with government and enterprise customers. Chin said PureCipher's mission is to ensure AI is on the human side, and that she wants AI to serve humanity, not the other way around. Nelson said American Fusion is still operating and testing the Texatron on a daily basis, and that its data is getting better.

Wong said Robo.ai's ALIF Holding was recently awarded its first contract by a federal government-owned company, and discussed the recent appointment of W Motors founder Ralph R. Debbas as Group President. Malhotra said a growing mix of higher-margin U.S. business, together with a pending acquisition in Europe, should help margins continue to expand. Chin said PureCipher is in discussions with a large company about applying its capability to physical AI. Nelson said his priorities for the next six months include filing the company's quarterly report, closing on its North Texas Ranch facility, which American Fusion expected to complete by Thanksgiving, and building its own testing bunker there. Nelson said the company is evaluating four or five of the top proposals from roughly 15 it has received from prospective financial partners.

New to The Street was founded in 2009 and is a sponsored and syndicated business television platform serving public companies and emerging-growth businesses. As of November 21, 2026, New to The Street TV has 5.48M+ subscribers and NewsOut has 1.24M+ subscribers, together reaching 6.72M+ YouTube subscribers. Following the broadcast, every segment will be distributed across the New to The Street TV and NewsOut YouTube channels. New to The Street's Meet The Companies tour brings presenting companies face to face with family offices, accredited investors and high-net-worth individuals in three cities in 2027. The New York event is Thursday, January 7, 2027, at The Hudson Yards Penthouse, 455 Tenth Avenue PH, New York, NY 10018, the week before the Needham Growth Conference, with a cocktail reception on Wednesday, January 6.

The Atlantic City event is Thursday, January 28, 2027, and the Las Vegas event is June 17-18, 2027. Each event hosts up to 20 presenting companies, with 20-minute slots that include a 15-minute presentation and Q&A. For Atlantic City and Las Vegas presenters, New to The Street pays for your stay. Confirmed New York presenters include Glint, TMC the metals company Inc. (NASDAQ:TMC), American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN), Big Sky Industrial (NASDAQ:BSIN), T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA), Stewards, Inc. (NASDAQ:SWRD), Roadzen Inc. (NASDAQ:RDZN) and Smile Design Manhattan. Additional presenters will be announced, and accredited investors only may apply to attend at John@NewtoTheStreet.com.

Nelson said American Fusion is working toward an uplisting to the Texas Stock Exchange, Nasdaq or the New York Stock Exchange, a move he hopes to make in the next six months or so. Nelson said the company hopes the final independent review report will confirm that it is on the right track. Wong said Neurovia's goal is to store more visual data on the same servers, or the same data with less compute, power, water and land. Chin said once an AI system is given a mission, it looks for the fastest way to achieve it, which is why PureCipher is building real-time, intent-specific guardrails. The articles leave open the final results of the independent review, the terms of the pending European acquisition and the outcome of the uplisting effort.

stories.Headline: Northwestern opens undergraduate AI major with 28 students declared
stories.Summary:
In spring 2022, McCormick Prof. Sara Owsley Sood began noticing that employers hiring computer science majors struggled to find people with the specific skills they needed. Companies have begun seeking students with knowledge of AI technologies as artificial intelligence has risen, signaling a need to distinguish the subject from concentrations under the computer science major. According to McCormick Prof. Samir Khuller, the Peter and Adrienne Barris Chair of Computer Science, Northwestern began creating a new undergraduate AI major in spring 2023. The major opened for enrollment in the McCormick School of Engineering and the Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences this fall. Khuller said students and professors are happy with its results so far.

Students pursuing the AI major as a primary major in McCormick, a second major in McCormick or a second major outside McCormick must all take courses in specific areas of study. “Breadth” courses require students to explore topics in AI such as symbolic AI and theoretical foundations, Sood said. Technical electives focus on the foundations of programming and computer science, and Sood said they ensure students can pivot into software engineering if they choose. Students must also take one societal impact course, which engages them in discussions about the effects of AI and the tools they create. Sood said 28 students have declared a major in AI so far, including 20 McCormick and non-McCormick students taking it as a second major.

Sood, the program’s director of undergraduate studies, said “It’s going well” and “This is a long time coming.” She said the number of declarations surprised her, especially given the program’s heavy course load, and that students feel the need to augment their studies with deeper knowledge in AI. Khuller said allowing AI as a secondary major makes the program more accessible to students in other fields. Sood said breadth requirements give students a broader understanding beyond generative AI, and that ethics are “not as an afterthought” in design. She said it is important for people building these systems to have a strong ethical framework to evaluate them.

Khuller said the interaction between AI systems and people is vital when looking at societal effects, and he wants students to think about the impact on different people. Weinberg sophomore Charlotte Morton said the AI program pairs well with her primary major in cognitive science, and that understanding human cognition helps her understand how AI models reason and use logic. Morton said she hopes the program will require more ethics courses, since of the 22 major-specific units required for primary or secondary majors and the 19 units for non-McCormick second majors, students need only one societal impact course. McCormick Prof. Kristian Hammond said programs like ChatGPT, Claude and Google Gemini are “damaging” because they decrease cognitive skills instead of enhancing them. Hammond said the major helps students develop systems that augment what humans do well rather than replace them.

Northwestern launched its Master of Science in Artificial Intelligence in fall 2018, and Kellogg School of Management and McCormick launched their MBAi program in fall 2021 to integrate AI into business. McCormick launched the undergraduate AI minor in fall 2024. Before the curriculum was announced, Sood said she saw confusion from people who thought the major would teach students to use AI rather than create it. Hammond said he could make his teachings accessible to thousands with AI, and that he encourages students to explore AI’s positive impacts rather than run from it. Morton said the most important thing will be integrating AI into companies and professions ethically, in a way that assists humans and genuinely adds to society.

Sood said she hopes the program takes students beyond generative AI models and explores areas supporting a longer career in AI, and that students have broad knowledge in AI, “Not just the thing that’s hot right now.” Hammond said the world is changing and “we have to help direct it,” and that students can build systems that expand their impact to a larger audience. Morton said increasing the number of societal impact courses required will help students understand AI’s potential positive and negative impacts. Faculty of the undergraduate AI major remain hopeful that students will use AI systems to be leaders within their communities. The articles do not say what the program will require next or when any changes will be decided.

stories.Headline: Human Frontier Mission launches globally to apply AI agents to open science questions
stories.Summary:
The Human Frontier Mission Committee announced on November 21, 2026, that Human Frontier Mission will launch globally on November 24, according to a paid press release distributed by PR Newswire and carried by Yahoo Finance. The initiative puts advances in artificial intelligence to work on unsolved scientific and engineering questions and makes the experiments they generate available for public review. The committee said the launch will open to a global audience a program of research led by domain experts and carried out with autonomous AI agents. The announcement was issued from Seattle.

So far, HFM has recorded 2,391 experiments across 54 challenges in 12 fields, with 23 studies running at the time of the snapshot. The questions range from improving global weather forecasts to coordinating road signals and scheduling wind power and energy storage. In structural materials, HFM is testing whether a model can predict how steel reacts to repeated loads it has not encountered during development. The public experiment record shows where an approach gained ground, where it fell short and what another researcher could investigate next. The global launch invites researchers, engineers and institutions to propose questions, share evidence or evaluation methods, and help assess results.

The committee said that in a research setting a more capable model makes it possible to test ideas that would otherwise compete for limited time and resources. It said whether those ideas advance a field depends on the questions scientists ask, the standards they set and the results that hold up under examination. Domain experts define the challenges and establish criteria for evaluating progress, while autonomous AI research agents develop and test candidate approaches. HFM brings scientific and engineering expertise, autonomous AI research agents and research resources together in a shared research program organized by the committee. The experiment record gives other researchers a way to examine a result before putting the approach to work on new questions.

stories.Headline: SBE Council reports 82% of small employers use AI tools
stories.Summary:
SBE Council published its Small Business Insider newsletter on 21 November 2026 at 10:09 am, covering AI, Small Business Saturday, and policy. The newsletter included an op-ed in the Washington Reporter by SBE Council President and CEO Karen Kerrigan and American Edge Project President and CEO Doug Kelly. SBE Council applauded the U.S. Department of Labor's final independent contractor rule, issued on 19 November. SBE Council also urged New York City lawmakers to reject the proposed Delivery Protection Act, Intro. 0518-2026.

Freelance Busting published a Q&A with Kerrigan on 17 November, and Inc. published an article on 11 November. SBE Council's 2026 Technology Use Survey found that 82% of small business employers use AI tools, two-thirds report AI-driven revenue gains, and 93% plan to continue investing in AI. Small Business Saturday is November 28, and American Express research found that 88% of U.S. consumers say they are likely to shop at small businesses this holiday season, the highest level of intent since 2012. The 2026 Shop Small Impact Study found that 72% of consumers shop small for memorable gifts and 70% enjoy discovering new small businesses. 35% of consumers plan to use AI to discover small businesses, while 90% of surveyed small business owners expect to use AI tools during the holiday season.

SBE Council's October 2026 Small Business Check Up Survey found that 47% of small business employers use independent contractors, and MBO Partners research reports that a record 74.9 million Americans engaged in independent work in 2026. Kerrigan and Kelly wrote that America's AI leadership will not be decided only in Silicon Valley but also in millions of small offices, shops and job sites. They called for a clear national AI framework, expanded training opportunities, and policies that encourage infrastructure investment, including data centers. They wrote that it matters which country builds the future and that Main Street is ready to help. Kerrigan said independent contractors provide essential expertise and capacity that help small businesses compete, innovate, and grow.

Kerrigan emphasized the importance of policies that protect independent business relationships and the way individuals want to work. SBE Council joined ten other business and health care organizations in coalition letters to Rep. Kevin Hern (R-OK) and Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-MT) urging passage of the CHOICE Act, H.R. 5643 and S. 2875, during the lame-duck session. The bills would provide participating employers with tax credits of up to $1,200 per employee in the first year and $600 in the second year. The letters note that employer health costs are projected to rise an average of 10% in 2027, and 73% of surveyed small businesses are considering dropping traditional health insurance benefits.

More than two-thirds of small businesses currently offering CHOICE arrangements previously provided no health coverage to employees. SBE Council warned that the Delivery Protection Act could devastate independent delivery businesses, eliminate thousands of jobs, and increase delivery costs, and noted that many affected businesses are minority and veteran-owned. SBE Council is a founding partner of Small Business Saturday and encouraged entrepreneurs to make the most of the entire holiday shopping season. Carol Roth released her 2026 Small Business Holiday Gift Guide featuring products and services from small businesses across the country.

SBE Council supported the DOL rulemaking through formal comments and will continue working with the department on implementation guidance. SBE Council said it will remain focused on advancing long-term legislative certainty and opposing restrictive state and local policies. Chicago is among other cities considering the delivery policy, and SBE Council called on city leaders to listen to affected small business owners and workers. SBE Council will continue working with the Department of Labor on implementation guidance reflecting modern work arrangements, including digital platforms and collaborative business relationships.

Lawmakers are urged to include the CHOICE reforms in legislation before the end of the 119th Congress. SBE Council is calling on New York City leaders to pursue solutions that improve safety without destroying businesses, jobs, and economic opportunity. The newsletter offers eight practical steps to help entrepreneurs prepare for Small Business Saturday, along with five ways to put AI to work immediately. The articles leave open whether the Delivery Protection Act will pass and whether Congress will act on the CHOICE Act before year-end.

stories.Headline: GE Vernova's Ateret says AI can handle seven of ten software vulnerability types
stories.Summary:
Suspected Iran-linked hackers forced a small British power generator offline for four days in July, according to Ynetnews. Around the same time, water treatment and supply systems across at least 12 U.S. states were targeted in a wave of cyberattacks. British authorities said the attack affected only a small generator and posed no threat to the country's wider electricity supply. The incidents showed attackers increasingly targeting physical infrastructure, not merely stealing information or disrupting websites. Lior Ateret heads global cybersecurity research and GE Vernova's cybersecurity center in Israel.

Ateret leads a team of dozens of researchers, software developers and ethical hackers from GE Vernova's offices in Ramat Gan, near Tel Aviv. GE Vernova says its equipment helps generate approximately 25% of the world's electricity. Ateret told Yenergya that products do not go live without passing through Israel, whether power plants or distribution systems. GE Vernova was spun off as an independent publicly traded company in April 2024. Its order backlog reached approximately $197 billion in its latest quarterly report.

Ateret said there is not a moment when someone isn't attacking power plants, and that nothing is 100% secure. He said the standard in Israel is very high and the situation is definitely above average in terms of protection. He said attacking one power station might generate publicity, but countries are built to deal with that and the system balances itself within minutes. He said what is truly frightening is a sophisticated attack by a major power against many stations simultaneously. He said AI is replacing the hacker, not completely, but it can perform tasks that previously required a human.

Ateret said an AI model given access to software code can handle approximately seven of the 10 traditional categories of software vulnerabilities. He said results that would take a human hacker a week can be achieved in just a few hours. He warned the technology can transform one person into an entire army of hackers. He said no operational technology system is managed by AI, describing them as deterministic real-time systems. He said the red button that stops electricity generation isn't in AI's hands.

Ateret began in Jerusalem, where as a high school student he enrolled in a gifted students' program at the Hebrew University. After earning his bachelor's degree through an academic program linked to military service, he joined the Israel Defense Forces' Communications and Cyber Defense Directorate. He began testing military systems in the evenings, and the initiative developed into the IDF General Staff's red team, which he established and led. His work earned him recognition from the head of the Shin Bet. In 2012, Ateret left the military with the rank of major and received an approach from General Electric the same day.

Ateret attributes Israel's relative strength to centralized cybersecurity monitoring by a security operations center in Be'er Sheva, jointly operated by Israel's National Cyber Directorate and Energy Ministry. He also cites strict regulation and one-way communication technology, sometimes called a data diode, some supplied by Israeli company Waterfall Security using fiber-optic technology. He said in most recent incidents controllers were connected directly to the internet, and that is how the attack was carried out. GE Vernova's gas turbines are used in converting the Orot Rabin power station in Hadera from coal to natural gas. GE Vernova is also involved at the Eshkol and Alon Tavor power stations, the Tzafit private power facility and the Kochav Hayarden pumped-storage project.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal agencies to replace artificial intelligence with super intelligence
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term artificial intelligence with super intelligence on September 29. He signed an executive order for this change because he believes the word artificial makes the technology sound fake. On October 4, the president established a super intelligence force to coordinate government efforts and maintain American global leadership. This new body reports directly to the president and his chief of staff to streamline federal actions. The task force has 120 days to submit a report regarding the risks and opportunities of this technology.

The force is led by Jay Clayton, who serves as the director of national intelligence and was previously the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Other members include Federal Trade Commission chair Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael, and federal workforce leader Scott Kupor. This initiative follows a morally binding accord signed by firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Nvidia for internal evaluations and audits. Private investment in the United States reached 285.9 billion dollars in 2025, which is roughly 23 times the 12.4 billion dollars spent by China. Major American tech companies are expected to spend more than 650 billion dollars on capital investments this year.

Jay Clayton stated that the risk of the United States not being first in this race is high. However, Democratic senator Mark Warner criticized the move as merely renaming the technology while telling private companies to regulate themselves. Critics argue that the White House has not disclosed a budget or clarified if the force has regulatory powers. They also note that the performance gap between the best American and Chinese models narrowed to 2.7 percentage points by 2026. The lack of an enforcement mechanism for the voluntary industry accord suggests that the government may have limited leverage.

The effectiveness of this strategy depends on whether the body secures a budget and gains authority over infrastructure and hiring. Recent midterm elections shifted control of Congress toward the Democrats, which could change future funding and oversight. Because the president revoked Joe Biden's previous executive order on his first day in office, these new actions could also be undone. There is a tension between the goals of winning a global race and protecting the public from potential harms. The leadership comes from defense and intelligence sectors rather than from experts focused specifically on safety.

stories.Headline: Clark Hill lawyers present a webinar on three emerging legal threats in healthcare AI
stories.Summary:
Clark Hill, a law firm, announced a webinar titled Healthcare AI in 2027: Three Emerging Legal Threats You Haven't Been Warned About, scheduled for December 16, 2026, from 10:00 to 11:00 AM Pacific Time and running through the corresponding hours in Mountain, Central and Eastern time. The session will be presented by Paul F. Schmeltzer and John F. Howard, according to the firm's announcement dated November 20, 2026. The webinar is aimed at the growing integration of artificial intelligence into healthcare operations and clinical decision-making, which the firm says is producing a new generation of legal, cybersecurity and patient safety risks. The firm states that the discussion will go beyond traditional AI governance and HIPAA compliance to examine three cutting-edge threats.

The first threat covered is autonomous AI agents that make or influence clinical decisions with limited human oversight. The second is AI-targeted cyberattacks, including prompt injection and data poisoning, which can manipulate AI systems, compromise clinical workflows and potentially put patients at risk. The third is AI-driven operational failures that can lead to patient misidentification, inaccurate medical records, or automated decisions that are difficult to reconstruct or explain. The presenters will examine the evolving legal and regulatory implications of these threats, including cybersecurity obligations, medical malpractice exposure and vendor liability.

The firm also plans to address the importance of continuous monitoring, meaningful human oversight and safeguards meant to prevent the uncritical acceptance of AI-generated decisions. Clark Hill lists the webinar under its healthcare industry group and its cybersecurity, privacy and technology litigation and data privacy, protection and cybersecurity practice areas. The announcement does not name any clients, patients or specific AI products affected by the threats described. It also does not state whether the webinar carries continuing legal education credit or what the registration fee is.

The page offers a registration link for the event but gives no further details on the agenda beyond the three threats and the legal topics listed. No enforcement actions, lawsuits or regulatory deadlines are mentioned in connection with the webinar. The announcement appears alongside other Clark Hill legal updates, including one on expanded Medicare revocation powers and one on a federal court ruling vacating a Department of Homeland Security rule. Nothing in the announcement indicates what, if anything, will follow the December 16 session.

stories.Headline: Review finds only two of fourteen tuberculosis studies directly integrate GIS with AI modelling
stories.Summary:
A systematic literature review published by Nur Adibah Mohidem and Sharifah Norkhadijah Syed Ismail in the International Journal of Health Geographics found that only two of fourteen eligible studies directly embedded spatial structures within artificial intelligence modelling frameworks for tuberculosis research. The authors searched Scopus, PubMed, the Cochrane Library, ScienceDirect, and Taylor & Francis for literature published up to July 7, 2025, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines. After systematic screening, eligibility checks, and quality appraisal using the MI-CLAIM framework, fourteen primary studies met all criteria for final analysis. The review examined how geographic information systems and artificial intelligence currently converge in tuberculosis research, a field marked by persistent spatial heterogeneity in incidence, mortality, and healthcare access.

Most of the included studies concentrated on tuberculosis incidence and case counts, while others examined diagnostic procedures, medical treatment, mortality patterns, community-based public health applications, and the geographic distribution of Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains. Researchers used geographic information systems for spatial mapping, spatial autocorrelation, hotspot analysis, spatial clustering, spatial regression, general spatial modelling, and spatial accessibility assessments including network analysis of healthcare access. The artificial intelligence methods spanned neural networks, deep learning architectures, tree-based and ensemble machine learning, kernel-based machine learning, Bayesian modelling, time-series and regression-based frameworks, and explainable artificial intelligence. However, twelve of the fourteen studies applied the two approaches independently, in parallel, or through sequential pipelines rather than integrating them into unified structures.

The authors concluded that combining geographic information systems and artificial intelligence in tuberculosis investigations is an emerging field with limited technical integration. They said future research must prioritize standardized spatially incorporated artificial intelligence frameworks to translate analytical outputs into operational real-time disease surveillance. The review emphasizes the need for high-resolution geocoded data, spatially sensitive validation protocols, and emerging concepts such as GeoAI, digital twins, explainable artificial intelligence, and tailored implementation strategies. The article was published on November 22, 2026, with a DOI of 10.1186/s12942-026-00506-1.

stories.Headline: Civil Guard arrests four for using AI to spread jihadist content and radicalize youth
stories.Summary:
The Civil Guard has arrested four people in three provinces and in the autonomous city of Melilla for spreading jihadist content on social networks with the aim of indoctrinating people in terrorism, in an investigation that also detected the use of artificial intelligence to improve radicalization processes. In a first action, officers arrested three people in San Sebastián in Guipúzcoa, Vilanova i la Geltrú in Barcelona and Fuengirola in Málaga, after confirming that they had become radicalized over recent years, especially because of greater access to terrorist propaganda spread on the internet. A parallel operation in Melilla led to the arrest of a young man for his active work in spreading jihadist ideology, and he is attributed with large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially content used by young people. The detainees also recorded videos in which they expressed their jihadist affiliation and displayed bladed weapons, according to material seized during the investigation.

Among the analyzed materials are content related to Daesh and Hamas, used with the aim of indoctrinating for terrorist purposes, and the investigation has also located material that justifies violence and the carrying out of attacks. The Civil Guard considers this terrorist propaganda material to be of special danger because of the intrinsic risk of fostering jihadist radicalization, especially among a young and vulnerable group. The operations were carried out with the cooperation of the National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States, within an investigation focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for the recruitment and radicalization of users on social networks. The report was published on November 22, 2026, and the arrests were made in San Sebastián, Vilanova i la Geltrú, Fuengirola and Melilla.

The General Directorate of the Civil Guard provided the information on the analyzed materials, and the force described the propaganda as especially dangerous because it can foster radicalization among young and vulnerable people. The investigation attributes to the Melilla detainee large quantities of jihadist multimedia content on social networks, especially material used by young people, and the seized material shows that the detainees recorded videos expressing their jihadist affiliation and displaying bladed weapons. The National Intelligence Center and the FBI of the United States cooperated in the operations, which focused on the spread of terrorist propaganda and the use of new technological tools for recruitment and radicalization. The articles do not say what charges the four detainees face or what happens to them next.

stories.Headline: Higher-income parents more often encourage kids to use AI for schoolwork, RAND finds
stories.Summary:
A report from the research group RAND, published in Education Week on November 20, 2026, found a connection between how much money parents make and how often their kids use AI for schoolwork. The report was written by Arianna Prothero. RAND surveyed nationally representative groups of parents and teens in the winter and spring of 2025 and the spring of 2026. The more parents earn, the more likely they are to use AI themselves and encourage their kids to use it to complete schoolwork. Parental encouragement is positively correlated with teens’ AI use.

There was a 15-percentage-point gap in AI use among high- and low-income parents in February 2025, with the former using AI more. That gap grew to 21 percentage points in May 2026, even as AI use increased among all income groups. About two-thirds of parents who made $150,000 a year or more said in the most recent survey they had encouraged their kids to use AI for schoolwork compared with just under half of parents making less than $50,000. Nearly 1 in 5 parents in that highest-income category (17%) encourage their kids to use AI whenever possible within school rules. Four in 10 teens reported in May 2025 that they used AI to complete schoolwork, rising to nearly 5 in 10 a year later.

Heather Schwartz, the vice president and director of education, employment, and infrastructure for RAND, said the report shows parents are encouraging their children to use AI for school in greater numbers than might have been realized. She said parents therefore need messages about when AI can be helpful and when AI is harmful. Schwartz said many students are unfamiliar with their schools’ AI policies, if they even exist. She said schools should have coherent AI policies and communicate them to parents, and need buildingwide rules rather than depend on teachers to craft their own in individual classrooms. Schwartz said the all-essential ingredient is how higher-income teens are using AI, and that if teens are using AI to do the work for them, this could harm highest-income teens’ performance.

Among parents who don’t think that AI harms their kids’ critical thinking, most encouraged AI use, but even among parents who believe that AI use undermines critical thinking, more than half (53%) still encouraged their kids to use it. In a subset of survey data that matched parents with their own children, which was not a nationally representative sample, teens whose parents reported frequent AI use were more likely to use the technology themselves to help with homework than their peers whose parents didn’t use AI (63% vs. 40%). Teens from high-income families were more likely than their peers to use AI for schoolwork: 57% of teens in the highest-income families (those making more than $150,000 a year) reported using AI to do their homework in 2026 compared with 43% of teens from the lowest-income families (those making less than $50,000 a year). AI use among those wealthiest teens grew by 17 percentage points from May 2025 to May 2026. Teachers accounted for the loudest voices discouraging AI use, with 57% of teens saying teachers discouraged them from using the technology.

Among parents who nudge their kids to use AI for schoolwork, most say they counsel them to use restraint, such as using AI as a brainstorming partner rather than allowing it to do all their thinking for them. Teens are getting mixed messages on AI use from the people in their lives, whether parents, other family members, friends, teachers, or other school staff. If parents, friends, and teachers discouraged teens from using AI, they were much less likely to do so, but if at least one group was pushing for AI use, teens were significantly more likely to use it for homework. Schwartz said that if teens are using AI to supplement their thinking, such as asking a tool for feedback after writing the first draft of an essay themselves, that’s a more enriching way to use the technology that could boost learning. Schwartz said that in the real world, she thinks kids are using AI as a shortcut and, in general, they’re getting AI to do the work for them.

Whether this gap in AI use will harm or hurt wealthier students is to be seen, Schwartz said. Schwartz said schools need to give parents clear talking points about either recommended or mandated do’s and don’ts on their children’s AI use for school. The report states that families play a crucial role in teaching students healthy AI habits that won’t undermine their learning. The articles do not say what specific policies schools have adopted in response to the findings. The articles do not say whether further RAND surveys are planned.

stories.Headline: Ireland's Data Protection Commission blocks or delays nine AI launches over five years
stories.Summary:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission published a report on September 25, 2026, regarding its reviews of artificial intelligence. The regulator examined roughly 180 AI products and services between 2021 and 2025. Most of these reviews occurred before the products reached users in Europe. Nine of these launches were delayed or cancelled because of interventions by the regulator. These reviews were conducted by the Technology Multinational Supervision Unit.

The report, titled Responsible Artificial Intelligence Innovation, covers companies including Meta, Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, TikTok, and X. It includes other firms like Airbnb, Apple, Deepseek, LinkedIn, and Pinterest. The DPC noted that 59 percent of AI products launched in 2024 and 2025 received recommendations. Transparency problems appeared in 72 percent of those recommendations. The regulator requires a minimum lead time of 8 weeks for substantive engagement.

The Technology Multinational Supervision Unit is responsible for engaging with large multinational tech companies based in Ireland. This unit operates separately from other regulatory functions like complaints or inquiries. The DPC stated that this voluntary process acts as a quasi-regulatory sandbox. The regulator noted that recommendations are non-binding in nature. However, the DPC may use other regulatory powers if redline issues are not addressed.

The report affects large platforms that sell advertising in Europe because the DPC is their lead regulator. Some companies, such as X, refused to stop training AI models when requested. The DPC applied to the Irish High Court on August 8, 2024, regarding X. Eurostat data shows 52.7 percent of EU firms avoiding AI due to privacy concerns. AI use among EU enterprises rose from 13.5 percent to 20 percent in 2025.

Generative AI drove most growth, accounting for 79 percent of all engagements. The DPC counted 25 generative AI engagements in 2023, 36 in 2024, and 82 in 2025. Non-generative AI engagements totaled 37 over the whole period. AI engagements with large technology controllers grew tenfold from 2021 to 2025. This activity included technologies like facial recognition, age assurance, and large language models.

The DPC now says training AI on private messages faces a very difficult legal threshold. The regulator believes training new AI models will likely require a Data Protection Impact Assessment. Future monitoring will include how mitigations, such as objection forms, work in practice. The report does not name most companies involved in the specific case studies. It remains open whether companies can justify training AI on private messages under legitimate interests.

stories.Headline: Analysts see over 100% upside for Ciena, Tower Semiconductor and Lumentum after steep AI stock declines
stories.Summary:
The AI boom has rewarded early investors handsomely, but the opportunity now looks considerably less straightforward, according to an article by Faheem Tahir published on Yahoo Finance on Sunday, November 22, 2026. After months of enthusiasm surrounding artificial intelligence, investors are increasingly questioning whether the enormous spending behind the technology can generate adequate returns. According to Reuters on November 19, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index had lost nearly 30% since early October, even as estimates for major technology companies' capital expenditure remained largely unchanged. Barclays strategists noted that hyperscaler spending forecasts for next year had yet to be revised downward, suggesting that the market's retreat has outpaced changes in investment expectations. Rising financing costs, regulatory uncertainty, and potential restrictions on data center construction have complicated the outlook.

The article screened U.S.-listed companies with exposure to AI through chips, cloud computing, software, or supporting infrastructure, using data as of November 20, 2026. It selected stocks that had declined by at least 25% over the preceding month and offered at least 50% upside to their median analyst price targets. The final ten are presented in ascending order of analyst upside potential, and the top five are presented in the article. Hedge fund interest was considered as of the third quarter of 2026, using Insider Monkey's hedge fund database, which tracked 994 hedge funds during the quarter. Ciena Corporation had a 27.95% one-month decline and 104.30% upside potential, with 83 hedge fund holders.

Reuters reported on November 18 that 83% of analyst ratings on key AI stocks were Strong Buy recommendations, despite mounting concerns over profitability and debt. Bank of America's November fund manager survey revealed that nearly 40% of respondents believed companies were overinvesting, while more than half anticipated at least one hyperscaler cutting capital expenditure within six months. On November 16, TD Cowen retained its Buy rating on Ciena while reducing its target to $375 from $400, arguing that strong demand made substantial near-term earnings estimate cuts difficult to justify. On November 3, Craig-Hallum maintained its Buy rating on Tower Semiconductor while cutting its target to $250 from $325, highlighting strong photonics demand and capacity expansion running ahead of schedule. UBS maintained Neutral on Lumentum on November 10, noting accelerating optical demand but identifying the acquisition as the principal near-term share-price driver.

Tower Semiconductor shares fell 39.38% over the past month, while the median analyst price target implied 111.30% upside as of November 20, and it had 49 hedge fund holders. Lumentum Holdings had a 40.75% monthly decline, with its median analyst target implying 111.60% upside, and 122 hedge fund holders. Marvell Technology had a 45.29% monthly decline, with 118.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 108 hedge fund holders. Sandisk Corporation had a 49.87% monthly decline, with 164.80% upside to its median analyst target, and 122 hedge fund holders. On November 11, Evercore maintained Outperform on Sandisk, arguing that supply discipline and long-term customer agreements could make earnings more predictable.

Ciena's fiscal third-quarter revenue rose 37% to $1.67 billion, while adjusted operating margin reached 22.5%, compared with 10.7% a year earlier, and management expected fiscal year-end backlog to exceed $10 billion. Tower Semiconductor generated approximately $240 million in silicon photonics revenue during the third quarter, nearly half its total, overall revenue increased 33% to $526 million, net income reached $120 million, and fourth-quarter revenue guidance was $600 million. Lumentum reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $1.26 billion and a 42.3% adjusted operating margin, and management secured purchase commitments exceeding $5 billion for a second major win in optics positioned near or alongside chips. Marvell generated $2.17 billion in fiscal second-quarter data-center revenue, up 46% year-over-year, and in November preliminary third-quarter revenue remained consistent with its earlier guidance. Sandisk reported fiscal first-quarter revenue of $11.03 billion, up 23% sequentially, and data-center revenue increased 61% sequentially to approximately $4.8 billion.

Under the proposed transaction, Lumentum shareholders would receive 4.5 Marvell shares per share owned, and completion remains subject to shareholder and regulatory approvals, with expected completion in the first half of 2028. Ciena's Hyper-Rail optical platform, designed to support distributed AI training, should begin contributing meaningful revenue during fiscal 2027, and Ciena trades at approximately 22.1 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, with consensus anticipating roughly 66% EPS growth. Tower Semiconductor trades at approximately 18.2 times estimated 2027 earnings, against projected EPS growth of roughly 72%, and has approximately $1.47 billion in cash against $154 million in debt. Lumentum trades at approximately 21.5 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings, and short interest stood at 8.97% of float on October 30, before the deal announcement. Marvell trades at approximately 32.8 times estimated fiscal 2027 earnings and 18.8 times fiscal 2028 earnings, and Stifel retained Buy on November 20 while reducing its target to $280 from $370.

Management expected silicon photonics manufacturing capacity at year-end to approximately double the level supporting third-quarter shipments, and Lumentum's next-quarter revenue guidance was $1.575, $1.625 billion. Management attributed roughly 60% of Sandisk's total sequential revenue growth to volume and 40% to pricing, indicating that the expansion was not solely a pricing story. The article states that the announced $1,132 equivalent for Lumentum is not a guaranteed cash payout, and that the consideration fluctuates with Marvell's stock. The article leaves open which companies' growth prospects remain intact and which valuations have further to fall, and it notes that additional production capacity takes time to become recognized revenue. The article also leaves open how the proposed Lumentum acquisition will affect customer conflicts and regulatory uncertainty for Marvell.

stories.Headline: Atlassian's Sherif Mansour says PMs should steer AI work rather than code
stories.Summary:
Sherif Mansour, who leads AI and product craft at Atlassian and has spent 17 years at the company according to The Futurist account of the conversation, told Lenny's Podcast that the product manager job did not disappear when AI coding arrived but narrowed to direction. He said an early experiment that turned PMs and designers into full-time AI builders fell apart after a month, and that throughput was not the problem because direction was. That failed experiment is why Mansour argues PMs own decision making velocity rather than the decisions themselves, and why the best PMs build a shared brain, a common understanding of customer, product and business context that lets engineers and designers act without waiting for a spec. He names three contexts to fill, customer context, product and market context, and the business you operate in, and said trust breaks once a group grows past 20 or 30 people unless someone maintains that shared base.

The workflow change he describes is concrete, since Mansour said he tries never to do a customer interview without engineers in the room. He cited PMs who send every engineer to test AI tools and report back, plus engineers staffing booths with him at customer events. He pointed to a 2010 Confluence interview where customers used red and green stars to mark unfinished work, and said an engineer in the room proposed the checkbox in the page, an idea he said did not exist on the web at the time. Hiring is where he gets prescriptive, and Mansour uses a triangle credited to Geoff Redfern with general manager, scientist and artist as the three corners describing how a PM naturally does discovery, from TAM and revenue math to hypothesis testing to vision-led taste.

He said few people do all three well, so leaders should stop throwing PM bodies at a problem and match the archetype to the work, with all-rounders reserved for zero-to-one teams. He admitted the model is aimed at medium to large organizations rather than startups, and he joked that he is a strong artist and a terrible general manager. Mansour said on Lenny's Podcast that the idea you no longer need to hire juniors is a misconception, in part because they bring new working norms. His example was his 12-year-old son, who he said went straight to vibe coding games without learning syntax and treats that as normal.

The article closes by telling teams to watch for groups that hire for a spike, state the weakness plainly, and pair opposites, as Mansour said he does with his colleague Jamille, rather than asking every PM to ship code. The piece was written by the StartupHub.ai staff and reviewed by editor Daniel Singer, and it draws on Lenny's Podcast as its source.

stories.Headline: Meghan Markle's As Ever brand promotes holiday sale with an AI-generated image
stories.Summary:
Meghan Markle's lifestyle brand As Ever drew scrutiny after a holiday sale promotion reportedly used an AI-generated image, according to the Daily Mail. The image was shared on the brand's Instagram account on Thursday, November 19. It advertised the brand's holiday sale with the words "As Ever Holiday Sale: 25% off sitewide." The graphic reportedly contained SynthID, a digital watermark developed by Google to identify AI-generated content. The outlet claimed the graphic was created or edited using technology developed by OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.

The promotion also included a separate photograph of the Duchess wearing cream-colored clothes beside a Christmas-decorated fireplace. The brand announced a 25% reduction across its website, but the Daily Mail reported that its $148 Holiday Advent Calendar was excluded. The limited-edition product contains 24 chocolates produced with Los Angeles chocolatier Compartés. It features a sketch of the California mansion where Meghan and Harry have lived, along with countdown numbers based on the Duchess's handwriting. Other products, including the brand's fruit spreads and gift baskets, were included in the holiday promotion.

The discovery does not establish who created the graphic or whether the Duchess personally used AI. Meghan previously said on Bloomberg's The Circuit with Emily Chang in August 2025, "Aren't you a little bit scared for, by AI?" She said someone had recently introduced her to ChatGPT, which she had not previously experienced. She admitted, "I'm a little bit vintage in many ways," and said she prefers handwritten notes and traditional ways of communicating. She also revealed that Siri was not enabled on her phone and that she did not use location services.

In August 2026, Meghan and Harry publicly criticized technology companies over the dangers of AI-generated sexual images. In a statement on their official website, the Sussexes supported efforts to stop AI tools from creating nonconsensual intimate images, especially those involving women and children. They criticized companies that challenged stronger safeguards and asked, "Can AI make our world better while it enables the worst in humans?" The statement argued that technology companies were investing enormous sums in artificial intelligence while resisting measures to protect vulnerable users.

During his September 2026 appearance at the Clinton Global Initiative in New York, Harry warned that AI companion applications could pose a greater threat to young people than conventional social media. According to remarks published on the Sussexes' official website, Harry described AI companion apps as the "ultimate sycophant." He warned, "It doesn't just want your attention, it wants your attachment." He expressed concern that children could confide in artificial intelligence instead of developing relationships with real people. The Duke also called for greater accountability from technology companies, arguing that rapid AI development should not come at the expense of public safety.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Libya trains officials to use AI for Agenda 2063 reporting
stories.Summary:
Libya opened its Third Training Programme on Domesticating Agenda 2063 through artificial intelligence in Tripoli this week, according to a report by Kanto Kai Okanta published by TechReviewAfrica on Sunday, November 22, 2026. The programme brings together data governance, alignment, analysis and national reporting, with a focus on translating continental commitments into measurable national outcomes. Libya recorded an overall performance of 84% in its national Agenda 2063 implementation report, which the article describes as a foundation for the next phase of its implementation efforts. The training is using alignment maps, AI-assisted reports and live dashboards to strengthen the country's capacity to monitor and report progress under Agenda 2063.

According to the African Union Development Agency-NEPAD, the priority is now to turn plans into delivery by making every figure verifiable, accelerating reporting and ensuring that decisions are informed by reliable evidence. Dr. Mohamed Al-Fadil Gubran, Chairman of Libya's Permanent Committee for Monitoring and Implementing Agenda 2063, described the country's 84% performance as a milestone rather than a finish line. He called for stronger national systems and capacity to ensure that every number can be verified, explained and trusted. The programme seeks to strengthen national reporting, data governance and evidence-based decision-making to accelerate the implementation of the African Union's development blueprint.

Opening the programme, Dr. Ziad Elhajjaji, Minister of State for Digital Economy and Artificial Intelligence, highlighted the transformative potential of responsible AI, trusted data and human judgement in helping institutions plan better, report faster and serve citizens more effectively. Representing AUDA-NEPAD, Director of Operations Ola Ehinmoro reaffirmed the Agency's commitment to supporting Libya beyond alignment and into delivery. He emphasised the importance of capable institutions and reliable data in translating continental commitments into results that people can see and feel in their daily lives. The articles do not say what happens after the training programme or give any further next steps.

stories.Headline: Forrester says firms will fold AI token costs into security budgets by 2027
stories.Summary:
Rising cybersecurity risks linked to the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence are forcing global businesses to strengthen their safeguards before 2027. Throughout 2026, companies worldwide faced repeated disruptions caused by single points of failure, including accidental undersea cable cuts across Africa, Asia, and West Asia. A major security flaw in PHP software also caused significant issues, with Check Point Software Technologies reporting that India was the eleventh hardest hit among eighteen affected nations. These events have renewed concerns regarding the dangers of relying on a single technology vendor without having a comprehensive backup plan.

The integration of artificial intelligence into daily operations will require companies to reshape their financial planning for the coming year. According to Forrester Research, businesses will soon need to treat AI usage costs, which are known as tokens, as a core part of their security budgets. This shift is necessary because the growing dependence on single technology providers creates vulnerabilities that hackers can exploit. Organizations must now prepare for new operational risks as AI becomes more integral to their standard business operations.

Experts from Forrester Research, Fortinet, and Gartner are responsible for identifying these emerging threats to essential services. They suggest that the current landscape is changing because artificial intelligence is giving hackers a significant head start in their attacks. These analysts indicate that the risks associated with AI will likely outweigh the disruptions seen during the previous year. Businesses are being urged to move away from single-vendor dependence to avoid the catastrophic outages that have recently plagued critical global services.

stories.Headline: German courts grant urgent deepfake injunctions when rights holders act fast and preserve evidence
stories.Summary:
A convincing fake of a chief executive, brand ambassador or advertising campaign can be created and circulated within hours, Global Advisory Experts reported on November 22, 2026. The guide said deepfakes have become a live enforcement issue in Germany in 2026 rather than a technology curiosity. It described a deepfake as synthetic audio, video or imagery produced or altered by artificial intelligence so a person appears to say or do something they never said or did. Typical incidents it listed include cloned brand ambassadors endorsing products they never used, invented celebrity interviews and voice clones used to defraud. The guide said the common element is output realistic enough to mislead an ordinary audience, which can create liability under several German regimes at once.

The guide said Germany has no single deepfake statute and rights holders rely on a mix of civil, constitutional, competition and criminal provisions. It set out five pillars, beginning with personality and image rights under Articles 1 and 2 of the Basic Law and §22 KUG, which requires consent to distribute images of a person. It said copyright under the UrhG offers removal, injunctive relief and damages where a protected work is copied or adapted. It said the MarkenG lets a proprietor stop confusing use of registered brand elements, with national marks registered at the DPMA. It said the UWG provides injunctions and, where fault is shown, damages for misleading commercial content, and that the GDPR, BDSG and StGB may apply to voice cloning, defamation, fraud, extortion and non-consensual intimate imagery.

The guide was written by Global Advisory Experts and featured Markus Koerner of Bird & Bird in Germany as its Gold featured expert on the matter. It said the guide explains which route suits which situation, how quickly each works and what evidence German courts expect before granting urgent relief. It said urgency under the Zivilprozessordnung rules on preliminary injunctions is applied strictly and that delay after discovering a deepfake can forfeit the expedited route. It said orders can be backed by penalties for non-compliance, including Ordnungsgeld and in some cases Ordnungshaft. It said a focused application with a clean evidence bundle and a narrowly drafted request is far more likely to succeed than a sprawling one.

The guide said it is for brand owners, talent agents, celebrities, in-house teams and marketing departments needing enforcement and takedown options in Germany against AI-generated fakes. It said a single deepfake often causes reputational, commercial and endorsement-misuse harm at once, which is why combining remedies is frequently the strongest approach. It said platform takedowns rest on platform terms and the EU Digital Services Act, which imposes notice-and-action duties on hosting and online platform intermediaries operating in the EU. It said a clear, well-evidenced notice identifying the content, the infringed right and the rights holder will normally prompt removal, but platforms differ in responsiveness. It said rights holders should never rely on a takedown alone, should preserve evidence in parallel and should keep a court application ready in case removal stalls or the content reappears.

The guide said the general right of personality derives from Articles 1 and 2 of the Basic Law and has been developed at length by the Federal Constitutional Court. It said the Kunsturhebergesetz protects the right to one's own image and that German courts have consistently regarded unauthorised use of a likeness as a serious interference. It said proving a voice clone is fake may call for acoustic expert analysis, while video deepfakes usually benefit from frame-level forensic review. It said purely machine-generated output generally does not attract copyright itself, but the material fed into the system often does. It said trademark claims can be particularly effective against fake adverts because the holder has an enforceable right on the register and does not need to prove reputational harm from scratch.

The guide said the right answer in many matters is a sequence rather than a single step, a platform takedown within hours followed by a personality rights or UWG injunction to secure a binding court order. It said damages under the UrhG and MarkenG may be calculated by licence analogy, by the infringer's profits or by actual loss. It said claims for information and accounting are normally pleaded alongside the main relief because quantifying loss usually requires disclosure of the infringer's sales and reach. It said the guide includes an evidence and interim relief checklist, sample claim wording and a simple framework for picking the right remedy quickly. It said the analysis of personality and image rights is both constitutional and statutory, and that good drafting counts as much as good theory.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as NVIDIA chief amid investigation into foreign intelligence threat
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the president, chief executive, and director of NVIDIA on 11 November 2026. This leadership rupture followed an announcement that the company had launched an independent investigation into reports of a possible foreign intelligence effort. The NVIDIA board initiated this specific investigation on 8 November 2026 to address the reported threat. These events exposed a structural vulnerability in the global artificial intelligence infrastructure that depends on a few corporations and individuals. The company has not established that any corporate secrets or national security data were actually compromised.

The situation requires a new governance approach for an industrial system with concentrated credit commitments and legal permissions. On 17 November 2026, NVIDIA established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson. The company appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as the interim chief executive and named Harvey C. Jones as the chair. Additionally, a rule from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security on 16 November 2026 expanded scrutiny of overseas data centers and remote computing. These changes affect the compliance architecture for technology suppliers, cloud operators, and cross-border investments in AI infrastructure.

The NVIDIA board is responsible for the investigation and stated there was no reason to believe secrets were compromised. The company reported revenue of 115.844 billion dollars and GAAP net income of 65.287 billion dollars for the quarter ending 25 October 2026. These financial results suggest that the governance crisis has not yet caused a documented collapse in operating performance. However, the company faces 518 billion dollars in future commitments, including 390 billion dollars for supply and capacity. This includes 222 billion dollars assigned to fiscal 2028 and 103 billion dollars for fiscal 2029.

The broader context involves high exposure in U.S. export policy, Taiwanese manufacturing, South Korean production, and Israeli networking technology. Disruption to research or semiconductor production in Israel could negatively impact that country's national accounts and technology sector. Separately, the U.S. Department of Commerce investigated Singaporean operator Megaspeed starting in 2024 and interviewed chief executive Alice Huang. NVIDIA placed Megaspeed on a no-sell list in June 2025 after officials inspected the operator. Future stability depends on whether governments can govern a system where critical components are concentrated across a handful of firms.

stories.Headline: Researchers launch autonomous AI agent to analyze neutron scattering data at China Spallation Neutron Source
stories.Summary:
Researchers recently introduced DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous AI agent designed to analyze neutron scattering data at the China Spallation Neutron Source. This agent utilizes a large language model to perform joint neutron powder diffraction and pair-distribution-function analysis without any human intervention. By employing a hierarchical framework of reasoning and acting, the system orchestrates established refinement software to interpret complex materials data. The tool aims to eliminate the time-consuming iterative cycles of data reduction and modeling that typically challenge both experts and novices.

The system relies on Agentic Context Operation to maintain a working memory of file paths, domain rules, and intermediate results during processing. In tests using Si, CsAgTe, and Bi2MoO6, the agent produced structural parameters that were statistically indistinguishable from those derived by human experts. An 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite mechanisms under 50k-token context compression. Full implementation of these components yielded a mean composite score of 0.9316 and a repeatability stability of 0.9905, while Memo alone improved performance by 20.2 percent.

The developers integrated the agent with a permission-controlled data interface at the facility to ensure the secure analysis of proprietary user data. They stated that the agent can move beyond simple recommendations to become a reliable partner in complex structural science. This integration allows for on-demand analysis and automatic archiving of results within the secure facility environment. The researchers believe this technology could potentially accelerate the overall rate of materials discovery at pulsed neutron sources across the entire world.

stories.Headline: Medical students who use reasoning scaffolding before an AI assistant achieve higher diagnostic accuracy, trial finds
stories.Summary:
A randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students, of whom 389 were analysed, tested whether the order in which trainees receive AI support affects their clinical reasoning, and the preprint by Yizhou Fan, Luzhen Tang, Mengyu Xia, Jiaqi Xu, Zijian Li, Naping Chen and 10 more was posted on Research Square on 21 November 2026 without peer review. The students worked through clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were assigned to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the assistant, the assistant followed by scaffolding, or both at once. The scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their own reasoning without giving direct answers, while the assistant supplied requested information and answers. The study ran an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn, and frontier large language models completed the same tasks as a benchmark. Students first performed below the language models but later exceeded them following the interventions.

Students who began with AI scaffolding reached higher diagnostic accuracy than those given the assistant from the outset, both during the later intervention phase at 75.2% versus 66.0% (OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12, 2.68]) and after withdrawal at 24.6% versus 14.4% (OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15, 4.14]). After withdrawal, the scaffold-first groups were the only ones to outperform both unsupported students, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 9.0% (ORs 3.77, 3.87, 95% CIs [1.25, 12.00]), and the language models, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 8.6% (ORs 3.48, 3.50, 95% CIs [1.22, 9.89]). Introducing the assistant after scaffolding lowered intrinsic cognitive load (t(50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and raised metacognitive evaluation (t(50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). The authors state that there is no competing interest and provide supplementary information in an appendix file.

The authors conclude that their findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding comes before answer-providing assistance. They say this order strengthens diagnostic performance both while AI-supported learning is under way and after AI support is withdrawn. The abstract frames the question as whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use generative AI effectively and independently, given that such tools could improve physicians' clinical performance. Because the paper is a preprint, it has not been peer reviewed by a journal, and the articles give no further details on publication or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Nvidia tightens AI financing after Huang resigns as interim CEO Kress pledges stricter oversight
stories.Summary:
The global artificial intelligence industry is facing a funding crisis after Nvidia began tightening its financial support following the resignation of former CEO Jensen Huang. This shift occurred as the Nasdaq plunged 5.28 percent on Friday, erasing all of its gains for the current year. Investors are now anxious because Nvidia previously acted as a central bank for the sector by providing liquidity and assuming financing risks for its clients. This circular financing structure made many data center builders and technology companies heavily dependent on the company's continuous financial backing.

The new approach requires more rigorous scrutiny and systematic investing, which may withdraw over 50 billion dollars from the market according to analyst Tim Arcuri. Nvidia's current investment portfolio exceeds 100 billion dollars, including 48 billion dollars in eight public companies as of September. Specific obligations include a 6.3 billion dollar agreement from September 2025 to buy computing capacity from CoreWeave, where Nvidia holds a 10 percent stake. Additionally, the company reportedly guaranteed 105 billion dollars for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary developing a data center for OpenAI.

Interim CEO Colette Kress stated on Tuesday that the company will continue supporting the AI ecosystem but will apply stricter oversight to its investments. This announcement follows a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigation into the accounting practices of the semiconductor giant. Former SEC Chair Gary Gensler told CNN on November 16 that AI is in a bubble and predicted an economic slowdown before November 2028. IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva also warned on November 16 that a sudden investment retreat could tighten financial markets and slow global growth.

The International Monetary Fund estimates that AI circular financing exceeds 1 trillion dollars, with two-thirds of that amount funded by debt. This environment puts immense pressure on neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Nebius that rely on Nvidia's guarantees to obtain loans. If Nvidia continues to retreat, analysts suggest that Google and other suppliers of customized AI chips could gain a competitive advantage. The industry now faces a double squeeze of rising borrowing costs and fewer advance purchase commitments to reassure lenders.

Articles.Title: Nvidia’s pullback sparks fears of an AI funding shock

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework for gradient-flow PDEs
stories.Summary:
Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 that proposes a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework, which they call ONTS, for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the framework uses spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, the authors develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme called E-ONTS, an implicit variational scheme called I-ONTS, and a predictor-corrector scheme called PC-ONTS that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. The paper is listed as arXiv identifier 2611.20563.

For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions, according to the abstract. The authors also rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, Fokker-Planck, and coupled Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework. The abstract does not give numerical error values or timing results for those experiments.

The paper is credited to Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou, and the arXiv listing names Qiao and two other authors in its byline for the PDF. The abstract states that the framework is unified and that the implicit schemes carry unconditional discrete energy stability under a suitable descent criterion. It describes the three schemes as complementary and the numerical experiments as showing accuracy, robustness and structure-preserving properties. The articles do not include separate comments from the authors beyond the abstract text.

The context given in the articles is limited to the abstract and the standard arXivLabs boilerplate about openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. stories.Headline: Researchers present MAGE framework for transferable multimodal graph learning without target-domain parameter updates
stories.Summary:
Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 describing a framework they call MAGE, which stands for Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting, and which is built for transferable multimodal graph learning. Multimodal graphs combine textual and visual attributes with relational structures, giving a rich representation of complex real-world data, and the authors argue that models trained on source graphs need to generalize to unseen graph domains so that graph models can be broadly applied and reused. The authors say this is hard because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. They frame the problem as two key challenges, adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variation across nodes and domains, and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information each target node needs to support prediction by a large language model. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components.

Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation, or MAMP, adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning, or EGIT, selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal large language model. Together, the authors say, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without any parameter updates on the target domains. The authors report experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs that show strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, again without requiring parameter updates on the target domains. The paper lists five authors, Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin, and is identified on arXiv as 2611.20449.

The abstract presents the work as a response to the two challenges of adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion and target-specific evidence selection, and it describes the frozen multimodal language model as the component that receives the selected evidence through instructions. The posting page offers the paper as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source, and it also carries the standard arXivLabs notice about collaborators who develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the posting of the preprint and the results the authors report. No venue, publication date or peer review outcome is given, and the articles do not describe any deployment or follow-up work. The only stated plan is the framework itself, which the authors present as a way to transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates.

stories.Headline: Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner warns that no kill switch can stop rogue AI
stories.Summary:
Former OpenAI board member Helen Toner appeared on Fox News Sunday on November 22, 2026, to discuss several critical technology issues. She addressed the causes of recent nationwide tech outages and the growing danger of autonomous artificial intelligence cyber threats. Toner also spoke about the necessity of establishing AI guardrails between the United States and China. Her appearance highlighted the urgent need for better oversight of rapidly evolving software systems.

The situation requires a shift in how officials communicate about software patching, which Toner believes caused the recent nationwide outages. She specifically questioned why government or corporate officials have not been clear about these technical failures. Furthermore, she warned that no single kill switch exists to stop autonomous AI systems that operate outside of United States jurisdiction. This lack of control means that rogue AI could potentially function without any way to shut it down.

Helen Toner is the person responsible for these warnings based on her previous experience on the OpenAI board. She suggested that the rush to patch software may have inadvertently triggered the widespread technical disruptions seen across the country. Regarding the threat of rogue AI, she emphasized that jurisdictional boundaries make it impossible to implement a universal emergency stop. Her comments serve as a warning about the inherent risks of autonomous systems running in foreign territories.
